options: No — rule 13 applies before the start like any Part 2 rule; while tacking Black had to keep clear of you
Yes — before the starting signal boats manoeuvring at the line are not subject to rules 10–13
No — but Black had the right to tack because she was approaching a starting mark
Yes — only rule 14 applies in the last minute before the start
questions.why: Rule 13 applies whenever Part 2 applies, from the time boats are sailing in the racing area intending to race.

questions.q: You tack from port to starboard and, instead of settling close-hauled, keep bearing away straight onto a reach to pass astern of Blue, who is on starboard. Blue claims you were «still tacking» when you passed her because you never sailed close-hauled. When did rule 13 stop applying to you?

figure.note: You bore away through close-hauled onto a reach

options: Only when you steadied on your new course on the reach
When your heading passed through a close-hauled course — rule 13 requires reaching that course, not holding it
When you passed head to wind — that is where every tack ends
Never on this manoeuvre — a boat that does not sail close-hauled after a tack keeps clear until the next mark
questions.why: Rule 13: «until she is on a close-hauled course»; a boat that turns through close-hauled onto a reach is no longer tacking.

questions.q: You and White are overlapped on port tack, you to leeward. White tacks onto starboard; you stay on port and the boats converge again a few seconds later. Who keeps clear during White's tack, and who afterwards?

figure.note: White is tacking onto starboard

options: White keeps clear throughout — she was the windward boat and stays the give-way boat until the boats separate
You keep clear throughout — a leeward boat must give room to a windward boat that wants to tack
White keeps clear while tacking (rule 13); once she is close-hauled on starboard you are on opposite tacks and you, on port, keep clear (rule 10)
Nobody — after a tack the boats start again with equal rights until one hails
questions.why: Rule 11 ends when White passes head to wind; rule 13 covers her tack, and rule 10 applies once she is close-hauled on starboard.

questions.q: You have just tacked from port to starboard and are now settled close-hauled, sheets in. Green, also on starboard, is three hull lengths directly behind you, having been there since before your tack. Which rule now governs the two of you?

figure.note: Your tack is complete; Green is three lengths astern

options: Rule 13 — you remain the tacking boat until you have sailed clear of Green
Rule 15 — having just acquired right of way you must keep clear of Green for a while
Rule 10 — Green is still treated as being on the tack you came from
Rule 12 — you are clear ahead on the same tack, so Green, clear astern, keeps clear of you
questions.why: Rule 13 ends at close-hauled; rule 12 then applies between boats on the same tack that are not overlapped.

questions.q: Wednesday club race on a lake, 8 knots. You are close-hauled on starboard tack in a J/24. Red, on port, is converging on a collision course and shows no sign of bearing away. Confident of rule 10, you hold your course and the boats touch, bow to shroud — a scuff, no damage. What does the protest committee decide?

figure.note: Neither boat alters course

options: Red broke rules 10 and 14; you also broke rule 14 by not avoiding contact when you could, but you are exonerated because there was no damage
Both of you are disqualified — rule 14 penalises every boat involved in a contact
Nobody broke a rule — contact without damage is not a breach of rule 14
Only Red broke a rule — a starboard-tack boat is never required to alter course for a port-tack boat
questions.why: Rule 14: a right-of-way boat must avoid contact once it is clear the other is not keeping clear; rule 43.1(c) exonerates her when there is no damage or injury.

questions.q: Evening race in 15 knots. You are on starboard tack in a 36-ft cruiser-racer. Grey, on port, is clearly not going to cross; a boat length before contact you could still bear away, but your tactician says 'we're on starboard, hold on'. The boats collide and Grey's pulpit is bent. How does this end in the protest room?

figure.note: You could still bear away

options: Only Grey is penalised — the right-of-way boat never has to avoid contact
Both boats are penalised: Grey under rules 10 and 14, you under rule 14 — with damage, a right-of-way boat is not exonerated for failing to avoid contact
Only you are penalised — the boat that could have avoided the collision last is responsible for it
Nobody is penalised — damage is a matter between the boats and their insurers, not the rules
questions.why: Rule 14: once it was clear Grey was not keeping clear you had to avoid contact if reasonably possible; with damage there is no exoneration under 43.1(c).

questions.q: District championship in ILCA 7s. You are close-hauled on starboard; a port-tack boat is converging two lengths away. Your coach always says 'never alter course on starboard'. Under rule 14, for how long may you hold your course?
options: Not at all — a right-of-way boat must alter course as soon as a collision is possible
Until the boats are one hull length apart — then both boats must turn away from each other
Until it is clear that the port-tack boat is not keeping clear — after that you must act to avoid contact if reasonably possible
For as long as you like — a right-of-way boat is never required to avoid contact
questions.why: Rule 14: a right-of-way boat need not act to avoid contact until it is clear the other boat is not keeping clear; then she must, if reasonably possible.

questions.q: Dragon regatta, beating in 20 knots. You are on starboard; Yellow, on port, is holding on, her helmsman looking at the mark and not at you. You hail 'Starboard!' three times and keep going; Yellow sees you too late and you hit her amidships, holing her topsides. Her owner says you should have avoided her. Is he right?

figure.note: You hail three times and hold course

options: Yes, but only because you did not back up the hails with a sound signal
No — a starboard-tack boat breaks rule 14 only if she changes course towards the other boat
No — three hails put the whole responsibility on Yellow; a boat that has been warned cannot complain
Yes — once it was clear Yellow was not keeping clear you had to try to avoid contact; hailing is no substitute, so you broke rule 14 and, with damage, are not exonerated
questions.why: Rule 14: a hail does not replace avoiding action; the right-of-way boat must act once it is clear the other is not keeping clear; damage removes exoneration.

questions.q: You are close-hauled on starboard. Blue, on port, is crossing ahead and would have passed a length clear of your bow. You bear away to 'close the door' and hit her quarter. Blue's skipper protests. Who broke what?

figure.note: You bear away toward Blue

options: You — by bearing away you broke rule 16.1 and then rule 14; Blue was keeping clear and is exonerated for any contact
Blue — a port-tack boat hit by a starboard-tack boat has broken rule 10, whatever the starboard boat did
Both — Blue broke rule 10 and you broke rule 14, so each takes a Two-Turns Penalty
Nobody — a right-of-way boat may sail any course she likes and the port-tack boat must stay out of it
questions.why: Rule 16.1: a right-of-way boat changing course must give room to keep clear; causing contact also breaks rule 14. Blue is exonerated under rule 43.1(a).

questions.q: Reaching leg in a 29er fleet. Black, overlapped to windward of you, drops down in a gust and her hull kisses your gunwale — no damage, nobody hurt. Her crew shouts 'no damage, no foul, carry on!'. What is the position?

figure.note: Black drops down in a gust

options: Both boats must take a Two-Turns Penalty, because any contact means both broke rule 14
Black broke rules 11 and 14 and should take a Two-Turns Penalty; the no-damage exoneration applies only to you, the right-of-way boat
You must take a penalty for not luffing away in time; Black is exonerated as the give-way boat
Nobody is penalised — rule 14 is broken only when the contact causes damage or injury
questions.why: Rule 14 binds every boat; rule 43.1(c) exonerates only the right-of-way boat when there is no damage. The windward boat still broke rules 11 and 14.

questions.q: Approaching the windward mark on starboard. Grey, on port, tacks onto starboard less than half a length ahead of your bow; before you can do anything your stem touches her transom. Grey protests you under rule 14. Will the protest committee penalise you?

figure.note: Grey has just completed her tack

options: No, but only because Grey did not hail 'Protest' before the contact
Yes — both boats touched, so both broke rule 14 and both are disqualified
No — avoiding contact was not reasonably possible for you; Grey broke rule 13 (or 15) and rule 14
Yes — the boat astern always has the last chance to avoid contact and is penalised for it
questions.why: Rule 14 requires only what is reasonably possible; a boat given no time to react does not break it. The tacking boat broke rule 13/15 and rule 14.

questions.q: Running in 18 knots in Melges 24s. You are to leeward of Red, overlapped by half a length. You luff hard to shake her off; Red tries to respond but her boom is pinned by the spinnaker and your rigs touch. Who broke what?

figure.note: You luff hard

options: Red — the windward boat must keep clear whatever the leeward boat does, so she broke rules 11 and 14
Nobody — a leeward boat may luff as she pleases on a run
Both of you broke rule 14 equally and both must retire
You — you broke rule 16.1 by not giving Red room to keep clear, and rule 14; Red is exonerated for breaking rule 11
questions.why: Rule 16.1: a right-of-way boat that changes course must give the other room to keep clear; a windward boat compelled to break rule 11 is exonerated (43.1(a)).

questions.q: Three J/70s reaching in a line: you to leeward, White overlapped to windward of you, Green overlapped to windward of White, all within a length. You luff hard without warning; White luffs to keep clear of you and hits Green, who had no room to respond. Which rules did you break?

figure.note: You luff sharply

options: Rule 16.1 and rule 14 — you gave White no room to keep clear and you caused contact between two boats; White is exonerated
Only rule 17, because you luffed above your proper course
Rule 11 — as the boat that started the chain you are treated as the windward boat
None — you had right of way over both boats and never touched either of them
questions.why: Rule 14 (2025): a boat shall not cause contact between boats; rule 16.1: a course change must give room to keep clear. White was compelled and is exonerated.

questions.q: Start of a Star class race, 30 seconds to go. You are to leeward of Blue, both close-hauled and creeping towards the committee boat. You luff Blue sharply; she has no room to respond and is pushed onto the committee boat's bow. Blue says she will protest. Who is penalised?
options: Both — Blue for touching the mark and you for luffing before the start, which rule 17 forbids
You — you broke rule 16.1 and rule 14 by causing contact between Blue and the committee boat; Blue is exonerated for touching the mark
Nobody — before the starting signal rules 14 and 16 do not yet apply
Blue — she touched a starting mark, so she takes a One-Turn Penalty, and you broke no rule
questions.why: Rule 14 (2025): a boat shall not cause contact between a boat and an object to be avoided; rule 16.1 required room. Blue is exonerated under 43.1(a).

questions.q: Dead run in 6 knots at a 470 regatta in Palma. You are to leeward; Green, overlapped to windward, lets her spinnaker pole swing and it touches your shroud — the hulls never touch. Green says 'no hull contact, no contact'. Is there a breach?

figure.note: Green's pole touches your shroud

options: No — rule 14 is about hull-to-hull contact only; touching sails or spars does not count
No — on a run the windward boat has right of way, so you should have kept clear of her pole
Yes — contact between any parts of the boats or their equipment counts; Green broke rules 11 and 14 and should take a Two-Turns Penalty
Yes, but it is you who broke rule 14 by not bearing away from Green's pole
questions.why: Contact under rule 14 includes any part of a boat or her equipment; the windward boat that touches the leeward boat broke rules 11 and 14.

questions.q: Two Hobie 16s collide on a beat, you on starboard and Blue on port. In the hearing Blue's crew argues: 'Rule 14 binds only the give-way boat; a right-of-way boat can do what she likes'. What does rule 14 actually say?
options: Both boats shall alter course away from each other as soon as there is any risk of collision
Only the give-way boat shall avoid contact; the right-of-way boat has no obligation at all
The right-of-way boat shall avoid contact only after the other boat has hailed for room
Every boat shall avoid contact if reasonably possible; the right-of-way boat may only wait until it is clear the other boat is not keeping clear
questions.why: Rule 14 applies to every boat; the right-of-way boat is only excused from acting until it is clear the other boat is not keeping clear.

questions.q: Leeward mark of a windward–leeward course. You are inside and entitled to mark-room; Red, outside, leaves you too little space and your quarter touches her bow as you round — no damage. Red says you should have gone wider. Who, if anyone, is penalised?

figure.note: You are inside; Red gives little room

options: Red — she broke rule 18.2 and rule 14; you broke rule 14 too but are exonerated, as a boat sailing within her mark-room with no damage
You — a boat entitled to mark-room must still keep clear of a leeward boat, so you broke rule 11
Nobody — contact without damage inside the zone is allowed
Both — any contact at a mark means both boats take a Two-Turns Penalty
questions.why: Rule 14: a boat sailing within her mark-room need not act until it is clear the other is not giving it; exonerated under 43.1(c) if there is no damage.

questions.q: Beating in 12 knots. Red, on port, ducks you and passes 30 cm behind your transom; you did not need to alter course and there was no contact. Your crew wants to protest her for passing too close. Did Red break a rule?

figure.note: Red passes 30 cm astern of you

options: Yes — passing within a boat length of a starboard-tack boat breaks rule 10 even without contact
No — she kept clear: you could sail your course without avoiding action, and there was no contact, so neither rule 10 nor rule 14 was broken
Yes — rule 14 requires a boat to pass at least one hull length from a right-of-way boat
Yes — she should have hailed before passing so close astern
questions.why: Keeping clear means the right-of-way boat can sail her course with no need for avoiding action; rule 14 concerns contact, and there was none.

questions.q: Big waves off Bodrum, 25 knots, running under spinnaker. You are clear astern of White and catch a wave; before you can bear away your bow hits her transom. White was holding a steady course. Who is at fault?

figure.note: You surf down a wave

options: Nobody — in waves a boat cannot be expected to control her speed, so there is no breach
White — a boat ahead must keep a lookout astern and move aside for a faster boat
You — as the boat clear astern you had to keep clear (rule 12) and avoid contact (rule 14); White did nothing wrong
Both — White broke rule 14 by not luffing and you broke rule 12
questions.why: Rule 12: the boat clear astern keeps clear; rule 14: she must avoid contact. A boat holding a steady course has no duty to anticipate a surfing boat.

questions.q: On a reach you are the windward boat and your rail touches the leeward boat's — no damage. You know you broke rules 11 and 14. What penalty should you take?

figure.title: Reaching leg
lines: Your rail touched the leeward boat

options: No penalty — rule 14 breaches are dealt with only by a protest committee
A 20% scoring penalty, signalled by displaying a yellow flag
A One-Turn Penalty — a breach involving only light contact counts as one turn
A Two-Turns Penalty, taken promptly after getting well clear — unless the contact caused serious damage or injury, when you must retire
questions.why: Rule 44.1: a breach of a Part 2 rule is answered by a Two-Turns Penalty, or by retiring if it caused injury, serious damage or a significant advantage.

questions.q: On port tack you misjudge a cross, hit a starboard-tack Farr 30 amidships and crack her hull at the waterline. You start your two turns at once. Is that enough?

figure.title: Collision on the beat
lines: You: port tack, misjudged the cross
Her hull is cracked at the waterline
You have started your two turns

options: No — when a breach causes serious damage the Two-Turns Penalty is not available and you must retire (rule 44.1(b))
Yes — two turns settle any Part 2 breach, whatever the consequences
No — you must take four turns: two for rule 10 and two for rule 14
Yes, as long as you also report the damage to the race committee after finishing
questions.why: Rule 44.1(b): if the breach caused injury or serious damage, or gave a significant advantage, the penalty is to retire.

questions.q: Approaching the leeward mark, your bow touches the transom of Blue, who is clear ahead of you, as she slows to round — no damage. Your helm says there is nothing to do because nothing was broken. Is he right?

figure.note: Blue was clear ahead at the zone

options: Yes — contact without damage never breaks rule 14
No — you broke rule 12 and rule 14; the absence of damage exonerates only the right-of-way boat, not the give-way boat
No — but the only rule you broke is rule 31, touching a mark
Yes — at a mark the boat astern is entitled to mark-room, so Blue should have kept clear
questions.why: Rule 43.1(c) exonerates only a right-of-way boat (or one entitled to room) for contact without damage; a give-way boat still broke rules 12 and 14.

questions.q: You are on starboard; a port-tack boat is converging five lengths away. Rather than wait, you bear away ten degrees now to pass astern of her. Have you given anything up or broken a rule?

figure.note: You bear away early to pass astern

options: No, but the port boat must now take a Two-Turns Penalty for making you alter course
Yes — a starboard-tack boat that alters course for a port-tack boat loses her right of way
No — rule 14 allows a right-of-way boat to hold on but never obliges her to; you may avoid early, subject to rule 16.1 if you change course close to her
Yes — by altering course you broke rule 16.1, because the port boat was keeping clear
questions.why: Rule 14 lets the right-of-way boat wait until it is clear the other is not keeping clear; it does not forbid avoiding earlier. Rule 16.1 governs the turn.

questions.q: You finished, cleared the line and are sailing home on port tack through the fleet still racing. Green, racing on starboard, hits you and breaks her bowsprit. You say you are no longer racing, so no rule applies. Can you be penalised?

figure.title: After your finish
lines: You finished and cleared the line

options: No — only rule 23.1 (interfering with a boat racing) can apply after finishing, never rule 14
No — once you have finished none of the Part 2 rules applies to you
Yes — and also under rule 10, because Part 2 applies in full to any boat on the course area
Yes — Part 2 applies to a boat that has been racing, and a boat not racing can be penalised under rule 14 when the contact causes injury or serious damage
questions.why: Part 2 preamble: a boat not racing is penalised under Part 2 only for rule 14 when the incident caused injury or serious damage, or for rule 23.1.

questions.q: Ducking a starboard-tack boat in a 470, your bow touches Blue's transom as she passes — a bump, no damage. Her crew says 'you owe us turns'. Are they right?

figure.note: Your bow touches Blue's transom

options: Yes — you broke rule 10 and rule 14; take a Two-Turns Penalty promptly after getting clear
Yes, but one turn is enough, because the contact caused no damage
No — a touch on the transom while passing astern is not a breach, because you were astern of her
No — the starboard-tack boat should have borne away to make room for you to pass astern
questions.why: Rule 10: port keeps clear; rule 14: avoid contact. A give-way boat that makes contact broke both and takes a Two-Turns Penalty (rule 44.1).

questions.q: You are on starboard with Grey overlapped a length to windward of you. Red, on port, bears away to duck you far too late; the only way to avoid her is to luff into Grey. You hold on and Red hits your bow, denting it. Did you break rule 14?

figure.note: Red bears away too late

options: Yes — with damage the right-of-way boat is always penalised under rule 14 along with the other boat
No — rule 14 requires only what is reasonably possible, and turning into another boat is not; Red broke rules 10 and 14
No — rule 14 never applies to a starboard-tack boat
Yes — you should have luffed into Grey, who as the windward boat had to keep clear of you anyway
questions.why: Rule 14 asks a boat to avoid contact 'if reasonably possible'; avoiding one collision by causing another is not reasonably possible.

questions.q: On a reach Blue, overlapped to windward of you, shouts 'I can't hold her up, give me room!' and bears down onto your deck before you can react. Did her hail change anything?

figure.note: Blue hails, then bears down

options: No, but you broke rule 14 because you were warned and did not bear away
Yes — after a hail for room the leeward boat must bear away and give it (rule 16.1)
No — a hail gives Blue no rights; as the windward boat she had to keep clear (rule 11) and avoid contact (rule 14)
Yes — a boat that hails before contact is exonerated under rule 43
questions.why: No rule lets a windward boat demand room by hailing; she must keep clear (rule 11) and avoid contact (rule 14).

questions.q: Blue is doing her penalty turns near the windward mark and her gybe brings her across your bow while you are on starboard; contact, no damage. Blue says boats doing turns are protected. Who broke a rule?

figure.note: Blue is doing penalty turns

options: Both — rule 14 always penalises both boats in a contact
You — a boat taking a penalty must be given room, so you broke rule 23.2 by interfering with her
Nobody — a boat taking a penalty is not racing while she turns, so Part 2 does not apply
Blue broke rule 21 and rule 14 — a boat taking a penalty keeps clear of others; you are exonerated for the contact as there was no damage
questions.why: Rule 21: a boat taking a penalty keeps clear of a boat that is not; rule 14 still binds her. The right-of-way boat is exonerated under 43.1(c) without damage.

questions.q: In the hearing you, the leeward right-of-way boat, admit you could have borne away to avoid the windward boat but did not. Which single fact decides whether you are penalised under rule 14?

figure.title: Hearing after the race
lines: You: leeward boat, right of way
Red: windward, did not keep clear
You could have borne away, did not

options: Whether the contact caused damage or injury — with none, rule 43.1(c) exonerates you; with damage, you are penalised
Whether the other boat took a Two-Turns Penalty — if she did, you cannot be penalised
Whether you hailed before the contact — a hail exonerates the right-of-way boat
Whether the contact was hull to hull — contact with sails or rigging is never penalised
questions.why: Rule 43.1(c): a right-of-way boat that breaks rule 14 is exonerated if the contact caused no damage or injury.

questions.q: You tack from port onto starboard directly ahead and to leeward of Blue, who is close-hauled on starboard. When your tack is complete she is one length away and has to luff hard at once to miss your transom. Which rule did you break?

figure.note: You have just completed your tack

options: Rule 10 — you were on port tack when the incident began
Rule 15 — having acquired right of way by your own tack you had to give Blue room to keep clear at first
None — a boat that completes her tack ahead of another boat is clear ahead and has right of way
Rule 17 — you may not tack within two hull lengths of another boat
questions.why: Rule 15: a boat acquiring right of way shall initially give the other boat room to keep clear, unless she acquires it because of the other boat's actions.

questions.q: Running on port tack in a Finn, a length to windward of Red, who is also on port. You gybe onto starboard. Red must now keep clear under rule 10 — what do you owe her at that moment?

figure.note: You have just gybed onto starboard

options: Nothing — a starboard-tack boat never owes anything to a port-tack boat
You must sail no higher than your proper course, as the boat that just became leeward (rule 17)
Room to keep clear, initially — you acquired right of way by your own gybe, so rule 15 applies
You must hold your course until Red has gybed too (rule 16.2)
questions.why: Rule 15 applies to any way of acquiring right of way, a gybe included: initially give the other boat room to keep clear.

questions.q: You are close-hauled on port. Grey, on starboard, crosses ahead and tacks onto port a length to windward of you, becoming the windward boat. Must you give her room to keep clear under rule 15?

figure.note: Grey has just tacked onto port

options: Yes — and you must also bear away to your proper course under rule 17
Yes — whenever a boat becomes the right-of-way boat she must initially give the other room
No — because you were already the right-of-way boat as the port-tack boat
No — you acquired right of way because of Grey's own tack, so rule 15 does not apply; Grey must keep clear at once (rules 13 and 11)
questions.why: Rule 15 does not apply when a boat acquires right of way because of the other boat's actions — here Grey's tack made you the leeward boat.

questions.q: Broad reach in 15 knots. You are catching Blue from clear astern and establish an overlap to leeward, within a length of her. What do you owe Blue at that moment, and what limits you afterwards?

figure.note: You came from clear astern

options: At first, room to keep clear (rule 15); then, while overlapped within two lengths, you may not sail above your proper course (rule 17)
You must keep clear of her until she has had time to respond; then she keeps clear of you
Nothing — as the leeward boat you have right of way and may luff her at once
You must pass at least two hull lengths to leeward of her, or stay astern
questions.why: Rule 15: the new right-of-way boat initially gives room; rule 17: a leeward overlap from clear astern within two lengths bars sailing above proper course.

questions.q: Two lengths ahead and to leeward of a port-tack boat you tack onto starboard. She has ample room and bears away a little to pass astern, but ten seconds later, as the boats converge again, she has to duck you sharply. Did you break rule 15?

figure.note: You tacked ten seconds ago

options: No — because rule 15 never applies to a tack, only to a gybe
No — rule 15 requires room to keep clear only at the moment you acquire right of way; after that the port-tack boat simply has to keep clear under rule 10
Yes — a boat that tacks within three hull lengths of another always breaks rule 15
Yes — rule 15 protects the other boat for the whole time the boats are converging
questions.why: Rule 15 says 'initially': once the other boat has been given room to keep clear, her ordinary obligation (here rule 10) takes over.

questions.q: First beat of a 470 national championship. You lee-bow a starboard-tack boat, tacking half a length to leeward and slightly ahead of her. She begins luffing to avoid your stern while you are still head to wind, and is still luffing when you reach close-hauled. What is the ruling?

figure.note: You have just lee-bowed Blue

options: Nobody broke a rule — a lee-bow tack is a legitimate manoeuvre and the windward boat must simply respond
She broke rule 11 — once you were close-hauled to leeward of her she was the windward boat and had to keep clear
You broke rule 15 (and rule 13 if she had to act before you were close-hauled) — she was not given room to keep clear; take a Two-Turns Penalty
She broke rule 16.1 by luffing without giving you room
questions.why: Rule 13 while tacking, then rule 15: the boat that becomes leeward by tacking must give the windward boat room to keep clear at first.

questions.q: Reaching in a Dragon. Red comes up from clear astern and establishes an overlap to windward of you. Her helmsman hails 'Give me room, you've just got right of way!'. Is he right?

figure.note: Red's overlap came from astern, to windward

options: Yes — and you must also sail no higher than your proper course under rule 17
No — but you must hold your course until Red has passed (rule 16.2)
Yes — the moment an overlap begins the leeward boat acquires right of way and owes room under rule 15
No — you were already the right-of-way boat (clear ahead, rule 12) and remain so (rule 11); you acquired nothing, so rule 15 does not apply
questions.why: Rule 15 applies only when right of way changes hands; a boat clear ahead that becomes the leeward boat keeps right of way throughout.

questions.q: After you tack onto starboard clear ahead of a port-tack boat, your crew says: 'Now she has to keep clear immediately — not our problem any more.' What does rule 15 add to that?

figure.title: Just after your tack
lines: You: port to starboard, now clear ahead
Blue: port tack, one length astern
Blue had no warning of your tack

options: That you, having just acquired right of way, must at first give her room to keep clear — she is not required to anticipate your tack
That she must keep clear only after you hail 'Starboard!'
That you must keep clear of her for the next two hull lengths
Nothing — rule 15 applies only to boats that acquire right of way by gybing
questions.why: Rule 15: a boat that acquires right of way by her own action initially gives the other boat room to keep clear.

questions.q: You were over the line at the gun and dip back to restart on starboard. The moment your hull is wholly on the pre-start side you are overlapped to leeward of Green, who until then was keeping clear of you under rule 21; Green now has to luff immediately. Who broke what?

figure.note: You have just returned below the line

options: You — a boat that was OCS keeps clear of everyone until she has started correctly
You — by returning you acquired right of way through your own action, so rule 15 required you to give Green room to keep clear at first
Green — once you were back on the pre-start side she was simply the windward boat and had to keep clear
Nobody — a boat returning to start is always the right-of-way boat
questions.why: Rule 21 ends when the returning boat is wholly on the pre-start side; she then acquires right of way by her own action and rule 15 applies.

questions.q: You tack onto starboard two lengths ahead and to leeward of White, who is on port. You give her room and she bears away to pass astern. You then luff sharply towards head to wind to stop her crossing your stern; she cannot respond and hits you. Which rule did you break?

figure.note: You luff as White passes astern

options: No rule — a starboard-tack boat may luff as high as she likes and the port boat must keep clear
Rule 16.2 — a starboard boat must not luff when a port boat is passing astern on a beat
Rule 16.1 — after giving initial room you changed course without giving White room to keep clear; rule 15 was satisfied but 16.1 was not
Rule 15 — your obligation to give room lasts until the boats have separated
questions.why: Rule 15 covers the moment of acquiring right of way; each later course change by the right-of-way boat must give room under rule 16.1.

questions.q: You tack onto starboard ahead of Green, on port. To pass astern of you she has to bear away 20 degrees at once, which she does easily and without contact. Green protests that she was 'denied room under rule 15'. Will she win?

figure.note: Green bears away 20° and passes astern

options: Yes — after tacking you must hold your course until the other boat has passed
No — rule 15 does not apply when the other boat is on port tack
Yes — any boat forced to alter course by a boat that has just tacked has been denied room under rule 15
No — rule 15 requires room to keep clear, not a course free of alterations; she could respond promptly and in a seamanlike way, so you complied
questions.why: Room is the space to manoeuvre promptly in a seamanlike way; rule 15 is satisfied when the other boat can keep clear by such a manoeuvre.

questions.q: Approaching the leeward gate in a J/70 fleet. You are on port, clear ahead of Grey (also port) by half a length. You gybe onto starboard across her bow; Grey has to luff instantly and still clips your quarter. What is your position?

figure.note: You have just gybed onto starboard

options: You broke rule 15 — you acquired right of way by gybing but gave Grey no room to keep clear; the contact also breaks rule 14
Grey broke rule 12 — she was clear astern and had to keep clear of you whatever you did
Grey broke rule 10 — the moment you were on starboard she had to keep clear
Nobody — a gybe is not a change of tack under rule 13, so right of way did not change
questions.why: Rule 15: a boat acquiring right of way (here by gybing onto starboard) must initially give the other boat room to keep clear.

questions.q: On a run you gybe your 49er onto port and find Blue, on starboard, a length away — she had been hidden behind your spinnaker, holding a steady course the whole time. You hit her. Does rule 15 help you?

figure.note: Blue was hidden behind your spinnaker

options: Yes — a boat hidden behind another boat's spinnaker must hail before claiming right of way
No — Blue did not acquire right of way, she had it all along; you broke rule 10 and rule 14, and a boat must keep a lookout
No — but Blue broke rule 16.1 by holding her course when she saw you gybe
Yes — Blue appeared suddenly and had to give you room to keep clear
questions.why: Rule 15 applies only to a boat that acquires right of way; a boat that already had it owes nothing. Failing to see her is no defence under rules 10 and 14.

questions.q: Blue tacks onto starboard three lengths ahead of you while you are on port; you have plenty of time to duck but would rather protest her for 'tacking too close'. Does any rule set a distance within which a boat may not tack in front of another?

figure.note: Blue has just tacked, three lengths away

options: Yes — rule 15 forbids tacking within two hull lengths of another boat
No — but a boat that tacks ahead of another must hail 'Tacking' first
No — rules 13 and 15 require only that she keeps clear while tacking and then gives you room to keep clear; three lengths was ample, so she broke nothing
Yes — rule 13 forbids tacking in front of a boat that is within hailing distance
questions.why: There is no distance rule: rule 13 governs the tack itself and rule 15 requires room to keep clear once it is complete.

questions.q: Running by the lee in 10 knots. Blue, overlapped to windward of you on starboard, gybes onto port to head for the pin. Now you are on starboard and she is on port. Blue calls 'You've just got right of way, give me room!'. Is she right?

figure.note: Blue has just gybed onto port

options: Yes — and you must also hold your course under rule 16.2 until she is clear
No — because on a run the windward boat always has right of way
Yes — every change of right of way is followed by a period in which the new right-of-way boat gives room
No — you got right of way because of her gybe, not by your own action, so rule 15 does not apply; she must keep clear under rule 10 at once
questions.why: Rule 15 does not apply when a boat acquires right of way because of the other boat's actions — Blue's gybe put her on port.

questions.q: Twenty seconds before the start you come from astern and poke your bow to leeward of Red, half a length apart. The instant the overlap begins you luff hard; Red cannot respond and your bows touch. Who broke a rule?

figure.note: 20 s to the start; you luff at once

options: You — you acquired right of way by establishing the overlap and had to give Red room initially (rule 15); your immediate luff also broke rule 16.1
Red — before the start the windward boat must keep clear instantly and rule 15 does not apply
You — you broke rule 17 by sailing above your proper course before the start
Nobody — before the starting signal a leeward boat may luff as she pleases
questions.why: Rule 15: initially give room to keep clear; rule 16.1: give room when changing course. Rule 17 cannot apply — there is no proper course before the start.

questions.q: In a post-race debrief your crew asks which boat rule 15 binds: the one that gains right of way, or the one that loses it?
options: The boat that loses right of way — she must immediately keep clear without being given any room
The boat that acquires right of way — she must initially give the other boat room to keep clear, unless she got it through the other boat's actions
Both boats equally — each must give the other room for one hull length
Neither — rule 15 is about the race committee giving room at the starting line
questions.why: Rule 15 binds the boat acquiring right of way: initially give the other boat room to keep clear.

questions.q: Reaching to the wing mark in 12 knots. Green is overlapped to windward of you, a metre away, and keeping clear. Without warning you throw the helm over and luff 30 degrees; Green's bow hits your quarter before she can respond. Who broke a rule?

figure.note: You luff sharply

options: Both — Green for rule 11, you for rule 17
Green — the windward boat must keep clear whatever the leeward boat does
You — a right-of-way boat that changes course must give the other boat room to keep clear (rule 16.1); Green is exonerated for breaking rule 11
Nobody — a leeward boat may luff up to head to wind at any time
questions.why: Rule 16.1: when a right-of-way boat changes course she shall give the other boat room to keep clear.

questions.q: You are the leeward boat on a reach and luff gradually, a few degrees at a time, over ten seconds. Blue, to windward, has room to respond but sails on, and her boom hits your shroud. Blue claims you broke rule 16.1. Did you?

figure.note: You luff slowly over ten seconds

options: Yes — a leeward boat may not luff at all while the boats are overlapped
Both boats are equally at fault, because the contact involved only rigging
Yes — rule 16.1 requires the leeward boat to hail before every course change
No — you gave her room to keep clear; Blue broke rule 11 (and rule 14) by not responding
questions.why: Rule 16.1 is satisfied when the windward boat is given room to keep clear; if she then fails to keep clear she breaks rule 11.

questions.q: Twenty seconds before the start you are clear ahead of Red, who is a third of a length astern on the same tack. You luff head to wind to kill speed; Red cannot avoid hitting your transom. Who broke what?
options: You broke rule 16.1 — as the right-of-way boat (rule 12) you changed course without giving Red room to keep clear; Red is exonerated for breaking rule 12
You broke rule 17 — you sailed above your proper course before the start
Red broke rule 12 — the boat clear astern must keep clear of the boat ahead whatever she does
Nobody — before the starting signal a boat may luff head to wind at will
questions.why: Rule 16.1 binds a boat clear ahead as much as a leeward boat: a course change must leave the other boat room to keep clear.

questions.q: On a beat Blue, the windward boat, bears away sharply towards you without warning and you have to bear away to avoid her. You protest her under rule 16.1 for changing course without giving you room. Will the protest succeed under that rule?

figure.note: Blue bears away toward you

options: No — Blue broke no rule, because a windward boat may bear away at any time to gain speed
Not under rule 16.1 — it limits only the right-of-way boat; Blue, the windward boat, broke rule 11 by failing to keep clear
Yes — rule 16.1 applies to any boat that changes course towards another
Yes — and Blue also broke rule 17 by sailing below her proper course
questions.why: Rule 16.1 restricts the right-of-way boat when she changes course; a give-way boat that sails into the right-of-way boat breaks rule 11.

questions.q: In 25 knots and a big sea you, the leeward boat on a broad reach, luff Grey 15 degrees in two seconds. In flat water she could have followed; in these waves her spinnaker collapses, she broaches and hits you. Did you give Grey room to keep clear?

figure.note: 25 knots, big sea; you luff 15° in 2 s

options: Yes — 15 degrees in two seconds is always a reasonable rate of luff, whatever the weather
No — rule 16.1 forbids any luff in more than 20 knots of wind
No — room is the space needed to respond promptly and in a seamanlike way in the existing conditions; in that sea your luff broke rule 16.1
Yes — a windward boat that broaches has lost control and is herself breaking rule 11
questions.why: Room (definition) is judged in the existing conditions; rule 16.1 requires room that allows a seamanlike response in that wind and sea.

questions.q: Ninety seconds before the start of a J/24 race you are to leeward of White, overlapped, both luffing slowly. You then luff hard to head to wind; White responds but cannot avoid touching your rail. White says there is no proper course before the start, so you were free to luff as you liked. Who is right?

figure.note: 90 s to the start

options: You — before the starting signal the leeward boat may luff at any speed and the windward boat must simply keep clear
White — before the start a leeward boat may not luff above close-hauled at all
Neither — before the starting signal Part 2 does not apply
White is partly right: rule 17 does not apply before the start, but rule 16.1 always does — you had to give her room to keep clear, and you did not
questions.why: Rule 16.1 applies at all times a right-of-way boat changes course; the absence of a proper course before the start only switches off rule 17.

questions.q: On a run in a Melges 24 fleet you are to leeward of Black, who established the overlap from windward. You luff her three times in a row, each time slowly enough for her to respond, and she does. Black says repeated luffing is harassment and against rule 16.1. Is it?

figure.note: Black's overlap was from windward

options: No — rule 16.1 is satisfied each time Black is given room to keep clear; there is no limit on the number of course changes
Yes — you broke rule 17: a leeward boat may never sail above her proper course on a run
Yes — you broke rule 2: more than one luff is unsportsmanlike by definition
Yes — a right-of-way boat may change course only once while the boats are overlapped
questions.why: Rule 16.1 requires room to keep clear at each course change and nothing more; rule 17 does not apply to an overlap gained from windward.

questions.q: On a reach Red, clear astern, is trying to pass you to leeward. You bear away sharply below your proper course to block her; she has to crash-gybe to avoid you. Red cites 'the rule against sailing below proper course'. Which rule actually applies?

figure.note: You bear away to block Red

options: Rule 16.2 — a right-of-way boat may not bear away towards a boat that is keeping clear
Rule 16.1 — bearing away is a change of course too, and you must give Red room to keep clear; the old ban on sailing below proper course no longer exists
No rule — Red was clear astern and had to keep clear whatever you did
Rule 17 — a boat may not sail below her proper course to block a boat passing to leeward
questions.why: Old rule 17.2 (no sailing below proper course) was deleted in 2013; a right-of-way boat bearing away is bound only by rule 16.1.

questions.q: On a reaching leg you are on starboard; Blue, on port, is converging and will pass close astern of you. You bear away to go for a puff, and Blue has to bear away hard too in order to still pass astern. Which rule governs your course change?

figure.note: Reaching leg; you bear away

options: Rule 16.2 — a starboard-tack boat may never bear away towards a port-tack boat passing astern
Rule 17 — you sailed below your proper course
Rule 16.1 — this is not a beat, so rule 16.2 does not apply; you broke 16.1 only if Blue was not given room to keep clear
No rule — a starboard-tack boat may sail any course she likes
questions.why: Rule 16.2 applies only on a beat to windward; on other legs a right-of-way boat's course change is judged under rule 16.1 alone.

questions.q: Close-hauled on starboard, you are clear ahead of Grey. To slow down for a shift you ease everything and stop almost dead in the water; Grey, two lengths astern, has to bear away hard to miss you. Grey says you broke rule 16.1. Did you?

figure.note: You slow almost to a stop on a steady course

options: Yes — a boat clear ahead may not reduce speed while another boat is within two lengths
Yes — slowing down suddenly is treated as a change of course under rule 16.1
No — but you broke rule 17 by sailing slower than your proper course
No — rule 16.1 is about changing course, not speed; you held your course, and Grey had to keep clear of you under rule 12
questions.why: Rule 16.1 is triggered by a change of course; a boat that slows down on a steady course does not change course, and the boat astern keeps clear (rule 12).

questions.q: You are on starboard and decide to luff to cross ahead of a port-tack boat that is ducking you. Your crew asks what rule 16.1 requires of you when you do. What is the answer?

figure.note: You luff as A sets up to pass astern

options: That you give her room to keep clear — she must be able to respond promptly and in a seamanlike way
That you give her room only if she is within one hull length of you
That you hold your course until she has passed — a right-of-way boat may not alter course near a give-way boat
That you hail before changing course
questions.why: Rule 16.1: when a right-of-way boat changes course she shall give the other boat room to keep clear.

questions.q: Reaching, you are the leeward boat and luff Green slowly; she has time to respond and does. Afterwards Green insists you broke rule 16.1 because you did not hail 'Coming up' before luffing. Is she right?

figure.note: You luff slowly, no hail

options: Yes — a right-of-way boat must hail before any change of course under rule 16.1
No — rule 16.1 requires room to keep clear, not a hail; a hail is good practice but its absence is no breach
No — because on a reach a leeward boat may not luff at all
Yes — on a reach the windward boat is entitled to a warning before a luff
questions.why: Rule 16.1 says nothing about hailing; it requires that the other boat be given room to keep clear.

questions.q: Approaching the windward mark on starboard, clear ahead of Red, you shoot head to wind to make the mark. Red, a length astern, bears away and passes clear of your stern without contact. Red protests you under rule 16.1. What is the outcome?

figure.note: You shoot head to wind for the mark

options: You broke rule 16.1 — a boat clear ahead may not luff above close-hauled with a boat astern of her
Red broke rule 12 — she should have luffed with you rather than bear away
No breach — you changed course but gave Red room to keep clear, and she kept clear; rule 12 required her to do so
You broke rule 13 — shooting head to wind counts as tacking
questions.why: Rule 16.1 is satisfied when the other boat is given room to keep clear; a boat astern that keeps clear by bearing away had that room.

questions.q: Beat in 10 knots. Red, on port, could keep clear of you either by tacking or by bearing away; you luff 5 degrees. Red chooses to bear away, misjudges it and hits your transom. Red says your luff took away her room. Who broke what?

figure.note: You luff 5°; Red bears away and misjudges

options: You — rule 16.1 requires that whichever response the port boat picks must still work after your course change
Nobody — a luff of only 5 degrees is too small to count as a change of course
Both — you for rule 16.1 and Red for rule 10, so both take two turns
Red — your luff still left her a seamanlike way to keep clear; choosing the wrong one is her problem, so she broke rules 10 and 14
questions.why: Rule 16.1 requires room to keep clear in a seamanlike way, not room for every possible manoeuvre; a give-way boat that misjudges breaks rules 10 and 14.

questions.q: Blue, on port, hails 'Hold your course!' as she sets up to cross you. You luff ten degrees to make her duck instead; she has room and does so. Blue protests, saying that once she hailed you had to hold your course. What is the decision?

figure.note: Blue hails 'Hold your course!'; you luff

options: Blue loses — no rule obliges a right-of-way boat to hold her course on request; you only had to give her room to keep clear, which you did (rule 16.1)
Blue wins — on a beat a starboard-tack boat may not luff towards a port-tack boat (rule 16.2)
Blue loses — but only because her hail was not loud enough to be heard
Blue wins — a hail of 'Hold your course' binds the starboard boat under rule 16.1
questions.why: A hail creates no obligation; the right-of-way boat may change course provided she gives room to keep clear (rule 16.1). Rule 16.2 restricts bearing away only.

questions.q: On the run you are on starboard; Grey, on port, is clear astern and heading to pass behind you. You bear away to put yourself in her path and make her gybe. Grey has room to respond each time. Is this allowed?

figure.note: Running leg; you bear away toward Grey

options: Yes — and because you are the right-of-way boat you need not give Grey any room
Yes, if you give Grey room to keep clear each time you change course (rule 16.1); rule 16.2 applies only on a beat to windward
No — rule 16.2 forbids a starboard-tack boat from bearing away towards a port-tack boat on any leg
No — a right-of-way boat may not change course at all when another boat is keeping clear of her
questions.why: Rule 16.1 allows a right-of-way boat to change course as long as she gives room to keep clear; rule 16.2 is limited to a beat to windward.

questions.q: Reaching in 14 knots with an anchored spectator boat to windward of the course. Red is overlapped to windward of you, between you and the spectator boat. You luff Red towards it; the only way she can keep clear of you is to hit the anchored boat. Which rules did you break?

figure.note: You luff Red toward the anchored boat

options: None — the windward boat must keep clear, and whether she can is her own problem
Rule 17 only — you luffed above your proper course while overlapped
Rule 16.1 — room to keep clear means room to respond without hitting anything — and rule 19.2(b), which required you to give Red room between you and the obstruction
Rule 14 only — a right-of-way boat may luff as she likes but must not cause contact
questions.why: Room includes space to comply with the rules and avoid objects; rule 16.1 requires it when a right-of-way boat changes course, rule 19.2(b) at an obstruction.

questions.q: Running in 12 knots. You are clear ahead of Blue, who is sailing lower and faster on your leeward quarter. You bear away sharply across her bow to gybe; she has to crash-gybe to miss you. Which rule did you break?

figure.note: You bear away across Blue's bow

options: None — a boat clear ahead may change course freely and the boat astern must keep clear
Rule 10 — by bearing away you changed tack and became the give-way boat
Rule 17 — you sailed below your proper course while Blue was passing to leeward
Rule 16.1 — a boat clear ahead has right of way under rule 12, but when she changes course she must give the boat astern room to keep clear
questions.why: Rule 16.1 binds every right-of-way boat, including a boat clear ahead under rule 12: a course change must give room to keep clear.

questions.q: On a reach Red, overlapped to windward of you, is keeping clear by a boat's width. You luff gently; she luffs with you and the gap stays the same. Did you break rule 16.1?

figure.note: You luff gently; Red follows

options: No — you changed course and gave her room to keep clear; that is all rule 16.1 asks of you
Yes — any luff by a leeward boat while overlapped breaks rule 16.1
Yes — you should have hailed before luffing
No — but you broke rule 17 by luffing while overlapped
questions.why: Rule 16.1 requires the right-of-way boat to give room to keep clear when she changes course; a luff the windward boat can follow complies.

questions.q: Beat, 12 knots. Blue, on port, is crossing you with a length to spare. 'To be safe' you bear away to pass further astern of her; at the same moment she bears away to duck you. The boats collide and both bows are damaged. Who is penalised?

figure.note: Both boats bear away at the same moment

options: Both — each boat changed course towards the other, so each broke rule 16.1
You — a right-of-way boat that changes course must give the other boat room to keep clear (rule 16.1); Blue was keeping clear until your bear-away, and is exonerated
Nobody — when both boats alter course at the same moment the collision is nobody's fault
Blue — a port-tack boat that hits a starboard-tack boat has broken rule 10, whatever the other boat did
questions.why: Rule 16.1: the right-of-way boat's course change deprived a boat that was keeping clear of room to continue doing so; rule 43.1(a) exonerates the other boat.

questions.q: Beating in 10 knots. Blue, on port, bears away early to duck you. When she is a length away you bear away at her, so that she must immediately bear away further to still pass astern. Which rule did you break?

figure.note: You bear away at Blue as she ducks

options: Rule 17 — you sailed below your proper course
None — a starboard-tack boat may alter course as she likes and the port boat must simply keep clear
Rule 16.2 — on a beat a starboard-tack boat shall not bear away if a port-tack boat passing astern would immediately need to change course to keep clear
Rule 10 — by turning towards her you became the give-way boat
questions.why: Rule 16.2: on a beat, a starboard-tack boat shall not bear away if a port-tack boat passing to leeward would immediately need to change course to keep clear.

questions.q: On the first beat Grey, on port, is about to cross ahead of you by half a length. You luff to force her to duck instead; she has time and room to bear away and does so. Grey protests under rule 16.2. What happens?

figure.note: You luff; Grey ducks

options: Grey wins — rule 16.2 forbids any course change by the starboard-tack boat on a beat
Grey loses — rule 16 does not apply to a boat on starboard tack at all
Grey wins — a starboard-tack boat may not luff above close-hauled on a beat
Grey loses — rule 16.2 forbids only bearing away at a port-tack boat passing astern; a luff is governed by rule 16.1, and you gave her room
questions.why: Rule 16.2 (2025 wording) restricts a starboard-tack boat from bearing away; a luff is judged under rule 16.1 — room to keep clear.

questions.q: Running leg in 10 knots. You are on starboard; White, on port, is passing astern of you. You bear away towards her; she has to change course at once but does so cleanly and passes astern. White protests under rule 16.2. What is the decision?

figure.note: Running leg; White passes astern

options: No breach of rule 16.2 — it applies only on a beat to windward; your bear-away is judged under rule 16.1, and White had room to keep clear
You broke rule 10 — by bearing away towards White you gave up your right of way
You broke rule 16.2 — bearing away at a port-tack boat passing astern is forbidden on every leg
You broke rule 17 — a starboard-tack boat may not sail below her proper course on a run
questions.why: Rule 16.2 is limited to a beat to windward; elsewhere only rule 16.1 applies, and it is satisfied when the other boat can keep clear in a seamanlike way.

questions.q: Beating in 8 knots. Blue, on port, is five lengths away and already bearing away to pass astern of you. You bear away 15 degrees towards better pressure; Blue carries on without altering and still passes comfortably astern, but protests you under rule 16.2. Will she win?

figure.note: Blue is five lengths away

options: Yes — on a beat a starboard-tack boat may never bear away while a port-tack boat is in sight
No — rule 16.2 is broken only if the port-tack boat would immediately need to change course; five lengths away, she did not
No — rule 16.2 applies only within one hull length
Yes — any bear-away towards a port-tack boat on a beat breaks rule 16.2
questions.why: Rule 16.2 bites only when, as a result of the bear-away, the port-tack boat would immediately need to change course to continue keeping clear.

questions.q: A 15-degree header hits and you bear away to stay close-hauled on starboard, just as Red, on port, is passing a length astern of you; she has to bear away hard at once to miss your transom. You say you were only following the wind. Did you break a rule?

figure.note: A 15° header; you bear away to stay close-hauled

options: No — following a header is sailing your proper course, which rule 16.2 allows
No — you broke rule 16.1 at most, and rule 16.2 does not apply to wind shifts
Yes, rule 16.2 — it has no exception for wind shifts; a starboard-tack boat may not bear away if the port-tack boat ducking her must immediately change course
No — Red broke rule 10: a port-tack boat must allow for the starboard boat's wind shifts
questions.why: Rule 16.2 is absolute: on a beat the starboard-tack boat shall not bear away if the port-tack boat passing astern would immediately need to change course.

questions.q: Beat in 12 knots. Blue, on port, decides to keep clear by tacking under your lee bow rather than ducking. Just before she tacks you bear away a few degrees; she has to tack earlier than she wanted. Blue protests under rule 16.2. What should the committee find?

figure.note: Blue is about to tack under your lee bow

options: Neither rule 16.1 nor 16.2 applies — a starboard-tack boat is never limited by rule 16
Rule 16.2 applies but Blue broke it — a port-tack boat may not tack in front of a starboard-tack boat
Rule 16.2 applies and you broke it — any bear-away at a port-tack boat on a beat is forbidden
Rule 16.2 does not apply — Blue was not sailing to pass astern (to leeward) of you; your bear-away is judged by rule 16.1 alone
questions.why: Rule 16.2 applies only when the port-tack boat is keeping clear by sailing to pass to leeward of the starboard-tack boat; otherwise rule 16.1 governs.

questions.q: Halfway up the beat you realise you bore away at a ducking port-tack boat and she had to react instantly; there was no contact and she did not hail. What should you do?

figure.title: On the beat
lines: You bore away; she had to react at once

options: Take a Two-Turns Penalty promptly — you broke rule 16.2, a Part 2 rule, contact or not
Nothing — a breach counts only if the other boat hails 'Protest'
Take a One-Turn Penalty — rule 16.2 is a minor breach
Nothing — a rule is only broken if contact follows
questions.why: Basic principle Sportsmanship and the Rules, and rule 44.1: a boat that breaks a Part 2 rule takes a Two-Turns Penalty, whether or not there was contact.

questions.q: Beating in 8 knots. Blue, on port, starts to duck you from four lengths away. Your helm wants to bear away to make her duck even deeper. Under rule 16.2, when may he?

figure.note: Blue is ducking from four lengths

options: Always — a starboard-tack boat may sail any course and the port boat must keep clear
Only if Blue would not immediately need to change course to keep clear — otherwise the bear-away breaks rule 16.2
Only after hailing 'Starboard!' once more
Never — a starboard-tack boat may not bear away while a port-tack boat is ducking her
questions.why: Rule 16.2: on a beat the starboard-tack boat shall not bear away if the ducking port-tack boat would immediately need to change course to keep clear.

questions.q: You hold a steady course on starboard up the beat. Red, on port, leaves her duck too late and her bow hits your transom; no damage. Red's helm says you should have luffed to let her through under rule 16.2. Who broke a rule?

figure.note: You hold course; Red ducks too late

options: You — rule 16.2 requires a starboard-tack boat to luff and let a ducking boat pass astern
Nobody — a touch without damage during a duck is not a breach
Red — she broke rules 10 and 14; rule 16.2 only restricts a starboard-tack boat that bears away, and you did not change course at all
Both — Red for rule 10 and you for rule 16.2
questions.why: Rule 16.2 restricts only a starboard-tack boat that bears away; a boat holding course breaks nothing, and the port-tack boat broke rules 10 and 14.

questions.q: In the bar after the race your crew says rule 16.2 forbids a port-tack boat from changing course while she ducks a starboard-tack boat. Whom does rule 16.2 actually restrict?
options: The port-tack boat — she must hold a steady course while passing astern of a starboard-tack boat
Both boats — neither may change course once they are within two hull lengths
The windward boat on any leg — she may not bear away towards a leeward boat
The starboard-tack boat on a beat — she may not bear away if a port-tack boat passing astern would immediately have to change course
questions.why: Rule 16.2 is a limit on the starboard-tack boat on a beat: no bearing away that would force a ducking port-tack boat to change course immediately.

questions.q: On the beat you first luff to make Yellow, on port, give up her cross and duck you; then, as she is passing astern, you bear away onto her and she has to react at once. Which part of your manoeuvre broke a rule?

figure.note: First you luffed; now you bear away at Yellow

options: The bear-away — once Yellow was passing astern you bore away and she had to change course immediately (rule 16.2); the earlier luff was legal under rule 16.1, as she had room
The luff — a starboard-tack boat may not luff towards a port-tack boat on a beat
Both — any course change by a starboard-tack boat towards a port-tack boat is illegal on a beat
Neither — a starboard-tack boat may do as she likes and the port boat must keep clear
questions.why: Rule 16.1 allows a luff that leaves room to keep clear; rule 16.2 forbids a bear-away that forces a ducking port-tack boat to change course immediately.

questions.q: Beating in 18 knots. You bear away at Green, on port, as she is ducking you; she reacts immediately but cannot avoid you and her bow damages your quarter. In the hearing you argue that as the starboard-tack boat you cannot be penalised. What is the decision?

figure.note: You bear away at Green; contact with damage

options: Nobody is penalised — the damage was caused by both boats equally
You broke rules 16.2 and 14 and, as there was damage, are not exonerated; Green is exonerated for breaking rule 10 because you compelled her
Green is disqualified under rule 10 and rule 14; a starboard-tack boat is never penalised for a collision
Both boats are disqualified — Green under rule 10, you under rule 14 only
questions.why: Rule 16.2 forbids the bear-away; rule 14 is broken too, with no exoneration where there is damage. Rule 43.1(a) exonerates the boat compelled to break rule 10.

questions.q: You are on port tack, ducking Red on the beat. Red bears away at you; you react instantly and pass astern without contact. Should you take a penalty for having to alter course twice to keep clear?

figure.note: Red bears away at you as you duck

options: Yes — a port-tack boat that has to alter course twice to keep clear has broken rule 10
Yes — rule 16.2 requires the port-tack boat to hold her course while ducking
No — you kept clear; it is Red who broke rule 16.2 by bearing away so that you had to change course immediately, and you may protest her
No — because no rule applies when there is no contact
questions.why: Rule 16.2 restricts the starboard-tack boat; a port-tack boat that keeps clear despite the bear-away breaks nothing and may protest.

questions.q: Reaching leg in ILCA 7s, 12 knots. You come from clear astern and establish an overlap to leeward of Red, a length apart. You now want to luff her well above the course to the mark. May you?

figure.note: You came from clear astern

options: Yes — the leeward boat has right of way and may luff up to head to wind
Yes — but only once, and after hailing 'Up!'
No — a boat that establishes an overlap from astern must keep clear of the boat ahead
No — having become overlapped to leeward from clear astern within two of your hull lengths, you may not sail above your proper course while the overlap lasts (rule 17)
questions.why: Rule 17: a boat that becomes overlapped to leeward from clear astern within two of her hull lengths shall not sail above her proper course while so overlapped.

questions.q: On a reach Green comes from astern and overlaps you to windward. You, now the leeward boat, luff her well above your proper course, giving her room each time. Green cites rule 17. Who is right?

figure.note: Green overlapped you from astern, to windward

options: You — rule 17 limits only a boat that became overlapped to leeward from astern; Green created the overlap to windward, so you may luff (subject to rule 16.1)
You — because rule 17 applies only on a run
Green — a leeward boat may never sail above her proper course while overlapped
Green — rule 17 applies to whichever boat is to leeward, however the overlap began
questions.why: Rule 17 binds the boat that becomes overlapped to leeward from clear astern; when the overlap is made from windward the leeward boat may luff, with room (16.1).

questions.q: Running in a Finn fleet. You establish a leeward overlap on Blue from clear astern, but three hull lengths to leeward of her. You then luff up towards her. Does rule 17 restrict you?

figure.note: Three hull lengths apart

options: Yes — any leeward overlap established from clear astern limits you to your proper course
No — rule 17 applies only when the overlap begins within two of your hull lengths; from three lengths away you may luff, subject to rule 16.1
Yes — rule 17 applies within three hull lengths, the same distance as the zone
No — rule 17 never applies on a run
questions.why: Rule 17 is triggered only by an overlap that begins within two of the leeward boat's hull lengths; beyond that she is limited only by rule 16.1.

questions.q: You are close-hauled on starboard. Grey crosses ahead of you on port and tacks. She passes head to wind clear ahead, and while she is still turning to close-hauled you sail into an overlap a length to leeward of her. Once she is close-hauled you luff her hard above close-hauled, giving her room. Grey says you broke rule 17. Did you?

figure.note: Grey has just tacked to windward of you

options: Yes — on a beat no boat may sail above close-hauled while overlapped
No — rule 17 does not apply when the overlap began while the windward boat was still tacking
Yes — you became overlapped to leeward from clear astern within two lengths after she passed head to wind; since 2025 rule 17 applies even while she is still tacking
No — because Grey acquired right of way by her tack and had to give you room (rule 15)
questions.why: The 2025 rules deleted rule 17's last sentence: an overlap from clear astern that begins after the windward boat passes head to wind counts, so you may not sail above your proper course.

questions.q: On port you duck Black, on starboard, and immediately tack onto starboard a length to leeward of her and slightly ahead, so that you are overlapped the moment your tack is complete. Does rule 17 stop you luffing above your proper course?

figure.note: You have just tacked into the overlap

options: Yes — any boat that becomes overlapped to leeward within two hull lengths is limited to her proper course
No — because rule 17 does not apply on a beat
Yes — a lee-bow tack always triggers rule 17
No — you did not become overlapped from clear astern; the overlap began as you completed your tack, so rule 17 does not apply (rules 13, 15 and 16.1 do)
questions.why: Rule 17 applies only to a boat that becomes overlapped to leeward from clear astern; a boat that tacks straight into an overlap was not clear astern.

questions.q: Forty seconds before the start you come from astern and establish a leeward overlap on White within a length. You luff slowly, up to head to wind, giving her room all the way. White says you may not sail above your proper course. Is she right?

figure.note: 40 s to the start

options: No — a boat has no proper course before her starting signal, so rule 17 cannot limit you; only rule 16.1 (room to keep clear) applies
Yes — rule 17 applies from the preparatory signal
Yes — before the start a leeward boat may not luff above close-hauled
No — because rule 17 never applies within the starting area
questions.why: Definition Proper Course: a boat has no proper course before her starting signal, so rule 17 has nothing to bite on; rule 16.1 still applies.

questions.q: At the starting signal you are overlapped to leeward of Blue, from an overlap you gained from astern within a length, and you are holding her head to wind. What must you do now?

figure.note: The starting signal has just been made

options: Tack immediately — a leeward boat may not stay overlapped after the start
Bear away promptly to your proper course — from the starting signal you have one, and rule 17 forbids sailing above it while overlapped within two lengths
Hold Blue head to wind until she drops back clear astern
Nothing — a luff begun before the start may be continued until the windward boat tacks away
questions.why: From the starting signal a boat has a proper course; a leeward boat subject to rule 17 may no longer sail above it.

questions.q: On a reach you are overlapped to leeward of Red within a length, from astern, so rule 17 applies. You want to tack. You luff above your proper course, pass astern of Red and tack. Red protests under rule 17. Did you break it?

figure.note: You luff to pass astern of Red and tack

options: Yes — you may pass astern of Red only by bearing away
Yes — once rule 17 applies you may not luff until Red has broken the overlap
No — rule 17 allows you to sail above your proper course if in doing so you promptly sail astern of the other boat
No — because rule 17 does not apply on a reaching leg
questions.why: Rule 17's exception: the leeward boat may sail above her proper course if she promptly sails astern of the other boat.

questions.q: Running, you overlapped Grey to leeward from astern and were limited by rule 17. Grey then surfed clear ahead by half a length; a minute later you caught her again and re-established the leeward overlap from astern within a length. Does rule 17 apply now?

figure.note: The overlap was broken and re-established

options: No — you must now keep clear of Grey as the boat that was astern
No — rule 17 never applied, because on a run there is no proper course
No — the limitation is lifted for good once the first overlap is broken
Yes — a new overlap from clear astern within two lengths starts the limitation afresh
questions.why: Rule 17 applies each time a boat becomes overlapped to leeward from clear astern within two of her hull lengths.

questions.q: You are overlapped to leeward of Blue on starboard, from an overlap gained from astern, and rule 17 applies to you. You gybe onto port. Which rule now governs the boats?

figure.note: You have just gybed onto port

options: Rule 17 no longer applies — the boats are on opposite tacks; rule 10 now applies, and you, on port, must keep clear
Rule 17 still applies until the overlap is broken
Rule 17 still applies, but now to Blue as the boat to windward
Rule 11 — you remain the leeward boat with right of way
questions.why: Rule 17 applies only while the boats remain on the same tack; after the gybe rule 10 governs.

questions.q: Running on port, you are overlapped to windward of Red, both within a length. You gybe together onto starboard and you are now the leeward boat. May you luff Red above your proper course, giving her room?

figure.note: Both have just gybed onto starboard

options: Yes — but only because gybing resets all rights for both boats under rule 15
Yes — you did not become overlapped from clear astern; the boats were already overlapped when you became the leeward boat, so rule 17 does not apply
No — rule 17 carries over from the previous tack
No — the moment you become the leeward boat within two lengths, rule 17 applies
questions.why: Rule 17 is triggered by becoming overlapped to leeward from clear astern; a boat that becomes leeward through a simultaneous gybe did not.
questions.ref: RRS 17, RRS definition Leeward and Windward

questions.q: On a run Blue is trying to pass you to leeward. You bear away below your proper course to block her, giving her room as you go. Blue cites 'the rule against sailing below your proper course'. Does it exist?

figure.note: You bear away to block Blue

options: Yes — rule 17 forbids sailing below proper course when a boat is passing to leeward
Yes — a boat may change course only to windward while overlapped
Not any more — old rule 17.2 was deleted in 2013; only rule 16.1 limits your bear-away
No — but you must hold your course under rule 16.2 on a run
questions.why: Rule 17 today limits only sailing above proper course; the old 17.2 on sailing below it was removed in 2013. Rule 16.1 governs the course change.

questions.q: Mixed club race. Your 29er comes from astern and establishes a leeward overlap on a 40-ft keelboat; the gap between the boats is 12 metres. Does rule 17 apply to you?

figure.note: Gap 12 m — nearly three of your lengths

options: Yes — two of the keelboat's hull lengths is 24 m, and you are well within that
No — rule 17 does not apply between boats of different classes
Yes — rule 17 applies whenever a leeward overlap begins from astern, whatever the distance
No — the distance is measured in the leeward boat's hull lengths; two 29er lengths are under 9 m, so at 12 m rule 17 does not apply
questions.why: Rule 17 says 'within two of her hull lengths' — the lengths of the boat that becomes overlapped to leeward.

questions.q: Running to the leeward gate with rule 17 applying to you as the leeward boat. You sail 10 degrees higher than Black because you plan to gybe later and the hotter angle is faster for you. Black says you are above her proper course. Are you breaking rule 17?

figure.note: You sail 10° higher than Black

options: No — rule 17 refers to your own proper course, which may differ from Black's; sailing your fastest course to the gate is not above it
No — because rule 17 never applies on a running leg, only on a reach
Yes — the leeward boat must sail the windward boat's proper course, not her own
Yes — on a run the proper course is always dead downwind to the next mark
questions.why: Proper course is the course the boat herself would sail to finish soonest in the absence of the other boat; two boats may have different proper courses.

questions.q: Limited by rule 17 on a run, you luff 15 degrees to avoid a floating pallet directly ahead, then bear back down. Red, to windward, protests. Did you break rule 17?

figure.note: You luff round the pallet, then bear away

options: Yes — you should have borne away round the pallet, below Red's course
No — avoiding an obstruction is part of your proper course, the course you would sail in Red's absence; rule 16.1 still applies to the luff
No — because rule 17 does not apply when an object is in the water
Yes — once rule 17 applies you may not luff for any reason until the overlap ends
questions.why: Proper course is the course a boat would sail without the other boat present — it includes a luff to avoid an obstruction. Rule 16.1 still requires room.

questions.q: You are limited by rule 17 on a reach. Blue, to windward, calls 'You're under 17 — keep clear of me!'. What does rule 17 actually require of you?

figure.note: Blue hails 'Keep clear!'

options: That you sail at least one hull length below your proper course
That you keep clear of Blue until the overlap is broken
Only that you do not sail above your proper course; you are still the right-of-way boat and Blue must keep clear (rule 11)
That you hold a straight course until Blue has passed
questions.why: Rule 17 limits how high the leeward boat may sail; it does not change right of way — the windward boat still keeps clear under rule 11.

questions.q: Rule 17 applies to you on a reach. Your proper course to the mark converges with Blue's course, and she will have to luff to keep clear. May you hold your proper course?

figure.note: Your proper course converges with Blue's

options: No — under rule 17 you must bear away whenever the windward boat would have to alter course
No — a boat limited by rule 17 loses her right of way
Yes — and Blue must also take a penalty for being forced to luff
Yes — rule 17 forbids only sailing above your proper course; Blue must keep clear under rule 11, and you give her room if you alter course (rule 16.1)
questions.why: Rule 17 does not oblige the leeward boat to sail below her proper course; the windward boat keeps clear (rule 11), with room under rule 16.1 for course changes.

questions.q: Limited by rule 17 on a reach, you sail 10 degrees low for clear air and then come back up to your proper course, giving Red, to windward, room as you do. Red says the luff back up breaks rule 17. Does it?

figure.note: You come back up to your proper course

options: No — you may sail anywhere up to your proper course; coming back up to it is not sailing above it (rule 16.1 still applies to the luff)
No — because rule 17 only applies for the first two hull lengths of the overlap
Yes — once you have sailed below your proper course you may not luff again while overlapped
Yes — rule 17 fixes your course at the moment the overlap began
questions.why: Rule 17 forbids sailing above proper course; a boat below it may luff back up to it, giving room under rule 16.1.

questions.q: Running on starboard, you are overlapped to leeward of Grey, who is on port (both sailing more than 90 degrees from the wind, so the boats are overlapped). You got there from astern within a length. Grey says rule 17 limits you. Does it?

figure.note: You on starboard, Grey on port

options: No — because on a run the windward boat has right of way
No — rule 17 applies only between boats on the same tack; here rule 10 applies and Grey, on port, must keep clear
Yes — on a run rule 17 applies whatever the tacks
Yes — rule 17 applies to any leeward overlap gained from astern
questions.why: Rule 17 is in Section B 'on the same tack'; between boats on opposite tacks rule 10 governs.

questions.q: Rule 17 applies to you on the run. You head 20 degrees high to reach a band of pressure 200 metres to windward of the rhumb line; Red, overlapped to windward, protests that you are above your proper course. How will the committee decide?

figure.note: You head high for pressure

options: Against you — on a run the proper course is always the rhumb line to the next mark
Against you — a leeward boat under rule 17 may not change course at all
