On the facts — if heading for the pressure is the course you would sail to finish soonest with Red absent, it is your proper course and rule 17 is not broken
For you — rule 17 does not apply when the leeward boat is going for more wind
questions.why: Proper course is a question of fact: the course the boat would sail to finish as soon as possible in the absence of the other boat, pressure included.

questions.q: Blue, to windward and overlapped, believes rule 17 means you must get out of her way as she bears down towards the mark. She bears away onto you and you have to bear away to avoid contact. Who broke a rule?

figure.note: Blue bears down on you

options: You — a boat limited by rule 17 must keep clear of the windward boat
Both — Blue for rule 11 and you for not holding your course under rule 16.2
Nobody — the windward boat may bear away at any time when the leeward boat is under rule 17
Blue — rule 17 only limits how high you may sail; it gives her no right of way, and by bearing down into you she broke rule 11
questions.why: Rule 17 does not alter right of way: the windward boat still keeps clear under rule 11.

questions.q: You established a leeward overlap on Green two and a half lengths to leeward of her, then the boats converged to half a length while staying overlapped. Green says rule 17 now applies. Does it?

figure.note: The overlap began 2.5 lengths apart

options: No — what counts is the distance when the overlap began; it began beyond two lengths, so rule 17 never applied (rule 16.1 still limits your luffs)
Yes — rule 17 applies to every leeward overlap on the same tack
No — but rule 17 will apply once the boats are within one hull length
Yes — rule 17 starts to apply as soon as the boats come within two hull lengths
questions.why: Rule 17 is triggered when a boat becomes overlapped within two of her hull lengths; converging later does not start a new overlap.

questions.q: Protest hearing after a reaching leg: you came from clear astern and overlapped Blue to leeward within a length; you then luffed her 20 degrees above the course to the mark; she responded and there was no contact; Blue protested under rule 17. What should the committee decide?

figure.title: Protest hearing
lines: You: leeward overlap from clear astern
Gap at the start of the overlap: 1 length
You luffed Blue 20° above the course

options: No breach — Blue kept clear and nobody touched, so no rule was broken by anyone
You broke rule 17 — a leeward boat whose overlap came from clear astern within two lengths may not sail above her proper course; you are penalised
No breach — without contact rule 17 cannot be broken, whatever the course sailed
Blue broke rule 11 — she should have luffed sooner and higher to keep clear
questions.why: Rule 17 is broken by sailing above proper course while overlapped from astern within two lengths; no contact is needed for a breach.

questions.q: Approaching the finishing line on starboard, limited by rule 17 as the leeward boat, you luff head to wind to shoot the line, giving White, to windward, room to respond. White protests under rule 17. Is she right?

figure.note: You luff to shoot the line

options: Yes — rule 17 forbids luffing within two lengths of the finishing line
No — because rule 17 stops applying when the boats enter the zone of a finishing mark
No — shooting the line is your proper course if it gets you across sooner; rule 17 is not broken, and rule 16.1 was satisfied
Yes — a boat under rule 17 may not luff above close-hauled for any reason
questions.why: Proper course is the course that finishes the boat soonest without the other boat; a shoot at the line can be that course. Rule 16.1 still requires room.

questions.q: Black comes from astern and establishes an overlap to windward of you within a length. Who is limited by rule 17?

figure.note: Black overlapped you from astern, to windward

options: Both — neither boat may luff while they are overlapped within two lengths
Black — having come from astern she may not sail above her proper course
You — once the boats are overlapped you may not sail above your proper course
Nobody — rule 17 limits a boat that becomes overlapped to leeward from astern; Black is simply the windward boat and must keep clear (rule 11)
questions.why: Rule 17 applies only to a boat that becomes overlapped to leeward from clear astern; an overlap made to windward triggers nothing but rule 11.

questions.q: Wednesday club race, windward mark to be left to port. You are close-hauled on port tack, one hull length from the mark and inside Red, who is close-hauled on starboard tack and fetching it. You hail "Room at the mark!" Does Red have to give you mark-room?

figure.note: Both boats are beating; the mark is to be left to port

options: No — rule 18 does not apply between boats on opposite tacks on a beat; you must keep clear of Red under rule 10
No — but only because you hailed too late; a hail before the zone would have secured the room
Yes — you are the inside boat in the zone, so Red must give you mark-room under rule 18.2
Yes — the boat nearer the mark is entitled to room whatever her tack
questions.why: Rule 18.1(a)(1): rule 18 does not apply between boats on opposite tacks on a beat to windward; rule 10 governs.

questions.q: Wing mark of a trapezoid course, 8 knots, both of you on port tack on a beam reach. Blue is overlapped inside you (closer to the mark) and the bow of your Melges 24 has just crossed the three-length circle; Blue's bow is still a metre outside it. Blue hails for mark-room. Does rule 18 apply between you yet?

figure.note: Your bow is in the zone; Blue's is just outside

options: No — rule 18 applies only once the inside boat is in the zone
Yes — rule 18 applies as soon as at least one of the two boats is in the zone, and you are
No — rule 18 applies only when both boats are inside the zone
Yes — but only because Blue hailed; without a hail rule 18 starts at two lengths
questions.why: Rule 18.1(a): rule 18 applies between boats required to leave the mark on the same side when at least one of them is in the zone.

questions.q: National championship, windward mark to be left to port. You are on starboard tack, fetching the mark comfortably. Grey approaches on port tack; she cannot lay the mark and will have to tack to round it. As you converge inside the zone Grey shouts that she is inside and wants room. Does rule 18 apply between you?

figure.note: Grey cannot lay the mark on port tack

options: Yes — rule 18 applies between any two boats in the zone that must leave the mark to port
Yes — Grey is inside and in the zone, so you must give her mark-room to tack round the mark
No — the boats are on opposite tacks and the proper course at the mark for Grey, but not for you, is to tack; rule 10 applies
No — rule 18 never applies at a windward mark, only at leeward and gate marks
questions.why: Rule 18.1(a)(2): rule 18 does not apply between boats on opposite tacks when the proper course at the mark for one but not both is to tack.

questions.q: You have just rounded the windward mark of a trapezoid course and are bearing away onto the reach, still inside the zone. Yellow is coming up close-hauled on starboard tack towards the same mark, which she must also leave to port. You are both on starboard and overlapped. Yellow hails for mark-room. Is she entitled to it?

figure.note: You are leaving the mark; Yellow is approaching it

options: No — rule 18 switches off for both boats the moment either of them passes the mark
Yes — a boat that has rounded must always keep clear of boats still approaching the mark
Yes — both of you are on starboard, overlapped and in the zone, so the outside boat gives mark-room
No — rule 18 does not apply between a boat approaching a mark and one leaving it; the ordinary Section A rules decide who keeps clear
questions.why: Rule 18.1(a)(3): rule 18 does not apply between a boat approaching a mark and one leaving it; rules 11 or 12 apply instead.

questions.q: Thirty seconds before the start of a J/70 race you are approaching the committee boat end of the line on starboard tack. Black is overlapped to leeward of you, also on starboard, and is squeezing you up towards the committee boat. You hail "Room at the mark!" What are your rights?

figure.note: 30 seconds to the start; no mark-room at the committee boat

options: None under rule 18 — at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water Section C does not apply while boats approach it to start; you must keep clear under rule 11
Black must give you room because the committee boat is an obstruction under rule 19
Black must give you mark-room because you are the inside boat at the committee boat
Black must let you through if you hail for room before the zone, but not after
questions.why: Section C preamble: rule 18 does not apply at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water while boats approach it to start; rule 11 applies.
questions.ref: RRS Part 2 Section C preamble, RRS 11

questions.q: Pin end of a start line, 20 seconds to go, 12 knots. You are on starboard tack, overlapped and to leeward of White, who is also on starboard. You are right at the pin and realise you cannot quite lay it, so you hail White for room to pass the pin on its course side. She holds her course and you have to tack away and start late. You protest. Who, if anyone, broke a rule?

figure.note: 20 seconds to the start; you cannot quite lay the pin

options: White — at the pin end the boat nearer the mark always has the right to room
Nobody — rule 18 is off at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water; as the leeward boat you could luff White under rule 11, but not demand room at the pin
You — you broke rule 31 by sailing so close to a starting mark before the start
White — you were the inside boat at the pin, so she had to give you mark-room under rule 18.2
questions.why: Section C preamble: no mark-room at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water when approaching to start; rule 11 decides between overlapped boats.
questions.ref: RRS Part 2 Section C preamble, RRS 11

questions.q: Finish of a lake regatta: the finishing line runs from the committee boat to a pin and you are beating up to it. You are on starboard tack, overlapped inside Green (between her and the committee boat), both of you in the zone of the committee boat, which you must leave to starboard. Green, to leeward, luffs and squeezes you towards the committee boat. Who is right?

figure.note: You are between Green and the committee boat

options: Green — a committee boat is a starting and finishing mark, and Section C never applies at it
You — but only because the committee boat is an obstruction and rule 19 applies
You — rule 18 applies at a finishing mark, so Green, the outside boat, must give you mark-room even though she is the leeward boat
Green — as the leeward boat she has right of way under rule 11, and that overrides rule 18
questions.why: The Section C exception covers starting marks only; at a finishing mark rule 18.2(a)(1) applies and the outside boat gives mark-room.
questions.ref: RRS 18.2(a)(1), RRS Part 2 Section C preamble

questions.q: River race with current. The sailing instructions make the end of a 300-metre stone pier a mark of the course, to be left to port. You and Blue, both on starboard tack, run down along the pier overlapped; Blue is inside, between you and the pier. Which rule governs the room Blue gets at the pier end?

figure.note: The pier end is a mark; Blue is between you and the pier

options: Rule 18 at the end of the pier and rule 19 along its side; Blue may claim both
Neither — a shore structure is not a mark or an obstruction in the sense of the rules
Rule 18 — the pier end is a mark of the course, so Blue is entitled to mark-room as the inside boat
Rule 19 — the mark is a continuing obstruction, so rule 18 does not apply and rule 19 does
questions.why: Rule 18.1(a)(4): if the mark is a continuing obstruction, rule 18 does not apply and rule 19 applies instead.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 15 knots. You are running on port tack and Red is running on starboard tack; your bows are level, Red is inside (closer to the mark) and you both enter the zone together. Red hails for room. Are you overlapped for the purposes of rule 18, and who gives room?

figure.note: Both boats running, bows level, entering the zone together

options: Yes — the terms overlap and clear astern apply to boats on opposite tacks when rule 18 applies, and on a run it does; you give Red mark-room
No — you are on opposite tacks at a mark, so rule 18.1 switches off as it does on a beat
No — boats on opposite tacks are never overlapped, so rule 18 cannot apply and only rule 10 decides
Yes — but as the inside boat Red must still keep clear of you because you are to windward
questions.why: Definition Overlap: boats on opposite tacks are overlapped when rule 18 applies; 18.1 excludes opposite tacks only on a beat, so 18.2(a)(1) applies.
questions.ref: RRS definition Clear Astern and Clear Ahead; Overlap, RRS 18.2(a)(1)

questions.q: Gybe mark of a triangle, Saronic Gulf, 18 knots. You and Grey are broad reaching on starboard tack, overlapped as the first of you reaches the zone, the mark to be left to port; Grey is inside and to leeward. Just at the mark Grey starts her gybe and you, outside, hold on so close that she has to delay it and sail past the mark. You say she had room to pass the mark and could gybe later. Who is right?

figure.note: First reach of a triangle; Grey is inside at the gybe mark

options: You — mark-room is only room to pass the mark without touching it; the gybe is her own business
Grey — mark-room includes the room to round the mark as needed to sail the course, and at a gybe mark that includes the gybe
Grey — but only because she is to leeward; a windward inside boat gets no room to gybe
You — a boat entitled to mark-room must sail past the mark first and gybe only when she is clear of the outside boat
questions.why: Definition Mark-Room: room to round or pass the mark on the required side; at a gybe mark the rounding includes the gybe (rule 18.2(a)(1)).

questions.q: Windward–leeward course, two fleets. Your 470 fleet is rounding the leeward mark to port while the earlier Finn fleet is already beating back up through it. A Finn on starboard tack passes close to the mark as you, also on starboard, round it. He hails for mark-room. Does rule 18 apply between you?

figure.note: The Finn is on her beat; the mark is not a mark of her leg

options: Yes — both boats are on starboard, in the zone and leaving the mark to port, so the outside boat gives room
No — rule 18 never applies between boats of different fleets or classes
No — the Finn is not required to leave that mark on any side on her leg, so you are not boats required to leave it on the same side
Yes — rule 18 applies between any boats racing that are in the zone of a mark of either course
questions.why: Rule 18.1(a): rule 18 applies only between boats required to leave the mark on the same side; a boat for whom it is not a mark of her leg is not.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port. You were the outside boat and gave Blue mark-room; she has rounded, hardened up to close-hauled and is now a length past the mark, overlapped to windward of you, both close-hauled on starboard. You luff slowly and she has to respond. Blue protests that you took away "her" mark-room. Who is right?

figure.note: Blue has rounded and been given mark-room; you are now luffing

options: Blue — a boat entitled to mark-room keeps it until she is clear ahead or the boats separate
You — but only because you are the longer boat and so the zone belongs to you
Blue — mark-room lasts for three hull lengths after the mark, the same distance as the zone
You — once mark-room has been given rule 18 no longer applies between you, and Blue is simply the windward boat under rule 11 (you must give her room to keep clear under 16.1)
questions.why: Rule 18.1(b): rule 18 no longer applies between boats when mark-room has been given; afterwards rule 11 and 16.1 govern.

questions.q: Offset mark 60 metres to the left of the windward mark, both to be left to port. You have rounded the windward mark and are reaching to the offset on starboard tack; Yellow rounded just behind you and is overlapped outside and to windward of you as you enter the offset mark's zone. She says "a spreader mark isn't a real mark" and tries to squeeze in between you and the mark. What are the rights at the offset mark?

figure.note: Short reach from the windward mark (off the picture, right) to the offset

options: Yellow must give you mark-room and, as the windward boat, keep clear — an offset mark is a mark of the course like any other
Nobody owes anybody room — an offset mark is not a mark of the course under rule 18
Yellow must only keep clear under rule 11; there is no mark-room on a reaching leg
You must let Yellow through because she is the faster boat and was clear ahead at the windward mark
questions.why: Definition Mark and rule 18.2(a)(1): an object the SI require to be left on a side is a mark; overlapped at the zone, the outside boat gives mark-room.

questions.q: Leeward gate, 25 knots and waves. You are clear ahead of Black as you enter the zone of the right-hand gate mark, which you intend to round. Black, two lengths behind and to your left, bears off for the left-hand gate mark. At the last moment you change your mind and swing across towards the left mark too, and Black, now overlapped with you, has to bear away hard to avoid your transom. Who broke a rule?

figure.note: The right gate mark is about eight lengths to the right, off the picture

options: Black — you were clear ahead when you entered the zone of the gate, so she had to give you mark-room at either gate mark
Probably you — entering the zone of the right mark gave you nothing at the left mark; rule 18 starts afresh at its zone, and your change of course had to give Black room to keep clear (16.1)
Black — a boat clear astern must keep clear under rule 12 whatever the leading boat does at the gate
Nobody — at a gate rule 18 does not apply, and each boat may round whichever mark she likes
questions.why: Each gate mark has its own zone; rule 18.2(a) is judged at the left mark when the first boat reaches its zone, and rule 16.1 applies to your course change.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, light wind. You and Blue are running down on port tack, overlapped, with you on the outside, when Blue's bow reaches the zone. You are the leeward boat and have right of way under rule 11. Blue hails for mark-room. What must you do?

figure.note: Blue's bow has just reached the zone; she is inside

options: Luff Blue head to wind before the mark, as the leeward boat is allowed to do
Give room only if Blue was overlapped two lengths before the zone as well
Give Blue mark-room — you were the outside boat when the first of you reached the zone, and that obligation does not depend on who has right of way
Nothing — as the leeward right-of-way boat you may sail your course and Blue must keep clear
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(1): the boat outside when the first boat reaches the zone must thereafter give the inside boat mark-room, right of way or not.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port. You are clear ahead of Grey by half a length as your bow enters the zone, both of you running on port tack with spinnakers. Just before the mark Grey, faster in the puff, gets an overlap on your inside and hails for room. Must you give it?

figure.note: You enter the zone clear ahead; Grey is faster in the puff

options: Yes — Grey is the faster boat and a boat that establishes an overlap from astern has right of way
No — but only because Grey hailed after the overlap instead of before it
Yes — an inside overlap at the mark always entitles the inside boat to mark-room
No — you were clear ahead when you reached the zone, so Grey must give you mark-room even though she later became overlapped inside
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(2): not overlapped when the first boat reaches the zone — the boat that has not reached the zone must thereafter give the other mark-room.

questions.q: Palma, 40-boat fleet, leeward mark to be left to port. You are running on starboard tack and establish an inside overlap on Red from clear astern about four hull lengths from the mark, well before either of you is in the zone. Red says you came "from nowhere" and refuses room. Who is right?

figure.note: The overlap began four lengths out, before the zone

options: You — the overlap existed when the first boat reached the zone, so Red, the outside boat, must give you mark-room
Red — a boat that gets an inside overlap from clear astern is never entitled to mark-room
You — but only because you are on starboard tack and Red must keep clear anyway
Red — the overlap must exist from at least five hull lengths to count at the mark
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(1): what matters is whether the boats are overlapped when the first of them reaches the zone; an overlap gained before that counts.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 10 knots. White's bow enters the zone clear ahead of you by about a metre; a few seconds later, still before the mark, you get an inside overlap and call for room. White sails her rounding without giving you any, and you have to brake behind her. Was White right?

figure.note: White's bow reached the zone a metre ahead of yours

options: No — once you are overlapped inside in the zone, the outside boat must give you mark-room
Yes — the moment the first boat reached the zone you were clear astern, so you must give White mark-room no matter what overlap you gain later
Yes — but only because White entered the zone on starboard tack and you were on port
No — a lead of one metre is within the margin of error, so the boats count as overlapped
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(2): a boat clear astern when the leader reaches the zone must give mark-room; a later inside overlap changes nothing.

questions.q: In the protest room after a leeward-mark incident. You say you had an inside overlap when Blue's bow reached the zone; Blue says you were half a metre clear astern. Neither of you has a witness, and the protest committee finds it cannot tell who is right. How should it decide the overlap question?

figure.title: Protest hearing
lines: You: "I was overlapped at the zone"
Blue: "You were half a metre astern"

options: It must dismiss the protest, because without witnesses no facts can be found
It gives the benefit of the doubt to the boat that hailed first
It presumes you did not obtain the overlap in time — when there is reasonable doubt, the overlap is presumed not to have existed
It gives the benefit of the doubt to the inside boat, because the rules favour the boat nearer the mark
questions.why: Rule 18.2(e): if there is reasonable doubt that a boat obtained or broke an overlap in time, it is presumed she did not.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port. You are inside and overlapped with Green when she reaches the zone, so she must give you mark-room. In a lull she rolls over you and briefly gets clear ahead, then you surge back and the overlap is re-established just before the mark. Green now says you lost your rights when the overlap broke. Is she right?

figure.note: Overlapped at the zone, then briefly broken, then re-established

options: Yes — the moment the overlap broke she was clear ahead in the zone and you had to give her mark-room
No — but only because you were on starboard and she was on port
Yes — rule 18 is re-assessed every time the overlap changes inside the zone
No — a boat required to give mark-room must keep doing so for as long as rule 18.2(a) applies, even if the overlap is later broken or a new one begins
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a): a boat required to give mark-room continues to do so while the rule applies, even if later an overlap is broken or a new one begins.

questions.q: Leeward mark, Bodrum, dying breeze. You entered the zone clear ahead of Red and then slowed badly in a hole; Red, with the last of the wind, rolls up on your inside and is overlapped by half a length as you both reach the mark. She hails "Room!" Who must give what?

figure.note: You entered the zone clear ahead, then stopped in a hole

options: Red must give you mark-room — you were clear ahead at the zone, and her later inside overlap does not change that
Neither — once a leading boat slows, rule 18 no longer applies and rule 12 decides
You must give Red mark-room — she is overlapped inside at the mark, which is what counts
You must give Red mark-room — a boat that slows down loses her rights at the mark
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(2): clear ahead at the zone keeps her entitlement; the boat astern must give mark-room even after becoming overlapped inside.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, three Dragons running on starboard tack, all overlapped as the first of them reaches the zone: you are the outside boat, Blue is in the middle and Grey is inside. Blue hails you for room and Grey hails Blue. What do you owe, and to whom?

figure.note: Three boats overlapped at the zone; you are outside

options: Nothing — with three boats overlapped the leeward boat has right of way and sails her own rounding
Mark-room to both Blue and Grey — you must leave enough room for Blue to give Grey mark-room as well as for Blue herself
Mark-room to Blue only — Grey is Blue's problem, not yours
Mark-room to Grey only — Blue was not overlapped with you directly, only through Grey
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(1) with the definition Room: the outside boat gives room to the inside boats, including room for them to comply with their own obligations.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, both of you on port tack. You are the inside boat, overlapped to windward of Blue when she reaches the zone. Rounding, you come down onto her and your boom touches her shroud; no damage. Blue protests you under rule 11. What should the protest committee decide?

figure.note: Blue did not give you room; your boom touched her shroud, no damage

options: Blue is exonerated — a leeward boat need not give room to a windward boat under any rule
You are disqualified — a windward boat always keeps clear under rule 11, and mark-room does not change that
If you were sailing within the mark-room you were entitled to, you are exonerated for breaking rule 11 (43.1(b)); Blue broke 18.2(a)(1) by not giving mark-room
Both boats are disqualified — you for rule 11 and Blue for rule 18, because there was contact
questions.why: Rule 43.1(b): a boat sailing within the mark-room she is entitled to is exonerated for breaking a Section A rule in an incident with the boat owing that room.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, both on port tack. You are the inside boat, overlapped and to windward of Yellow at the zone. You sail two lengths wide of the mark so as to come out close-hauled right at it, and Yellow, to leeward, hits your wide loop and has to bear away. She protests. Did your mark-room cover the wide-and-tight rounding?

figure.note: Your wide loop (dashed) took you down onto Yellow

options: Yes — mark-room includes the room a boat needs to round the mark in the fastest way
Yes — the inside boat decides how she rounds, and the outside boat must keep out of her way
No — because mark-room never allows an inside boat to sail more than one length from the mark
No — mark-room is room to sail to the mark and round it, not room for a tactical rounding; as the windward boat you had to keep clear of Yellow where you went beyond that
questions.why: Definition Mark-Room: room to sail to the mark and to round or pass it; sailing wide for a tactical rounding is not within it, so rule 11 applied.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, both of you on starboard tack. You are the inside and the leeward boat, overlapped with Grey to windward of you when you reach the zone. You bear away to sail wide, then harden up tight around the mark, and Grey has to alter course both times to keep clear. Grey protests. Who is right?

figure.note: You are inside and to leeward; Grey is to windward

options: You — as the inside right-of-way boat you may round as you like, provided that when you change course you give Grey room to keep clear (rule 16.1)
You — a leeward boat can alter course at a mark without any limitation at all
Grey — the inside boat is limited to a seamanlike rounding, and a wide-and-tight is tactical
Grey — a boat entitled to mark-room must sail directly to the mark and leave it at once
questions.why: A right-of-way boat is not limited to mark-room; she may sail a tactical rounding, subject to rule 16.1 when she changes course.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 14 knots, both on port tack. Black is clear ahead and has already started her turn at the mark when you, surfing a wave, poke your bow between her transom and the mark and hail "Room!" Black cannot do anything but continue her turn and your bows touch, no damage. Who broke a rule?

figure.note: Black is already turning when your bow appears inside

options: Black — once you were overlapped inside in the zone she had to give you mark-room
You — the overlap came from clear astern when Black was already unable to give mark-room, so rule 18.2 gave you nothing; you broke rules 12 and 14
Black — a boat ahead must always leave a gap at the mark in case a boat comes up on her inside
Nobody — contact without damage at a mark is not a breach of any rule
questions.why: Rule 18.2(d): an inside overlap from clear astern when the outside boat has been unable to give mark-room since it began gives no entitlement.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port, 12 knots. You are on starboard tack a little below the layline, planning two short tacks to round. Blue crosses you on port and tacks right between you and the mark, half a length to windward and overlapped; you cannot bear away without hitting her. She then has to luff to shoot the mark and hails you for room. Is she entitled to mark-room?

figure.note: Blue tacks here, half a length to windward of you

options: Yes — she is inside, in the zone and overlapped, and an inside boat gets mark-room however she got there
No — because she was on port tack when she entered the zone and rule 18 never protects a port-tack boat
No — she obtained the inside overlap by tacking to windward of you when you were unable to give mark-room from the start, so rule 18.2 does not apply between you (18.2(d))
Yes — under rule 18.3 a boat that tacks in the zone is protected as long as she is fetching the mark
questions.why: Rule 18.2(d): an inside overlap gained by tacking to windward, when the outside boat has been unable to give mark-room since it began, gives no entitlement.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, J/24s, 10 knots. You establish an inside overlap on Grey from clear astern about two hull lengths before the zone. Grey, still sailing straight for the mark with two lengths of water between her and it, says she "cannot give room now" and rounds tight, forcing you outside. Was Grey entitled to refuse?

figure.note: Overlap gained two lengths before the zone; Grey has plenty of water

options: Yes — an inside overlap established from clear astern never entitles a boat to mark-room
Yes — the outside boat decides whether she is able to give room, and her word is final
No — but only because you hailed for room before the overlap began
No — she was able to give mark-room when the overlap began, so the exception in rule 18.2(d) does not help her; she had to give you mark-room
questions.why: Rule 18.2(d) excuses the outside boat only if she has been unable to give mark-room from the time the overlap began; here she could.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port, club championship. You are close-hauled on starboard tack, fetching the mark, and have been on starboard since well before the zone. Yellow, on port, tacks inside the zone right under your bow; her tack is complete, but to avoid her transom you have to luff above close-hauled for a few seconds. Did Yellow break a rule?

figure.note: Yellow tacks here, just under your bow

options: Yes — having passed head to wind in the zone she must not cause you to sail above close-hauled to avoid contact (rule 18.3(a))
Yes — she broke rule 13, because a boat may not tack at all inside the zone of a windward mark
No — once her tack was complete she was the leeward boat and you, to windward, simply had to keep clear
No — a boat that completes her tack clear ahead has right of way, and luffing briefly is no hardship
questions.why: Rule 18.3(a): a boat that passes head to wind in the zone must not cause a boat on starboard since entering it to sail above close-hauled to avoid contact.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port, 15 knots. You are on starboard tack fetching the mark. Red, on port, tacks inside the zone two hull lengths ahead of you and sails on to round the mark without you having to alter course at all. You protest her under rule 18.3 because "you can't tack in the zone". What will the protest committee decide?

figure.note: Red tacks two lengths ahead of you and clears

options: Red is disqualified — she tacked within three hull lengths of a right-of-way boat
Red broke no rule — 18.3 is broken only if the tacking boat makes you sail above close-hauled or fails to give mark-room when you overlap inside; neither happened
Red is penalised but exonerated, because she completed her tack before you reached her
Red is disqualified — a port-tack boat may not pass head to wind inside the zone of a windward mark
questions.why: Rule 18.3 does not forbid tacking in the zone; it imposes obligations (a) and (b) on the boat that tacks, and here neither was breached.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port. Grey, on port tack, tacks inside the zone a little above the layline and ahead of you. You, on starboard since before the zone, sail on and become overlapped to leeward of her, between her and the mark. She bears away to round and squeezes you onto the mark. Who is right?

figure.note: Grey tacks here, above the layline; you come up inside her

options: Grey — she completed her tack clear ahead, so under rule 18.2(a)(2) you had to give her mark-room
You — but only under rule 11, because after her tack she was the windward boat
You — once you became overlapped inside her, Grey, having passed head to wind in the zone, had to give you mark-room (rule 18.3(b))
Grey — the inside boat at a windward mark must be overlapped at the zone, and you were not
questions.why: Rule 18.3(b): a boat that passed head to wind in the zone shall give mark-room if the starboard boat becomes overlapped inside her.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port, crowded Laser fleet. Both you and White came into the zone on port tack; you tacked onto starboard first, then White tacked a length to leeward and ahead of you, and you had to luff above close-hauled to miss her. You protest under rule 18.3. Does it apply?

figure.note: Both of you tacked inside the zone; White tacked last

options: Yes — the boat that tacks last inside the zone always loses under rule 18.3
Yes — White passed head to wind in the zone and made a starboard-tack boat sail above close-hauled
No — rule 18.3 only applies when the starboard boat is a different class
No — 18.3(a) protects only a boat that has been on starboard tack since she entered the zone, and you tacked inside it; rule 18.2 is off too, so 13, 15 and 16 decide
questions.why: Rule 18.3: (a) and (b) apply only if the other boat has been on starboard since entering the zone; 18.2 does not apply between them, so 13 and 15 decide.

questions.q: Unusually, the sailing instructions for this regatta require the windward mark to be left to starboard. You are on port tack fetching it; Blue, on starboard tack, tacks onto port inside the zone just ahead of you and you have to luff above close-hauled to clear her. Which rule, if any, did Blue break?

figure.note: The mark is to be left to starboard; Blue tacks here

options: Not 18.3 — it applies only at a mark to be left to port; between you rules 13, 15 and 18.2 decide, and Blue had to give you room to keep clear when she acquired right of way
Rule 18.2(a)(2) — you were clear ahead at the zone, so she had to give you mark-room
Rule 18.3 — a boat tacking in the zone must not make a boat that was fetching sail above close-hauled
No rule — a mark to be left to starboard switches off the whole of rule 18
questions.why: Rule 18.3 is limited to marks to be left to port; at a starboard rounding the general rules 13, 15, 16 and 18.2 apply.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port. You are on starboard tack fetching the mark; Green tacks from port inside the zone and completes her tack a clear hull length ahead and to leeward of you. You could have held your close-hauled course and passed astern of her comfortably, but you luff above close-hauled "to be safe" and protest her under 18.3. What should the protest committee find?

figure.note: Green has completed her tack a length ahead; no avoiding action was needed

options: No breach — but only because Green hailed before she tacked
No breach — 18.3(a) is broken only when the tacking boat causes you to sail above close-hauled to avoid contact, and no avoiding action was needed
A breach — Green tacked within a hull length of a right-of-way boat, which rule 13 forbids
A breach — any luff above close-hauled by the starboard boat after a tack in the zone penalises the tacking boat
questions.why: Rule 18.3(a): the question is whether the tacking boat caused the starboard boat to sail above close-hauled to avoid contact; an unnecessary luff is not that.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port, 20 knots. You are on starboard tack fetching the mark when Red, on port, throws a tack right in front of you inside the zone. She is still head to wind, sails flapping, when you have to bear away sharply to miss her stern. Which rule did Red break?

figure.note: Red is head to wind, sails flapping, right ahead of you

options: Rule 18.2(a)(1) — she was not overlapped inside you when you reached the zone
No rule — a boat may tack in the zone, and the starboard boat has to allow for it
Rule 13 — she was still tacking when you had to take avoiding action; 18.3 would apply after she had passed head to wind, and 18.2 does not apply between you
Rule 10 — a port-tack boat must keep clear of a starboard-tack boat until she has rounded the mark
questions.why: Rule 13: a boat tacking keeps clear until she is on a close-hauled course; in the zone, 18.3 adds its obligations once she has passed head to wind.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port. Black, on port tack, tacks onto starboard about four hull lengths from the mark, just outside the zone, and ends up clear ahead of you on the starboard layline. She then enters the zone a length ahead of you. Who must give whom room?

figure.note: Black tacked just outside the zone and is clear ahead

options: Nobody — a boat that tacks within five lengths of the mark loses all rights under rule 18
Black must give you mark-room — she tacked in front of a starboard boat that was fetching the mark
Black must keep clear of you all the way round under rule 10, because she was on port when you first met
You must give Black mark-room — she passed head to wind outside the zone and was the first to reach it (18.2(a)(2)); 18.3 is not involved
questions.why: Rule 18.3 applies only to a boat that passes head to wind in the zone; when boats are not overlapped, the first to reach the zone is entitled to mark-room under 18.2(a)(2).

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port, light wind. You are on starboard tack fetching the mark, on starboard since before the zone. Blue tacks from port inside the zone just ahead of you and immediately shouts "Starboard!" as you have to luff above close-hauled to avoid her. Does her hail change anything?

figure.note: Blue has just completed her tack and hails "Starboard!"

options: No — hails do not create rights; having passed head to wind in the zone she must not make you sail above close-hauled to avoid contact (18.3(a))
Yes — the first boat to hail at a mark establishes her right to room
Yes — once she is on starboard and hails it, you are two starboard boats and rule 11 makes you keep clear
No — because a boat may never tack within the zone of a windward mark
questions.why: Rule 18.3(a) binds the boat that passed head to wind in the zone regardless of any hail; a hail is not a rule.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 12 knots. You are running on starboard tack and Grey, on port, is overlapped outside you as you reach the zone, so you have both right of way and mark-room. To round for the beat you must gybe. You sail on past the mark for two lengths before gybing, to get a better angle, holding Grey out wide. She protests. Who is right?

figure.note: You sail two lengths past the mark (dashed) before gybing

options: You — you had right of way under rule 10 and mark-room, so Grey had to keep clear of whatever rounding you chose
Grey — as the inside right-of-way boat that must gybe at the mark to sail her proper course, you may not sail farther from the mark than needed until you gybe (18.4)
Grey — because a starboard-tack boat must gybe before she enters the zone
You — a boat entitled to mark-room may sail a tactical wide-and-tight rounding
questions.why: Rule 18.4: an inside overlapped right-of-way boat that must gybe at the mark sails no farther from it than needed for her proper course until she gybes.

questions.q: Leeward gate, 15 knots. You are running on starboard tack, overlapped inside Red, who is on port, as you reach the zone of the left-hand gate mark. You have right of way and must gybe to round it. You carry on past the gate mark for a length and a half before gybing, and Red has to sail wide to stay clear. Did you break rule 18.4?

figure.note: The right gate mark is about eight lengths to the right, off the picture

options: No — because at a gate rule 18 does not apply at all
Yes — rule 18.4 applies at every mark that must be left to port
No — rule 18.4 does not apply at a gate mark; you were still subject to rule 16.1 when you changed course, but not to the no-farther-than-needed limit
Yes — an inside right-of-way boat that must gybe must gybe as soon as she can at any mark
questions.why: Rule 18.4 (last sentence): the rule does not apply at a gate mark; the inside right-of-way boat remains bound by rule 16.1 when changing course.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port. You are running on port tack, overlapped inside Blue, who is on starboard tack and outside you, as the first of you reaches the zone. Blue claims that under rule 18.4 you must round the mark as tightly as possible. To round, you only have to harden up; no gybe is needed. Does 18.4 limit you?

figure.note: You can round by hardening up; no gybe is needed

options: Yes — every inside boat at a leeward mark must sail no farther from it than needed
No — because Blue, on starboard, has to keep clear of you as the inside boat
Yes — rule 18.4 limits any boat that is overlapped inside when she reaches the zone
No — rule 18.4 applies only to an inside right-of-way boat that must gybe at the mark; you need not gybe and you are the keep-clear boat anyway
questions.why: Rule 18.4 applies only to an inside overlapped right-of-way boat that must gybe to sail her proper course; this inside boat need not gybe.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, Hobie 16s, 12 knots. You and Yellow are both running on starboard tack, overlapped at the zone; you are inside and to leeward, so you have right of way under rule 11 and are entitled to mark-room. You must gybe to round. You keep going a length beyond the mark before gybing, pushing Yellow wide. Is rule 18.4 in play here?

figure.note: Both on starboard; you are inside and to leeward

options: Yes — you are an inside overlapped right-of-way boat that must gybe at the mark, so you may sail no farther from it than your proper course needs until you gybe
No — a leeward boat with right of way under rule 11 may round the mark as she pleases
No — rule 18.4 only applies between boats on opposite tacks
Yes — but only because you hailed Yellow before the gybe
questions.why: Rule 18.4 applies to any inside overlapped right-of-way boat that must gybe at the mark, whether her right of way comes from rule 10 or rule 11.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, both running on port tack. You are inside and to windward of Grey, overlapped at the zone, so Grey must give you mark-room but she has right of way under rule 11. You gybe onto starboard well before the mark to round from the other side, then sail a length past the mark before gybing back. Grey protests you under 18.4. Who is right?

figure.note: Both on port tack; you are inside and to windward

options: Grey — rule 18.4 forbids any inside boat to sail past the mark before gybing
Grey, but not under 18.4 — that rule binds only a right-of-way boat; as the keep-clear boat you simply had no mark-room beyond what a rounding needed, and had to keep clear otherwise
You — once you gybed onto starboard you had right of way under rule 10 and could round how you liked
You — rule 18.4 lets an inside boat choose where she gybes as long as she stays within the zone
questions.why: Rule 18.4 applies only to an inside right-of-way boat; a keep-clear inside boat is confined to her mark-room (18.2(a)(1)) and otherwise keeps clear.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 25 knots and big waves, 36-ft cruiser-racers. You are inside Blue on starboard tack with right of way and must gybe at the mark. You bear away and wait for a flat spot, gybing about a length later than you would in 10 knots, and Blue has to sail a little wider. She protests under 18.4. How should the protest committee look at it?

figure.note: 25 knots and waves; you wait for a flat spot to gybe

options: It must dismiss the protest — rule 18.4 does not apply in winds above 20 knots
It must disqualify you — 18.4 requires the gybe at the earliest possible moment regardless of conditions
By asking what your proper course was in those conditions — 18.4 allows you to sail as far from the mark as your proper course requires, and a safe gybe in 25 knots may well require it
It must disqualify Blue — a boat required to give mark-room may never protest the inside boat
questions.why: Rule 18.4 limits the inside right-of-way boat to what is needed to sail her proper course; proper course depends on the existing conditions.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port, 10 knots. You are close-hauled on port tack below the mark; Red is overlapped with you, to windward and closer to the mark, also on port tack, as the first of you reaches the zone. To round the mark Red must tack onto starboard, and after her tack she would be fetching it. She hails for room to tack. Must you give it?

figure.note: Both on port tack; Red is inside and to windward

options: No — you are the leeward boat with right of way under rule 11, and she must keep clear while tacking under rule 13
Yes — but under rule 20, because the mark is an obstruction and she hailed for room to tack
No — mark-room never includes room to tack; she must wait until you have tacked or passed
Yes — mark-room includes room to tack when the boat is overlapped inside and to windward of the boat required to give mark-room and would be fetching the mark after her tack
questions.why: Definition Mark-Room: it includes room to tack when the boat is inside and to windward of the giving boat and would be fetching the mark after her tack.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port, 8 knots. You are close-hauled on port tack with Green overlapped to windward of you and nearer the mark as you enter the zone, both on port. Green hails for room to tack, but she is so far below the mark that even after tacking she would not lay it and would need another tack. Must you give her room to tack now?

figure.note: Green is well below the layline; a tack now would not fetch the mark

options: No — mark-room includes room to tack only if she would be fetching the mark after her tack; as she would not, her hail gives her nothing under rule 18
Yes — under rule 20, because any boat may hail for room to tack when a mark is near
Yes — an inside windward boat in the zone is always entitled to room to tack
No — because a leeward boat never has to give room to a windward boat
questions.why: Definition Mark-Room: room to tack is included only when the inside windward boat would be fetching the mark after her tack.
questions.ref: RRS definition Mark-Room, RRS definition Fetching

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port, 6 knots. You and Blue are close-hauled on starboard tack, overlapped at the zone; you are inside and to leeward, Blue outside and to windward. You are not quite laying the mark, so at the last moment you luff head to wind to shoot it, and Blue has to luff with you. Blue protests under rule 16.1. Who is right?

figure.note: You luff head to wind to shoot the mark; Blue is outside and to windward

options: Blue — luffing head to wind in the zone is a tack, and under rule 13 you had to keep clear of her
You — Blue had to give you mark-room, which includes room to round the mark; shooting it head to wind is part of that rounding, and you did not pass head to wind
You — but only because you hailed "Shooting!" before you luffed
Blue — a leeward boat may not luff above close-hauled when another boat is within a hull length
questions.why: Mark-room is room to round the mark; a luff to head to wind without passing it is within it, and rule 43.1(b) exonerates a breach of 16.1 inside that room.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, both on port tack. Grey gave you, the inside windward boat, room to reach the mark and round it, but as soon as your bow was past the mark — with the mark still alongside your cockpit — she luffed hard and you had to luff into the mark's side to avoid her. Grey says mark-room ended when you reached the mark. Did it?

figure.note: The mark is still alongside you when Grey luffs

options: Yes — mark-room is only room to reach the mark; the rounding itself is covered by rule 11
No — because mark-room always continues for three hull lengths after the mark
No — mark-room is room to sail to the mark, round or pass it on the required side and leave it astern; Grey luffed before you had left it astern
Yes — mark-room ends the moment any part of the inside boat passes the mark
questions.why: Definition Mark-Room (2025): room to sail to the mark, round or pass it on the required side and leave it astern; rule 18 ends only when that has been given.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 24 knots and short steep waves, 29ers. You are outside and must give Red mark-room. You leave her the gap you would in 10 knots — barely a boat width — and Red, rounding with her spinnaker still coming down, broaches and hits you. Red says the room was not enough for the conditions. Is she right?

figure.note: 24 knots, steep waves; you leave Red a 10-knot gap

options: No — room is a fixed amount, roughly one boat width, whatever the weather
Yes — because the inside boat always decides how much room she needs
No — a boat that broaches has lost control and has broken rule 22, so she cannot claim room
Yes — room is the space a boat needs in the existing conditions to manoeuvre promptly in a seamanlike way; in 24 knots and waves that is more than a boat width
questions.why: Definition Room: the space needed in the existing conditions, including to comply with Part 2 and rule 31, while manoeuvring promptly in a seamanlike way.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 12 knots. You are outside Blue and must give her mark-room. You give her just enough space to get round without touching you, but her rounding is so tight that her quarter brushes the mark. You tell her she must do a one-turn penalty. Who is right?

figure.note: Blue's quarter brushes the mark in the gap you left

options: Blue — mark-room includes room to comply with rule 31, so you did not give enough; she is exonerated for touching the mark and you broke rule 18.2(a)(1)
Nobody — touching a mark while being given mark-room is simply not a breach of rule 31
You — room is only space to avoid the other boat; keeping off the mark is the inside boat's own problem
You — a boat that touches a mark must take a one-turn penalty whatever the reason
questions.why: Definition Room includes space to comply with rule 31; a boat forced to touch the mark while sailing within her mark-room is exonerated (43.1(b)).

questions.q: Handicap race, leeward mark to be left to port. Your boat is 7.5 m long; Black, a 12 m cruiser-racer, is approaching the mark close behind you. Black's crew shout that you are "already in their zone" at about 30 metres from the mark. How big is the zone between the two of you?

figure.note: The circle is three of YOUR hull lengths while you are nearer

options: Three hull lengths of the boat astern, because she is the one who must give room
Three hull lengths of the boat nearer the mark — while you are nearer, 22.5 m; Black's longer hull does not enlarge it
A fixed 50 metres at every mark, whatever the boats' lengths
Three hull lengths of the longer boat — 36 m, so you are already in it
questions.why: Definition Zone: the area within three hull lengths of the boat nearer to the mark; a boat is in the zone when any part of her hull is in it.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port, 470s. You are on the starboard layline, clear ahead of Red when you reach the zone. Red, directly astern, luffs to come up between you and the mark and calls "Inside!" as she gets an overlap. Is she entitled to room?

figure.note: Red luffs to get inside after you entered the zone clear ahead

options: Yes — as soon as she becomes the leeward boat she has right of way and you must keep clear
Yes — the boat nearer the mark is inside and the inside boat always gets mark-room
No — you were clear ahead when you reached the zone, so Red must give you mark-room; her later inside overlap changes nothing
No — but only because she luffed instead of bearing away
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(2): when the boats are not overlapped as the first reaches the zone, the boat that has not reached it must give the other mark-room.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, sportsboats with long bowsprits, 10 knots. You are overlapped inside Blue. Your bowsprit, with the gennaker still up, crosses the three-length circle a second before Blue's hull does, but your hull is still outside it at that moment. Blue says that she, not you, reached the zone first. Who is right?

figure.note: Your bowsprit is over the line of the zone; your hull is not yet

options: You — the bowsprit is part of the hull once it is fixed to the boat
Neither — the zone is measured from the mast, not from the bow
You — any part of the boat or her equipment in normal position counts for the zone
Blue — a boat is in the zone when any part of her hull is in it; bowsprits and sails do not count
questions.why: Definition Zone: a boat is in the zone when any part of her hull is in the zone; equipment such as a bowsprit does not count.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port, 12 knots. You and Blue are both close-hauled on starboard tack, overlapped as the first of you reaches the zone. Blue is to leeward of you and a little nearer the mark. Which of you is the inside boat, and what follows?

figure.note: Both on starboard; Blue is to leeward and nearer the mark

options: Blue — at a port rounding approached on starboard tack the mark is on the leeward side, so Blue is inside; you give her mark-room and keep clear under rule 11
You — at a windward mark the windward boat is always the inside boat, so Blue must give you mark-room
Neither — boats on the same tack at a windward mark are governed only by rule 11, not by rule 18
Blue — but as the leeward boat she must give you, the windward boat, room to round the mark
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(1): overlapped at the zone, the outside boat gives mark-room; approaching a port rounding on starboard the inside boat is the leeward one.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port, Optimists in a dying breeze. You enter the zone clear ahead of Red, both on starboard tack, but you realise you cannot lay the mark and tack onto port to take two more hitches. Red, still on starboard, has to bear away to avoid you as you come round and complain that she owed you mark-room. Who is right?

figure.note: You are tacking onto port inside the zone; Red is still on starboard

options: You — Red had to give you room to tack because the mark was an obstruction
Red — when you passed head to wind your entitlement under 18.2(a) ended (18.2(b)); on opposite tacks on a beat rule 18 is off and you had to keep clear under 13, then 10
You — a boat clear ahead at the zone keeps her mark-room until she has rounded the mark, whatever she does
Red — because a boat may never tack inside the zone of a windward mark
questions.why: Rule 18.2(b): 18.2(a) no longer applies once the entitled boat passes head to wind; thereafter 18.1(a)(1) switches rule 18 off and rules 13 and 10 govern.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 18 knots. You enter the zone clear ahead of Grey, so she owes you mark-room, but your spinnaker wraps, you lose control, sail right out of the zone to leeward and come back. When you re-enter you are overlapped with Grey — and now you are the outside boat. Who owes whom room at the mark now?

figure.note: You left the zone with a wrapped spinnaker (dashed) and are coming back outside Grey

options: Grey owes you room — but only because you left the zone involuntarily
Grey still owes you mark-room — a boat clear ahead at the zone keeps her entitlement until she has rounded
You owe Grey mark-room — your entitlement under 18.2(a) ended when you left the zone (18.2(b)); now that 18.2(a) does not apply and you are overlapped, the outside boat gives room (18.2(c))
Nobody owes anybody room — once a boat leaves the zone rule 18 is finished between those boats for that mark
questions.why: Rule 18.2(b) ends 18.2(a) when the entitled boat leaves the zone; rule 18.2(c) then applies to boats overlapped at the mark — the outside boat gives mark-room.

questions.q: Downwind finish at a lake regatta, the line between a pin and the committee boat. You and Red are running on starboard tack towards the pin end, overlapped, you inside (nearer the pin), when the first of you reaches the zone of the pin. Red, to leeward, holds her course and you cannot pass the pin on the line side without hitting her. Who is right?

figure.note: Running finish; you are the inside boat at the pin

options: Red — rule 18 does not apply at the ends of a starting or finishing line surrounded by navigable water
Red — the leeward boat has right of way under rule 11 and need not give room to a windward boat at the finish
You — but only because at the finish the rules of Part 2 no longer apply
You — a finishing mark is an ordinary mark under rule 18, so Red, outside at the zone, must give you mark-room even though she has right of way
questions.why: The Section C exception covers only starting marks; at a finishing mark rule 18.2(a)(1) applies and the outside boat gives mark-room.
questions.ref: RRS 18.2(a)(1), RRS Part 2 Section C preamble

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, both on port tack. You are inside and overlapped with Yellow when she reaches the zone. Rounding, Yellow closes the gap, your hulls touch and you are pushed within a hand's width of the mark; no damage. Yellow protests you for the contact. What should the protest committee decide?

figure.note: Yellow closes the gap; hulls touch, no damage

options: Yellow broke rule 18.2(a)(1) and rule 14; you are exonerated for the contact under 43.1(c) because you were sailing within your mark-room and there was no damage
You are penalised — the windward boat must keep clear under rule 11 even while being given mark-room
Both boats are penalised — rule 14 applies to both and there was contact
Nobody is penalised — contact without damage is never a breach of any rule
questions.why: Rule 43.1(c): a boat sailing within the mark-room she is entitled to is exonerated for breaking rule 14 when the contact causes no damage or injury.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, Split, 12 knots. Blue was inside you at the zone and you gave her mark-room; she rounded tight and is now close-hauled a length ahead and to windward of you, still overlapped. You start to luff her. Blue insists that while you remain overlapped she is entitled to room to sail her proper course. Is she?

figure.note: Blue has been given mark-room and is now to windward of you

options: Yes — rule 18.2(c)(2) gives a boat entitled to mark-room room to sail her proper course while the boats remain overlapped
No — the old provision giving the inside boat room for her proper course is gone; once mark-room has been given rule 18 no longer applies, and you may luff under rule 11 (subject to 16.1)
No — but only because she is more than a hull length ahead of you
Yes — rule 17 forbids you to sail above your proper course while overlapped to leeward of her
questions.why: Rule 18.1(b): rule 18 no longer applies once mark-room has been given; rule 17 does not limit a leeward boat whose overlap did not begin from clear astern.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, three boats running on port tack. You are the outside boat; Grey is overlapped between you and the mark; White is inside Grey and overlapped with her, but White's bow is a metre behind your transom. All three are in this position when the first boat reaches the zone. Do you owe White mark-room?

figure.note: White's bow is behind your transom, but Grey overlaps you both

options: Yes — but only because White is on the same tack as you
No — you owe room only to the boat you are directly overlapped with, Grey
Yes — Grey, the intervening boat, is overlapped with both of you, so you and White are overlapped too, and you must give room to both inside boats
No — White is clear astern of you, so she must give you mark-room under 18.2(a)(2)
questions.why: Definition Overlap: boats are overlapped if a boat between them overlaps both; rule 18.2(a)(1) then makes the outside boat give room to both.
questions.ref: RRS definition Clear Astern and Clear Ahead; Overlap, RRS 18.2(a)(1)

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 9 knots. You are overlapped inside Black when she reaches the zone, but you say nothing. Black shouts "No room, you didn't hail!" and rounds tight on you. Does rule 18 require a hail for you to be entitled to mark-room?

figure.note: You are inside and overlapped at the zone; nobody has hailed

options: Yes — the first boat to hail at a mark establishes her rights, and Black hailed first
No — but a hail would also have given you the right to a tactical wide-and-tight rounding
Yes — the inside boat must hail "Room" before the first boat reaches the zone, otherwise she gets none
No — rule 18 has no hailing requirement; your entitlement depends on the positions when the first boat reached the zone, so Black must give you mark-room
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(1) turns on the overlap when the first boat reaches the zone; unlike rule 20, rule 18 has no hail requirement.

questions.q: Finish of a Wednesday race, the line between the committee boat and a pin, the last leg a beat. You are on port tack approaching the committee boat end; Green is on starboard tack, also heading for the committee boat end, and you are nearer the committee boat than she is. You hail for mark-room. What are your rights at the committee boat?

figure.note: Beat to the finish; the committee boat is at the right-hand end

options: None under rule 18 — you are on opposite tacks on a beat to windward, so rule 18 does not apply and you must keep clear of Green under rule 10
Green must keep clear because at the finish the boat nearer the committee boat has priority
Green must give you mark-room because you are the inside boat at a finishing mark
Green must give you room because the committee boat is an obstruction under rule 19
questions.why: Rule 18.1(a)(1): rule 18 does not apply between boats on opposite tacks on a beat to windward, even at a finishing mark; rule 10 governs.

questions.q: Leeward gate, 14 knots. You and White are running on starboard tack, overlapped, both heading for the right-hand gate mark, which is rounded to starboard. You are to leeward of White and have right of way under rule 11; White is to windward and nearer the right-hand mark. At that gate mark, who is inside and what do you owe?

figure.note: The left gate mark is about eight lengths to the left, off the picture

options: Nobody is inside — rule 18 does not apply at gate marks, only rule 11
White is inside — at the right-hand mark the boat nearer it is inside, so when the first of you reaches its zone you, outside, must give her mark-room despite your right of way
White is inside, but as the windward boat she must still keep clear and cannot claim room
You are inside — the leeward boat is always the inside boat at a leeward gate
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(1): the inside boat is the one between the other and the mark; at the right-hand gate mark that is the boat nearer it, whatever her right of way.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 15 knots, a tight pack. You are coming up fast on Red's inside and honestly cannot tell whether your bow was level with her transom when her bow reached the zone — it was a matter of centimetres. What should you do?

figure.note: Was your bow level with Red's transom at the zone? Nobody is sure

options: Take the room — in a doubtful case the benefit goes to the inside boat
Take the room and offer to do a one-turn penalty afterwards if Red objects
Treat yourself as not overlapped and give Red mark-room — if there is reasonable doubt that an overlap was obtained in time, it is presumed that it was not
Hail "Overlap!" loudly; if Red does not answer at once the overlap is deemed established
questions.why: Rule 18.2(e): if there is reasonable doubt that a boat obtained or broke an overlap in time, it is presumed that she did not.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, both on starboard tack. You are the inside boat entitled to mark-room. Blue, outside, gives you less room than she should, but you can see it coming and could easily have slowed down; instead you hold on and your bow punches a hole in her topsides. What is your position?

figure.note: You could have avoided the contact; there is damage

options: Only Blue is penalised — the boat that fails to give mark-room carries all the blame for any contact
You broke no rule — a boat entitled to mark-room never has to avoid the boat that owes her room
You are exonerated under 43.1(b) because you were sailing within your mark-room
You broke rule 14 and are not exonerated — a boat entitled to mark-room is excused a breach of rule 14 only if there is no damage or injury
questions.why: Rule 14 and 43.1(c): a boat entitled to mark-room must still avoid contact if reasonably possible and is exonerated only when there is no damage or injury.

questions.q: You were over the line at the pin end and are returning to start: you have come round the pin and are now on port tack just below the line, with Grey, starting correctly on starboard tack, bearing down on the pin and you between her and it. You hail for room at the mark. What are your rights?

figure.note: You are returning to restart round the pin; Grey is starting

options: None — the pin is a starting mark surrounded by navigable water and you are still approaching it to start, so rule 18 is off; you must keep clear under rules 10 and 21
Grey must keep clear of you because a boat returning to start has priority at the line
Grey must give you room under rule 19 because the pin is an obstruction
Grey must give you mark-room because you are the inside boat at the pin
questions.why: Section C preamble: no rule 18 at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water while approaching it to start; a returning boat also keeps clear under rule 21.
questions.ref: RRS Part 2 Section C preamble, RRS 21, RRS 10

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, club race. Blue, an older sailor, says you had to be overlapped "at two lengths" to claim room, and since you got your inside overlap at two and a half lengths from the mark you were in time. Where in fact does the zone begin?
options: Wherever the sailing instructions say; the rule book itself sets no fixed distance
Three hull lengths from the mark — the two-length zone is the pre-2009 rule; an overlap at two and a half lengths was obtained after the zone had been reached
Four hull lengths, since the 2025 rules extended it to protect the inside boat
Two hull lengths — the zone is two lengths of the boat nearer the mark, as it has always been
questions.why: Definition Zone: the area within three hull lengths of the boat nearer the mark; an overlap gained inside it is too late under 18.2(a).

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 12 knots. You are inside Red at the zone. Red refuses room, saying a mark is an obstruction and under rule 19 the right-of-way boat (she is to leeward) chooses which side to pass. Is she right?

figure.note: Red says the mark is an obstruction and she chooses the side

options: Yes — a mark is an obstruction, and at an obstruction the right-of-way boat chooses the side
Yes — rules 18 and 19 both apply, and the right-of-way boat picks whichever suits her
No — rule 19 does not apply at an obstruction that is also a mark the boats must leave on the same side; rule 18 governs, and she must give you mark-room
No — because a buoy is never an obstruction, only solid objects are
questions.why: Rule 19.1: rule 19 does not apply at an obstruction that is also a mark the boats are required to leave on the same side; rule 18 applies instead.

questions.q: Handicap race, leeward mark to be left to port. You are in a 24-ft boat, overlapped inside Black, a 45-ft racer, when she reaches the zone. Her helmsman shouts that a boat your size has to keep out of the way of a big boat at a mark. Who is right?

figure.note: Overlapped at the zone; you are the smaller boat, inside

options: Black — a larger boat is harder to manoeuvre and so is treated as an obstruction
You — but only because the smaller boat always has right of way
Black — in a handicap fleet the boat with the higher rating has priority at marks
You — mark-room depends only on the positions at the zone, not on size or speed; Black must give you mark-room
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(1) makes the outside boat at the zone give mark-room; there is no rule giving a larger or faster boat priority.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 16 knots. You are overlapped inside Yellow when she reaches the zone. In the last length Yellow accelerates on a wave, gets her transom just ahead of your bow, rounds tight and you have to brake hard behind her. She says that as she was clear ahead at the mark she owed you nothing. Is she right?

figure.note: Overlapped at the zone; Yellow surfs clear ahead in the last length

options: No — a boat required to give mark-room must keep doing so even if the overlap is later broken; Yellow had to leave you room to round
Yes — once she broke the overlap you were clear astern and had to keep clear under rule 12
No — but only because the overlap was broken inside the last hull length
Yes — rule 18 is applied at the mark itself, and there she was clear ahead
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a): a boat required to give mark-room continues to do so as long as the rule applies, even if later an overlap is broken.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port, 5 knots and a big swell. Blue, inside and to leeward of you when you reached the zone, both on starboard, stalls almost head to wind at the mark with no steerage way. There is a gap between her and the mark, and you steer into it to round ahead of her. Were you allowed to?

figure.note: Blue is stalled near the mark; you steer for the gap inside her

options: Yes — a boat that has stopped at a mark has given up her mark-room and others may pass inside
No — Blue was entitled to mark-room and still is; sailing between her and the mark denies her room to round, and as the windward boat you also had to keep clear
Yes — rule 18 only applies to boats that are moving; a stationary boat is an obstruction
No — but only because you did not hail before going through the gap
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(1): the outside boat gives mark-room for as long as the rule applies; a slow or stalled inside boat remains entitled to room to round the mark.

questions.q: Two classes share a leeward mark, both leaving it to port. You, in a Laser, are overlapped inside a 29er from the other fleet when the first of you reaches the zone; the 29er says rule 18 is only between boats in the same race. Does rule 18 apply between you?

figure.note: Different classes, same mark, both leaving it to port

options: Yes — but only if the sailing instructions say the fleets share the rules of Part 2
No — the faster class always has priority at shared marks
Yes — rule 18 applies between boats racing that are required to leave the mark on the same side, whatever their class or fleet; the 29er must give you mark-room
No — rule 18 applies only between boats in the same race and class
questions.why: Rule 18.1(a): rule 18 applies between boats required to leave the mark on the same side when one is in the zone; Part 2 applies between all boats racing.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 12 knots. You are running on port tack, overlapped inside Blue, who is on starboard tack and outside you, when she reaches the zone. Blue hails "Starboard!" and holds her course for the mark. What does Blue owe you, and what do you owe her?

figure.note: Blue on starboard outside; you on port inside

options: She must give you room only after you gybe onto starboard
She must keep clear of you — the inside boat at a mark has right of way over the outside boat
Nothing on her side — a starboard-tack boat never has to give room to a port-tack boat
Blue must give you mark-room although she has right of way under rule 10; you must keep clear of her, but you are exonerated if you break rule 10 while sailing within your mark-room
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(1) makes the outside right-of-way boat give mark-room; rule 43.1(b) exonerates the inside boat for breaking rule 10 within that room.

questions.q: River race, leeward mark to be left to port, two knots of current setting the fleet towards the mark. You are outside Grey and must give her mark-room. You leave her the room you would in slack water; the current sets her down and she has to push off the mark with her hand. Grey says you did not give her enough room. Is she right?

figure.note: Two knots of current setting the boats onto the mark

options: Yes — room is the space needed in the existing conditions, and the current is one of them; she is exonerated for touching the mark and you broke 18.2(a)(1)
No — a boat set onto a mark by current has simply misjudged it and must take a one-turn penalty
No — the room owed is measured in still water; current is the inside boat's problem
Yes — but Grey must still take a one-turn penalty for touching the mark
questions.why: Definition Room: the space needed in the existing conditions, including to comply with rule 31; the outside boat must allow for the current.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 10 knots. Blue is overlapped inside you five hull lengths from the mark and starts demanding room at once, steering towards you and telling you to go wide now. From what moment does your obligation to give her mark-room begin?

figure.note: Blue demands room well before the zone

options: From the moment the overlap is established, however far from the mark
From the moment the first of you reaches the zone — until then only the ordinary right-of-way rules apply between you
From the moment the inside boat hails for room
From five hull lengths, the distance at which boats must settle their positions for the mark
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a): the obligation is fixed when the first boat reaches the zone and applies thereafter; before that rules 10–12 govern.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port, 10 knots. You and Red are close-hauled on port tack, overlapped at the zone, you inside and to windward, and after a tack you would fetch the mark, so your mark-room includes room to tack. You tack; while you are between head to wind and close-hauled Red has to bear away a little to avoid you. She protests under rule 13. What is the result?

figure.note: You are tacking within your mark-room; Red is to leeward

options: Red is disqualified — a boat that must give mark-room may not protest the boat she owes it to
You are disqualified — rule 13 has no exceptions, and a tacking boat always keeps clear
You broke rule 13 but are exonerated — you were sailing within the mark-room you were entitled to, and rule 43.1(b) covers a breach of a Section A rule in that situation
Nobody broke a rule — rule 13 does not apply inside the zone of a windward mark
questions.why: Rule 43.1(b): a boat sailing within the mark-room she is entitled to is exonerated for breaking a Section A rule (here 13) with the boat owing that room.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 20 knots. You enter the zone clear ahead of Blue, a faster Melges 24. She overtakes you on the outside, gets clear ahead a length before the mark, then cuts across your bow to round tight and you have to bear away to miss her transom. Blue says that being clear ahead at the mark she owed you nothing. Is she right?

figure.note: Blue overtook outside and now cuts across your bow (dashed)

options: Yes — a boat that becomes clear ahead before the mark may round as she likes, and you keep clear under rule 12
No — but only because she overtook you to windward rather than to leeward
Yes — rule 18 is judged at the mark, not at the zone, and there she was ahead
No — she was astern when you reached the zone, so she must give you mark-room for as long as the rule applies; cutting across your course to the mark denied it
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(2) and its last paragraph: the boat that had not reached the zone gives mark-room thereafter, even if the positions later change.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 12 knots. You are running on port tack towards the mark. Red, behind you, gybes onto starboard and comes in from your port side so that when the first of you reaches the zone she is overlapped with you and inside. Who gives room, and who has right of way?

figure.note: Red gybed onto starboard and is overlapped inside at the zone

options: You give Red mark-room — the boats are overlapped for rule 18 although on opposite tacks — and she also has right of way under rule 10
Red gives you room — a boat that gybes to get inside has gained her overlap unfairly
Nobody gives room — boats on opposite tacks cannot be overlapped, so rule 18 is off and rule 10 alone applies
You give Red mark-room, but she must keep clear of you because you were ahead before she gybed
questions.why: Definition Overlap applies to opposite tacks when rule 18 applies, as on a run; 18.2(a)(1) makes the outside boat give mark-room, and rule 10 also applies.
questions.ref: RRS 18.2(a)(1), RRS 10, RRS definition Clear Astern and Clear Ahead; Overlap
