questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port, 12 knots. You and Blue are close-hauled on port tack, overlapped, about six hull lengths from the mark. Blue, to leeward, luffs you slowly. You protest that she may not do that "this close to the mark". Which rules apply between you here?

figure.note: Six lengths from the mark, outside the zone

options: Rule 18.3 — a boat may not make another sail above close-hauled near a windward mark
Rules 11 and 16.1 only — neither of you is in the zone yet, so rule 18 does not apply and the leeward boat may luff, giving you room to keep clear
No rule — before the zone anything goes between boats on the same tack
Rule 18 — within ten hull lengths of a mark the inside boat is protected from luffing
questions.why: Rule 18.1(a): rule 18 applies only when at least one boat is in the zone; before that rules 11 and 16.1 govern the luff.

questions.q: This leeward mark must be left to starboard. You are running on port tack, overlapped inside Grey, who is on starboard tack and outside you, as the first of you reaches the zone; to round you must gybe. You sail on past the mark for a length and a half before gybing and Grey has to sail wide. Grey protests under 18.4. Does the rule apply to a starboard rounding?

figure.note: The mark is to be left to starboard; you are inside on port tack

options: No — rule 18.4 applies only at marks to be left to port, so a starboard rounding is outside it
Yes — rule 18.4 applies at every mark, and you broke it by sailing past the mark before gybing
Yes, at any mark — but it binds only an inside right-of-way boat; on port tack you keep clear of Grey under rule 10, so it does not limit you here
No — because at a starboard rounding the outside boat always keeps clear of the inside boat
questions.why: Rule 18.4 binds an inside overlapped right-of-way boat; an inside port-tack boat is not the right-of-way boat (rule 10), so the rule does not apply to her.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 14 knots. You are overlapped inside Black when she reaches the zone, but instead of heading for the mark you luff up for clear air, sailing a course two lengths wide of it, and Black has to go up with you. Then you bear away for the mark. Black protests. Was all of that within your mark-room?

figure.note: You luff away from the mark for clear air (dashed), then come back

options: Yes — mark-room includes room to sail your proper course, and clear air was your proper course
No — because mark-room only begins one hull length from the mark
Yes — a boat entitled to mark-room may sail any course she likes inside the zone
No — mark-room is room to sail to the mark when your proper course is to sail close to it, and then to round it; sailing high for clear air was not that, and rule 11 applied
questions.why: Definition Mark-Room: room to sail to the mark when her proper course is to sail close to it; beyond that the inside windward boat keeps clear under rule 11.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port, 10 knots. You are on port tack, five hull lengths from the mark, and duck Red, who is on starboard, then tack to leeward of her a length and a half astern. Red hails that you "can't tack inside the zone". Is rule 18 involved at all?

figure.note: You tack five lengths from the mark, outside the zone

options: No — nobody is in the zone yet, so rule 18 does not apply; rules 10 and 13 covered your duck and tack, and now rule 12 applies
No — but only because Red hailed instead of protesting
Yes — rule 18.3 forbids tacking within five lengths of a windward mark
Yes — the moment you tack near a mark the zone is deemed to begin
questions.why: Rule 18.1(a): rule 18 applies only once a boat is in the zone — three hull lengths; outside it the Section A rules govern.

questions.q: The race committee shortens the course and finishes you at the leeward mark: flag S on a committee vessel beside the mark, the line between the two. You are overlapped inside Yellow when the first of you reaches the zone; Yellow says that at a finish the mark is no longer a rounding mark and rule 18 is off. Is she right?

figure.note: Shortened course: the finishing line runs from the mark to the S-flag vessel

options: Yes — when a course is shortened Part 2 ceases to apply at the shortened finish
No — the mark is now a finishing mark that you must leave on the required side, and rule 18 applies; Yellow must give you mark-room
No — but only because the committee vessel is an obstruction under rule 19
Yes — rule 18 applies only at rounding marks, not at the ends of a finishing line
questions.why: Rule 18.1(a) applies at any mark the boats must leave on the same side; the Section C exception is only for starting marks, not finishing ones.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, both on port tack. You enter the zone clear ahead of Grey. Just before the mark Grey establishes an overlap to leeward of you, between you and the mark, and as the new leeward boat starts luffing you away from the mark. She says rule 11 now gives her right of way. Who is right?

figure.note: Grey came up from astern on your leeward side and is luffing you off the mark

options: You — a boat clear ahead at the zone keeps right of way over any boat that comes up from astern
Grey — the inside boat at the mark is always entitled to round first
You — Grey may be the right-of-way boat under rule 11, but she must still give you mark-room (18.2(a)(2)); luffing you off the mark denies it, and rule 15 also required her to give you room at first
Grey — once she is the leeward boat, rule 11 overrides rule 18 and you must keep clear wherever she sends you
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(2): the boat astern at the zone must give mark-room even after acquiring right of way under rule 11; rule 15 adds the initial room to keep clear.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 18 knots. You are outside Blue and owe her mark-room. Blue's crew fumble the spinnaker drop, the sail goes in the water and she rounds extremely wide, far wider than a normal rounding needs, and brushes your bow. She says you failed to give her mark-room. What is the right analysis?

figure.note: Blue's spinnaker is in the water; she rounds far wider than normal

options: You are entirely in the clear — a boat that drops her spinnaker in the water has broken rule 22 and lost all rights
Blue is right — in 18 knots any amount of room the inside boat uses is seamanlike
Blue is right — the inside boat decides how much room she needs, and the outside boat must give it
Room is the space needed for a seamanlike rounding in the conditions; the extra width caused by her own mishandling is not within it — but you still had to try to avoid contact under rule 14
questions.why: Definition Room: the space needed to manoeuvre promptly in a seamanlike way; an unseamanlike rounding is not within it, but rule 14 still applies.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 11 knots. You are running on port tack and enter the zone clear ahead of Red, who is running on starboard tack directly astern of you. Red hails "Starboard!" and demands that you leave her room at the mark. Who gives room to whom?

figure.note: Red is directly astern, on the other tack, when you reach the zone

options: Red gives you mark-room — the terms clear ahead and clear astern apply between opposite-tack boats when rule 18 applies, and you were clear ahead at the zone
Nobody — on opposite tacks the terms clear ahead and clear astern do not apply, so rule 18 cannot be applied
Red gives you room, but only once she gybes onto port tack
You give Red room — a starboard-tack boat is always entitled to room from a port-tack boat at a mark
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(2): the boat astern at the zone gives mark-room; the definition applies clear ahead and clear astern to opposite tacks when rule 18 applies.
questions.ref: RRS 18.2(a)(2), RRS definition Clear Astern and Clear Ahead; Overlap

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 13 knots. You are inside and overlapped with Green when the first of you reaches the zone, but you are two hull lengths wide of the mark's track while Green is sailing straight at it. You bear away towards the mark and Green has to go up to let you in. Green says she only had to give room where you were, not where you wanted to go. Is she right?

figure.note: You are inside but wide; you bear away to sail to the mark

options: Yes — mark-room only covers the rounding itself; the approach is governed by rule 11 alone
No — mark-room is room to sail to the mark when your proper course is to sail close to it, so Green must give you room to converge on the mark, not only room where you are
Yes — an inside boat more than a length from the mark's track is not inside at all
No — because an inside boat may sail any course she likes once in the zone
questions.why: Definition Mark-Room: room to sail to the mark when her proper course is to sail close to it; the outside boat gives room for that approach.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 10 knots. You are inside White at the zone and she gives you a generous two boat widths of room. You misjudge your own turn and your transom clips the mark. You claim exoneration because you were sailing within your mark-room. Are you right?

figure.note: White left you two boat widths; your transom still clips the mark

options: Yes — a boat entitled to mark-room is never penalised for touching the mark while she rounds it
No — and the penalty for touching a mark while being given mark-room is two turns, not one
No — 43.1(b) exonerates only a breach caused by the boat owing you room; with enough room given, touching the mark was your own error and you owe a one-turn penalty
Yes — the outside boat is always responsible for keeping the inside boat off the mark, so White is penalised
questions.why: Rule 43.1(b) exonerates a boat only when, within her mark-room, she breaks a rule because of the boat owing it; otherwise rule 31 and a one-turn penalty apply.

questions.q: Leeward gate, 15 knots. You round the right-hand gate mark to starboard and come out close-hauled on starboard tack. Blue rounded the left-hand mark to port at the same moment and comes out close-hauled on port tack; you converge a few lengths after the gate. Blue says that as she was "inside at the gate" she has priority. Who must keep clear?

figure.note: Blue rounded the left mark (off the picture); you are now converging on opposite tacks

options: Nobody — boats leaving a gate on opposite tacks may hold their courses until one tacks
You — the boat that rounds the left-hand gate mark always has priority after the gate
You — Blue was the inside boat at her gate mark and keeps mark-room until the boats separate
Blue — rule 18 never applied between you, since you were rounding different marks; after the gate you are boats on opposite tacks and rule 10 makes her keep clear
questions.why: Rule 18.1(a) applies between boats required to leave the same mark on the same side; after rounding different gate marks rule 10 governs the convergence.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, both on port tack, 12 knots. Black enters the zone clear ahead of you and deliberately sails wide of the mark to make a tactical rounding. You dive into the gap between her and the mark; as she turns back in to round tight she closes the gap and you have to brake to avoid her stern. You protest. Who is right?

figure.note: Black's wide-and-tight rounding (dashed); you dive into the gap

options: Black — she was entitled to mark-room and you had to give it; she may sail a wide-and-tight rounding and you went inside at your own risk, subject only to her rule 16.1 obligation
You — once Black sailed wide she abandoned her mark-room and the gap belonged to you
Black — because a boat clear ahead has right of way over a boat astern in all circumstances
You — a boat entitled to mark-room must sail directly to the mark and may not sail wide
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(2): the boat astern at the zone gives mark-room; a wide rounding does not forfeit it, and the boat astern enters the gap at her own risk.

questions.q: Championship course: the windward mark is a race committee boat that the sailing instructions require you to leave to port. You are overlapped inside Blue, both on starboard, when she reaches the zone. Blue refuses room, saying mark-room is for buoys and a vessel is an obstruction, not a mark. Is she right?

figure.note: The windward mark is a committee vessel, to be left to port

options: Yes — a vessel can only be a starting or finishing mark, never a rounding mark
No — an object the sailing instructions require a boat to leave on a specified side is a mark, so rule 18 applies and Blue must give you mark-room
No — but only because the committee boat is anchored
Yes — a committee boat is an obstruction, so rule 19 applies and the right-of-way boat chooses the side
questions.why: Definition Mark: an object the sailing instructions require a boat to leave on a specified side; rule 18.2(a)(1) then applies.

questions.q: Second reach of a triangle, port tack, 14 knots, approaching the leeward mark to be left to port — so the mark is on your windward side. You are the leeward boat with right of way under rule 11; Red is overlapped to windward of you, between you and the mark, when the first of you reaches the zone. Must you give her room?

figure.note: Port-tack reach; the mark is to windward, Red is inside

options: Yes — but only if she hails "Room" before you reach the zone
No — the leeward boat has right of way and the windward boat must keep clear all the way round the mark
Yes — Red is the inside boat, so you, the outside boat, must give her mark-room although you have right of way
No — on a reaching leg rule 18 does not apply and rule 11 alone decides
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(1): overlapped when the first boat reaches the zone — the outside boat gives mark-room, whatever her right of way under rule 11.

questions.q: Handicap race, leeward mark to be left to port. Your 24-footer is clear astern of Grey, a 36-footer, as you both approach the mark. You get an inside overlap on her about 25 metres from the mark and hail for room. Grey says you were too late. Were you?

figure.note: Grey, nearer the mark, is 36 ft; the zone is three of HER lengths

options: No — in a handicap fleet the zone is always measured by the smallest boat in the race
Yes — but only because the zone in a handicap race is a fixed 50 metres from the mark
No — the zone is three of your own hull lengths, about 22 m, so an overlap at 25 m was in time
Yes — the zone is three hull lengths of the boat nearer the mark; Grey was nearer, so the zone was about 33 m, and your overlap at 25 m came after she had reached it
questions.why: Definition Zone: three hull lengths of the boat nearer to the mark; rule 18.2(a)(2) fixes the positions when she reaches it.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 12 knots. You have rounded the mark and are close-hauled on starboard tack, still inside the zone. White is still running down to the mark on starboard tack, and your courses converge close to the mark. She hails that you must keep clear of a boat approaching the mark. Which rule decides?

figure.note: You are leaving the mark; White is still approaching it

options: Rule 18 does not apply between a boat leaving a mark and one approaching it; as you are both on starboard, rules 11 or 12 apply according to your positions
Rule 10 — a boat beating always keeps clear of a boat running
Rule 18 — a boat that has rounded must give mark-room to every boat still approaching
Rule 18.4 — the approaching boat must gybe before she reaches you
questions.why: Rule 18.1(a)(3): rule 18 does not apply between a boat approaching a mark and one leaving it; the Section A rules apply instead.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 9 knots. You were the inside boat and Yellow gave you mark-room; you have rounded and left the mark astern, and now you are both close-hauled on starboard, you to windward. Yellow says that now you owe her the same room back and must bear away to let her up. Is there such an obligation?

figure.note: Both boats have rounded; Yellow is now to leeward

options: Yes — a boat that was given mark-room must give the outside boat equal room on the next leg of the course
No — mark-room is not a debt to be repaid; once given, rule 18 no longer applies and you simply keep clear as the windward boat under rule 11
No — because after a mark rounding neither boat has any obligation to the other at all
Yes — after a rounding the boat that was outside has right of way for three hull lengths
questions.why: Rule 18.1(b): rule 18 no longer applies once mark-room has been given; thereafter rule 11 governs the overlapped boats.

questions.q: Wing mark of a trapezoid, beam reach on port tack, 12 knots, the mark to be left to port — so it is on your windward side. You are the leeward boat with right of way; Black is overlapped to windward of you, between you and the mark, when you reach the zone. You hold your course and Black has to luff over the mark's wrong side to avoid you. Who broke a rule?

figure.note: Port-tack beam reach; Black is inside, to windward

options: Black — she should have hailed for room; without a hail the outside boat has no obligation
Black — a windward boat must keep clear under rule 11, and that includes keeping clear at a mark
You — Black was the inside boat and you, outside, had to give her mark-room even though you were the right-of-way boat
Nobody — rule 18 does not apply on reaching legs, only at windward and leeward marks
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(1): the outside boat at the zone gives the inside boat mark-room; her right of way under rule 11 does not excuse her.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 16 knots. You are the outside boat, overlapped with Red, and it is YOUR bow that crosses the three-length circle first — Red, inside, is a little behind. Red calls for room; you answer that the inside boat must reach the zone first to be entitled. Who is right?

figure.note: Your bow reaches the zone first; Red is overlapped inside, slightly behind

options: You — the test is whether the inside boat reaches the zone, so rule 18 was not yet triggered
You — the first boat into the zone is entitled to room from all boats that enter it later
Red — but only because she hailed for room before your bow reached the zone
Red — the test is the overlap when the first of the two boats reaches the zone, whichever boat that is; you were outside at that moment and must give mark-room
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(1): if the boats are overlapped when the first of them reaches the zone, the boat outside at that moment thereafter gives mark-room.

questions.q: Protest hearing after a leeward-mark incident. Facts found: you got an inside overlap on Blue from clear astern three and a half lengths from the mark; Blue says she then pulled clear ahead again just before her bow reached the zone, you say the overlap never broke. The committee cannot decide whether it broke in time. What should it conclude?

figure.title: Protest hearing
lines: Blue: "I broke it before the zone"

options: That the overlap was not broken in time — reasonable doubt about whether an overlap was broken in time is resolved by presuming it was not, so you were entitled to mark-room
That no decision is possible and both boats must be scored as they finished
That the overlap was broken — the benefit of the doubt always goes to the boat ahead
That the overlap was broken — an overlap from clear astern must be held for at least five lengths
questions.why: Rule 18.2(e): if there is reasonable doubt that a boat obtained or broke an overlap in time, it is presumed that she did not.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 14 knots. You are running on starboard tack, overlapped inside Grey, who is on port tack and outside you, when the first of you reaches the zone. You must gybe to round. Grey says that as the outside boat with no right of way she will simply keep clear and you can round as you like. What limits you?

figure.note: You are inside on starboard and must gybe to round

options: Nothing — you have right of way under rule 10 and mark-room, so you may round the mark any way you wish
Rule 18.4 — as the inside right-of-way boat that must gybe, you may sail no farther from the mark than your proper course needs until you gybe, and rule 16.1 when you change course
Rule 17 — you may not sail above your proper course while overlapped with Grey
Rule 18.2(d) — an inside boat on starboard tack must gybe before she reaches the mark
questions.why: Rule 18.4: an inside overlapped right-of-way boat that must gybe at the mark sails no farther from it than needed for her proper course until she gybes.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port, 12 knots, both of you close-hauled on starboard tack and overlapped when the first of you reaches the zone; you are inside and to leeward, Blue outside and to windward. Blue says that "port–starboard" is all that matters at marks and, as you are both on starboard, she may hold her course. Which rules actually decide?

figure.note: Both on starboard; you are inside and to leeward

options: No rule — two boats on the same tack at a mark may both hold their courses
Rule 10 only — at a windward mark the tack is the only thing that matters
Rule 18.2(a)(1) and rule 11 — Blue must give you mark-room as the outside boat and keep clear of you as the windward boat
Rule 18.3 only — any boat on starboard at a windward mark is protected
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(1): the outside boat at the zone gives mark-room; between overlapped boats on the same tack rule 11 also applies.

questions.q: Leeward mark to be left to port, 22 knots. Red enters the zone clear ahead of you and broaches right at the mark, lying on her side with the spinnaker flogging for ten seconds. You are coming down fast behind her. What may you do?

figure.note: Red has broached at the mark; you are coming down fast behind her

options: Sail between her and the mark — a boat that has broached has lost her mark-room
Round the mark on the wrong side and correct it later, as rule 28 allows
Hold your course straight at her — she must get out of your way as soon as she recovers
Pass her on the outside if you can, giving her mark-room — she is still entitled to it; you may not force your way between her and the mark, and you must avoid contact
questions.why: Rule 18.2(a)(2): the boat astern at the zone gives mark-room for as long as the rule applies; rules 14 and 22 also require avoiding a boat out of control.

questions.q: Wednesday evening club race, 8 knots. You and Blue are close-hauled on starboard tack, overlapped, you to leeward, heading straight at a large yacht anchored in the middle of the leg. Which of you decides whether to pass her to port or to starboard?

figure.note: Both on starboard, Blue to windward

options: You — the right-of-way boat chooses the side; if you change course to do so you must give Blue room to keep clear
Blue — whichever boat hails her choice first decides
Neither — both must pass an anchored vessel on the side nearer the next mark
Blue — the windward boat chooses because she can see over the obstruction
questions.why: Rule 19.2(a): the right-of-way boat may pass an obstruction on either side; if she changes course to do so, she gives the other boat room to keep clear.

questions.q: You are reaching on port tack, overlapped inside Red — between her and the end of a long concrete pier you both have to pass. Red, outside and to leeward, holds her course and the gap closes. Does Red have to give you room?

figure.note: Both on port tack, reaching east along the pier

options: No — room at an obstruction is owed only to a boat that was clear ahead when it was first reached
Yes — once overlapped, the outside boat gives the inside boat room between her and the obstruction, even though Red is the right-of-way boat
No — Red is the leeward boat and has right of way, so you must keep clear by slowing down
Yes, but only if you hailed "Water" before Red reached the pier
questions.why: Rule 19.2(b): when boats are overlapped, the outside boat gives the inside boat room between her and the obstruction, unless unable since the overlap began.

questions.q: Dying breeze, 5 knots, running on starboard. Grey, clear astern of you, surges on a puff and gets an overlap on your inside only a boat length before you both reach a line of moored motor boats. You cannot open a gap in time; she wedges in and touches both a mooring buoy and your quarter. Who broke a rule?

figure.note: Grey has just got the overlap, one length from the moorings

options: You — as the boat ahead at an obstruction you should have slowed to let Grey through
Nobody — a boat astern may squeeze in as long as she gets the overlap before the obstruction
Grey — the outside boat need not give room when she has been unable to do so from the time the overlap began
You — an outside boat must always give room to an inside overlapped boat at an obstruction
questions.why: Rule 19.2(b): the outside boat gives room unless she has been unable to do so since the overlap began; Grey must then keep clear (rule 11).

questions.q: 470 nationals, you are beating along a beach on starboard tack, clear astern of 4471. You sail a little lower and faster and become overlapped between her and the shore at a point where there is not enough room for a boat to pass. 4471 does not move over and you have to tack out. Were you entitled to room?

figure.note: You have just got an overlap between 4471 and the beach

options: Yes — you were the leeward boat, so under rule 11 4471 had to luff and make space
Yes — once overlapped the outside boat must always give room at an obstruction
No, but 4471 had to tack away at once as the boat farther from the shore
No — at a continuing obstruction a boat that gets an inside overlap from clear astern where there is no room is not entitled to it, and must keep clear
questions.why: Rule 19.2(c): at a continuing obstruction a boat from clear astern that gets an inside overlap with no room is not entitled to it; rules 10 and 11 are off.

questions.q: Saronic Gulf, reaching on starboard along a rocky shore in 12 knots. You come up from clear astern of Red and get an overlap between her and the rocks where there are three lengths of clear water. A minute later the shore juts out, the gap narrows, and Red bears away toward the rocks to close you out. Who is right?

figure.note: The shore juts out ahead; Red bears away toward you

options: You — there was room between Red and the shore when the overlap began, so rule 19.2(b) applies and Red must give you room; 19.2(c) does not bite
Red — at a continuing obstruction a boat that comes from clear astern is never entitled to inside room
Red — a leeward boat cannot claim room against a boat that was ahead of her
Red — she may bear away at you as long as she gives you room to keep clear under rule 16.1
questions.why: Rule 19.2(c) denies room only when there was no room between the other boat and the obstruction at the moment the overlap began; otherwise 19.2(b) applies.

questions.q: You and Blue, overlapped on starboard tack, approach the committee boat end of the finishing line. Blue is inside and hails "Room — obstruction!", claiming room under rule 19 to pass between you and the committee boat. Which rule actually governs?

figure.note: Finishing at the committee boat end, Blue inside

options: Rule 19 — a committee boat is a vessel, so it is an obstruction and the inside boat gets room between you and it
Rule 18 — the committee boat is a mark you both must leave on the same side, so Blue is entitled to mark-room, not room under rule 19
Neither — at a finishing mark surrounded by navigable water no room is owed, just as at the start
Rule 19 — because the committee boat is anchored it counts like any other anchored vessel
questions.why: Rule 19.1(a): rule 19 does not apply when the obstruction is a mark the boats must leave on the same side; rule 18 applies at a finishing mark.

questions.q: Leeward mark to port, three boats overlapped on starboard: Red inside, Blue in the middle, you outside. Blue is entitled to mark-room from you under rule 18. Blue also hails you for room under rule 19 to pass Red, saying Red is an obstruction to her. Is she right?

figure.note: Leave the mark to port; Red inside, you outside

options: Yes — rule 19 always applies at a boat, and rule 18 only at the mark itself
Yes — Red is a boat Blue must keep clear of, so she is an obstruction and rule 19 adds room to the mark-room
No — when rule 18 applies between you and the obstruction is another boat overlapped with each of you, rule 19 does not apply; rule 18 alone governs
No — a boat racing can never be an obstruction, so rule 19 never involves other boats
questions.why: Rule 19.1(b): rule 19 does not apply when rule 18 applies between the boats and the obstruction is another boat overlapped with each of them.

questions.q: Beat in 12 knots. You and Yellow are close-hauled on port, overlapped, you to leeward, Yellow a length to windward. Grey crosses on starboard. You decide to bear away and pass astern of Grey, but Yellow, who also has to duck, is bearing down on you. What must Yellow do?

figure.note: Grey on starboard; both port-tack boats will have to duck her

options: Hold her course — at an obstruction the boat nearest to it must find her own way round
Tack at once — a windward port-tack boat must always tack when a starboard-tack boat crosses
Nothing — Yellow is clear of Grey; if you cannot duck in time you must tack
Give you room to pass astern of Grey between her and Grey — Grey is an obstruction to you both and you, the right-of-way boat, chose the side
questions.why: A right-of-way boat is an obstruction to boats that must keep clear of her; rule 19.2(a)–(b): you choose the side and Yellow, outside, gives you room.

questions.q: Palma, 36-ft cruiser-racers running on port gybe. You are clear ahead of Blue, who is a length and a half astern on the same tack, and a trawler lies at anchor dead ahead. At the last moment you alter course sharply to starboard; Blue, who was already going that way, has to gybe to miss your stern. Was that allowed?

figure.note: You bear away hard to starboard at the last moment

options: You may choose either side, but when you change course to do it you must give Blue room to keep clear — you did not
No — you had to pass on the side Blue had committed to, because she chose first
No — you had to hail your choice; without a hail the boat astern picks the side
Yes — a boat clear ahead has no obligation whatever to a boat clear astern
questions.why: Rule 19.2(a): the right-of-way boat may pass either side, but if she changes course to do so she gives the other boat room to keep clear (as in rule 16.1).

questions.q: You are close-hauled on port tack. Red, close-hauled on starboard, is converging and will cross just ahead of you. Your crew asks: is Red an obstruction to us?

figure.note: Red on starboard, you on port

options: No — a boat is an obstruction only when she is capsized, anchored or aground
Yes — a boat racing is an obstruction to boats that must keep clear of her, so Red is one to you, though you are not one to her
Yes, and that means Red must also give you room to pass her
No — only fixed objects, anchored vessels and the shore are obstructions
questions.why: Definition Obstruction: a boat racing is an obstruction to other boats only if they must keep clear of her or avoid her under rule 22.

questions.q: A race committee RIB is holding station on her engine 40 m below the windward mark; the sailing instructions do not list her as a mark. You and Grey, overlapped and close-hauled on starboard, must pass her; Grey is inside, between you and the RIB. What are Grey's rights?

figure.note: Grey inside, between you and the RIB

options: None — a vessel with her engine running is never an obstruction to boats racing
None — Grey is the windward boat and must keep clear of you whatever is in her way
Grey is entitled to room to pass between you and the RIB under rule 19 — the RIB is an obstruction, not a mark
None — the RIB is a mark boat, so rule 18 applies and Grey gets mark-room only if overlapped at the zone
questions.why: Definition Obstruction and rule 19.2(b): a vessel you cannot pass without a substantial course change is an obstruction; the outside boat gives room.

questions.q: Lake regatta. The sailing instructions declare the swimming area, marked by yellow buoys, a prohibited area. You and Blue are overlapped on starboard, reaching along its edge, you inside. Blue says no room is owed because "a few buoys are not an obstruction". Who is right?

figure.note: Reaching west along the prohibited area, you inside

options: Blue — only a solid object you could hit can be an obstruction under the rules
Blue — the prohibited area binds each boat separately and creates no rights between boats
You, but only because the buoys themselves are marks of the course
You — an area that a rule prohibits boats from entering is an obstruction by definition, so Blue, outside, must give you room
questions.why: Definition Obstruction (c): an object, area or line so designated by a rule that boats may not enter or cross; rule 19.2(b) then applies.

questions.q: You are overlapped inside Red, to windward, passing the head of a pier on port tack. Red, the leeward boat, luffs you toward the pilings and you touch a piling and then her hull; no damage. Who is penalised?

figure.note: Red luffs you toward the pier head

options: Red — she had to give you room; you are exonerated for breaking rule 11 and for the contact, as you were sailing within the room you were entitled to
Both — Red for luffing and you for the contact, because rule 14 applies to every boat
Nobody — luffing is allowed and touching a pier is not a breach of any racing rule
You — a windward boat must keep clear whatever the obstruction; the pier is your problem
questions.why: Rule 19.2(b) binds the outside boat; rule 43.1(b)–(c): the inside boat sailing within her room is exonerated for breaking rules 11 and 14 (no damage).

questions.q: Lake race in 6 knots. A tall navigation post stands in the middle of the second leg; it is not a mark of the course. You and Black are overlapped on starboard, you inside and nearer the post. Black says you cannot claim room "because it isn't a mark". Is she right?

figure.note: You inside, nearer the post

options: Yes — a post with navigable water all round can be passed either side, so no room is owed
No — the post is an obstruction and, being overlapped, Black as the outside boat must give you room to pass between her and it
Yes — room is owed only at marks of the course and at other boats
No, but only if you were clear ahead when the post was two lengths away
questions.why: Definition Obstruction (an object a boat could not pass without a substantial course change) and rule 19.2(b); a post needs no status as a mark.

questions.q: Bodrum, 15 knots. Blue, inside and to windward of you, is given room to pass between you and an anchored gulet. She swings out much wider than she needs, well clear of the gulet, and her boom hits your shrouds. She says she was "within her room". Was she?

figure.note: Blue swings wide of the gulet and into you

options: Yes — rule 19 gives the inside boat right of way until both boats are clear of the obstruction
Yes — an inside boat may use all the space the outside boat gives up until both are past the obstruction
No — room is the space needed to pass in a seamanlike way; sailing wider than that she was no longer within it and broke rule 11 as windward boat
No, but you are penalised too, for not giving extra room in the waves
questions.why: Definition Room: space to manoeuvre promptly in a seamanlike way; rule 43.1(b) exonerates only a boat sailing within that room.

questions.q: Run in 10 knots. You are on starboard tack, Blue on port, both sailing more than 90° from the wind and side by side, approaching an anchored ship. Blue is nearer the ship. Must you give her room to pass between you and the ship?

figure.note: Both running; Blue inside, nearer the ship

options: No — rule 10 gives you right of way and a port-tack boat is never entitled to room from a starboard-tack boat
No — boats on opposite tacks cannot be overlapped, so rule 19.2(b) cannot apply
Yes, but only once Blue has gybed onto starboard tack
Yes — boats on opposite tacks are overlapped when both sail more than 90° from the wind, so rule 19.2(b) applies and you, outside, give room
questions.why: Definition Overlap: opposite-tack boats are overlapped when both sail more than 90° from the true wind; rule 19.2(b) then applies between them.

questions.q: Thirty seconds to the start. Blue, overlapped to windward of you, squeezes between you and the committee boat and hails "Room — obstruction!". Must you give her room?

figure.note: 30 s before the start; Blue barging at the committee boat

options: No — the committee boat is a starting mark in navigable water: rule 18 is off while approaching to start and rule 19 does not apply at a mark; rule 11 governs
Yes — a boat overlapped inside when the pair reaches the zone of the committee boat is entitled to mark-room under rule 18.2(a)
Yes — the committee boat is a vessel, so it is an obstruction and the inside boat is entitled to room under rule 19 until she is past it
No — before the starting signal no boat has a proper course, and therefore no boat can be entitled to room of any kind
questions.why: Rules 18.1 and 19.1(a): no mark-room at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water and no rule 19 room at a mark; the windward boat keeps clear (rule 11).

questions.q: Just after the start, you and Red are close-hauled on starboard, overlapped, heading between the committee boat and the small buoy marking her anchor 25 m upwind of her. You are inside, nearer the anchor line. Red says the anchor line is part of the mark and no room is owed. What is the anchor line?

figure.note: You inside, heading between the committee boat and her anchor buoy

options: Part of the mark — touching it is a rule 31 breach and rule 18 applies to it
An obstruction, not part of the mark — overlapped boats passing it are subject to rule 19, so Red must give you room
A mark — anything attached to a mark boat, including her ground tackle, is part of her
Nothing — only the hull of the committee boat has any status under the rules
questions.why: Definition Mark: an anchor line is not part of the mark; it is an object you cannot pass without changing course substantially, so an obstruction (rule 19).

questions.q: Reaching leg, you are the windward boat overlapped with Red, who is to leeward. A spectator boat is anchored on the course ahead. Red bears away to pass to leeward of her. Must you pass on the same side as Red?

figure.note: Red bears away to pass to leeward of the spectator boat

options: No — as the windward boat you choose your side first and Red adjusts to it
Yes — the windward boat always follows the leeward boat's side at an obstruction
No — Red, the right-of-way boat, chooses her side and you must keep clear of her; if you can pass the other side while keeping clear, you may
Yes — overlapped boats must pass an obstruction on the same side, the side chosen by the right-of-way boat
questions.why: Rule 19.2(a) gives the right-of-way boat the choice of side; the other boat's duty is to keep clear (rule 11), on whichever side she can do so.

questions.q: The fleet beats up a narrow river. To port is a quay with forty yachts moored along it; ahead a small fishing boat lies at anchor. Which of them is a continuing obstruction?

figure.note: A small fishing boat is anchored further up the river

options: Both — any object you cannot pass without a substantial course change is a continuing obstruction
The fishing boat — a vessel at anchor is always a continuing obstruction
Neither — only natural shoreline counts as a continuing obstruction
The line of moored yachts along the quay — the small anchored fishing boat is an ordinary obstruction
questions.why: A continuing obstruction is one boats sail alongside for some time (a shore, a long quay, a line of moored boats); a short object is an ordinary obstruction.

questions.q: River race with two knots of current under you. You and Blue are overlapped on port, reaching toward the bridge arch the sailing instructions tell you to use; you are inside, nearer the pier of the bridge. How much room must Blue give you?

figure.note: Current sets you toward the upper pier

options: Room to pass between her and the pier in a seamanlike way in the existing conditions — which here includes space for the set of the current
None — a bridge pier is not an obstruction because the arch is a designated passage
Exactly one hull length between you and the pier; the current is your own problem
Only room to keep clear of Blue herself; the pier is not her concern
questions.why: Rule 19.2(b) and definition Room: the space needed in the existing conditions to manoeuvre promptly in a seamanlike way — current included.

questions.q: You are close-hauled on port, Red close-hauled on starboard; your courses converge right at an anchored barge. Red hails that she is the inside boat and demands room between you and the barge. Does she get it?

figure.note: Courses converge at the barge

options: No — both boats must pass the barge on the side nearer the next mark, and neither owes room
No room is owed — on a beat opposite-tack boats are not overlapped, so rule 19.2(b) cannot apply; rule 10 governs and you keep clear of Red
Yes — Red, as right-of-way boat, is entitled to room between you and the barge under rule 19.2(b)
No — you are the inside boat and are entitled to room, so Red must bear away
questions.why: Definition Overlap: boats on opposite tacks on a beat are not overlapped; rule 19.2(b) needs an overlap, so only rule 10 applies.

questions.q: Beating along a sea wall on starboard tack. Blue came from clear astern and wedged in between you and the wall where there was no room; you had to pinch to avoid contact. Now the wall falls away and there is plenty of water. Still overlapped, Blue hails "Leeward boat — up, up!" May she now claim rights under rule 11?

figure.note: Blue got the overlap earlier where there was no room

options: Yes — as soon as there is room between you and the wall the normal rules return and she is the leeward boat
Yes — rule 19.2(c) only applies at the moment the overlap begins, not afterwards
No — for as long as that overlap lasts she must keep clear and rules 10 and 11 do not apply; the gap opening later gives her nothing
No — but you must now give her room under rule 19.2(b) because room has become available
questions.why: Rule 19.2(c): a boat that got the inside overlap without room is not entitled to it and, while the overlap lasts, keeps clear; rules 10 and 11 do not apply.

questions.q: The course passes through a 40 m gap in a breakwater. Three boats arrive overlapped on starboard: White nearest the gap wall, you in the middle, Grey outside. Who owes room to whom?

figure.note: The gap is between the two walls; White nearest the left wall

options: Nobody — a gap in a breakwater is a passage, not an obstruction, so rule 19 is off
Grey gives room to White only; the middle boat has no rights and no duties under rule 19
You give room to White, but Grey owes you nothing because you are not nearest the wall
Grey must give you room, and you must give White room — each outside boat gives the boat inside her room to pass between her and the obstruction
questions.why: Rule 19.2(b) applies between each pair of overlapped boats: the outer gives the middle room, and the middle, as outside boat to the inner, gives her room too.

questions.q: Split, a Mediterranean regatta. A rock awash is marked on the chart but has no buoy. You and Red are overlapped on port, reaching, you inside and nearer the rock. Red says that without a buoy it is "not an obstruction under the rules". Who is right?

figure.note: You inside, nearer the rock

options: You — an object a boat one length away heading at it could not pass without a substantial course change is an obstruction, buoyed or not; Red gives you room
You, but only because the chart counts as part of the sailing instructions
Red — only objects marked on the water or listed in the sailing instructions are obstructions
Red — a rock is part of the seabed, and the rules deal only with objects on the surface
questions.why: Definition Obstruction (a): an object a boat could not pass without substantially changing course if she were one hull length from it; rule 19.2(b) applies.

questions.q: You are close-hauled on port tack, three lengths from a stone quay, with Blue close to windward of you so that you cannot tack without hitting her. You hail "Room to tack!". Is your hail allowed?

figure.note: You will hit the quay in three lengths unless you tack

options: No — a leeward boat may not hail; room to tack is for the windward boat
Yes — you are close-hauled, approaching an obstruction, and will soon need a substantial course change to avoid it safely
No — you may hail only when you are already within one hull length of the obstruction
Yes, but only if you first hailed "Water" and waited for a reply
questions.why: Rule 20.1: a boat may hail for room to tack when approaching an obstruction, about to need a substantial course change, and sailing close-hauled or above.

questions.q: You are on a reach, about 20° below close-hauled, with the shore coming up and Blue just to windward. You hail "Room to tack!"; Blue tacks at once and then protests you. What should the protest committee decide?

figure.note: You are reaching, well below close-hauled

options: Both are penalised: you for hailing and Blue for responding to an invalid hail
Blue is penalised: a boat that responds to a hail accepts it and cannot protest afterwards
You are penalised: you hailed while not sailing close-hauled, breaking rule 20.1; Blue was right to respond, as she must even to an improper hail
Nobody: on a reach the hail is simply void and Blue could have ignored it
questions.why: Rule 20.1(b): hail only when sailing close-hauled or above; rule 20.2(b): the hailed boat responds even if the hail breaks rule 20.1.

questions.q: Beating up a shoreline, Red, close to leeward of you on the same tack, hails "Room to tack!". Which responses satisfy the rule?

figure.note: Red to leeward hails for room to tack

options: Reply "You tack" and keep your course; Red must then tack and keep clear of you
Tack as soon as possible, or ignore the hail if you can see she could still bear away
Reply "Hold your course" and bear away to give her room to tack beneath you
Tack as soon as possible, or reply "You tack" at once and then give Red room to tack and to avoid you
questions.why: Rule 20.2(c): the hailed boat either tacks as soon as possible or immediately replies "You tack" and gives the hailing boat room to tack and avoid her.

questions.q: You hail Blue, to windward, for room to tack at a pier. She replies "You tack!" but then holds her course and you have to abort your tack to avoid her stern, ending up pinching along the pier. Who broke a rule?

figure.note: Blue replied "You tack" but did not move over

options: Blue — after replying "You tack" she had to give you room to tack and to avoid her
You — once Blue replied you had to tack and keep clear of her under rule 13 whatever room there was
Nobody — "You tack" transfers the whole responsibility to the hailing boat
You — you should have tacked before hailing instead of waiting for Blue's answer
questions.why: Rule 20.2(c): a hailed boat that replies "You tack" must then give the hailing boat room to tack and to avoid her.

questions.q: A 20° header hits you on the beat, far from any shore or boat you must avoid. Grey is sitting on your windward quarter, so you cannot tack without fouling her. You hail "Room to tack!" to get across onto the lifted tack. Is that allowed?

figure.note: The wind has headed you 20°; no obstruction anywhere

options: No, and Grey may simply ignore the hail because there is no obstruction
No — the hail is allowed only when approaching an obstruction; Grey must still respond, but she may protest you
Yes — a boat may hail for room to tack whenever another boat prevents her from tacking
Yes — a header of 20° or more is a reason that justifies requiring room to tack
questions.why: Rule 20.1: a hail is permitted only when approaching an obstruction; rule 20.2(b): the hailed boat responds even if the hail breaks rule 20.1.

questions.q: Windward mark to be left to port. You and Red are both close-hauled on starboard in the zone, Red to windward and fetching the mark, you a little below the layline and heading straight at the mark. You hail Red "Room to tack!" to avoid hitting the mark; she tacks away and you round. What happened under the rules?

figure.note: Red is fetching the mark; you are heading straight at it

options: Both acted correctly — Red's tack counted as giving you mark-room under rule 18.2(a)
Nothing wrong — the mark is an obstruction and you were close-hauled, so the hail met every condition of rule 20.1
You broke rule 20.1 — no hail for room to tack when the obstruction is a mark and a boat fetching it would have to change course; Red nevertheless had to respond
Red broke rule 20.2 — a boat fetching a mark may refuse to respond to a hail for room to tack, and she should have
questions.why: Rule 20.1, last sentence: no hail when the obstruction is a mark and a boat fetching it would have to change course; rule 20.2(b): she still responds.

questions.q: Three boats close-hauled on port toward a sea wall: Yellow to leeward, you in the middle, Black to windward. Yellow hails you "Room to tack!". You cannot tack because Black is right beside you to windward. What do you do?

figure.note: Yellow has hailed you; Black is close to windward of you

options: Wait until Black tacks of her own accord; you may not hail unless you are the leeward boat
Reply "You tack" to Yellow — a boat that cannot tack is excused from responding
Bear away under Yellow's stern; the hail does not bind a boat that has another boat to windward
Hail Black for room to tack at once, then tack as soon as she responds — between you and Black rule 20.2 applies
questions.why: Rule 20.3: a hailed boat that intends to tack may hail another boat on the same tack for room to tack, even if her own hail would not meet rule 20.1.

questions.q: Approaching a shoal marked by a pole, you hail "Room to tack!" and put the helm down in the same breath. Red, to windward, has no time to react and your bow hits her quarter. Who broke a rule?

figure.note: You hailed and tacked at the same moment

options: You — after hailing you must give the hailed boat time to respond before you tack; until she responds you have no right to tack into her
Red — once hailed she had to tack instantly, and she did not
Nobody — the collision was caused by the shoal, which is nobody's fault
Red — a windward boat must anticipate a hail whenever an obstruction is near
questions.why: Rule 20.2(a): after hailing, a boat gives the hailed boat time to respond; tacking at once she also breaks rule 13 while past head to wind.

questions.q: Blue tacked immediately when you hailed her for room to tack at a rocky point. Now, with Blue gone, you look again and think you can just squeeze past the point without tacking. May you hold on?

figure.note: Blue has already tacked in response to your hail

options: No — you had to tack before Blue did; the hailing boat always tacks first
No — once the hailed boat has responded, you must tack as soon as possible
Yes — if the obstruction can be cleared after all, the hail is cancelled automatically
Yes — the hail only obliges the hailed boat; the hailer may then do as she pleases
questions.why: Rule 20.2(d): when the hailed boat responds, the hailing boat shall tack as soon as possible.

questions.q: Beat along a lee shore off Split in 25 knots and breaking waves. You need room to tack and hail Red at the top of your voice, but her crew, hiking hard, clearly hear nothing. What does the rule require of you?

figure.title: Beat along a lee shore, Split
lines: You: close-hauled on port, 3 lengths off the shore
Red: close to windward, same tack
You hail "Room to tack" — no reaction

options: You cannot ask for room; in heavy weather rule 20 is suspended for safety
You must call Red on VHF channel 16; no other method is recognised
You must also make a signal that clearly indicates your need for room to tack — in such conditions the hail alone is not enough
Nothing more — a loud hail satisfies the rule whether or not it is heard
questions.why: Rule 20.4(a): when conditions mean a hail may not be heard, the boat must also make a signal that clearly indicates her need for room to tack (or her response).

questions.q: You hail Blue, to windward, for room to tack at a harbour wall. Blue replies "You tack!", but Red is close to windward of Blue and Blue cannot move over; you are forced to bear away along the wall. Who broke a rule?

figure.note: Blue replied "You tack" but Red pins her

options: Red — the outermost boat is always responsible for making room when a hail is made
Nobody — Blue did all she could; rule 20 does not apply when three boats are involved
You — you should have hailed Red directly, as the boat that was actually in the way
Blue — having replied "You tack" she had to give you room; she should have tacked, or passed the hail on to Red and then tacked
questions.why: Rule 20.2(c): after "You tack" the hailed boat must give room; rule 20.3 lets her instead hail a third boat and tack when that boat responds.

questions.q: You are close-hauled on port, a few lengths from the shore. Grey, close-hauled on starboard, is crossing just ahead of you. You hail Grey "Room to tack!". What is the effect?

figure.note: Grey is on starboard, you on port

options: None — rule 20 works only between boats on the same tack; Grey keeps her rights under rule 10 and you must keep clear of her
Grey must respond, because an obstruction cancels rule 10 between boats near it
Grey must respond by tacking or replying "You tack" — the hail binds any boat within hearing
Grey may ignore the hail, but she must still give you room under rule 19
questions.why: Rule 20.1: a boat may hail for room to tack and avoid a boat on the same tack; across tacks rule 10 applies and the hail has no effect.

questions.q: The windward mark, to be left to port, is laid three lengths off a rocky point. You and Blue are close-hauled on port in the zone, Blue to windward and inside for the rounding; the rocks are dead ahead. You hail Blue "Room to tack!" and she tacks; you tack after her. Blue later protests that you failed to give her mark-room. Decision?

figure.note: The rocks are dead ahead; the mark is in reach after one tack

options: You broke rule 20.1 — a boat may never hail for room to tack inside the zone of a mark
No breach — from your hail until you had tacked and avoided Blue, rule 18.2 did not apply between you; Blue had to respond to the hail
You broke rule 18.2(a) — Blue was the inside boat at the zone and mark-room overrides any hail for room to tack
Blue broke rule 20.2 — a boat entitled to mark-room may refuse a hail for room to tack
questions.why: Rule 20.2(e): from the time a boat hails for room to tack until she has tacked and avoided the hailed boat, rule 18.2 does not apply between them.

questions.q: In 20 knots you hail Red for room to tack at a breakwater. Red, to windward, takes four or five seconds to ease sheets, get the crew across and tack. You protest her for not tacking "at once". Decision?

figure.title: Breakwater, 20 knots
lines: You hail "Room to tack" at four lengths
Red (to windward) eases sheets, crew crosses
Red tacks after about five seconds
You clear the breakwater with room to spare

options: Breach — a hailed boat that cannot tack instantly must reply "You tack" instead
Breach — the hailed boat must begin her tack within two seconds of the hail
No breach — Red tacked as soon as possible in a seamanlike way for the conditions; the rule does not require an instant tack
No breach, because a hailed boat is never required to tack, only to give room
questions.why: Rule 20.2(c): the hailed boat tacks "as soon as possible" — promptly and in a seamanlike way in the conditions, not instantly regardless of them.

questions.q: You hail Blue, to windward, for room to tack as the shore comes up. Blue says nothing and holds her course; you run out of water and have to crash-tack under her transom, touching her rudder. Who broke a rule?

figure.note: Blue holds her course in silence

options: You — a boat that cannot tack safely must slow down and wait until the windward boat has passed
Nobody — Blue may choose not to respond if she judges the hail unjustified
You — you had to hail a second time before tacking, and you did not
Blue — she had to respond by tacking or by replying "You tack" and giving room; silence and holding course is not a response
questions.why: Rule 20.2(c): the hailed boat shall respond either by tacking as soon as possible or by replying "You tack" and giving room; Blue did neither.

questions.q: You hail Grey, to windward, for room to tack at a line of moored boats. Grey replies "You tack!" and luffs to give you room. Instead of tacking you bear away and pass astern of her, then carry on. Grey protests. What did you break?

figure.note: Grey has luffed to give you room; you bear away instead

options: Rule 20.2(d) — once the hailed boat responds, the hailing boat must tack as soon as possible, not bear away under her stern
Rule 20.1 — bearing away proved that you did not need a substantial course change after all
Rule 16.1 — by bearing away you changed course without giving Grey room to keep clear
Nothing — once room is given, the hailing boat may use it to tack or to bear away as she sees fit
questions.why: Rule 20.2(d): when the hailed boat responds, the hailing boat shall tack as soon as possible.

questions.q: You are close-hauled on port with Yellow a length to windward, overlapped. Red is approaching on starboard; you are too close to her to bear away under her stern. You hail Yellow "Room to tack!". Is the hail valid?

figure.note: Red on starboard is too close for you to duck

options: No — at another boat your only option is to bear away under her stern under rule 19
Yes — Red, a boat you must keep clear of, is an obstruction; you are close-hauled and need a substantial course change, so Yellow must respond
No — only fixed objects, the shore and anchored vessels are obstructions for the purposes of rule 20
Yes, but Yellow may respond by holding her course if she judges that you could still duck Red
questions.why: Definition Obstruction: a right-of-way boat is an obstruction to a boat that must keep clear of her; rule 20.1 allows the hail and 20.2 requires a response.

questions.q: Same beat: you to leeward and Yellow to windward, both close-hauled on port and overlapped, with Red on starboard approaching. You could either bear away under Red's stern or tack. Yellow shouts "Just duck her!". Who decides what the pair does?

figure.note: You may duck Red or hail for room to tack

options: Yellow — the windward boat decides whether the pair tacks or ducks, because she has the bigger move to make
Neither — the rules require both port-tack boats to tack when a starboard-tack boat is an obstruction
You — as the right-of-way boat between the two port-tack boats you may duck (and Yellow gives room under rule 19) or hail for room to tack under rule 20
Red — the starboard-tack boat may hail "Hold your course" and fix what the port-tack boats do
questions.why: Rule 19.2(a) gives the right-of-way boat the choice of side; rule 20.1 lets her hail for room to tack instead; the windward boat must comply either way.

questions.q: You hail Blue for room to tack at a shore; she replies "You tack!" and bears away only slightly. You tack as fast as you can, but in the tack your transom brushes her bow — no damage. The protest committee finds Blue could easily have borne away more. Who is penalised?

figure.note: Blue bore away only a little; you are mid-tack

options: Both — Blue for the room and you for the contact; rule 14 is never excused
Nobody — contact without damage during a room-to-tack exchange is not a breach
You — a tacking boat must keep clear under rule 13 whatever room she was given
Blue — she failed to give room to tack and to avoid her; you are exonerated for breaking rules 13 and 14 while sailing within the room you were entitled to
questions.why: Rule 20.2(c) binds the hailed boat; rule 43.1(b)–(c) exonerates the hailing boat sailing within her room for breaking rule 13 and rule 14 (no damage).

questions.q: A small dinghy lies at anchor ahead of you on the beat. Bearing away ten degrees for a couple of lengths would take you clear of her. Instead you hail Blue, close to windward, "Room to tack!" because the other tack suits you. What are the consequences?

figure.note: A small bear-away would clear the dinghy

options: Your hail broke rule 20.1 — avoiding the dinghy did not require a substantial course change; Blue must still respond but may protest you
None — any object you must steer round is an obstruction and justifies a hail for room to tack
Blue may ignore the hail, since a dinghy at anchor is too small to be an obstruction
None — the hailing boat alone judges whether a course change is substantial
questions.why: Rule 20.1(a): the boat must be about to need a substantial course change to avoid the obstruction safely; rule 20.2(b): the hailed boat still responds.

questions.q: Red is a length clear ahead and to windward of you, both close-hauled on starboard, as a long pier approaches. You are not overlapped, but if you tack now you will tack straight into her path. May you hail her for room to tack?

figure.note: Red clear ahead and to windward; no overlap

options: No — a boat clear astern has no rights at all against a boat clear ahead
Yes — rule 20 needs no overlap; you may hail a boat on the same tack whose position prevents your tack, and Red must respond
Yes, but Red may answer "You tack" only, since she is ahead of you
No — room to tack can be claimed only from a boat you are overlapped with
questions.why: Rule 20.1 speaks of a boat on the same tack, not an overlapped one; the hailed boat responds under rule 20.2(c).

questions.q: You hailed Blue for room to tack at a mole and she has replied "You tack!". Who tacks first now?
options: Both together — the rule requires simultaneous tacks after that reply
Whichever boat is nearer the mole decides who tacks first
You, the hailing boat — as soon as possible, while Blue gives you room to tack and to avoid her
Blue — "You tack" means she will tack and you follow her round
questions.why: Rule 20.2(c)–(d): after "You tack" the hailed boat gives room and the hailing boat tacks as soon as possible.

questions.q: On the final beat of a club race you hail Blue, to windward, for room to tack as a jetty approaches. Blue says nothing for several seconds, keeps sailing, and only when you are a length from the jetty shouts "You tack!" and bears away. You tack and barely miss the piles. Did Blue comply?

figure.note: Blue answered only when you were a length from the piles

options: No — she had to tack herself; "You tack" is only allowed when she cannot tack
Yes — she replied "You tack" and gave room, which is all the rule requires
Yes — a hailed boat may take time to assess whether the hail was justified before answering
No — she had to respond either by tacking as soon as possible or by replying "You tack" immediately; a late answer is not a response
questions.why: Rule 20.2(c): the reply "You tack" must be immediate; rule 20.2(a) gives the hailed boat time to respond, not time to wait and see.

questions.q: The notice of race says that a boat needing room to tack shall hail "Room to tack" and raise one arm, and that the response shall be a hail plus a hand signal. Your crew only shouts in Greek and Red does not react. Who is right?

figure.title: Notice of race, hails under rule 20
lines: Hail "Room to tack" and raise one arm
Response: hail and clear hand signal
You: hail in Greek, no arm signal

options: Red — the notice of race may prescribe an alternative communication for the hail and the response and require boats to use it; make the prescribed signal
You — any clear hail in any language satisfies rule 20, and the notice of race cannot add to it
You — only the sailing instructions, not the notice of race, can change how rule 20 hails are made
Neither — when the notice of race prescribes a signal, a boat need not hail at all; she may just tack
questions.why: Rule 20.4(b): the notice of race may specify an alternative communication for the hail and the response and require boats to use it.

questions.q: Windward mark to port. You are close-hauled on starboard, heading straight at the mark — you cannot pass it without a substantial course change. Red is close to windward of you but below the layline, not fetching the mark. You hail Red "Room to tack!". Is that allowed?

figure.note: Neither of you is fetching the mark; you are aimed at it

options: Only if Red agrees — at a mark the hailed boat may refuse to respond
Yes — the ban on hailing at a mark applies only when a boat fetching the mark would have to change course; Red is not fetching, so she must respond
No — a boat may never hail for room to tack when the obstruction is a mark of the course
No — inside the zone rule 18 replaces rule 20 completely
questions.why: Rule 20.1, last sentence: the hail is barred when the obstruction is a mark and a boat fetching it would be required to change course — not otherwise.

questions.q: Red, to leeward of you on port tack, hails "Room to tack!" as a moored barge approaches. You judge that she could easily bear away under the barge and do nothing. Red has to bear away hard at the last moment. In the hearing the protest committee agrees that Red's hail did not meet rule 20.1. Who is penalised?

figure.title: Protest hearing: Red v. You
lines: Red hailed "Room to tack" at a moored barge
You held course, judging the hail unjustified
Red bore away hard, no contact
PC finds: the hail did not meet rule 20.1

options: Nobody — the committee found the hail invalid, so the whole exchange is void
Only Red — an invalid hail imposes no obligation on the hailed boat
Both — Red for hailing when rule 20.1 did not allow it, and you for not responding, because the hailed boat must respond even to a hail that breaks 20.1
Only you — once a boat hails, the hailed boat alone is responsible for what follows
questions.why: Rule 20.2(b): the hailed boat shall respond even if the hail breaks rule 20.1; the remedy for an improper hail is a protest, not refusal.

questions.q: You are close-hauled on starboard with Blue close to windward, and the beach is two lengths ahead. You need her to let you tack. What should you hail?

figure.note: Two lengths to the beach

options: "Water!" — and then tack at once; the traditional hail needs no reply
"Protest!" — a hail for room must be preceded by a protest hail to be valid
"Starboard!" — it is the only hail the rules recognise between boats on a beat
"Room to tack!" — loudly and in time for Blue to respond before you have to turn
questions.why: Rule 20.1: the hail is "Room to tack"; rule 20.2(a): after hailing, the boat gives the hailed boat time to respond.

questions.q: Flag X goes up with one sound after the start and you realise your bow was over the line. You bear away and sail back toward the pre-start side on starboard tack, straight into the boats still starting. What are your obligations?

figure.note: You are returning after the start; A and B are starting

options: You must keep clear of every boat that is not returning, until your hull is completely on the pre-start side
Only to avoid contact; the starting boats must give you room to get back
None beyond the normal rules — on starboard tack you keep right of way over port-tack boats
To keep clear only of boats that have already crossed the starting line
questions.why: Rule 21.1: a boat sailing toward the pre-start side after her starting signal keeps clear of a boat not doing so until her hull is completely on that side.

questions.q: You were OCS and are returning. Your bow is now back across the line but your stern is still on the course side when Grey, starting on port, converges with you on starboard. Grey keeps clear of you, saying you are "back". Who had to keep clear at that moment?

figure.note: Your stern is still on the course side of the line

options: Neither — boats returning to start and boats starting have no obligations to each other
You — your obligation under rule 21.1 lasts until your hull is completely on the pre-start side, and your stern was still over
Grey — as soon as any part of your hull is back on the pre-start side you regain your rights
Grey — a port-tack boat keeps clear of a starboard-tack boat whatever the circumstances
questions.why: Rule 21.1: the returning boat keeps clear until her hull is completely on the pre-start side of the line or its extensions.

questions.q: One minute after the start Blue, scored over early, is beating back toward the line on starboard tack. You started correctly and are close-hauled on port, on course to cross her bow. Blue hails "Starboard!". Must you keep clear?

figure.note: Blue is returning to the pre-start side; you have started

options: Yes — rule 10 applies regardless of what either boat is doing, and you are on port
No, but only because Blue failed to hail before you became overlapped
No — while rule 21.1 applies between you, the rules of Section A do not; Blue, returning to start, must keep clear of you
Yes — a boat returning to start may hail for right of way and you must respond
questions.why: Part 2 Section D preamble: when rule 21 applies between two boats, the rules of Section A (10–13) do not; rule 21.1 puts the duty on the returning boat.
questions.ref: RRS 21.1, RRS Part 2 Section D preamble

questions.q: After touching Red at the windward mark you are taking a Two-Turns Penalty. Halfway through your first turn you are on starboard tack, bow pointing at Grey, who is close-hauled on port. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: You are in the middle of your Two-Turns Penalty

options: Grey — a boat doing turns has right of way so that she can complete them promptly
Grey — you are on starboard and rule 10 applies throughout your turns
Both must keep clear of each other equally; neither has right of way during a penalty
You — a boat taking a penalty keeps clear of a boat that is not, whatever tack either boat is on
questions.why: Rule 21.2: a boat taking a penalty keeps clear of one that is not; Section A does not apply between them.

questions.q: Twenty seconds before the start you are early at the committee boat. You back your jib and the boat starts moving astern through the water. Black, close astern of you, is luffing slowly toward the line. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Your jib is backed; you are moving astern

options: You — a boat moving astern through the water by backing a sail keeps clear of a boat that is not
Both equally — before the start there is no right of way at all
Black — before the starting signal no boat may sail into a boat that is holding position
Black — a boat clear astern keeps clear of the boat ahead under rule 12
questions.why: Rule 21.3: a boat moving astern, or sideways to windward, through the water by backing a sail keeps clear of a boat that is not.

questions.q: You hit the leeward mark and start your One-Turn Penalty right away, a length from the mark, while three boats are rounding behind you. Blue, one of them, has to luff to miss you and protests. You say she had to stay clear of a boat doing a penalty. Who is right?

figure.note: You began your turn a length from the mark, in the traffic

options: Nobody — penalty turns are taken outside the rules of Part 2
Blue — a boat taking a penalty keeps clear of others; Blue's duty under rule 23.2 not to interfere applies only "if reasonably possible" and does not give you rights
You — a One-Turn Penalty must be started at once, and other boats must make space for it
You — rule 23.2 forbids interfering with a boat taking a penalty, so Blue had to keep clear
questions.why: Rule 44.2: get well clear before the turns; rule 21.2: a boat taking a penalty keeps clear; rule 23.2 asks others not to interfere only if reasonably possible.

questions.q: Flag I was displayed. You were over the line in the last minute, so you must sail round an end. You are now sailing along the course side of the line toward the pin, then round it, crossing the line's extension. Red is starting correctly on starboard. Until when must you keep clear of her?

figure.note: Flag I; you must round the pin end to return

options: Never — a boat complying with rule 30.1 has right of way so that she can get back quickly
Only while you are on the course side; on the extension of the line rule 21 does not apply
Until your hull is completely on the pre-start side of the line or its extension — the whole way round the end you are a returning boat
Only until you cross the line itself; once past the pin you have normal rights
questions.why: Rule 21.1: a boat sailing toward the pre-start side of the line or its extensions to comply with rule 30.1 keeps clear until her hull is completely there.

questions.q: Fifteen seconds before the starting signal you realise you are already over the line. You bear away and sail back toward the pre-start side on starboard, meeting Grey on port who is coming up to start. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: 15 s before the starting signal

options: You — a boat that is over the line early loses her rights from the moment she crosses it
You — a boat sailing back toward the pre-start side always keeps clear of boats approaching the line
Both — before the start neither boat has right of way
Grey — rule 21.1 applies only after your starting signal; before it the ordinary rules apply, and you are on starboard
questions.why: Rule 21.1 begins with the boat's starting signal; before it, Section A applies — rule 10 puts the duty on the port-tack boat.

questions.q: Crowded start, 10 seconds to go. Holding position at the committee boat, you push your boom out to windward; the boat does not go astern but slides sideways to windward through the water, into the gap where Red is luffing up beside you. Red protests. What rule applies?

figure.note: Your boom is pushed out to windward; you slide sideways toward Red

options: Rule 21.3 — a boat moving sideways to windward through the water by backing a sail must keep clear of a boat that is not; you broke it
Rule 12 — Red was clear astern of you when the contact began
Rule 11 — you were the leeward boat and Red, to windward, had to keep clear of you
No rule — moving sideways is not moving astern, so rule 21.3 did not apply
questions.why: Rule 21.3 (2025 wording): a boat moving astern or sideways to windward through the water by backing a sail keeps clear of a boat that is not.

questions.q: You were OCS, sailed back, and your whole hull is now on the pre-start side; you tack and head for the line again on starboard. Yellow, who was also OCS and is still on the course side returning, converges with you on port. Flag X is still displayed. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: You are starting again; Yellow is still on the course side

options: You — a boat that was OCS keeps clear until the race committee lowers flag X
Yellow — once your hull was completely on the pre-start side your rule 21.1 obligation ended; Yellow is still returning, so she keeps clear of you
Neither owes the other anything — two returning boats have no obligations between them
You — while flag X is displayed every boat that was OCS keeps clear of all other boats
questions.why: Rule 21.1 ends when the hull is completely on the pre-start side; the boat still returning keeps clear of the boat that is no longer doing so.

questions.q: You touched the offset mark and are taking a One-Turn Penalty. During the turn your bow strikes Grey, who was sailing the leg on a steady course and did not alter to avoid you; a stanchion is bent. Who broke which rules?

figure.title: Offset mark, after the rounding
lines: You touched the mark, began a One-Turn Penalty
Grey sailing the leg on a steady course
Your bow hit Grey's side; stanchion bent
Grey did not alter course at all

options: Only you, and only rule 14 — a boat doing turns keeps her normal right of way during them
Only Grey — rule 23.2 forbids interfering with a boat taking a penalty, and she sailed into your turn

You broke rule 21.2 (a boat taking a penalty keeps clear) and rule 14; Grey, as the boat with rights, broke rule 14 too if she could have avoided the contact once it was clear you were not keeping clear
Nobody — a penalty turn is a manoeuvre the other boats must allow for, and damage is a matter for insurance
questions.why: Rule 21.2: the penalised boat keeps clear; rule 14: every boat avoids contact when reasonably possible, and with damage neither boat is exonerated.

questions.q: Two sounds and First Substitute: general recall. Half the fleet turns back toward the pre-start side on starboard; you are among them. Red, on port, is sailing the other way to get a clear look at the pin. She claims you must keep clear as "a boat returning to start". Is she right?

figure.note: General recall signalled; both are on the course side

options: Yes — every boat sailing toward the pre-start side after a starting signal keeps clear of boats not doing so
No — after a general recall no racing rules apply at all until the next warning signal
Yes — after a general recall the whole fleet was over early, so all are bound by rule 21.1
No — after a general recall nobody is returning to start under rule 21.1; the ordinary Part 2 rules apply between boats intending to race, so Red on port keeps clear
questions.why: Rule 21.1 covers a boat returning after her starting signal to start; a general recall cancels that start, and Part 2 applies between boats intending to race.

questions.q: Blue, returning after being OCS, sails on starboard into Black, who has started correctly on port and holds her course to the end. The boats touch; no damage. Black took no avoiding action at all. What does the protest committee decide?

figure.note: Blue returning; Black started and held course

options: Blue broke rule 21.1 and rule 14; Black broke rule 14 but is exonerated because she was the boat with rights and there was no damage or injury
Black is penalised — on port she had to keep clear of a starboard-tack boat, returning or not
Nobody — contact without damage is not a breach of any rule
Both are disqualified — rule 14 applies equally to both boats and both made contact
questions.why: Rule 21.1 and 14 against Blue; rule 43.1(c): a boat with rights that breaks rule 14 is exonerated when the contact causes no damage or injury.

questions.q: Red is clear ahead of you on the run and begins a Two-Turns Penalty for an earlier incident. As she heads up and tacks she comes back across your bow. You are clear astern and sailing straight down the leg. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Red has begun her turns ahead of you

options: You — Red is turning to starboard tack and rule 10 gives her right of way
