Red — a boat taking a penalty keeps clear, and rule 12 does not apply between you while she does so
You — a boat clear astern keeps clear of the boat ahead under rule 12 until she has passed her
Both — the rules require both boats to keep clear during penalty turns
questions.why: Rule 21.2 puts the duty on the penalised boat; the Section D preamble switches off Section A (rules 10–13) between the two boats while rule 21 applies.
questions.ref: RRS 21.2, RRS Part 2 Section D preamble

questions.q: Gusty 18 knots on the run. The ILCA ahead of you broaches and capsizes, mast flat on the water, right in your path. You are on starboard, she was on port. What must you do?

figure.note: A has capsized, mast in the water, directly ahead of you

options: Hold your course — a capsized boat is not racing and has left the race
Hold your course — she was on port tack and must keep clear of you even capsized
Avoid her if possible — a boat shall avoid a capsized boat, whatever tack either was on
Hail "Starboard!" and bear away only if she fails to right herself in time
questions.why: Rule 22: if possible, a boat shall avoid a boat that is capsized or has not regained control after capsizing.

questions.q: Squall on the reach. A 470 ahead of you is knocked flat, gunwale under, the crew hanging from the trapeze in the water, but the mast is still well above the surface. Her helm hails "Capsized — keep off!". Is she a capsized boat under the rules?

figure.title: Squall on the reach
lines: Crew in the water on the trapeze
Masthead well clear of the water

options: Yes — any boat with crew in the water counts as capsized
Yes — a boat heeled past 45° is capsized under the definition
No — only a boat that has turned turtle is capsized under the rules
No — a boat is capsized only when her masthead is in the water; she is a boat under way and the normal rules apply between you
questions.why: Rule 22, last sentence: a boat is capsized when her masthead is in the water.

questions.q: A 29er ahead of you capsized, has just been righted and is upright again, but the helm is still climbing over the gunwale, the sails are flogging and the boat is drifting sideways. You are approaching fast on a reach. Is she still protected by rule 22?

figure.note: A is upright but drifting; helm not yet back aboard

options: Yes — a boat that has not yet regained control after capsizing is still one you must avoid if possible
Yes, but only if she displays a protest flag or hails for room
No — once the crew are back aboard the normal right-of-way rules apply at once
No — the protection ends the moment the boat comes upright
questions.why: Rule 22: avoid, if possible, a boat that is capsized or has not regained control after capsizing.

questions.q: River race, falling tide. Blue has run aground on a sandbank on the inside of the bend and sits heeled over with her keel in the mud. Your course takes you close past her. What are your obligations?

figure.note: Blue is aground on the sandbank

options: Give her room to get off — a boat aground has right of way over boats that are afloat
Avoid her if possible — a boat shall avoid a boat that is aground; she is also an obstruction between you and other boats
None — a boat aground is out of the race and no longer a boat under the rules
Keep clear of her only if she is on starboard tack
questions.why: Rule 22: if possible, avoid a boat that is anchored or aground; being a boat you must avoid, she is an obstruction (definition).

questions.q: The breeze dies to nothing and the ebb starts to carry the fleet backwards past the leeward mark. Red drops an anchor and lies head to tide. A puff comes and you, on port tack, find your course leads straight to her. She was lying with her boom to port. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Red is anchored against the tide; a puff has filled in

options: Red — she is on starboard tack by her boom, so rule 10 applies and you keep clear
Neither — an anchored boat is not racing, and rule 23.1 only asks her not to interfere
You must avoid her if possible — she is anchored, and while rule 22 applies between you the Section A rules do not, so her tack is irrelevant
Red — she must keep clear of boats that are sailing, because anchoring is not allowed while racing
questions.why: Rule 45 allows anchoring; rule 22: avoid an anchored boat if possible; Section D preamble: Section A does not apply while rule 22 applies.
questions.ref: RRS 22, RRS 45, RRS Part 2 Section D preamble

questions.q: Grey sees a windsurfer from another event in the water, clearly exhausted, and stops to hold him up until the rescue boat arrives. You are beating up toward her on starboard; she lies stopped, across your course. What are your obligations, and what can Grey expect afterwards?

figure.note: Grey has stopped to hold up a swimmer in difficulty

options: You must avoid her, but she gets no redress because helping is a personal choice
You keep clear only if she is on starboard; afterwards she can only ask the race committee for a resail
Nothing — a stopped boat is not racing, so she must get out of your way under rule 23.1
You must avoid her if possible — she is helping a person in danger — and Grey may request redress for the places she lost while giving help
questions.why: Rule 22: avoid, if possible, a boat trying to help a person or vessel in danger; rule 1.1 obliges her to help and rule 61.4(b)(4) allows redress.

questions.q: A Laser capsized at the gybe mark is lying on her side, mast on the water, bow pointing to starboard tack. You are approaching on port, could easily go behind her, but hold your course on the theory that she is "not sailing". Your bow touches her hull; no damage. Did you break a rule?

figure.note: A capsized beside the mark; you could pass astern of her

options: Yes — rule 22 required you to avoid her if possible, and rule 14 required you to avoid contact; her former tack is irrelevant
Yes, but only rule 10, because her bow pointed to starboard tack
No — a capsized boat is not a boat under way and cannot be fouled
No — contact without damage is never a breach when the other boat is capsized
questions.why: Rule 22: avoid a capsized boat if possible; rule 14: avoid contact; a capsized boat has no tack obligations, so Section A is not the issue.

questions.q: Twenty-five knots, 49er fleet. White capsizes to leeward of you; in the same gust you capsize too and, while you are both in the water, the wind blows your hull onto hers. Her crew protest you under rule 22. What should happen?

figure.title: 49er fleet, 25 knots
lines: White capsizes to leeward of you
You capsize in the same gust
Your hull blows down onto White's

options: Both boats are penalised — each failed to avoid the other
No penalty — rule 22 requires a boat to avoid a capsized boat only "if possible"; capsized yourself, you could do nothing
You are penalised — rule 22 is absolute and contact with a capsized boat is always a breach
You are penalised unless you took a Two-Turns Penalty immediately after righting
questions.why: Rule 22 applies "if possible"; a boat that is herself capsized and out of control cannot avoid another and breaks no rule.

questions.q: Just before the start Red hails "Room to tack!" to you from close to leeward on starboard, pointing at an anchored motor boat ahead. Having room to spare, you decide to tack rather than reply "You tack". Red shouts that she wanted to keep going on starboard. Did you respond correctly?

figure.note: Red hailed; you choose to tack

options: No — before the starting signal a boat may only reply "You tack", never tack herself
Yes, but only because the hail was made before the starting signal
Yes — tacking as soon as possible is a valid response; the choice between tacking and replying "You tack" belongs to the hailed boat
No — the hailing boat may specify which response she wants, and you must comply
questions.why: Rule 20.2(c): the hailed boat responds either by tacking as soon as possible or by replying "You tack" and giving room — her choice.

questions.q: Blue went aground on a shoal at the edge of the course. Her crew have rowed out a kedge in the dinghy and are winching her off; she is still touching bottom and swinging slowly. You are reaching toward her. Is she still a boat you must avoid under rule 22?

figure.note: Blue is aground and kedging off

options: No — a boat using her anchor to move is breaking rule 42 and has no protection
Yes, but only until her crew get back aboard from the dinghy
No — once a boat starts getting herself off she is sailing again and the normal rules apply
Yes — she is still aground; until she is afloat and under way you must avoid her if possible
questions.why: Rule 22: if possible, avoid a boat that is anchored or aground; the protection lasts while she is in that state.

questions.q: A J/24 from your fleet has anchored in the dying breeze, lying across the leg. You and Blue, overlapped on starboard, approach her; you are inside, nearer the anchored boat, and Blue, to leeward, says she is not going to "give room for someone's parking". Who is right?

figure.note: You are inside, nearer the anchored boat

options: You — both of you must avoid the anchored boat under rule 22, so she is an obstruction to you both, and as outside boat Blue must give you room to pass her
Blue — an anchored boat from your own fleet is a competitor, not an obstruction, so rule 19 is off
Blue — the leeward boat has right of way and the windward boat must find her own way past
Neither — the anchored boat must weigh anchor and keep clear of boats still sailing
questions.why: Definition Obstruction: a boat racing is an obstruction to boats that must avoid her under rule 22; rule 19.2(b): the outside boat gives the inside boat room.

questions.q: Red capsizes to windward of you on the beat; her crew, standing on the centreboard, shouts "Starboard! Keep clear!" as you approach on port. What is your obligation?

figure.note: Red is capsized; her crew hails "Starboard!"

options: To keep clear under rule 10 — she is on starboard tack and her hail confirms it
To avoid her if possible under rule 22 — her tack is irrelevant, because Section A does not apply while rule 22 applies between you
To keep clear under rule 10 only if she rights herself before you reach her
None at all — a capsized boat has no rights and you may pass as close as you like
questions.why: Section D preamble: when rule 22 applies between two boats, Section A does not; rule 22: avoid a capsized boat if possible.
questions.ref: RRS 22, RRS Part 2 Section D preamble

questions.q: Two knots of foul tide and no wind, 200 m from the finish. Grey drops her anchor and lies right in the approach you were drifting along. When a zephyr comes you have to steer round her and lose a place. Can you protest her for anchoring on the course?

figure.note: Grey anchored head to tide in the finishing approach

options: Yes — a boat may anchor only outside the zone of a mark and never on a finishing approach
Yes — anchoring while racing is prohibited by rule 45 unless the sailing instructions allow it
No — a boat may anchor while racing, and you had to avoid her under rule 22; she only had to recover the anchor before continuing, if possible
Yes — an anchored boat that obstructs others must be scored DNF
questions.why: Rule 45 allows a boat to anchor (recovering the anchor before continuing, if possible); rule 22: other boats avoid her if possible.

questions.q: Beating on port, you find a capsized Optimist dead ahead. To avoid her you tack onto starboard — straight into the path of Grey, who is close-hauled on starboard and has to bear away sharply to miss you. Grey protests. Are you exonerated because you were avoiding a capsized boat?

figure.note: A is capsized ahead; you tack into Grey's path

options: No, but Grey is penalised too, for not giving you room to avoid the capsized boat
Yes — rule 22 takes precedence over every other rule of Part 2 whenever a capsized boat is involved
Yes — a boat compelled to change course by an obstruction is exonerated for any resulting breach
No — you broke rule 13 (and 15) against Grey; the capsized boat broke no rule, so rule 43.1(a) gives no exoneration — you should have borne away or tacked earlier
questions.why: Rule 43.1(a) exonerates only a boat compelled to break a rule by another boat's breach; the capsized boat broke nothing, so rules 13 and 15 apply in full.

questions.q: Yellow capsized to windward of the leeward mark, righted, got the crew aboard and is now sailing again, close-hauled on starboard, sheets in and under full control. You come down on port and she hails that you must still avoid her "because she capsized". Must you?

figure.note: Yellow is upright, sailing close-hauled under control

options: You must keep clear of her under rule 10, as of any starboard-tack boat — rule 22 stopped applying when she regained control
No — rule 10 does not apply to a boat that has been capsized within the last two minutes
No — a boat that capsized loses her rights for the rest of the leg
Yes — a boat that has capsized in a race keeps rule 22 protection until she finishes
questions.why: Rule 22 covers a boat that is capsized or has not regained control after capsizing; once she is under control the normal rules return.

questions.q: You have finished, cleared the line, and are sailing back toward the harbour on a reach, straight through the boats still beating up to finish. Red has to tack to avoid you. Did you break a rule?

figure.note: You have finished and cleared the line; Red is still racing

options: No — you were the right-of-way boat under rules 10 and 11 against Red
Yes — a boat not racing shall not interfere with a boat racing if reasonably possible; sail round the fleet
Yes — rule 10, because Red was on starboard tack
No — once you have finished the racing rules no longer apply to you
questions.why: Rule 23.1: if reasonably possible, a boat not racing shall not interfere with a boat that is racing.

questions.q: Your spinnaker halyard breaks and you retire, hoisting nothing and heading home under main. On the way you tack right in front of Blue, who is still racing on the beat and has to duck you. What rule did you break?
options: None — a boat that has retired is outside the rules of Part 2
Rule 13 — a boat that tacks must keep clear of a boat that is not tacking
Rule 23.1 — a boat not racing shall not interfere with a boat racing if reasonably possible
Rule 42 — a retired boat may not sail through the racing area
questions.why: Rule 23.1: if reasonably possible, a boat not racing shall not interfere with a boat that is racing.

questions.q: Two fleets on the same course. You are running on port in the second fleet; the first fleet is beating up toward you on their last leg. You hold your proper course straight down the run, forcing a couple of their starboard-tack boats to go round you. Did you break rule 23.2?

figure.note: You run on your proper course; A and B are a different fleet, beating

options: No — rule 23.2 applies only between boats of the same fleet
Yes — a boat on another leg must always give way to boats beating
Yes — rule 23.2 forbids any interference with boats on another leg, proper course or not
No — after the starting signal rule 23.2 does not apply to a boat sailing her proper course; you still owe rule 10 to starboard-tack boats
questions.why: Rule 23.2: do not interfere with a boat on another leg if reasonably possible — but after the starting signal not when sailing your proper course.

questions.q: Club series: the Optimists started ten minutes before you and are on their run as you beat up. One of them is a clubmate you want to tease, so you sail well above your course to sit on her wind for a while. Harmless?
options: No — you interfered with a boat on another leg while not sailing your proper course; rule 23.2 does not excuse that
Yes — boats on different legs may do anything short of contact
Yes — the proper-course exception covers whatever course you choose after the start
No — rule 2, fair sailing, is the only rule you broke
questions.why: Rule 23.2: do not interfere with a boat on another leg if reasonably possible; after the start the exception covers only a boat sailing her proper course.

questions.q: Blue fouled you at the windward mark and sails off to one side to do her turns. You follow her and sail close to her so that she cannot complete her turns without hitting you. Allowed?
options: No — it breaks rule 21.2, which forbids others from approaching a penalised boat
No — if reasonably possible, a boat shall not interfere with a boat that is taking a penalty
Yes — rule 23 applies only between boats on different legs
Yes — the penalised boat must keep clear of you, so where you sail is your business
questions.why: Rule 23.2: if reasonably possible, a boat shall not interfere with a boat that is taking a penalty.

questions.q: Championship, two classes. The J/70s' warning signal is in twelve minutes; you (a J/70) are sailing near the committee boat while the Melges 24s are finishing their first race. (1) Right now, and (2) once your preparatory signal has gone — which rule limits you toward the finishing Melges?

figure.title: Two classes, one committee boat
lines: You (J/70) sailing near the finishing line

options: Rule 23.1 in both cases — you are not racing until your starting signal
Neither — boats of a different class owe nothing to each other under the racing rules
(1) Rule 23.1 — you are not yet racing and must not interfere with them if reasonably possible; (2) rule 23.2 — you are racing on another leg, with no proper-course exception before your start
Rule 23.2 in both cases, and after your preparatory signal you may sail any course since you have a proper course
questions.why: Definition Racing: from the preparatory signal; rule 23.1 covers a boat not racing, 23.2 a boat on another leg (proper-course exception only after the start).

questions.q: Black was OCS and is beating back toward the line. You have started correctly and, although it is not your fastest course, you tack on her wind twice to slow her down before she gets back. Black protests. Decision?

figure.note: You have tacked onto Black's wind as she returns

options: No breach — after the starting signal rule 23.2 never applies
You broke rule 21.1 — covering a returning boat counts as sailing toward the pre-start side
No breach — a returning boat keeps clear of you, so you may sail wherever you like
You broke rule 23.2 — a boat shall not interfere with a boat subject to rule 21.1 if reasonably possible, and you were not sailing your proper course
questions.why: Rule 23.2: do not interfere with a boat subject to rule 21.1 if reasonably possible; the proper-course exception did not cover tacking on her wind.

questions.q: You cross the finishing line at the pin end and immediately bear away to clear it, but before you are past the pin mark Blue, finishing behind you on starboard, is on a collision course with you (you are now on port). Blue says you must keep clear under rule 23.1 as a boat that is no longer racing. Is she right about the rule?

figure.note: You have finished but not yet cleared the pin; Blue is finishing

options: No — you are still racing until you have cleared the finishing line and marks, so the ordinary rules apply: you keep clear of Blue under rule 10, not under rule 23.1
Yes, and in addition rule 10 applies, so you are doubly obliged to keep clear
Yes — a boat stops racing the moment she finishes, and from then on rule 23.1 alone applies to her
No — a boat that has finished has right of way over boats still finishing
questions.why: Definition Racing: a boat is racing until she finishes and clears the finishing line and marks; until then Part 2 applies as usual and rule 23.1 does not.

questions.q: You retired after a gear failure and are sailing home through a crowded leeward-mark rounding of another fleet. Boxed in by boats on both sides and a committee RIB astern, you cannot avoid forcing one of them to alter course slightly. That boat protests you under rule 23.1. Likely outcome?

figure.title: Retired, sailing home
lines: Crowded leeward mark of another fleet
You boxed in: boats both sides, RIB astern
One racing boat alters course slightly

options: Disqualification — a boat not racing must never interfere with a racing boat, whatever the circumstances
No penalty if the protest committee finds that avoiding the interference was not reasonably possible — rule 23.1 is limited to what is reasonably possible
No penalty — rule 23.1 cannot be the subject of a protest by a boat
A Two-Turns Penalty, which you must take even though you have retired
questions.why: Rule 23.1 applies "if reasonably possible"; whether avoidance was reasonably possible is a question of fact for the protest committee.

questions.q: After finishing race 2 and clearing the line, Grey sails back through the fleet still racing and forces several boats to alter course. A protest under rule 23.1 is upheld. Grey argues that she cannot be penalised because she was not racing. To which race does the penalty apply?

figure.title: Protest: Grey, rule 23.1
lines: Grey finished race 2 and cleared the line
Sailed back through the racing fleet
Several boats forced to alter course
Protest upheld; Grey: "I was not racing"

options: None — a boat that is not racing cannot be penalised under the racing rules
The next race she sails, because the penalty must affect a future result
To the race sailed nearest in time to the incident — here race 2; a breach while not racing is penalised in that race
All races of the day, because the breach was not tied to any single race
questions.why: Rule 60.5(c): when a boat has broken a rule while not racing, her penalty applies to the race sailed nearest in time to the incident.

questions.q: Running on port on your proper course, you meet a boat from the earlier fleet close-hauled on starboard. You hold on, telling your crew that rule 23.2 lets a boat on her proper course ignore boats on other legs. She has to bear away to avoid you. Who broke a rule?

figure.note: A is from the earlier fleet, beating on starboard

options: She did — a boat on another leg must keep clear of a boat sailing her proper course
Nobody — between boats on different legs only rule 23.2 applies, and you met it
She did — a beating boat always keeps clear of a running boat
You — rule 23.2's proper-course exception only removes the duty not to interfere; rule 10 still requires a port-tack boat to keep clear
questions.why: Rule 23.2 limits interference between boats on different legs; it does not switch off Section A — rule 10 still applies between opposite-tack boats.

questions.q: Red was over the line at the start, never went back and knows she will be scored OCS, but sails the whole course anyway. On the second beat she meets you, port against her starboard, and you claim she must keep clear as "a boat that is not really racing". Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Red was OCS and did not return; both are on the second beat

options: You — Red is still racing until she finishes or retires; being OCS does not change her rights, so rule 10 applies and you keep clear
Red — a boat that will be scored OCS has no rights against boats that started correctly
Red — she is subject to rule 21.1 for the rest of the race because she never returned
Neither — a boat that did not start is not covered by Part 2 at all
questions.why: Definition Racing: a boat races from her preparatory signal until she finishes and clears the line or retires; scoring OCS later does not change Part 2.

questions.q: Black flag start. Yellow was in the triangle in the last minute, the race was recalled, and her sail number is displayed: she is BFD. Instead of leaving the course area she hangs around the line and tacks through the next fleet's start, forcing boats to alter course. Which rules has she broken?

figure.title: Black flag start, general recall
lines: Yellow in the triangle in the last minute
Tacks through the next fleet's start

options: None — a boat that has been disqualified may sail wherever she likes
Rule 30.4 (she had to leave the course area) and rule 23.1 — a boat not racing shall not interfere with boats racing, if reasonably possible
Only rule 21.1 — she is still a boat that started early and is returning
Only rule 30.4 — a disqualified boat is outside the rules of Part 2
questions.why: Rule 30.4: a boat disqualified under the black flag leaves the course area; rule 23.1: a boat not racing does not interfere with racing boats if she can.

questions.q: You have retired with a torn mainsail and are motoring back across the racing area. The fleet is still beating toward you. Which rule tells you how to behave toward them, and what does it say?
options: None — under engine you are a power-driven vessel and only the COLREGs apply to you
Rule 10 — racing boats on port must keep clear of you, and you of those on starboard
Rule 23.1 — a boat not racing shall not interfere with a boat racing if reasonably possible; motor round the fleet, not through it
Rule 22 — a boat under engine is treated like a boat anchored, and others must avoid you
questions.why: Rule 23.1 covers any boat not racing, under sail or power: if reasonably possible, do not interfere with a boat that is racing.

questions.q: Hobie 16 fleet reaching on port in 18 knots toward an anchored fishing boat. You come up from clear astern of White and get an overlap on her inside, four lengths before the fishing boat, with plenty of water between them. White holds her line and says she owes nothing to a boat that came from astern. Is she right?

figure.note: You got the inside overlap four lengths before the fishing boat

options: Yes — rule 19 applies only to boats that were overlapped at the start of the leg
No — but she must only give you room if you hail for it before reaching the fishing boat
Yes — a boat that establishes an overlap from clear astern is never entitled to room at an obstruction
No — the fishing boat is not a continuing obstruction, you were overlapped in time, and White was able to give room from the moment the overlap began, so she must
questions.why: Rule 19.2(b): the outside boat gives room unless unable since the overlap began; 19.2(c) limits overlaps from astern only at a continuing obstruction.

questions.q: Blue was over the line at the gun but has not noticed flag X and simply sails on up the beat on starboard. You, on port, having started correctly, consider ducking her unnecessary because "she is OCS and must keep clear". Must you keep clear?

figure.note: Blue was OCS but is sailing on up the beat

options: Yes — rule 21.1 applies only to a boat sailing back toward the pre-start side; Blue is not returning, so she has her normal rights under rule 10
Yes, but only because you did not hail "OCS" to her
No — a boat that was over the line keeps clear of all boats until the race committee lowers flag X
No — an OCS boat keeps clear of boats that started correctly for the whole first leg
questions.why: Rule 21.1 binds a boat sailing toward the pre-start side to start; a boat OCS who sails on is not doing that, and Section A applies normally.

questions.q: On the run you could have steered round a capsized Laser but cut it fine and brushed her hull; no damage, nobody hurt. You know you broke rule 22. What can you do on the water?
options: Retire — contact with a capsized boat always requires retirement
Take a Two-Turns Penalty promptly after getting well clear — rule 22 is a rule of Part 2, so rule 44.1 applies
Nothing — a breach of rule 22 can only be dealt with by a protest committee hearing
Take a One-Turn Penalty, as for touching a mark
questions.why: Rule 44.1: a boat that may have broken one or more rules of Part 2 may take a Two-Turns Penalty; rule 22 is in Part 2 Section D.

questions.q: The sailing instructions make the long harbour breakwater a mark, to be left to starboard on the way out. You and Grey, both on port, sail along it a length off; Grey is clear ahead. You get an overlap between her and the breakwater where there is not room for a boat. Grey holds her course. Who is right?

figure.note: The breakwater is both a continuing obstruction and a mark

options: Grey, but only because you failed to hail for room before becoming overlapped
You — a mark that boats must leave on the same side is governed by rule 18 and you were overlapped before the end of it
Grey — at a continuing obstruction rule 19 applies and rule 18 does not, even if the obstruction is also a mark; from clear astern with no room you get no entitlement
You — rule 18.2(a) protects the inside boat as soon as she is overlapped within the zone of a mark
questions.why: Rule 19.1, last sentence: at a continuing obstruction rule 19 always applies and rule 18 does not; rule 19.2(c) then denies room to the boat from astern.

questions.q: You are pinching hard, well above a normal close-hauled course, trying to clear a headland on port tack, with Blue overlapped close to windward. It is not going to work, so you hail "Room to tack!". Blue says the hail is invalid because you were "not close-hauled". Is she right?

figure.note: You are pinching above close-hauled toward the headland

options: No — the point of sailing is irrelevant; any boat may hail for room to tack at an obstruction
Yes — a boat that is pinching has already changed course substantially, so no further change is needed
Yes — a boat must be exactly on a close-hauled course when she hails
No — the rule allows the hail when sailing close-hauled or above; pinching above close-hauled still qualifies, and Blue must respond
questions.why: Rule 20.1(b): the hailing boat must be sailing close-hauled or above; rule 20.2(b)–(c): the hailed boat responds.

questions.q: Wednesday evening club race, a mixed fleet of ILCA 7s. You are reaching behind the line when the committee boat hoists the class flag with one sound. The notice of race says nothing unusual about the starting sequence. What has just happened and when is your start?
options: That was the warning signal — the starting signal comes 5 minutes later
That was the one-minute signal — start your watch for 60 seconds
That was the preparatory signal — the starting signal comes 4 minutes later
That was the starting signal — the class flag goes up when the race starts
questions.why: Rule 26: the class flag with one sound is the warning signal, 5 minutes before the start unless the NoR or SI say otherwise.

questions.q: A 470 national championship, 25 knots and waves. Four minutes before the start the committee boat hoists flag P with one sound. Your crew says the rules of Part 2 don't bite yet because the race hasn't started. From which moment are you actually racing, with everything that implies for penalties?

figure.title: Four minutes to go
lines: Flag P hoisted with one sound

options: From the warning signal five minutes before the start, when the class flag went up
From this preparatory signal — a boat is racing from her preparatory signal until she finishes and clears the line
From the starting signal — before it you are not racing and cannot be penalised
From the moment you cross the starting line after the starting signal
questions.why: Definition Racing: a boat is racing from her preparatory signal; rule 26: the preparatory flag is P, I, Z, U or black.

questions.q: Lake regatta, J/24s, a light 6-knot breeze. You see flag P come down on the committee boat and hear one long sound. The class flag is still flying. How long until your starting signal?
options: Zero — the long sound is the starting signal; cross the line now
Four minutes — the preparatory flag comes down four minutes before the start
One minute — lowering the preparatory flag with one long sound is the one-minute signal
Five minutes — the long sound restarts the sequence from the warning
questions.why: Rule 26: the preparatory flag is removed one minute before the start with one long sound.

questions.q: Saronic Gulf, a cruiser-racer regatta. You are hovering a boat length below the line. The class flag is lowered on the committee boat and you hear one sound. Flag P came down a minute ago. What does this signal mean?
options: It is a general recall — everybody returns behind the line
It is a postponement — the class flag down means wait for a new sequence
It is the one-minute signal — the sequence ends in 60 seconds
It is the starting signal — the class flag removed with one sound
questions.why: Rule 26: at 0 minutes the class flag is removed with one sound — that is the starting signal.

questions.q: Your crew on a Melges 24 missed the sequence while sorting a halyard. You look up: the preparatory flag came down 20 seconds ago, the class flag is still flying, no other flags. How long do you have until the starting signal?
options: 40 seconds — the preparatory flag comes down at one minute, so the start is 40 seconds away
You cannot tell — only the sound signals give the time
4 minutes 40 seconds — the preparatory flag comes down at five minutes
3 minutes 40 seconds — the preparatory flag comes down at four minutes
questions.why: Rule 26: the preparatory flag is removed at 1 minute; 60 s minus 20 s leaves 40 s to the start.

questions.q: A trapezoid course off Bodrum. Your timer shows that the class flag went up exactly 2 minutes 30 seconds ago. Flag P is still flying. With the standard sequence, how long to the start and when will P come down?

figure.title: Your timer
lines: Class flag up 2 min 30 s ago

options: 3 minutes 30 seconds to the start; flag P comes down in 2 minutes 30 seconds
2 minutes 30 seconds to the start; flag P comes down in 1 minute 30 seconds
2 minutes 30 seconds to the start; flag P comes down at the starting signal
1 minute 30 seconds to the start; flag P comes down in 30 seconds
questions.why: Rule 26: warning at 5 min, preparatory flag down at 1 min — 5:00 minus 2:30 is 2:30, and P drops 1:30 from now.

questions.q: A windy start on a river. You see flag P come down on the committee boat but hear no horn — the air horn has failed. Your helm says the sequence is void without the sound. What is the correct position?
options: Nothing has happened — a signal without its sound has no effect
The one-minute signal counts only if the race committee hails the time instead
The start is one minute away — times are taken from the visual signals and the absence of a sound is disregarded
The sequence is void — the race committee must postpone and restart the sequence
questions.why: Rule 26: times shall be taken from the visual signals; the absence of a sound signal shall be disregarded.

questions.q: Palma, a 36-ft cruiser-racer. Your stopwatch, started at the warning, reads 5:00 and you hear a horn from a neighbouring boat, but the class flag is still flying on the committee boat. Your tactician shouts "Go!". Have you been given the starting signal?
options: Yes — five minutes after the warning the race has started whatever the flag shows
Yes — any sound signal at the expected time is the starting signal
No — the start is only when the committee boat hails "Start" on the radio
No — the starting signal is the removal of the class flag; a horn without it is not the start
questions.why: Rule 26: times are taken from the visual signals; the starting signal is the class flag being removed.

questions.q: Two fleets at a lake championship: ILCA 7 then 470. At 12:00:00 the ILCA class flag comes down with one sound and, at the same moment, the 470 class flag goes up with another sound. A 470 sailor complains that two signals cannot be made at once. Is the committee right?

lines: ILCA class flag lowered, one sound

options: Yes — the warning signal of a following class is made with or after the starting signal of the preceding class
Yes, but only if both classes share the same preparatory flag
No — the next class's warning signal can only be made after its preparatory signal
No — the warning signal of the next class must wait at least one minute after the previous start
questions.why: Rule 26: the warning signal for each succeeding class shall be made with or after the starting signal of the preceding class.

questions.q: Four minutes before the start of a 29er fleet the committee boat hoists flag I instead of flag P. Your crew asks what changes for you compared with a normal P-flag start.
options: If you are over in the last minute you are disqualified without a hearing
If any part of your hull is on the course side in the last minute, you must sail round an end of the line to the pre-start side before starting
Nothing — flag I is just another preparatory flag; you may dip back across the line if you are over
If you are over in the last minute you get a 20 % scoring penalty without a hearing
questions.why: Rule 30.1: under flag I a boat on the course side in the last minute must sail across an extension of the line to the pre-start side before she starts.

questions.q: Big fleet of Optimists at a national event. At the preparatory signal the committee boat displays flag Z. Your coach asked you yesterday to know every preparatory flag. Which rule is now in force?
options: Rule 30.1 — a boat over in the last minute must return round an end
Rule 30.4 — disqualification that survives a general recall
Rule 30.2 — a 20 % scoring penalty for a boat in the triangle in the last minute
Rule 30.3 — disqualification unless the race is restarted or resailed
questions.why: Race signals: flag Z means rule 30.2 is in effect.

questions.q: After two general recalls of a 90-boat ILCA 6 fleet the committee boat shows a black rectangular flag as the preparatory signal. What does it mean for the last minute before the start?
options: Rule 30.2 applies — a boat over in the last minute gets a 20 % scoring penalty
Rule 30.1 applies — a boat over in the last minute must round an end to return
Rule 30.3 applies — disqualification only if this attempt is not recalled
Rule 30.4 applies — a boat identified in the triangle in the last minute is disqualified without a hearing, even if the race is recalled again
questions.why: Race signals: the black flag means rule 30.4 is in effect — the penalty survives a general recall.

questions.q: Split regatta, 20 knots. At four minutes the committee boat hoists flag U with one sound. A crew member who sails only club races asks what the U flag does.
options: Rule 30.3 — a boat in the triangle in the last minute is disqualified without a hearing unless the race is restarted or resailed
Rule 30.2 — a 20 % scoring penalty without a hearing
Rule 30.4 — disqualification that stands even after a general recall
Rule 30.1 — a boat over in the last minute must return round an end of the line
questions.why: Race signals: flag U means rule 30.3 is in effect.

questions.q: The notice of race for a J/70 event says: "Races will be started using rule 26 with the warning signal made 3 minutes before the starting signal." At 13:57:00 your class flag goes up with one sound. When is your start?
options: The sequence is invalid — rule 26 cannot be changed by the notice of race
14:00:00 — the notice of race may change the 5-minute interval, and the rest of the sequence is as in rule 26
14:02:00 — the warning is always 5 minutes before the start
13:58:00 — with a 3-minute warning the preparatory signal is the start
questions.why: Rule 26: the warning signal is 5 minutes before the start "or as stated in the notice of race or sailing instructions".

questions.q: Two minutes before your warning signal the wind drops to 3 knots. The committee boat hoists flag AP with two sounds. Your helm wants to head for the harbour for coffee. What does the signal tell you?

figure.title: Two minutes before the warning
lines: No pennant or other flag under it

options: Races are abandoned; the sequence will restart one hour later
The race is postponed and further signals will be made ashore
Races not started are postponed; the warning signal will be made one minute after AP is lowered — stay near the line
Racing is over for today — you may go ashore
questions.why: Race signals, AP: races not started are postponed; the warning signal will be made 1 minute after removal unless postponed again or abandoned.

questions.q: A Dragon regatta on a windless morning. Flag AP has been flying for an hour. At 11:40:00 it is lowered with one sound. Assuming the standard sequence, when is the warning signal and when is the start?
options: Warning at 11:40:00, start at 11:45:00
Warning at 11:41:00, start at 11:45:00
Warning at 11:45:00, start at 11:50:00
Warning at 11:41:00, start at 11:46:00
questions.why: Race signals, AP: the warning signal is made 1 minute after AP is lowered; rule 26: the start is 5 minutes after the warning.

questions.q: The first start of the day is scheduled for 11:00. At 10:30 the committee boat ashore shows AP over numeral pennant 2 with two sounds. What does the race committee mean?
options: Races are postponed 2 hours — the scheduled start is now 13:00
Two more general recalls will be followed by a black-flag start
Races are postponed for 2 minutes after the flag is lowered
Race 2 is postponed; race 1 will be started on time
questions.why: Race signals: AP over a numeral pennant 1–9 postpones races by that many hours from the scheduled starting time.
questions.ref: RRS race signals (AP over numeral pennant)

questions.q: After waiting all afternoon for wind, you see the committee boat hoist flag AP over flag A with two sounds. What should the fleet do?
options: Stay near the line — the warning signal comes one minute after the flags are lowered
Go ashore — races not started are postponed and there will be no more racing today
Listen on the VHF — further signals will be made by radio in one hour
Return to the starting area — all races in progress are abandoned and will be resailed
questions.why: Race signals: AP over A means races not started are postponed and no more racing today.

questions.q: Thunderstorms are forecast. Before the first warning signal the committee boat displays AP over H with two sounds and starts her engine. What are you being told?
options: Races are postponed; the warning signal will come one minute after the flags are lowered
All boats must return to the harbour and the race is abandoned
Races not started are postponed and further signals will be made ashore — go in and watch the official notice board
Races are postponed and there will be no more racing today
questions.why: Race signals: AP over H means races not started are postponed; further signals ashore.

questions.q: Ten minutes into the first beat of a club race the wind swings 60° and dies. A mark boat passes the fleet with flag N and you hear three sounds. What does the signal mean for you?

figure.title: On the first beat
lines: Flag N on a committee vessel

options: The course is shortened — finish at the next mark and the race will be scored
Racing is over for today — all races are abandoned and you may go ashore
Your race continues; only the classes that have not yet started are postponed
All races in progress are abandoned — return to the starting area; a warning signal will follow one minute after N is lowered
questions.why: Race signals, N: all races that have started are abandoned, return to the starting area; the warning signal follows 1 minute after N is lowered.

questions.q: A squall line arrives during the second race and the committee boat shows N over A with three sounds. What now?
options: All races in progress are abandoned and there is no more racing today — head for the harbour
The race is abandoned; a new warning signal will be made one minute after the flags come down
The race is abandoned; further signals will be made ashore
Only the race in progress is abandoned; the next race starts as scheduled
questions.why: Race signals: N over A means all races abandoned, no more racing today.

questions.q: During a Hobie 16 race a thick fog bank rolls in. The committee boat shows N over H with three sounds. What has the race committee decided?
options: All races are abandoned and there will be no more racing today
All races in progress are abandoned; further signals will be made ashore
The race continues but the next leg is changed; watch for the new bearing
The race is abandoned; the warning signal will be made one minute after the flags are lowered
questions.why: Race signals: N over H means all races abandoned, further signals ashore.

questions.q: You are sailing to the starting area for a Star-class race when the committee boat hoists flag L and sounds a horn. Nothing is posted on the notice board you can see. What should you do?
options: Start your watch — flag L is the warning signal for the first class
Wear your personal flotation device — flag L means the safety rule is in force
Come within hail of the committee boat or follow her — afloat, flag L means that
Return to the harbour — flag L means racing is cancelled for the day
questions.why: Race signals: flag L afloat means "come within hail or follow this vessel"; ashore it means a notice to competitors has been posted.

questions.q: At the warning signal of a 470 race in 25 knots, the committee boat also hoists flag Y with one sound. One of your crew has unclipped his buoyancy aid to adjust his trapeze harness. What does flag Y require?
options: Personal flotation devices are recommended but not compulsory until the start
Flag Y is the preparatory signal — nothing to do with buoyancy aids
Only the helm must wear a personal flotation device; the crew may choose
Everyone must wear a personal flotation device at all times during this race, except briefly while changing or adjusting clothing or personal equipment
questions.why: Rule 40.2(a): flag Y with one sound before or with the warning signal makes rule 40.1 apply for that race; rule 27.1 lets the RC signal it.

questions.q: The sailing instructions say: "The starting line is between a staff displaying an orange flag on the committee boat and the course side of the port-end mark." You are lining up on starboard near the committee boat. Where exactly is the line at the committee-boat end?

figure.note: Line from the pin to the orange-flag staff on the RC boat

options: At the staff with the orange flag — not at the committee boat's bow or stern
At the stern of the committee boat, where the race officer stands
Anywhere alongside the committee boat — she is a mark, so any part of her counts
At the bow of the committee boat, the nearest point to the course
questions.why: Race signals: the orange flag on a staff marks one end of the starting line; the SI define the line from that staff.

questions.q: Thirty seconds before the warning signal of a windward–leeward race the committee boat swaps the course board from "W2" to "W3" and sounds a horn. A competitor near you protests loudly that the course cannot be changed once boats are on the water. Who is right?
options: The competitor — the course may only be changed by the sailing instructions, never by a signal
The race committee — it may replace one course signal with another no later than the warning signal
The competitor — the course is fixed once the first boat has left the harbour
The race committee, but only if it also postpones and starts a new sequence
questions.why: Rule 27.1: no later than the warning signal the RC shall signal the course if not in the SI, and may replace one course signal with another.

questions.q: Three minutes before the start of a J/24 race — after the preparatory signal — the pin-end mark boat picks up the pin and re-lays it 40 m further to windward because the line was badly skewed. You had set up for the old pin. Was the race committee entitled to do this?
options: Yes — the race committee may move a starting mark at any time before the starting signal
Yes — the race committee may move a starting mark until one minute before the start
No — a starting mark may be moved no later than the preparatory signal; if the move made your score significantly worse you may request redress
No — a starting mark may never be moved after the warning signal
questions.why: Rule 27.2: the RC may move a starting mark no later than the preparatory signal; an improper action is a ground for redress under 61.4(b)(1).

questions.q: Thirty seconds before the start of a Dragon race the wind shifts 40° to the right, turning the first leg into a fetch. The committee boat hoists AP with two sounds. Your tactician says the race committee cannot postpone once the preparatory signal has been made. Is she right?
options: No — but the race committee must first finish the sequence and then recall the fleet
Yes — a postponement in the last minute is only allowed for a safety reason
Yes — after the preparatory signal the race may only be abandoned, not postponed
No — before the starting signal the race committee may postpone for any reason, including a shift that spoils the beat
questions.why: Rule 27.3: before the starting signal the RC may for any reason postpone (AP, AP over H or AP over A with two sounds) or abandon the race.

questions.q: Ten seconds before the start of an Optimist race the committee boat notices the windward mark has broken free and is drifting away. It displays flag N with three sounds. One coach shouts that the race should have been started and shortened later. Which action was correct?
options: Flag N — before the starting signal the race committee may abandon the race for any reason, with three sounds
Start the race and then abandon it — abandonment is only possible after the starting signal
Flag M on the committee boat — the committee boat becomes the windward mark
AP — a race may only be postponed, not abandoned, before its start
questions.why: Rule 27.3: before the starting signal the RC may abandon the race for any reason by displaying N, N over H or N over A with three sounds.

questions.q: P-flag start in a 20-boat Melges 24 fleet. At the gun your bow is half a metre over the line. You bear away, cross back behind the line until the whole hull is on the pre-start side, then harden up and cross again. Have you started?

figure.note: Over at the gun, back below the line, up again

options: Yes — you started at the gun; the second crossing was unnecessary
Yes — you started the moment your hull crossed the line the second time, having been entirely on the pre-start side after the starting signal
No — you started the first time you crossed, but you are OCS and cannot cure it
No — once over the line at the gun you must sail round an end of the line before you can start
questions.why: Definition Start: a boat starts when her hull crosses the line from the pre-start side after being entirely on that side at or after the starting signal.

questions.q: You sail a sportsboat with a 1.5-m fixed bowsprit. At the starting signal the bowsprit is clearly across the line but the stem of the hull is 30 cm behind it. The committee boat shows no flag X. A rival hails that you were over. Were you?

figure.note: Bowsprit over, hull behind at the gun

options: No, but only because the committee boat did not display flag X
Yes — the bowsprit is part of the hull for the purpose of starting
No — the definition of Start and rule 29.1 refer to the hull; a bowsprit or crew across the line does not make you OCS
Yes — any part of the boat or her equipment over the line at the signal makes her OCS
questions.why: Definition Start / rule 29.1: it is the hull that must be behind the line at the starting signal — not equipment or crew.

questions.q: Crowded committee-boat end, 30 knots, a 36-ft cruiser-racer. Squeezed out at the gun, you pass to windward of the committee boat — outside the line — and then bear away onto the first beat. Your hull was entirely behind the line's extension at the signal. Have you started?

figure.note: You passed outside the RC boat at the gun

options: Yes — you were on the pre-start side at the signal and are now on the course side
Yes — passing outside the committee boat is a legal "round-the-end" start
No — and because you passed the committee boat you must take a one-turn penalty before returning
No — to start you must cross the starting line itself between its ends; sail back to the pre-start side and cross the line properly
questions.why: Definition Start, rule 28.1: a boat starts by crossing the starting line from the pre-start side; sailing round the committee boat does not start her.

questions.q: P-flag start, a river with current pushing the fleet over. You are OCS at the gun near the middle of a 300-m line and flag X goes up. What is the quickest legal way to start?

figure.note: Flag X is up; you were over at the gun

options: Sail back across the line by any route until your hull is entirely on the pre-start side, keeping clear of boats that are starting correctly, then start
Keep racing — flag X is only a warning and the committee may accept your start
Take a two-turns penalty on the course side and carry on racing
Sail round the pin or the committee boat to the pre-start side — dipping back across the line is not allowed
questions.why: Under flag P a recalled boat may return across the line (definition Start); rule 21.1: while returning she keeps clear of boats not doing so.

questions.q: Club race, 40 Lasers. After the start flag X is displayed with one sound, but the race officer hails only "4471 and 1823". Your number is 2206 and you were over too. Your friend says you are fine because you were not called. Must you return?
options: No — only boats whose sail numbers are hailed are recalled
Yes — flag X with one sound is the individual recall; the race committee is not required to hail sail numbers, and the duty to start correctly is yours
No — if the race committee hails some numbers and not yours, it has accepted your start
Yes, but only if the hail was made within 30 seconds of the starting signal
questions.why: Rule 29.1 requires only flag X with one sound; hailing numbers is not required, and a boat that does not start correctly is scored OCS.

questions.q: You know you were over at the start of an ILCA 7 race and flag X is flying. You decide to "see what happens" and keep sailing. Four minutes after the starting signal flag X comes down. Your training partner says the committee has now accepted everyone who is still on the course. Is that right?
options: Yes — lowering flag X means all recalled boats have returned or been accepted
Yes — after 4 minutes an OCS boat can no longer be penalised
No — flag X must come down no later than 4 minutes after the start regardless of who has returned; you will be scored OCS
No — but you may still return and start until the first boat reaches the windward mark
questions.why: Rule 29.1: flag X is displayed until all recalled boats have returned, but no later than 4 minutes after the start; a boat that did not start is scored OCS.

questions.q: Two classes start five minutes apart. After the first start flag X is hoisted for several OCS boats. Three minutes after that start, with two boats still not back, the race committee lowers flag X. One of them later asks for redress, saying the flag was taken down too early. Was it?
options: Yes — flag X must stay up for a full 4 minutes after the starting signal
No — flag X may be lowered at any time once the first boat has been identified
Yes — flag X must stay up until every recalled boat has returned
No — flag X comes down no later than 4 minutes after the start or 1 minute before the next starting signal, whichever is earlier; here that is 3 minutes
questions.why: Rule 29.1: flag X stays up until all have returned, but no later than 4 min after the start or 1 min before any later starting signal, whichever is earlier.

questions.q: Pin-end start in a 60-boat Optimist fleet. You are sure your bow was a metre over at the signal, but no flag X is displayed and no sound is made — the committee did not see you. What should you do?
options: Go back and start correctly — until you do, you have not started; if you carry on, you have not sailed the course and should retire
Take a two-turns penalty when convenient; that cures a starting error
Keep racing and tell the race committee after finishing so it can add a 20 % penalty
Keep racing — without flag X you have started correctly by definition
questions.why: Definition Start, rule 28.1: a boat over at the signal has not started until she returns and crosses again; the flag is the RC's duty, starting is hers.
questions.ref: RRS definition Start, RRS 28.1, Basic Principle Sportsmanship

questions.q: The results of race 3 show you OCS. You are certain you were behind the line — your crew filmed the start from the bow. You ask the race office for a protest hearing against the race committee. What is the right procedure?

figure.title: Results, race 3
lines: You believe you were behind the line

options: Protest the race committee under rule 60 — a protest form with a red flag is required
Request redress within the time limit — the race committee scores OCS without a hearing, and a wrong scoring is an improper action to be corrected through redress
Nothing can be done — a scoring decision of the race committee is final
Ask the race committee to hold a hearing on the water with the two boats nearest you as witnesses
questions.why: Rule A5: the RC scores OCS without a hearing; rule 61.4(b)(1): an improper action or omission of the RC is remedied through a request for redress.

questions.q: You were OCS and are sailing back to the pre-start side on port tack after the starting signal. Blue, who started correctly, is close-hauled on starboard and heading for you. Who must keep clear?

figure.note: You are returning after the gun; Blue has started

options: Both equally — the port–starboard rule is suspended while boats are returning
Blue — a boat that has started is clear ahead in the race and must give room to boats behind her
You — a boat sailing toward the pre-start side to start keeps clear of a boat that is not doing so, until her hull is entirely on the pre-start side
Blue — she must keep clear of a boat that is returning to start, as she would of a boat taking a penalty
questions.why: Rule 21.1: a boat sailing toward the pre-start side after her starting signal keeps clear of a boat not doing so until her hull is entirely on that side.

questions.q: You were OCS, returned and are now entirely on the pre-start side, sailing close-hauled on starboard tack towards the line to start. Red, who was late to the line, is approaching on port tack and hails "You were over — keep clear of me!" Who keeps clear now?

figure.note: You are fully back below the line

options: Red, but only because she hailed; without the hail you would have to keep clear
You — a boat that was OCS keeps clear of all other boats until she has started
You — a boat that was OCS must keep clear until she has crossed the line and cleared it
Red — rule 21.1 stopped applying to you when your hull was entirely on the pre-start side; you are now simply a starboard-tack boat under rule 10
questions.why: Rule 21.1 applies only until the returning boat's hull is entirely on the pre-start side; after that the ordinary Part 2 rules apply — here rule 10.

questions.q: A 90-boat ILCA 6 start. Right after the starting signal the committee boat hoists a yellow-and-blue triangular pennant — First Substitute — and sounds two horns. What does it mean and when will the new warning signal be?
options: General recall — everybody returns; the new warning signal is made one minute after First Substitute is lowered, with one sound
Postponement — the sequence starts again five minutes after the pennant is lowered
Individual recall — only the boats that were over must return; the race continues for the rest
General recall — the new warning signal is made immediately when the pennant is lowered
questions.why: Rule 29.2: general recall is First Substitute with two sounds; the warning signal for the new start is made 1 minute after it is removed, with one sound.

questions.q: After a general recall of your 470 fleet, First Substitute is still flying and boats are milling around behind the line. Your crew asks whether you are still "racing" in the sense of the rules while you wait. Are you?
options: Yes — you have been racing since the first preparatory signal and remain so until you finish
No — the general recall ended racing; you will be racing again from the new preparatory signal
No — you will be racing again only when you cross the starting line in the new start
Yes — you are racing until First Substitute is lowered
questions.why: Definition Racing: a boat stops racing when a general recall is signalled, and is racing again from her next preparatory signal.

questions.q: In the final seconds before a P-flag start you, to windward, touched Grey's leeward boat and broke rule 11. You start your two turns; halfway through them the committee signals a general recall. Grey hails that you still owe her a penalty in the restart. Do you?
options: Yes — a penalty started before the recall must be completed before the new preparatory signal
Yes — the breach carries over and you must take two turns after the new start
No — after a general recall a breach in the original start is not penalised unless it was under rule 2, 30.2, 30.4, 69 or caused injury or serious damage under rule 14
No — but you must retire from the restarted race because you did not complete the penalty
questions.why: Rule 36: a breach in the original start is not penalised in the restart, except under rules 2, 30.2, 30.4, 69 or rule 14 with injury or serious damage.

questions.q: At a national championship the line is 400 m long and 15 boats are over at the gun; the race officer can see that many are over but cannot read their numbers. The pin boat radios two numbers only. What may the race committee do?
options: Score every boat in the front row OCS, since it cannot tell them apart
Nothing — a general recall is allowed only when there has been an error in the starting procedure
Signal an individual recall and let the protest committee identify the boats afterwards
Signal a general recall — rule 29.2 allows it when the committee is unable to identify the boats that were on the course side
questions.why: Rule 29.2: when the RC cannot identify the boats that were OCS or subject to rule 30, or erred in the starting procedure, it may signal a general recall.

questions.q: Two classes: 420s at 13:00 and 29ers scheduled at 13:05. The 420 start is general-recalled at 13:00:05. The 29er sailors want their start at 13:05 as published. What does rule 29.2 say about the order of the starts?
options: The 420s get a new start one minute after First Substitute is lowered, and the 29er start follows that new start
The 29ers start at 13:05 as scheduled and the 420s are restarted after them
Both classes are restarted together with a single warning signal
The 29er start is cancelled for the day because the 420s were recalled
questions.why: Rule 29.2: the new warning for the recalled class is 1 minute after First Substitute is removed, and the starts of succeeding classes follow the new start.

questions.q: After a general recall of your fleet, First Substitute is lowered with one sound at exactly 12:08:00. With the standard sequence and no further signals, when is your new starting signal?
options: 12:09:00 — the lowering of First Substitute is itself the warning signal
12:14:00 — warning at 12:09, preparatory at 12:10, one-minute at 12:13
12:13:00 — the new sequence starts at once when the pennant comes down
12:15:00 — the fleet gets a full two minutes before the new warning
questions.why: Rule 29.2: the warning signal is made 1 minute after First Substitute is removed; rule 26: start 5 minutes after the warning.

questions.q: I-flag start, a 29er regatta in 15 knots. Forty seconds before the start you are pushed over the line near the middle; you dip straight back behind it and start with the fleet at the gun. The committee shows flag X and later scores you OCS. Is the committee right?

figure.note: Flag I: over at 0:40, dipped back, started

options: No — you were behind the line at the gun and started correctly, so flag X did not apply to you
No — flag X is for boats over at the signal only; a boat over earlier gets a 20 % penalty instead
Yes — under flag I a boat on the course side in the last minute must sail across an extension of the line, round an end, to the pre-start side before she starts; dipping back does not count
Yes, but only because you did not return within the four minutes that flag X was displayed
questions.why: Rule 30.1: in the last minute a boat over the line must return across an extension to the pre-start side before starting; rule 29.1 recalls her; otherwise OCS.

questions.q: Flag I is the preparatory signal for your J/70 fleet. With 1 minute 30 seconds to go you find yourself a length over the line while checking the pin-end transit. You bear away and are back behind the line by 1 minute 10 seconds, then start normally. Any penalty?

figure.note: 1:30 to go, you are over near the pin and bearing away

options: Yes — under flag I any boat that crosses the line after the preparatory signal must round an end
Yes — you are scored OCS unless you sailed round the pin or the committee boat
No, but you must take a one-turn penalty for crossing the line early
No — rule 30.1 applies only during the last minute before the start; before that you may return across the line itself
questions.why: Rule 30.1 concerns a boat on the course side "during the last minute before her starting signal"; earlier she may return any way she likes.

questions.q: I-flag start at a Bodrum regatta. With 30 seconds to go your bow is over near the pin. You bear away, sail round the outside of the pin to the pre-start side, come back up and cross the line 25 seconds after the gun. Flag X was displayed. Did you start correctly?

figure.note: Round the pin to the pre-start side, then start

options: Yes — you crossed an extension of the line to the pre-start side, as rule 30.1 requires, and then started
Yes, but you are still penalised 20 % for being over in the last minute
No — under flag I you had to go round the committee-boat end, not the pin
No — flag X means you were scored OCS the moment it was displayed
questions.why: Rule 30.1: a boat over in the last minute sails across an extension to the pre-start side before she starts — either end will do; then definition Start applies.

questions.q: I-flag start. Fifty seconds before the gun Yellow is clearly over the line; she dips back and is behind the line at the starting signal. Flag X goes up with one sound anyway. Yellow's skipper argues that flag X is only for boats over at the signal. Why did the committee display it?
options: The committee made an error — flag X may only be displayed for boats over at the starting signal
Because rule 29.1 also covers a boat that must comply with rule 30.1 — Yellow still has to sail round an end before she can start
Because under flag I every boat that was over at any time after the preparatory signal is OCS
Because flag X under flag I means a 20 % scoring penalty for Yellow
questions.why: Rule 29.1: flag X is displayed when a boat is over at the signal OR must comply with rule 30.1, and stays up until she has complied.

questions.q: Z-flag start, 50 ILCA 7s. With 40 seconds to go your bow pokes over the line in the middle; you bear away, are back behind it at 20 seconds and start with the fleet. You finish 8th. What happens to your score?

figure.note: Flag Z: over at 0:40, back by 0:20

options: Nothing — you were behind the line at the starting signal, so you started correctly
You are scored OCS because you did not return round an end of the line
You receive a 20 % scoring penalty without a hearing — being in the triangle in the last minute is enough, even though you were behind at the gun
You are disqualified without a hearing unless the race is restarted
questions.why: Rule 30.2: under flag Z a boat identified in the triangle in the last minute gets a 20 % scoring penalty under 44.3(c) without a hearing.

questions.q: Flag Z is flying for a Dragon start. At 1 minute 30 seconds to go you are a boat length over the line checking the transit; by 1 minute 05 seconds your whole hull is back behind it, and you start cleanly. Has the Z-flag penalty been triggered?
options: Yes — under flag Z a boat may not cross the line at any time after the preparatory signal
No, but you must sail round an end of the line before you may start
Yes — the 20 % penalty applies from the preparatory signal onward
No — rule 30.2 applies only to the last minute before the starting signal; you were back in time
questions.why: Rule 30.2: no part of the hull may be in the triangle "during the last minute before her starting signal" — earlier excursions do not count.

questions.q: Z-flag start, 30 boats entered. You are identified in the triangle in the last minute, start correctly and finish 5th. The sailing instructions do not change rule 44.3(c). What is your race score?
options: 11.2 points — 5 plus 20 % of 31 (the DNF score), which is 6.2
31 points — a Z-flag boat is scored as if she had not finished
6 points — 5 plus 20 % of your own finishing place, rounded up
11 points — 6.2 is rounded to a whole number and added to your 5th
questions.why: Rule 44.3(c): the penalty is 20 % of the score for DNF (entries + 1), rounded to the nearest tenth of a point (0.05 upward), added to the boat's score; not worse than DNF.

questions.q: Z-flag start of a 420 fleet. You are identified over the line with 30 seconds to go; at the gun the committee signals a general recall. In the restart you start cleanly. Your crew says the recall wiped the penalty. Did it?
options: No — and you may not sail in the restart at all
No — the Z-flag penalty stands even if the race is restarted; if you are identified again in the restart you get an additional 20 %
Yes — only the black-flag penalty survives a general recall
Yes — a general recall cancels all starting penalties from that attempt
questions.why: Rule 30.2: the penalty applies even if the race is restarted or resailed; a boat identified again in a later start gets another 20 %.

questions.q: Z-flag start on a lake in a dying breeze. You were over the line with 45 seconds to go and the committee noted your number. Twenty seconds before the starting signal the race committee postpones with AP and two sounds. Does the 20 % penalty apply in the race when it is finally sailed?
options: Yes — the penalty applies to the race whenever it is eventually started
Yes — a postponement counts as a restart, and the penalty survives restarts
No — the Z-flag penalty does not apply if the race is postponed or abandoned before the starting signal
No — because the race committee must display your sail number first
questions.why: Rule 30.2: the penalty applies if the race is restarted or resailed, but not if it is postponed or abandoned before the starting signal.

questions.q: Z-flag start, Saronic Gulf. In the last 30 seconds you are to the left of the pin, outside the line, and your bow is over the line's extension beyond the pin. At the gun you are still there. Do you get the 20 % penalty, and have you started?

figure.note: Over the extension beyond the pin, outside the triangle

options: 20 % penalty — any part of the hull over the line or its extensions in the last minute triggers rule 30.2
20 % penalty and OCS — both apply to a boat over the extension
No penalty and no problem — you were beyond the pin, so you may simply bear away onto the beat
No Z-flag penalty — you were not inside the triangle between the ends of the line and the first mark; but you have not started and must return to the pre-start side and cross the line
questions.why: Rule 30.2 covers only the triangle formed by the ends of the line and the first mark; a boat beyond the pin is outside it, but she still has to start.

questions.q: U-flag start of a J/70 fleet in 18 knots. You are identified inside the triangle with 20 seconds to go. The race is not recalled and you sail it, finishing 2nd. What will the results show?

figure.note: Flag U: in the triangle 20 s before the gun

options: UFD — disqualified without a hearing under rule 30.3
2nd — the U flag only applies if there is a general recall
OCS — unless you returned and started correctly
ZFP — a 20 % scoring penalty added to your 2nd place
questions.why: Rule 30.3: under flag U a boat identified in the triangle in the last minute is disqualified without a hearing unless the race is restarted or resailed.

questions.q: U-flag start, 80 Optimists. You are identified in the triangle in the last minute, but at the gun the race committee signals a general recall. May you start in the restart, and with what penalty?
options: Yes, but only after taking a two-turns penalty before the new preparatory signal
Yes, with no penalty — the U-flag disqualification does not apply when the race is restarted
No — your sail number will be displayed and you must not sail in the restart
Yes, but you carry a 20 % scoring penalty into the restart
questions.why: Rule 30.3: the boat is disqualified without a hearing "unless the race is restarted or resailed" — unlike the black flag.

questions.q: U-flag start. You were identified in the triangle 15 seconds before the gun, kept sailing and are leading on the first beat when the committee abandons the race with flag N because the windward mark has dragged. The race is resailed an hour later. Does your U-flag disqualification carry into the resail?
options: Yes — unless you were not identified in the resail as well
No — but you must get the race committee's permission before starting
No — rule 30.3 does not apply when the race is restarted or resailed; you may sail the resail without penalty
Yes — the disqualification was earned in the original start and stands
questions.why: Rule 30.3: disqualification without a hearing unless the race is restarted or resailed; rule 36 confirms the breach is not carried over.

questions.q: Black-flag start. You are identified in the triangle with 40 seconds to go; the race is sailed through. No flag X was displayed after the starting signal and you argue at the race office that you were never recalled, so the BFD cannot stand. Is the argument good?
options: Yes — the black flag only applies after a general recall, so the first start must use flag X
No — but the committee should have displayed your number before the start
Yes — without flag X and one sound a boat cannot be scored for a starting error
No — when rule 30.4 applies to a boat, rule 29.1 does not; the committee did not have to recall you, only to identify you
questions.why: Rule 29.1 (last sentence): if rule 29.2, 30.3 or 30.4 applies, rule 29.1 does not — no individual recall is signalled for a boat penalised under the black flag.

questions.q: Black-flag start of a 100-boat ILCA 6 fleet. You are identified in the triangle with 15 seconds to go; at the gun a general recall is signalled. What happens to you?
options: You are disqualified without a hearing; the committee displays your sail number before the next warning signal and you must not sail in the restart
Nothing — a general recall cancels the black-flag penalty like any other starting penalty
You may sail the restart; the disqualification applies only if the race is not recalled
You get a 20 % scoring penalty and may sail the restart
questions.why: Rule 30.4: disqualification without a hearing, surviving a general recall; after a recall the RC displays her sail number and she shall not sail in the restart.

questions.q: After a black-flag general recall your sail number 183455 is displayed on the committee boat. You sail the restart anyway and finish 3rd. The results show DSQ. May you discard this result as your worst race of the series?

figure.title: After the recall
lines: Your number displayed on the RC boat

options: No — because a black-flag disqualification is never excludable, whether or not you sail the restart
No — a boat that sails the restart after her number was displayed gets a disqualification that is not excludable from her series score
Yes — a black-flag disqualification is excludable like any other DSQ
Yes — because you finished the race, the normal discard rules apply
questions.why: Rule 30.4: if a boat whose number was displayed sails in the restart or resail, her disqualification shall not be excluded.

questions.q: Black-flag start of a 49er fleet. You are identified over the line with 35 seconds to go. Then, 10 seconds before the starting signal, the wind dies completely and the race committee postpones with AP. When the race is eventually started an hour later, are you still black-flagged?
options: No — but only if the race committee forgets to display your number
Yes — the black flag was flying when you were identified, and that is what counts
No — the black-flag penalty does not apply if the race is postponed or abandoned before the starting signal
Yes — the penalty survives restarts, resails and postponements alike
questions.why: Rule 30.4: the penalty applies if the race is restarted or resailed, but not if it is postponed or abandoned before the starting signal.

questions.q: Black-flag start at a Mediterranean championship. Thirty seconds before the gun your bow is over near the committee boat; you duck back, start behind the fleet and sail a fine race to 6th. No general recall was signalled. What is your result?

figure.note: Black flag, 30 s to go, bow over near the RC boat

options: 6th with a 20 % scoring penalty added
6th — you were behind the line at the starting signal and started correctly
OCS — because you did not round an end of the line before starting
BFD — disqualified without a hearing; returning behind the line does not undo a black-flag breach
questions.why: Rule 30.4: no part of the hull may be in the triangle in the last minute; a boat identified doing so is disqualified without a hearing.

questions.q: Black-flag general recall. Your number appears on the board on the committee boat, but you are certain you were behind the line in the last minute — your GPS track and a coach boat confirm it. The restart is in a few minutes. What should you do?

figure.title: Black-flag recall
lines: Your number on the RC board
GPS track shows you behind the line

options: Do not sail the restart; afterwards request redress with your evidence — sailing it would make the disqualification non-excludable
Sail the restart and protest the race committee on the water with a red flag
Sail the restart — if you were not over, the disqualification cannot stand anyway
Accept the disqualification — a black-flag decision cannot be reviewed
questions.why: Rule 30.4: a boat whose number is displayed shall not sail the restart; if she does, her DSQ is not excludable. An RC error is a redress ground (61.4(b)(1)).

questions.q: Black-flag start. You are identified in the triangle 50 seconds before the gun. The race starts, but 20 minutes later it is abandoned because the wind dies. The committee announces the race will be resailed tomorrow. What is your position for the resail?
options: You may sail the resail with a 20 % scoring penalty
The committee must display your sail number before the next warning signal for that race, and you may not sail the resail — the penalty applies to a resailed race
You may sail the resail because the committee did not display your number during the original race
You may sail the resail — abandonment after the start wipes all penalties from the original race
questions.why: Rule 30.4: if the race is abandoned after the starting signal, the RC displays her sail number before the next warning signal and she shall not sail the resail.
