questions.q: Black-flag start with 120 boats. You know you were over the line with 20 seconds to go, but the line was so crowded that the race committee could not identify anyone and signalled a general recall. No sail numbers are displayed. May you sail the restart?
options: Yes, but you must take a two-turns penalty before the new preparatory signal
No — after a black-flag general recall the whole front row is automatically disqualified
Yes — rule 30.4 penalises a boat that is identified; with no number displayed you may sail the restart, though you must stay out of the triangle in its last minute
No — a boat that knows she was over must retire from the restart even if not identified
questions.why: Rule 30.4: "if a boat is identified" she is disqualified and her number displayed; a boat not identified has no penalty under 30.4 for that start.

questions.q: You coach a youth team and want them to remember which starting penalties survive a general recall. In the last minute a boat is identified over the line, then the committee signals a general recall. Under which preparatory flags may she sail the restart?
options: Under P and Z only — I, U and black all exclude her from the restart
Under all of them — a general recall wipes every starting penalty
Under P and I only — Z, U and black all exclude her from the restart
Under P, I, U and Z she may sail the restart (with a 20 % penalty under Z); only under the black flag may she not
questions.why: Rule 30: only the black flag (30.4) excludes an identified boat from the restart; Z (30.2) adds 20 % but lets her sail; U (30.3) is cancelled by a restart.

questions.q: Reading the results after a championship day you see "BFD" against your sail number in race 4. What does it mean?
options: Disqualified under rule 30.4 — identified in the triangle in the last minute of a black-flag start
Did not finish within the time limit
A 20 % scoring penalty for being over in the last minute under flag Z
Broke rule 30.1 — failed to return round an end under flag I
questions.why: Appendix A scoring abbreviations: BFD is a disqualification under rule 30.4 (black flag).

questions.q: The provisional results of a 24-boat J/24 regatta show you "OCS" in race 2. What does that mean, and how many points is it?
options: You were disqualified after a hearing for a Part 2 breach; 25 points
You did not start — part of your hull was on the course side at the starting signal and you did not return; 25 points (entries plus one)
You started correctly but finished outside the time limit; 24 points
You started late, more than 4 minutes after the signal; 0 points
questions.why: Appendix A: OCS means on the course side at the starting signal and failed to start, or broke rule 30.1; scored as entries + 1.

questions.q: Twenty seconds before the start you are reaching along the line on starboard towards the committee boat, planning to squeeze in at the stern. Blue, to leeward and overlapped, also on starboard, luffs to close-hauled and there is no longer a gap between her and the committee boat. She hails "No room!" What are your rights?

figure.note: 20 s to go; Blue is leeward and luffing

options: You may hold your course and Blue must bear away because you hailed for room first
You are entitled to mark-room — you are inside and overlapped when you reach the committee boat
None at the committee boat — at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water rule 18 does not apply; under rule 11 you must keep clear of Blue, even if it means going behind the committee boat
Blue must hold her course — a leeward boat may not luff within three hull lengths of a starting mark
questions.why: Section C preamble: rule 18 does not apply at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water while boats approach it to start; rule 11: windward keeps clear.
questions.ref: RRS Part 2 Section C preamble, RRS 11

questions.q: Pin-end start in a 470 fleet. Ten seconds before the gun you approach the pin on port tack, intending to tack onto starboard right at the mark. Grey is coming at the pin close-hauled on starboard. You hail "Room at the mark!" Who must keep clear?

figure.note: 10 s to go at the pin

options: Grey — you are the inside boat at the pin and so entitled to mark-room under rule 18
Nobody — before the starting signal the rules of Part 2 are not yet in force
Grey — you hailed first, so she must give you room to tack at the mark
You — rule 10 applies, and there is no mark-room at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water; port keeps clear of starboard
questions.why: Section C preamble: no mark-room at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water; rule 10: port keeps clear of starboard; Part 2 applies from the prep signal.
questions.ref: RRS 10, RRS Part 2 Section C preamble

questions.q: Forty seconds before the start, Red comes from clear astern and becomes overlapped to leeward of you, a hull length away. She then luffs steadily above close-hauled, pushing you up towards the line. You protest that she is sailing above her proper course. Is Red breaking rule 17?

figure.note: 40 s to go; Red is luffing from leeward

options: No — before the starting signal a boat has no proper course, so rule 17 cannot limit her; she may luff, but under rule 16.1 she must give you room to keep clear
Yes — rule 17 applies from the preparatory signal onward
No — because she is more than a hull length away rule 17 does not apply, and she may luff as hard as she likes
Yes — a leeward boat that gained her overlap from clear astern may not sail above close-hauled
questions.why: Definition Proper Course: a boat has none before her starting signal, so rule 17 does not restrict her; rules 11 and 16.1 govern the luff.
questions.ref: RRS definition Proper Course, RRS 17, RRS 16.1

questions.q: You are the leeward boat, close-hauled on starboard, setting up to start by the committee boat. Black, overlapped to windward, is barging in and hails "Mark-room — give me room at the committee boat!" If you hold your close-hauled course she will not fit. What should you do?

figure.note: Black is barging at the RC boat

options: Tack away — a boat that hails for room at a mark must be given it, whoever has right of way
Hold your course — Black gets no mark-room at a starting mark and must keep clear of you under rule 11; if you change course, give her room to keep clear
Luff hard to head to wind to push her into the committee boat — she is windward and must keep clear whatever you do
Bear away to let her in — an inside overlapped boat is entitled to mark-room at any mark, the committee boat included
questions.why: Section C preamble: no mark-room at a starting mark surrounded by navigable water; rule 11: windward keeps clear; your course changes are subject to rule 16.1.
questions.ref: RRS Part 2 Section C preamble, RRS 11, RRS 16.1

questions.q: Five seconds before the gun you are to windward of Green, both on starboard, half a length from the committee boat's stern. Green suddenly luffs to head to wind; the only way to keep clear of her is to hit the committee boat, which you do. Who broke which rule?

figure.note: 5 s to go; Green luffs to head to wind

options: Only Green — a leeward boat may never luff above close-hauled near the committee boat
Only you — a windward boat must keep clear whatever the leeward boat does, and you touched the mark
Green broke rule 16.1 — she changed course without giving you room to keep clear; you touched a starting mark, but you were compelled to and may be exonerated
Nobody — contact with the committee boat before the start carries no penalty
questions.why: Rule 16.1: a right-of-way boat changing course gives room to keep clear, including space to comply with rule 31; rule 43.1(a) exonerates the compelled boat.

questions.q: Fifteen seconds before the start of a Star-class race, squeezing in at the committee-boat end, your quarter brushes the committee boat's topsides. No other boat was involved and there is no damage. What must you do?

figure.note: 15 s to go; your quarter touches the RC boat

options: Nothing — a boat is not racing before the starting signal, so rule 31 does not apply
Retire — touching the committee boat before the start is a disqualification
Take a two-turns penalty — touching the committee boat is a Part 2 breach
Take a one-turn penalty as soon as possible after getting well clear — you touched a starting mark while racing
questions.why: Rule 31: while racing (from the preparatory signal) a boat shall not touch a starting mark before starting; rule 44.1: a One-Turn Penalty for rule 31.

questions.q: P-flag start, light wind, a strong favourable current pushing the fleet over. You plan a "dip start": sit on the course side of the line before the gun, then after the starting signal dip back across the line to the pre-start side and cross again. Is this legal?

figure.note: Flag P; dip back after the gun, then start

options: Yes — under flag P you may return across the line itself; you start when your hull crosses after being entirely on the pre-start side after the signal
No — a boat on the course side in the last minute is disqualified without a hearing
Yes, but you must first take a two-turns penalty for being over the line
No — a boat on the course side at the starting signal must always sail round an end of the line
questions.why: Definition Start: a boat starts when her hull crosses the line after being entirely on the pre-start side after the signal; only flag I requires an end.

questions.q: Same tactic, different day: the preparatory flag is I. You sit above the line, and after the gun you dip back across the middle of the line and start again. The committee boat scores you OCS. Why?
options: Because under flag I you get a 20 % penalty, which the committee records as OCS
Because under flag I a boat on the course side in the last minute must return across an extension of the line — round an end — before she starts; dipping the line does not comply
Because the dip start is forbidden under every preparatory flag
Because under flag I a boat may not be on the course side at any time after the preparatory signal
questions.why: Rule 30.1, definition Start: a boat subject to rule 30.1 has not started until she has crossed an extension to the pre-start side and then crossed the line.

questions.q: Four and a half minutes before the start of a Hobie 16 race — thirty seconds after the warning signal — you misjudge a gybe and your hull bumps the pin-end buoy. Your crew wants to do a penalty turn. Do you owe one?

figure.note: 4:30 to go, before the preparatory signal

options: No — touching the pin never carries a penalty, only touching the committee boat does
Yes — a one-turn penalty, because you touched a starting mark
No — you are not yet racing; racing begins at the preparatory signal, and rule 31 applies only while racing
Yes — a two-turns penalty, because touching a mark before the start is more serious
questions.why: Definition Racing: a boat is racing from her preparatory signal; rule 31 applies to a boat racing — before the preparatory signal there is no penalty.

questions.q: Thirty seconds before the start you are sitting on the line, head to wind, and back your jib to drift astern and open a gap to leeward. White, close-hauled on starboard behind you, has to bear away sharply to avoid your transom. Who had to keep clear?

figure.note: You are backing the jib and drifting astern

options: White — a boat head to wind holds her position and others must avoid her
Nobody — before the starting signal boats may manoeuvre as they wish
White — she was clear astern and must keep clear of a boat ahead
You — a boat moving astern through the water by backing a sail keeps clear of a boat that is not
questions.why: Rule 21.3: a boat moving astern, or sideways to windward, through the water by backing a sail shall keep clear of one that is not.

questions.q: The sailing instructions of a club series say: "A boat that does not start within 4 minutes after her starting signal will be scored DNS without a hearing." A tangled spinnaker sheet keeps you behind the line, and you finally cross it 5 minutes after the gun. You sail the course and finish 9th. What is your score?
options: DNS — the sailing instructions set a time limit for starting, and you crossed after it
9th with a 20 % penalty for starting late
9th — a late start is not a breach of any rule
DNF — you started, but outside the time limit, so you count as not finishing
questions.why: Rules 25 and 90.2: the SI may set a starting time limit; a boat that does not start within it is scored as the SI say — here DNS (rule A5).

questions.q: The sailing instructions say: "No warning signal will be made after 15:30." The committee boat makes the warning signal for race 4 at 15:40. You had already started home and miss the race. What is your remedy, if any?

figure.title: SI: no warning after 15:30
lines: You had left for the harbour

options: None — you should have stayed on the water until the committee boat went in
Request redress — making a warning signal after the time stated in the sailing instructions is an improper action of the race committee
Protest the race committee with a red flag at the next opportunity
None — the race committee may start a race at any time it considers fair
questions.why: Rule 61.4(b)(1): redress for a score made significantly worse by an improper action of the RC — here a warning signal made contrary to the SI.

questions.q: Two classes start five minutes apart. The first class has just started and flag X is flying for its OCS boats. Your class flag is up and your preparatory flag goes up a minute later. A nervous crew asks whether flag X means your sequence is interrupted. Does it?

figure.title: Two classes
lines: First class started, flag X up
Your class flag up, then P up

options: No, but your start is delayed until flag X is lowered
Yes — while flag X is flying no other class may be in sequence
No — flag X is the individual recall for the class that has just started; your sequence continues as signalled
Yes — flag X cancels the warning signal and your class will be restarted
questions.why: Rule 29.1: flag X recalls the boats over at the previous start; rule 26: the next class's sequence is made with or after that start and continues.

questions.q: A 60-boat ILCA 7 start. Flag X goes up with one sound. You were in the front row, sighting the pin against the committee boat's flagstaff, and are confident your bow was behind the line. Four boats near you go back. Should you?
options: Yes — when flag X is displayed every boat in the front row must return to be safe, whether or not she was over
Yes — flag X means the committee could not identify the boats, so the whole fleet is recalled
No, and you cannot be scored OCS later because your sail number was not hailed by the committee
If you are sure your hull was behind the line, keep racing — flag X concerns only the boats that were over; if you are scored OCS anyway, request redress
questions.why: Rule 29.1: the recall is for boats whose hull was over at the signal; the RC may still score a boat OCS (A5); an RC error is corrected by redress (61.4(b)(1)).

questions.q: You were a metre over at the gun of a 420 race. The committee boat was slow: flag X went up 40 seconds after the starting signal, by which time you were two hundred metres up the beat. You return and start, losing most of the fleet. Were you obliged to return, and do you have a claim?
options: Yes — your duty to start correctly does not depend on the flag; the late signal is an improper action of the committee and may ground redress
No — once you are more than three hull lengths past the line an individual recall no longer applies to you
Yes, and there is no possible claim — the timing of flag X is entirely at the committee's discretion
No — flag X must be displayed promptly; shown late, it has no effect and you had started correctly
questions.why: Rule 29.1: the RC shall display flag X promptly; definition Start: she has not started until she returns; 61.4(b)(1): an improper RC action may ground redress.

questions.q: P-flag start, you are OCS at the pin end. Instead of dipping back across the line through the crowd, you bear away round the outside of the pin and sail across the line's extension until your whole hull is on the pre-start side, then tack and cross the line. Have you returned correctly?

figure.note: Round the pin, across the extension, then start

options: Yes, but you must also take a one-turn penalty for passing the pin on the wrong side
Yes — under flag P the hull need only be entirely on the pre-start side of the line or its extensions before you start; either route is fine
No — only a boat under flag I may go round the pin to return
No — under flag P a recalled boat must return across the line itself, not an extension
questions.why: Rule 29.1: the hull must be completely on the pre-start side of the line or one of its extensions; definition Start applies when she then crosses the line.

questions.q: At the preparatory signal of an Optimist start the committee boat hoists flag Z and, below it, flag I. Your coach had told you about them separately. Which rules apply in the last minute?
options: Rule 30.3 — the two flags together mean the same as flag U
Only rule 30.2 — flag I is cancelled when it is displayed with flag Z
Both rule 30.1 and rule 30.2 — a boat over in the last minute must return round an end and also gets a 20 % scoring penalty
Only rule 30.1 — flag Z is a reminder that the penalty is 20 % if you fail to return
questions.why: Rule 26: the preparatory signal may be "Z with I"; race signals: flag I means rule 30.1 applies and flag Z means rule 30.2 applies — both at once.

questions.q: At a regatta with Optimists starting first and 29ers second, the 29er class flag goes up with one sound 30 seconds before the Optimist starting signal. The 29er fleet is confused. Is this signal in accordance with the rules?
options: Yes — the race committee may overlap sequences as long as the preparatory signals do not coincide
No — the warning signal of the next class must be made exactly five minutes after the previous start
Yes — a warning signal may be made at any time once the previous class is in its last minute
No — the warning signal for a succeeding class shall be made with or after the starting signal of the preceding class
questions.why: Rule 26: the warning signal for each succeeding class shall be made with or after the starting signal of the preceding class.

questions.q: Lasers start at 12:05 and 470s follow. You are in a 470 and see flag P go up for your class at 12:06:00 with one sound. With the standard sequence, when is your start, and when will P come down?
options: Start at 12:10:00; flag P comes down at 12:09:00 with one long sound
Start at 12:10:00; flag P comes down at the starting signal
Start at 12:09:00; flag P comes down at 12:08:00
Start at 12:11:00; flag P comes down at 12:10:00
questions.why: Rule 26: the preparatory signal is 4 minutes before the start and the preparatory flag is lowered 1 minute before the start.

questions.q: The first race is scheduled for 11:00. At 10:55 the committee boat displays AP over numeral pennant 1 with two sounds. At what time should you now expect the warning signal, with a standard sequence?

lines: AP over numeral pennant 1, two sounds

options: 10:56 — the warning signal is made one minute after AP is displayed
11:55 — the start is postponed one hour to 12:00 and the warning signal is 5 minutes before it
11:00 — AP over a numeral pennant only postpones the start, not the warning
12:05 — the warning signal is one hour after the original one
questions.why: Race signals: AP over numeral pennant 1 postpones the race 1 hour from the scheduled start; rule 26: the warning is 5 min before the start.
questions.ref: RRS 26, race signals (AP over numeral pennant)

questions.q: A river start with 2 knots of current running towards the course. In the last 10 seconds the wind dies, you lose steerage and the current carries your bow over the line at the gun. Flag X goes up. You feel it was not your fault. What is your position?

figure.note: Current sets towards the course; no steerage

options: You may keep racing and ask for redress because the current, not you, moved the boat
You started correctly — a boat without steerage way cannot be OCS
You are OCS whatever the cause — return to the pre-start side and start; current or lack of wind is no ground for redress
You must retire — a boat carried over by current cannot return
questions.why: Definition Start and rule 29.1 look only at where the hull was at the starting signal; rule 61.4 gives no redress for weather or current.

questions.q: The sailing instructions say: "The preparatory signal will be flag P unless flag U or the black flag is displayed." At four minutes you see flag P. If you find yourself over the line in the last 30 seconds, what must you do?
options: Retire — you will be disqualified without a hearing
Accept a 20 % scoring penalty, which applies to any boat over in the last minute
Sail round an end of the line before starting — otherwise you are OCS
Get your whole hull back behind the line by any route and start after the starting signal — under flag P there is no extra penalty
questions.why: Under flag P only the definition Start applies: be entirely on the pre-start side at or after the signal, then cross; rules 30.1–30.4 need I, Z, U or black.

questions.q: After a general recall of your Finn fleet, First Substitute is flying and you drift about waiting. Before the new preparatory signal you misjudge a tack and your transom touches the pin. A rival hails "Penalty!" Do you owe one?

figure.note: First Substitute flying; before the new preparatory signal

options: No — the general recall ended racing, and you are not racing again until the new preparatory signal; rule 31 does not apply
No — but only because the pin was touched by the transom and not the bow
Yes — because you have been racing continuously since the first preparatory signal
Yes — a one-turn penalty, because the pin is a starting mark
questions.why: Definition Racing: racing ends at a general recall and resumes at the next preparatory signal; rule 31 applies only to a boat racing.

questions.q: AP has been flying for twenty minutes. The committee lowers it with one sound, and you start your watch for the warning signal — but ten seconds later AP goes up again with two sounds. What now?
options: The sequence has started — the second AP counts as the warning signal
The race is postponed again — no warning signal will be made until one minute after AP is next lowered
The warning signal is still due one minute after the first lowering — the second AP is for the next class
Racing is over for the day — AP displayed twice means AP over A
questions.why: Race signals, AP: the warning will be made 1 minute after removal "unless at that time the race is postponed again or abandoned".

questions.q: Just after the starting signal of your race the committee boat hoists a white flag with a blue St Andrew's cross and makes one sound. What does it mean?
options: Abandonment — return to the starting area
General recall — the whole fleet returns for a new start
Individual recall — one or more boats were over the line and must return to start
Shortened course — finish at the next mark
questions.why: Rule 29.1 and race signals: flag X with one sound is the individual recall.

questions.q: Seconds after the gun, the committee boat hoists a triangular pennant with blue and yellow vertical panels and sounds two horns. The leaders are already pointing at the first mark. What has happened?
options: The course has been changed — watch for a new compass bearing
Individual recall — only the boats that were over must return
The race is abandoned for the day
General recall — the whole fleet returns and the class will be restarted
questions.why: Rule 29.2 and race signals: First Substitute with two sounds is the general recall.

questions.q: You started your watch at the warning signal. It reads 4:00 when you see flag P come down and hear a long sound. At what reading will the starting signal be made?
options: 5:00 — the preparatory flag comes down one minute before the start
8:00 — the preparatory flag comes down four minutes before the start
4:30 — the long sound is the thirty-second signal
6:00 — the start is two minutes after the preparatory flag comes down
questions.why: Rule 26: the warning is at 5 minutes and the preparatory flag is removed at 1 minute, so the start is 60 s after it comes down.

questions.q: A Dragon start. The class flag went up at 14:00:00 and flag P at 14:01:00. You look up and see flag P being lowered. What time is it, and when is the starting signal?
options: 14:03:00 now; the starting signal is at 14:05:00
14:04:00 now; the starting signal is at 14:05:00
14:04:00 now; the starting signal is at 14:06:00
14:05:00 now; this is the starting signal
questions.why: Rule 26: warning 5 min, preparatory 4 min, preparatory flag down 1 min before the start.

questions.q: During a Melges 24 sequence the committee boat lowers flag P by mistake at three minutes to go, with a long sound, then hoists it again twenty seconds later. Half the fleet now has the wrong time. What may the race committee properly do, and what should you expect?

figure.title: Sequence error
lines: 3:00 to go: flag P lowered by mistake
3:00 to go minus 20 s: flag P re-hoisted

options: Nothing — once the preparatory signal has been made the sequence must run to the starting signal
Hail the correct time to the fleet — a hail replaces the visual signals
There has been an error in the starting procedure — the committee may postpone before the start or signal a general recall after it; expect AP or First Substitute
Score every boat that starts on the wrong time OCS without a hearing
questions.why: Rule 27.3 allows postponement before the start for any reason; rule 29.2 allows a general recall when there has been an error in the starting procedure.

questions.q: You were OCS and are sailing back to the line on port tack after the gun. Blue, close-hauled on starboard, has started correctly. You misjudge her speed and your bow hits her quarter — a scuff, no damage. Who broke which rules?

figure.note: You are returning; Blue has started

options: Blue broke rule 14 — a right-of-way boat must always avoid contact, and she did not
Both equally — each boat broke rule 14 and each must take a two-turns penalty
Nobody — contact without damage between a returning boat and a starter is ignored
You broke rule 21.1 (and rule 10) and rule 14; Blue, the right-of-way boat, is exonerated for the contact because there was no damage or injury
questions.why: Rule 21.1: a returning boat keeps clear; rule 14: she must avoid contact; rule 43.1(c): the right-of-way boat is exonerated under 14 absent damage or injury.

questions.q: Windward–leeward course, all marks to port, a 29er national championship in 18 knots. In the crush at the windward mark you end up passing it on the wrong side, leaving it to starboard; five lengths down the run you realise. What must you do?

figure.note: You rounded leaving the mark to starboard

options: Sail back and unwind: return upwind past the mark on the side you came, round it leaving it to port, then carry on — you may correct the error until you finish
Retire — once you have left the zone a rounding on the wrong side can no longer be corrected
Carry on; the race committee only scores a boat NSC if she misses a mark altogether, not if she rounds it the wrong way
Take a Two-Turns Penalty as soon as you are clear of other boats and carry on down the run — a mark error is a Part 2 breach
questions.why: Rule 28.2: a boat may correct any error in sailing the course until she finishes; penalty turns do not replace the unwinding.
questions.ref: RRS 28.2, RRS definition Sail the Course

questions.q: The sailing instructions give course Start – 1 – 2 – 3 – Finish, marks to port. On the leg from mark 1 to mark 2 you pass mark 4, a mark of another course, leaving it on your starboard side. Your crew is worried. Have you broken a rule?

figure.note: Leg from mark 1 to mark 2

options: Only if the leader left it to port; the first boat sets the required side for the fleet
No — a mark that does not begin, bound or end the leg you are sailing may be left on either side
Yes — every mark laid by the race committee for the regatta must be left to port
Yes — you must go back and leave mark 4 to port before continuing to mark 2
questions.why: Rule 28.1: a boat may leave on either side a mark that does not begin, bound or end the leg she is sailing.

questions.q: In a dying breeze on a lake you misjudge the leeward gate: you sail past the outside of the right-hand gate mark without passing between the two marks, then harden up for the beat. Your crew says it does not matter which gate mark you round. Are they right?

figure.note: The left-hand gate mark is 60 m to the left, off the picture

options: No — a gate error cannot be corrected and the race committee will score you NSC
Yes — at a gate you only have to leave one of the two marks on the required side, and you did
No — your string must pass between the gate marks from the direction of the previous mark; you must go back and sail through the gate
No — you broke rule 28 and must take a Two-Turns Penalty before continuing up the beat
questions.why: Definition Sail the Course: the string passes between the gate marks from the direction of the previous mark; rule 28.2 lets her correct it.
questions.ref: RRS 28, RRS definition Sail the Course

questions.q: A lake regatta uses a small island as a mark: the sailing instructions say "the island to starboard". The breeze is better on the island's western shore, so you sail down that side with the island on your left and carry on to the next mark. What is your position?

figure.note: SI: the island to starboard

options: You are fine — a natural feature used as a mark may be passed on either side if the SI do not name a rounding direction
You broke rule 31 by passing on the wrong side; a One-Turn Penalty puts it right
You are fine as long as you did not touch the island or its shoal water
You have not sailed the course — the island had to be on your starboard side; go back and pass it correctly before you finish, or you will be scored NSC
questions.why: Rule 28.1 and definition Sail the Course: each mark of the leg must be left on the required side; the island is a mark of the course.

questions.q: Thirty seconds after crossing the finishing line in a Melges 24 you realise that at the last gate you sailed outside the right-hand gate mark instead of between the two marks. You are still a few lengths past the line. What can you do?

figure.note: You passed outside the right-hand gate mark

options: Go back, pass through the gate correctly and cross the finishing line again — you may correct the error because you had not yet finished
Nothing — once you cross the finishing line your finish stands, and the race committee will score you NSC
Nothing is needed — the gate marks do not bound the final leg to the finish
Return to the course side of the line, take a Two-Turns Penalty and cross the line again
questions.why: Rule 28.2 allows correction until she finishes; by sailing back to correct, a boat that crossed the line "continues to sail the course" and has not finished.

questions.q: In race 3 of a J/70 regatta Blue, sail number 4471, leaves mark 2 to starboard although the marks are to be left to port, never goes back, and finishes third. Nobody protests her. What happens to her score?

figure.title: Race 3, after the finish
lines: Marks were to be left to port
She never went back to correct it

options: Nothing — a boat can only lose her place if another boat protests her within the time limit
The race committee scores her NSC without a hearing, because she did not sail the course
She keeps third place unless the race committee protests her and a hearing finds she broke rule 28
She is scored DNF — a boat that misses a mark is treated as not having finished
questions.why: Rule 28 and Appendix A5.1 (2025): a boat the race committee determines did not sail the course is scored NSC without a hearing.

questions.q: Two minutes before your start in a Dragon fleet you sail round the committee boat, go out onto the course side of the line and come back through the line to the pre-start side to set up. The helm of the boat next to you says you now have to "unwind" around the committee boat. Does he have a point?

figure.note: Two minutes before the start

options: Yes — having been on the course side you must now return around an end of the line before you may start
Only if flag I was displayed; under flag P the string starts at the starting signal
No — the string that must pass the marks correctly starts only when you begin approaching the line from the pre-start side to start; earlier manoeuvres do not count
Yes — every pass of a starting mark from the preparatory signal onward is part of the string and must be unwound
questions.why: Definition Sail the Course: the string runs from when she begins approaching the starting line from its pre-start side to start until she finishes.

questions.q: You are close-hauled on starboard, two lengths from the windward mark, to be left to port. Red, overlapped to windward, bears away onto you; to avoid contact you bear away hard and pass the mark on the wrong side. You hail "Protest". Do you still have to go back?

figure.note: Red bears away onto you at the mark

options: No — you are exonerated under rule 43.1(a) because Red compelled you to pass the mark on the wrong side
No — Red's breach means the protest committee will give you redress for the places you lost
No — but you must take a One-Turn Penalty for passing a mark of the leg on the wrong side
Yes — being forced the wrong side does not relieve you of sailing the course; unwind and round the mark correctly, and protest Red for breaking rule 11
questions.why: Rule 28 still applies: a boat forced past a mark on the wrong side must correct it (28.2); the other boat is penalised under rule 11.

questions.q: The course board shows W2 — two laps of a windward–leeward course. You round the leeward gate after the first lap, cross the finishing line, hear no sound signal, stop and drop the jib. A friend on the committee boat shouts that you have one more lap to sail. Where do you stand?

figure.title: Course W2 (two laps)
lines: You rounded the leeward gate once
No sound signal from the RC
You stopped and lowered the jib

options: You have not sailed the course; if you go on and sail the second lap your earlier crossing does not count and you finish when you cross the line after it
Your race is over — crossing the finishing line early is scored NSC and cannot be corrected
You have finished — the race committee must record the time of your first crossing of the line
You must take a Two-Turns Penalty for crossing the finishing line before completing the course
questions.why: Definition Finish: a boat that crosses the line and then continues to sail the course has not finished; rule 28.2 lets her complete the course.

questions.q: River race, two knots of current setting across the course. Approaching the leeward mark, to be left to port, the stream sweeps you past it on the wrong side before you can round. You turn back, sail up past the mark on the same side you came down, then round it correctly leaving it to port. What else do you owe?

figure.note: Current 2 kn setting to the right; marks to port

options: A One-Turn Penalty, taken as soon as you are well clear of other boats
Nothing — you corrected the error before finishing, as rule 28.2 allows, and no penalty is due for the error itself
A Two-Turns Penalty, because passing a mark on the wrong side is treated like a Part 2 breach
You must retire — a boat set onto the wrong side of a mark by current cannot correct her course
questions.why: Rule 28.2: an error in sailing the course may be corrected before finishing; rule 44 penalties are for Part 2 and rule 31 breaches only.

questions.q: At a Bodrum regatta the course board on the committee boat shows course 3, but you read it as course 2. You sail course 2 faultlessly — every mark of it on the correct side — and cross the finishing line fifth. What will the results show?

figure.title: Course board: 3
lines: Every mark of course 2 left correctly

options: DNF — a boat that sails the wrong course is treated as not having finished
Fifth place, unless the race committee protests you and a hearing finds you broke rule 28
NSC — you did not sail the course that was signalled, however well you sailed the other one
DSQ after a hearing — a wrong course is always a disqualification
questions.why: Rule 28 requires the course signalled to be sailed; Appendix A5.1 lets the race committee score NSC without a hearing.

questions.q: In the pile-up at the pin end of a Laser start you are squeezed out and pass outside the pin mark, leaving it to starboard; you never crossed the line between the pin and the committee boat. The fleet sails off. What is your position?

figure.note: You passed outside the pin

options: You started — part of your hull crossed the extension of the line after the starting signal
Sail on; the race committee will score you OCS and nothing you do now can change that
You broke rule 31 by passing a starting mark on the wrong side; take a One-Turn Penalty
You have not started — go back to the pre-start side and cross the line between the pin and the committee boat before sailing on
questions.why: Definition Start and rule 28.1: a boat starts by crossing the starting line between its marks; until then she has not sailed the course.

questions.q: Grey rounded the windward mark the wrong way and is now sailing back on starboard tack to unwind her rounding. You are approaching the mark close-hauled on port and will meet her. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: Grey is sailing back to unwind her rounding

options: You do — Grey is racing and on starboard; a boat correcting an error in sailing the course keeps her normal rights under Part 2
Grey — a boat sailing back to correct a course error must keep clear of boats sailing the course properly, like a boat returning to start
Grey — she is not racing while she unwinds, so she must not interfere with you
Nobody has to keep clear until Grey hails that she is unwinding; then you must give her room
questions.why: Rule 10 applies as usual; rule 21 lists boats returning to start, taking a penalty or moving astern, not a boat correcting a rule 28 error.

questions.q: The sailing instructions list an offset mark 1a, to be left to port, 50 m from the windward mark. In 25 knots your spinnaker hoist goes wrong and you pass 1a leaving it to starboard. Your crew says an offset mark is only an aid and does not count. Who is right?

figure.note: Mark 1 is just above the picture; you left 1a to starboard

options: Neither — passing 1a on the wrong side is a rule 31 breach cured by a One-Turn Penalty
You must go back — 1a begins the run and has a required side; the string must pass it to port
Your crew — an offset mark counts only for boats that have hoisted a spinnaker before reaching it
Your crew — only marks with a number in the course sequence have a required side
questions.why: Rule 28.1: a mark that begins, bounds or ends the leg being sailed must be left on the required side; the offset mark begins the run.
questions.ref: RRS 28.1, RRS definition Sail the Course

questions.q: The sailing instructions define the finishing line as between the committee boat and a yellow pin buoy. A press RIB has anchored 30 m from the committee boat. You cross the line between the committee boat and the pin, passing the RIB on your right. Blue says the RIB was a mark and you left it on the wrong side. Is Blue right?

figure.note: The SI mention only the committee boat and the pin

options: Only if the RIB was closer to the pin than to the committee boat
Yes — a race committee or press vessel is a mark whenever it displays a flag
No — the RIB is not a mark; only objects the sailing instructions require you to leave on a specified side are marks
Yes — any vessel anchored by the organising authority near a line is part of that line
questions.why: Definition Mark: an object the sailing instructions require a boat to leave on a specified side, or an RC vessel from which a line extends.

questions.q: Windward–leeward course with an offset mark 1a used on the run. On the second beat you want to tack right where 1a lies, leaving it on whichever side suits the shift. May you?

figure.note: Second beat; 1a is used only on the run

options: No — once a mark is part of the course it must be left to port on every leg
No — you may pass 1a on either side only if you keep more than two hull lengths from it
Yes, but only after the leading boat has shown which side the fleet will take
Yes — on the beat 1a does not begin, bound or end the leg you are sailing, so it may be left on either side
questions.why: Rule 28.1: a mark that does not begin, bound or end the leg a boat is sailing may be left on either side.

questions.q: Marks to port. You left the windward mark to starboard and are ten lengths down the run before you notice. Your tactician proposes simply circling the mark once in the direction you first passed it. Which route actually unwinds the error?

figure.note: Marks to port; you left this mark to starboard

options: Sail back upwind past the mark on the side you came down, then round it leaving it to port — the string pulled taut must lie on the port side of the mark
Circle the mark once in the same direction you first passed it; a full loop in either direction straightens the string
Return to the zone, take a One-Turn Penalty at the mark and continue down the run
Cross to the correct side below the mark and carry on — the string only has to end up on the correct side
questions.why: Definition Sail the Course: the string drawn taut must pass each mark on the required side; unwinding means retracing and rounding correctly.
questions.ref: RRS 28.2, RRS definition Sail the Course

questions.q: At the leeward gate of a windward–leeward course the leader passes between the gate marks and rounds the left-hand mark. You pass between the gate marks and round the right-hand one, as the breeze is better on that side. Is your rounding valid?

figure.title: Leeward gate
lines: SI: pass between the gate marks,

options: No — with marks to port only the left-hand gate mark may be rounded
Yes — having passed between the gate marks from the direction of the previous mark you may round either of them
Yes, but you must first hail the boats behind you which mark you are taking
No — all boats must round the same gate mark as the leading boat
questions.why: Definition Sail the Course: pass between the gate marks from the direction of the previous mark; either mark may then be rounded.
questions.ref: RRS 28, RRS definition Sail the Course

questions.q: Two laps of a windward–leeward course; the finishing line lies between the committee boat and a pin halfway up the beat. On the first beat you sail straight across the finishing line on your way to the windward mark. Any consequence?

figure.note: First beat of two laps

options: You must take a One-Turn Penalty for passing between finishing marks before completing the course
You must leave both finishing marks to port, since all marks of the course are to port
None — you are continuing to sail the course, so you have not finished, and the finishing marks have no required side on the first beat
You have finished and will be scored by that crossing unless you re-cross the line in the other direction
questions.why: Definition Finish (c): a boat that crosses the finishing line and continues to sail the course has not finished; rule 28.1 on marks of the leg.

questions.q: The results sheet scores you NSC in race 2: the race committee says you missed mark 3. Your GPS track shows you rounded it correctly. There are forty minutes left in the protest time limit. What is the right step?

figure.title: Results posted
lines: You are scored NSC in race 2
Your GPS track shows you rounded it

options: Protest the race committee under rule 28; the protest committee will then hear it like a protest between boats
Appeal straight to the national authority, since scoring decisions are not heard by the protest committee
Nothing can be done — a score given by the race committee without a hearing is final
Request redress within the time limit — an incorrect NSC score is an improper action of the race committee — and bring the track as evidence
questions.why: Rule 61.4(b)(1): a boat whose score was made significantly worse by an improper action or omission of the race committee may request redress.

questions.q: The course board on the committee boat shows 2. The sailing instructions define course 2 as Start – 1 – 2 – 3 – 1 – Finish, all marks to port. After rounding mark 3 the leader heads straight for the finishing line. Where should you go?
options: Back to mark 1 — course 2 requires mark 1 to be rounded again before the finish; the leader is making an error
Follow the leader to the finish — the first boat's course becomes the course for the fleet
To the finish — once every mark has been rounded at least once the course is sailed
Wait near mark 3 for the race committee to signal whether mark 1 is required again
questions.why: Rule 28.1: a boat shall sail the course described in the sailing instructions; other boats' errors change nothing.

questions.q: The sailing instructions say the windward mark is an orange inflatable. At the top of the beat you find an orange inflatable and, 100 m away, a yellow one. The leader rounds the yellow one and the next three boats follow. Which should you round?

figure.title: At the windward mark
lines: SI: mark 1 is an orange inflatable
You find an orange and a yellow one
The leader rounds the yellow one

options: Either — when two buoys are in the area the race committee must accept both
The orange one — the mark is the object the sailing instructions describe; following the leader is no defence against NSC
The yellow one — once the leading boats have rounded a buoy it becomes the mark for the fleet
The yellow one, then the orange one, to be safe
questions.why: Rule 28.1 and definition Mark: the course is the one the sailing instructions describe, however many boats round the wrong object.

questions.q: Two minutes before the start of a Wednesday evening club race you are luffing head to wind by the committee boat and your boom swings against its hull. Nothing is damaged. What must you do?

figure.note: Two minutes to the start; your boom touches the committee boat

options: Nothing — touching a mark before the starting signal is not a breach, because the race has not begun
Take a Two-Turns Penalty — contact with the committee boat is treated like a collision with another boat
Take a One-Turn Penalty — you are racing from the preparatory signal, and a starting mark must not be touched before you start
Return to the pre-start side round an end of the line and start again
questions.why: Rule 31: while racing, a boat shall not touch a starting mark before starting; racing begins at the preparatory signal; penalty under rule 44.2.

questions.q: Starting at the committee boat end in a 36-ft cruiser-racer, you cut it fine and your keel snags the committee boat's anchor line, which is slanting away from its bow. The hull never touches the boat. Have you broken rule 31?

figure.note: The dashed line is the committee boat's anchor line

options: Yes — anything attached to the committee boat is part of the mark; take a One-Turn Penalty
No, but you must retire if the anchor line stopped your boat for more than a few seconds
Yes — and because you fouled her ground tackle the penalty is two turns
No — the anchor line of a committee boat is not part of the mark, so touching it is not touching the mark
questions.why: Definition Mark: an anchor line of a race committee vessel is not part of the mark; rule 31 is not broken.

questions.q: You cross the finishing line in a 470, bear away to clear it and your transom bumps the pin-end finishing mark. You have not yet cleared the line. What is the right response?

figure.note: Your transom touches the pin just after crossing

options: Take a One-Turn Penalty and finish again: sail completely back to the course side, do the turn, then cross the line — you are still racing until you clear the line and marks
Nothing — you had already finished, and rule 31 does not apply after the finish
Take a One-Turn Penalty where you are; your finish stands because you crossed the line before the touch
Retire — a mark touched after finishing cannot be penalised by turns
questions.why: Rule 31 covers a finishing mark after finishing while still racing; definition Finish (a): a boat taking a 44.2 penalty after crossing has not finished.

questions.q: Rounding the windward mark in a J/24, your hull clears it by half a metre but the lazy spinnaker sheet hanging from the pole drags over the top of the buoy. Your bowman says only the hull counts. Is he right?

figure.note: Your spinnaker sheet drags over the mark

options: Yes — since 2021 only the hull counts for touching a mark, just as for finishing
No — a boat touches a mark with any part of her hull, crew or equipment; take a One-Turn Penalty
Yes — running rigging is not part of the boat for rule 31
No — and because a sail control touched the mark the penalty is two turns
questions.why: Rule 31 is broken when any part of the boat, her equipment or crew touches the mark; the hull-only wording belongs to the definitions Start and Finish.

questions.q: At a crowded leeward mark you are the outside boat, fail to give Blue the mark-room she is entitled to, touch her gunwale and, in the same tangle, bump the mark. No damage. How many turns do you owe?

figure.note: You touch both Blue and the mark

options: One turn — when a boat touches a mark the One-Turn Penalty replaces any other penalty
Three turns — a Two-Turns Penalty for the Part 2 breach plus a One-Turn Penalty for the mark
Two turns in all — one Two-Turns Penalty covers the Part 2 breach, and for breaking rule 31 in the same incident you need not take the One-Turn Penalty as well
Four turns — a Two-Turns Penalty for each rule broken
questions.why: Rule 44.1(a): a boat that may have broken a Part 2 rule and rule 31 in the same incident need not take the penalty for rule 31.

questions.q: You are the inside boat at the leeward mark, overlapped since well before the zone. Red, outside, does not give you mark-room, squeezes you and your hull is pushed against the mark. Who takes a penalty?

figure.note: Red squeezes you onto the mark

options: Both — Red for rule 18.2 and you a One-Turn Penalty for rule 31; the mark touch is always your own
Nobody — contact caused by crowding at a mark is exonerated for all boats
Only you — the boat that touches the mark is the one that broke a rule
Red takes a Two-Turns Penalty for breaking rule 18.2; you are exonerated for touching the mark because Red compelled you to
questions.why: Rule 43.1(a): a boat compelled to break a rule by another boat's breach is exonerated; the outside boat broke rule 18.2(a).

questions.q: You touch the leeward mark with the hull in a pack of twelve boats. You carry on for about thirty seconds to get out of the traffic, then make one turn — a tack followed by a gybe — and rejoin. Was the penalty taken correctly?

figure.title: Leeward mark, twelve boats around
lines: You carry on about 30 s to get clear
Then one turn: a tack and a gybe

options: Yes — after getting well clear of other boats as soon as possible you promptly made one turn including a tack and a gybe
No — the turn must be made immediately at the mark, among the other boats if need be
No — a turn for touching a mark must include two tacks, not a tack and a gybe
No — the penalty must be completed before you leave the zone of the mark you touched
questions.why: Rule 44.2: get well clear of other boats as soon after the incident as possible, then promptly make the turn, each turn with one tack and one gybe.

questions.q: Windward–leeward course with the starting line below the leeward gate. On the first beat, tacking in a lull, you brush one of the gate marks with your bow. Must you take a penalty?

figure.note: First beat; the gate is used only on the run

options: Yes — a One-Turn Penalty; any mark of the course touched while racing breaks rule 31
No — on the first beat the gate marks do not begin, bound or end the leg you are sailing, so touching one is not a breach
Yes — a Two-Turns Penalty, because the gate is a rounding mark of the course
No — but you must sail back and pass through the gate before continuing up the beat
questions.why: Rule 31 applies to a starting mark before starting, a mark that begins, bounds or ends the leg she is sailing, or a finishing mark after finishing.

questions.q: Ten seconds after starting at the committee boat end of a Star fleet, a gust heels you and your quarter touches the committee boat's topsides. You had already crossed the line. Is this a breach of rule 31?

figure.note: Ten seconds after starting your quarter touches the committee boat

options: No — rule 31 only protects a starting mark before the start, and you had started
No — a committee boat is never a mark once the starting signal has been made
Yes — the committee boat is a mark that begins the first leg; take a One-Turn Penalty after getting well clear
Yes — but the penalty is to return and start again round an end of the line
questions.why: Rule 31: a boat shall not touch a mark that begins, bounds or ends the leg she is sailing; the starting marks begin the first leg.

questions.q: You have finished, cleared the finishing line and are sailing back to the committee boat to hand over a declaration form. Coming alongside, your bow bumps its hull. Do you owe a penalty?

figure.title: After the finish
lines: You finished and cleared the line
You sail back to the RC boat
Your bow bumps the RC boat's hull

options: Only if the committee boat was also the starting-line boat
Yes — a One-Turn Penalty; the committee boat is a finishing mark and you touched it after finishing
Yes — and since you cannot take turns now, the race committee will score you DSQ
No — you stopped racing when you finished and cleared the line and marks, so rule 31 no longer applies
questions.why: Definition Racing: a boat is racing until she finishes and clears the finishing line and marks; rule 31 applies only while racing.

questions.q: The windward mark has a small pick-up float tied to it on a short line so the mark-layer can lift it. Rounding close, your rudder nudges the float but not the buoy itself. Your crew says the float is like an anchor line and does not count. Who is right?

figure.note: A small pick-up float is tied to the mark

options: You touched the mark — an object intentionally attached to a mark is part of it; only the anchor line is excluded
Your crew — only the inflatable buoy itself is the mark; anything tied to it is ground tackle
Nobody can say — whether an attachment counts is decided by the protest committee case by case
Your crew — a float is attached to the anchor line, which is not part of the mark
questions.why: Definition Mark: any object intentionally attached to the object or vessel is part of the mark; an anchor line is not.

questions.q: You fouled Grey on port tack at the windward mark and begin your Two-Turns Penalty as soon as you are clear. During the first turn you hit the mark. You complete the two turns and sail on. Have you done enough?

figure.title: Two-Turns Penalty at the windward mark
lines: You fouled Grey (rule 10) at the mark
You start your two turns at once
During the first turn you hit the mark
You complete the two turns and sail on

options: Yes — rule 44.1(a) says a boat taking a Two-Turns Penalty need not take a penalty for rule 31
No — touching the mark during the turns is a new incident; you owe a One-Turn Penalty in addition to the two turns
Yes — a boat taking a penalty is exonerated for any mark she touches while turning
No — hitting a mark during a penalty voids it; you must retire
questions.why: Rule 44.1(a) covers a Part 2 breach and rule 31 broken in the same incident; a touch during the turns is a separate incident with its own penalty.

questions.q: An Optimist sailor at a club race touches the leeward mark with her bow. Her coach has told her to "always do a 720 to be safe". What penalty does the rule actually require?

figure.title: Optimist club race
lines: Her bow touches the leeward mark

options: A Two-Turns Penalty — two full turns are required for any breach while racing
A 20 % scoring penalty, reported to the race committee at the finish
A One-Turn Penalty — one tack and one gybe; a Two-Turns Penalty is for breaking a rule of Part 2
No penalty — in dinghy classes rule 31 is deleted by the class rules
questions.why: Rule 44.1: a boat that may have broken rule 31 may take a One-Turn Penalty; the Two-Turns Penalty is for Part 2 breaches.

questions.q: Twenty-five knots and steep waves at the leeward mark. You round with room to spare, but a wave lifts your bow and drops it onto the mark. It was nobody's fault. Must you take a penalty?

figure.note: A wave drops your bow onto the mark

options: Yes — a Two-Turns Penalty, because heavy-weather contact is treated as serious
No — in a wind of 25 knots or more rule 31 is suspended for safety
No — a touch caused by sea state rather than by your handling is not a breach
Yes — rule 31 has no fault element; unless another boat compelled the touch, a One-Turn Penalty is due
questions.why: Rule 31 is broken by any touch while racing; exoneration under rule 43.1(a) requires another boat's breach, not a wave.

questions.q: You round the leeward mark cleanly, harden up onto the beat, and as you sheet in your transom swings and hits the mark. You are already heading up the next leg. Have you broken rule 31?

figure.note: Hardening up after rounding, your transom hits the mark

options: Yes — the mark ends the run and begins the beat, so it is a mark of the leg you are sailing; take a One-Turn Penalty
No — once your bow has passed the mark you are on the next leg and the mark no longer counts
Yes — but as the touch was after the rounding the penalty is two turns
No — only contact with the bow or the hull forward of the mast counts as touching a mark
questions.why: Rule 31: a mark that begins, bounds or ends the leg she is sailing; the leeward mark both ends the run and begins the beat.

questions.q: You sail through the leeward gate intending to round the left-hand mark. On the way through, your spinnaker pole end touches the right-hand gate mark, which you are not rounding. Your crew says only the mark you round matters. Right?

figure.note: The left-hand gate mark is off the picture to the left

options: Yes — a spinnaker pole is not part of the boat for the purposes of rule 31
No — both gate marks bound the leg, so touching either is a breach of rule 31; take a One-Turn Penalty
No — but the penalty is two turns because you touched a mark you were not rounding
Yes — rule 31 applies only to the gate mark you actually round
questions.why: Rule 31: a boat shall not touch a mark that begins, bounds or ends the leg she is sailing; both gate marks do.

questions.q: Red saw your mainsail leech brush the windward mark, hailed "Protest" and displayed her red flag. You felt nothing and took no penalty. At the hearing the protest committee finds that you did touch the mark. What is the penalty?

figure.title: Protest hearing
lines: Red: your leech brushed the windward mark
Red hailed and showed a red flag
You felt nothing, took no penalty
PC finds that you touched the mark

options: A One-Turn Penalty imposed by the protest committee, taken before the next race
A 20 % scoring penalty — the protest committee cannot disqualify for touching a mark
Disqualification — the One-Turn Penalty is available only at the time of the incident; a boat found at a hearing to have broken rule 31 is disqualified
No penalty — a touch you did not feel is not a breach
questions.why: Rule 60.5(c): a boat found to have broken a rule and not exonerated is disqualified unless another penalty applies; rule 44 is for the time of the incident.

questions.q: Approaching the pin end of the finishing line on starboard in light air, your bow touches the pin mark before any part of your hull has crossed the line. What must you do?

figure.note: Your bow touches the pin before your hull crosses

options: Cross the line, then take the One-Turn Penalty on the far side
Nothing — rule 31 covers a finishing mark only after finishing
Finish, then return and pass the pin again on the other side to cancel the touch
Take a One-Turn Penalty with your hull completely on the course side, then finish — a finishing mark bounds the last leg
questions.why: Rule 31 covers a mark that bounds the leg; rule 44.2: a penalty near the finishing line is taken with the hull completely on the course side before finishing.

questions.q: Rounding the windward mark tight in a Hobie 16, your crew reaches out and pushes the mark away with her hand so that the hulls do not hit it. Has the boat touched the mark?

figure.note: Your crew fends the mark off by hand

options: Yes — a crew member's hand on the mark is the boat touching it; a One-Turn Penalty is due
Yes — and because the touch was deliberate the penalty is two turns
No — only the hull, spars and sails count; a crew member is not the boat
No — fending off by hand is seamanlike and avoids a touch by the hull
questions.why: Rule 31: a boat touches a mark when her hull, equipment or crew touch it; fending off is still a touch.

questions.q: You touched the leeward mark and decide to take your penalty: you tack onto port, then bear away straight onto the new leg without gybing, because that was quicker and you ended up on the same heading as before. Is the penalty taken?

figure.title: Penalty for touching the mark
lines: Bear away onto the new leg

options: Yes — a tack followed by bearing away through 360° of heading counts as one turn
No — a turn must include one tack and one gybe; without the gybe you have not taken the One-Turn Penalty
No — the penalty must consist of two gybes, not a tack
Yes — for touching a mark a tack alone is enough; the gybe is only needed for Part 2 breaches
questions.why: Rule 44.2: each turn includes one tack and one gybe, made promptly in the same direction.

questions.q: Finishing upwind in an ILCA 7, your bow crosses the finishing line; you tack away at once, so the rest of the hull never crosses. The race officer took your time as the bow crossed. Have you finished?

figure.note: Your bow crosses, then you tack away

options: No — the whole hull must cross the line before a boat has finished
Yes, but only because the race officer recorded a time; otherwise you would not have finished
Yes — a boat finishes when any part of her hull crosses the line from the course side; she need not cross completely
No — tacking back onto the course side cancels the crossing and you must cross again
questions.why: Definition Finish: any part of the hull crossing from the course side; after finishing she need not cross completely (rule 28.1).

questions.q: Downwind finish. Your spinnaker, flying well ahead of the bow, is across the finishing line a full second before Blue's bow; Blue's hull then crosses, and your hull crosses after it. Who finished first?

figure.note: Your spinnaker is over the line; Blue's bow, then your hull, follow

options: You — any part of the boat or her equipment in its normal position crossing the line counts
You — on a downwind finish the spinnaker is taken as the foremost point of the boat
A dead heat — the race committee scores both boats in the same place
Blue — a boat finishes when part of her hull crosses the line; sails and other equipment do not count
questions.why: Definition Finish (2021 wording): any part of her hull crosses the finishing line; equipment such as a spinnaker is not counted.

questions.q: Two lengths before the finishing line you foul Red on port tack. Your bow crosses the line, and only then do you start a Two-Turns Penalty just beyond the line. Have you finished, and when?

figure.note: You fouled Red two lengths before the line and crossed it

options: Not yet — a boat that takes a rule 44.2 penalty after crossing has not finished; sail completely back to the course side, do the turns and cross again
Yes — provided you complete the two turns within the finishing window set by the SI
No — and you cannot finish now; a penalty after crossing the line means DNF
Yes — you finished when your bow crossed; the turns afterwards are a separate matter
questions.why: Rule 44.2: near the finishing line the hull must be completely on the course side before she finishes; definition Finish (a).

questions.q: You start a Two-Turns Penalty on the course side, close to the finishing line. In the second turn your bow pokes across the line; you complete the turn on the course side and then cross the line. Which crossing is your finish?

figure.title: Two-Turns Penalty near the finishing line
lines: You start the turns on the course side
In the second turn your bow pokes
across the line; you complete the turn
on the course side and cross the line

options: Neither — a boat that crosses the line during a penalty is scored DNF
The last one — after the penalty your hull had to be wholly on the course side before you could finish, so the poke across does not count
The first one, but with a 20 % scoring penalty added for crossing early
The first one — the moment your bow poked across the line during the second turn, as the race committee recorded it
questions.why: Rule 44.2 and definition Finish (a): a boat taking a penalty at or near the line has not finished until her hull is wholly on the course side and she crosses.

questions.q: You cross the finishing line in a 470 in the middle of the fleet. Your crew asks whether you must now sail on through the line or come back the way you came. What are the rules?
options: You must return to the course side so the race committee can see your sail number again
You must sail round the committee boat before leaving the finishing area
You may clear the line in either direction, but you must not interfere with boats that are still racing
You must continue across and clear the line in the direction you were sailing
questions.why: Rule 28.1: after finishing she need not cross the line completely; rule 23.1: a boat not racing shall not interfere with a boat racing.

questions.q: On the last leg of a coastal race you see a RIB anchored with a blue flag on a staff and, 80 m from it, a yellow buoy. No other committee vessel is in sight. What does the blue flag tell you?

figure.title: Last leg, coastal race
lines: A RIB anchored with a blue flag on a staff
A yellow buoy 80 m from it
No other committee vessel in sight

options: That the RIB is a mark of the course to be left to port
That a protest hearing will be held ashore; come within hail for instructions
That the course has been shortened and you finish at the next rounding mark
That the staff with the blue flag is one end of the finishing line — finish between it and the buoy
questions.why: Race signals: a staff displaying a blue flag marks one end of the finishing line.

questions.q: A 40° shift on the last beat lets you fetch the finishing line from the north, the side away from the last mark. You cross the line heading south, the opposite way to the fleet. Have you finished?

figure.note: You approach the line from the side away from the last mark

options: No — a boat finishes by crossing the line from the course side, the direction of the last mark; you must go round an end and cross correctly
Yes — the direction of crossing does not matter as long as the whole hull passes between the marks
Yes — the race committee must record any crossing of the line after the starting signal
No — and you can no longer finish, since a line crossed the wrong way is closed to that boat
questions.why: Definition Finish: any part of the hull crosses the finishing line from the course side; a crossing from the other side is not a finish.

questions.q: You cross the finishing line between the committee boat and the pin, from the direction of the last mark. There is no horn and nobody seems to be on deck. Your helm wants to go round and cross again to be sure. Have you finished?

figure.title: You cross the finishing line
lines: Between the RC boat and the pin
From the direction of the last mark

options: No — a boat has not finished until the race committee makes a sound signal for her
Yes — finishing is defined by your hull crossing the line from the course side, not by a sound signal or an acknowledgement
No — without an acknowledgement you must cross again until the committee reacts
Yes, but your finishing time will be the time of your second crossing
questions.why: Definition Finish: a boat finishes when any part of her hull crosses the line from the course side; the rules require no signal from the RC.

questions.q: The sailing instructions say: "Boats failing to finish within 20 minutes after the first boat sails the course and finishes will be scored DNF without a hearing." The breeze dies and you cross the line 22 minutes after the winner. How are you scored?

figure.title: SI 14.2: finishing window
lines: DNF if not finished within 20 min

options: DNC — a boat outside the finishing window is treated as not having come to the starting area
By your finishing place, but with a 20 % scoring penalty for finishing late
DNF — the finishing window in the sailing instructions had closed, and no hearing is needed
By your finishing place — once the first boat has finished within the time limit every boat that finishes is scored
questions.why: Rule 35 and A5.1: the SI may set a finishing window; a boat outside it is scored DNF without a hearing.

questions.q: A Wednesday evening race has a time limit of 90 minutes. The wind dies completely; at 90 minutes the leading boat is still 200 m from the finishing line and nobody has finished. What must the race committee do?

figure.title: Time limit 90 minutes
lines: Leader 200 m from the line at 90 min

options: Shorten the course to the last mark the leader rounded and score the boats as they passed it
Score the boats by their positions on the course at the moment the time limit expired
Wait until the leader finishes and then give every other boat a finishing window
Abandon the race — if no boat sails the course and finishes within the time limit the race is abandoned
questions.why: Rule 35: if no boat finishes within the time limit, the race committee shall abandon the race.

questions.q: The sailing instructions give a time limit of two hours but say nothing about a finishing window. The winner finishes after 1 h 50 min; the breeze then dies and you drift across the line after 2 h 40 min. The race committee is still there. How are you scored?

figure.title: Time limit 2 h, no finishing window
lines: You crossed the line at 2 h 40 min

options: By your finishing place — once one boat sails the course and finishes within the time limit, all boats that finish are scored, unless the SI set a finishing window
By your finishing place, but only if the race committee did not abandon the race
DNF — a boat must finish within 30 minutes of the winner unless the SI say otherwise
DNF — any boat finishing after the time limit has expired is scored as not having finished
questions.why: Rule 35: if one boat finishes within the time limit and the race is not abandoned, all boats that finish are scored by their finishing places.

questions.q: You have finished, cleared the line and marks, dropped the sails and are motoring back to the harbour across the course. A Laser still racing on the run has to bear away sharply to avoid you. Did you break a rule, and which?

figure.title: After finishing
lines: You finished and cleared the line
Sails down, motoring across the course
A Laser on the run bears away sharply

options: Yes — rule 10, since a boat under engine is on neither tack and must keep clear of every sailing boat
Yes — rule 23.1: a boat not racing shall not interfere with a boat that is racing; you may be protested and penalised
No — a boat racing must keep clear of a vessel under power under the collision regulations
No — once you have finished the racing rules no longer apply to you
questions.why: Definition Racing ends when she finishes and clears the line and marks; rule 23.1 then forbids interfering with a boat racing.

questions.q: The finishing line runs between the committee boat and a pin; the windward mark lies 50 m beyond the pin. Approaching on starboard, you could save a tack by passing between the pin and the windward mark. Would you finish?

figure.note: The windward mark lies 50 m beyond the pin

options: Yes — any crossing of the line or its extensions from the course side is a finish
Yes — the finishing line extends to the windward mark when it lies within 50 m of the pin
No — to finish your hull must cross the line between its two marks; passing outside the pin is not a crossing
No — but you may then take a One-Turn Penalty and be scored as finished
questions.why: Definition Finish: the hull must cross the finishing line, which runs between its marks; the extensions are not the line.

questions.q: A Saronic Gulf regatta sets a time limit of 90 minutes for the first boat and a finishing window of 30 minutes. The first boat finishes after 89 minutes. You are 15 minutes behind her in a dying breeze. What does this mean for the race?
options: Only the first boat is scored; the time limit applies to every boat individually
The race committee must shorten the course so that the rest of the fleet can finish
The race will be abandoned because most of the fleet will not finish within 90 minutes
The race stands — one boat finished within the time limit, and every boat that finishes within the next 30 minutes is scored by her place
questions.why: Rule 35: if one boat sails the course and finishes within the time limit, the race is scored; the SI finishing window applies to the rest.

questions.q: In a Melges 24 regatta the only boat to finish within the time limit is later disqualified after a protest hearing. The rest of the fleet finished a few minutes outside the limit but within the finishing window. Is the race still valid?

figure.title: After the protest hearing
lines: Only one boat finished within the limit
She is disqualified at the hearing
The rest finished within the window

options: Yes — a race is scored if one boat started, sailed the course and finished within the time limit, even if she is later disqualified or retires
No — the time limit is now unmet by every boat with a valid finish, so the race is abandoned
No — the protest committee must order the race to be resailed
Yes, but only if the protest committee decides to give the fleet redress
questions.why: Rule 90.3(a): a race is scored if not abandoned and one boat finished within the time limit, even if she afterwards retired or was disqualified.

questions.q: The sailing instructions add a mark 1 time limit: "If no boat has passed mark 1 within 40 minutes the race will be abandoned." In a fading sea breeze the leader is still 100 m short of mark 1 at 41 minutes. What should you expect?

figure.title: SI 13.3: mark 1 time limit 40 min
lines: At 41 min the leader is 100 m

options: Nothing until the overall time limit expires; a mark time limit is only guidance for the race committee
Flag N with three sounds — the race committee abandons the race under the sailing instructions; a resail may follow
Flag C — the race committee moves mark 1 closer so the leader can reach it in time
Flag S with two sounds — the course is shortened to finish at mark 1
questions.why: Rule 32.1 and 35: the RC abandons when the time limits set by the rules or the SI are not met, signalling N with three sounds.

questions.q: Halfway up the last beat you break a batten and decide to retire. The shortest way home is straight down through the fleet still beating towards you. A 470 on starboard has to tack to avoid you. Where do you stand?

figure.note: You have retired and are sailing straight home through the fleet

options: You broke rule 10 only; rule 23 applies only to boats that have finished
You are fine — a retired boat is no longer bound by any racing rule
A boat that has retired is no longer racing and must not interfere with a boat racing — you broke rule 23.1
You are fine — a retired boat keeps her Part 2 rights until she reaches the harbour
questions.why: Definition Racing: a boat is no longer racing once she retires; rule 23.1: a boat not racing shall not interfere with a boat racing.

questions.q: On the second beat you see a committee RIB anchored beside mark 3 displaying flag S, and you hear two sound signals. Where do you now finish?

figure.note: The committee RIB is anchored beside mark 3

options: At the original finishing line, but the race committee will score you as you pass mark 3
At mark 3 only if you are in the leading half of the fleet; the others sail the full course
Between mark 3 and the next mark of the course
Between mark 3 and the staff with flag S on the RIB — the course has been shortened to finish at that rounding mark
questions.why: Rule 32.2(a): when the course is shortened at a rounding mark, the finishing line is between the mark and a staff displaying flag S.

questions.q: Running down to the leeward gate you see flag S with two sounds on a committee RIB anchored 30 m to the right of the right-hand gate mark. Where is the finishing line?

figure.note: The left-hand gate mark is 60 m to the left, off the picture

options: Between the two gate marks — when a course is shortened at a gate, the line is between the gate marks
Between the right-hand gate mark and the RIB displaying flag S
Between whichever gate mark you choose to round and the RIB
Between the left-hand gate mark and the RIB, so that boats pass through the gate first
questions.why: Rule 32.2(c): when the course is shortened at a gate, the finishing line is between the gate marks.

questions.q: You are second, 100 m behind the leader, when a committee RIB at mark 2 hoists flag S with two sounds — a few seconds after the leader has already crossed the line between the mark and the RIB. You finish there. What is the position?

figure.title: Mark 2, flag S hoisted
lines: a few seconds before the hoist

options: The shortening is valid; the leader simply finishes at the original finishing line
The shortening was improper — the signal must be made before the first boat crosses the new finishing line — so boats whose scores suffer may request redress
The shortening is void and all boats must continue to the original finishing line
The shortening is valid for every boat except the leader, who must sail the full course
questions.why: Rule 32.2: the shortened-course signal shall be made before the first boat crosses the finishing line; a late signal is an RC error (rule 61.4(b)(1)).

questions.q: A trapezoid course in a dying breeze: at the halfway point the race committee calculates that no boat can finish within the time limit. May the race committee shorten the course, and under which provision?

figure.title: Trapezoid, breeze dying
lines: RC: no boat can finish in time

options: No — once a race has started the course may only be shortened for safety reasons
