Yes, but only with the agreement of a majority of the boats still racing
Yes — insufficient wind making it unlikely that any boat will finish within the time limit is a ground for shortening under rule 32.1
No — the race committee must let the time limit expire and then abandon
questions.why: Rule 32.1(b): the RC may shorten or abandon because of insufficient wind making it unlikely that any boat will finish within the time limit.

questions.q: On the first beat of a Dragon regatta off Split the committee boat hoists flag N and makes three sound signals. What does this mean for you?

figure.title: First beat, Dragon regatta
lines: You are halfway up the beat

options: No more racing today; all races are abandoned and you should return to the harbour
Your individual start was invalid; return to the pre-start side and start again
The course is shortened; finish at the next rounding mark, between the mark and the committee boat
All races are abandoned; return to the starting area — the warning signal will be made one minute after flag N is lowered
questions.why: Rule 32.3 and race signals: N with three sounds — all races abandoned, return to the starting area; a warning follows one minute after removal.

questions.q: At 15:00 on the last day of a Palma regatta, with a storm front approaching, the race committee abandons your race by displaying flag N over flag A with three sounds. What should you do?

figure.title: 15:00, storm front approaching
lines: Committee boat: flag N over flag A

options: Head for the harbour — all races are abandoned and there will be no more racing today
Finish the race, as N over A abandons only the races that have not yet started
Return to the starting area and wait for the warning signal of a new start
Sail to the committee boat; N over A means further signals will be made from there
questions.why: Race signals: N over A — all races abandoned, no more racing today (N over H — further signals ashore).

questions.q: Half the fleet, including you, has finished within the time limit when the wind dies completely and the rest of the boats are stuck a mile from the line. The race officer wants to abandon the race. May he?

figure.title: Wind has died
lines: Half the fleet finished within the limit
The rest are a mile from the line

options: No — once one boat has finished within the time limit the race can no longer be abandoned
He may abandon under rule 32.1(b), but as boats have already finished within the time limit he must first consider the consequences for all boats in the race or series
Yes, without restriction — abandoning after the start is entirely at the race committee's discretion
No — he must instead score the boats still sailing by their positions on the course
questions.why: Rule 32.1: if a boat has finished within the time limit, the RC shall not abandon without considering the consequences for all boats in the race or series.

questions.q: The regatta is behind schedule after a postponement. Twenty minutes into race 2, with good wind and no safety problem, the race committee displays flag S at mark 2 to shorten the course so that race 3 can be sailed. A competitor claims this is not allowed. Who is right?

figure.title: Race 2, behind schedule
lines: Flag S at mark 2, two sounds

options: The competitor — the schedule is a reason to postpone later races, never to shorten a race in progress
The competitor — after the start a course may be shortened only for weather, wind or a missing mark
The race committee — it may shorten the course so that further scheduled races can be sailed
Neither — the race committee may shorten only with the protest committee's approval
questions.why: Rule 32.1: in addition to the listed grounds, the RC may shorten the course so that other scheduled races can be sailed.

questions.q: Three classes are racing on the same course. At the leeward gate a committee RIB displays flag S over the Optimist class flag, with two sounds. You are sailing a 420. Where do you finish?

figure.title: Leeward gate, three classes
lines: Committee RIB: flag S over the

options: Nowhere yet — you must wait for a separate flag S for the 420 class before you may finish anywhere
At the gate, but only if the Optimists started before you
At the gate — a shortened course applies to every class on that course
At the original finishing line — a signal displayed over a class flag applies only to that class, so only the Optimists finish at the gate
questions.why: Race signals: a visual signal displayed over a class flag applies only to that class; rule 32.2 shortens the course for that class.

questions.q: The course has been shortened at mark 2, to be left to port; the flag S boat lies to the right of the mark. Approaching on the run, must you still round mark 2 before you finish?

figure.note: Marks to port; you come down the run

options: No — you finish when your hull crosses the line between mark 2 and the S boat from the direction of the last mark, leaving mark 2 on the required side
Yes — round mark 2 as usual and then cross the line from the other side
Yes — the shortened course only moves the finish; every mark must still be rounded
No — and you may cross the line from either direction, since it was not part of the original course
questions.why: Rule 32.2(a) and definition Finish: cross the line between the mark and the S staff from the course side; the mark keeps its required side.

questions.q: Ten minutes after the start the race officer realises the warning signal was made with the wrong class flag. He displays flag N with three sounds. Was he entitled to abandon for that reason after the start?

figure.title: Ten minutes after the start
lines: Warning signal was made with the

options: No — after the starting signal the race may be abandoned only for weather or a missing mark
Yes — an error in the starting procedure is a ground for abandoning after the start under rule 32.1
Yes, but only if a boat requests redress for the error
No — a starting error can only be dealt with by a general recall before the start
questions.why: Rule 32.1: after the starting signal the RC may abandon the race because of an error in the starting procedure.

questions.q: Finishing at a shortened course, you squeeze between mark 2 and the committee RIB flying flag S and your boom taps the RIB's hull as you cross. Does this matter?

figure.note: Your boom taps the S boat as you cross

options: No — rule 31 does not apply at a shortened-course finish
No — the RIB is a committee vessel, not a mark; only the buoy at the other end is a finishing mark
Yes — the RIB from which the finishing line extends is a finishing mark; take a One-Turn Penalty, sail completely back to the course side and finish again
Yes — but as you had already crossed you are finished, and only a protest can penalise you
questions.why: Definition Mark: a race committee vessel from which the finishing line extends is a mark; rule 31 and rule 44.2 near the finishing line.

questions.q: The sailing instructions require boats to pass through the start/finish line in the middle of every lap. On lap 1 of a three-lap race the committee boat displays flag S with two sounds. Where do you finish?

figure.title: Three-lap course
lines: SI: pass through the start/finish line
in the middle of every lap
Lap 1: committee boat shows flag S,

options: The signal is invalid, because a course can only be shortened at a rounding mark or a gate
At the start/finish line only after completing the lap you are sailing in full
At the next rounding mark, between the mark and a staff with flag S
At the start/finish line as you next cross it — a course may be shortened at a line boats are required to cross according to the course description
questions.why: Rule 32.2(b): the finishing line may be a line boats are required to cross according to the course description.

questions.q: You missed the flag S at mark 3 and, having crossed the line between mark 3 and the committee RIB, carried on round the rest of the course to the original finishing line, crossing it twenty minutes later. Which is your finish?

figure.title: Flag S at mark 3 missed
lines: Crossed the original line 20 min later

options: Your crossing of the shortened line at mark 3 — the course was complete there, so you finished then; the extra sailing changes nothing
Neither — a boat that does not see the shortening signal is scored DNF
Your crossing at mark 3, but with a penalty for sailing beyond the finish
Your crossing of the original finishing line — a boat is scored at the last line she crosses
questions.why: Rule 32.2 and definition Finish: she finished when her hull crossed the shortened finishing line from the course side; later sailing is irrelevant.

questions.q: You are leading on the last leg when the race committee abandons the race because the windward mark has dragged 300 m from its position and several boats rounded it in different places. You lose a certain win. Can you get redress?
options: No — redress is never available for anything that happens after the starting signal
No — abandoning because a mark is out of position is a proper action under rule 32.1(c), and redress requires an improper action or omission of the race committee
Yes — a boat leading when a race is abandoned is entitled to average points for that race
Yes — the race committee should have shortened the course instead, and failing to do so is improper
questions.why: Rule 32.1(c) allows abandonment for a mark missing or out of position; rule 61.4(b)(1) requires an improper action or omission.

questions.q: During race 4 of a 29er regatta on a lake, the committee boat displays flag N over flag H with three sounds. What is the race committee telling you?

figure.title: Race 4, 29er regatta
lines: Committee boat: flag N over flag H

options: All races are abandoned and there will be no more racing today
Return to the starting area; a new warning signal will be made in one minute
All races in progress are abandoned; go ashore and wait for further signals there
Race 4 is shortened; finish at the next mark where a staff with flag H is displayed
questions.why: Race signals: N over H — all races abandoned, further signals ashore (N over A — no more racing today).

questions.q: Approaching the windward mark on the first beat you see a committee RIB near the mark displaying flag C with repeated sound signals and a green triangle. What has changed?
options: The next mark has been moved to port; green marks the port side on the course board
The course has been shortened and the next mark is now the finish
The windward mark you are approaching has been moved and you must look for it to starboard
The position of the next mark has been changed — it has been moved to starboard of its original position
questions.why: Rule 33(a): flag C with repeated sounds and a green triangle — the direction of the next leg is changed to starboard.

questions.q: At the leeward gate a committee boat shows flag C with repeated sound signals and a board with a minus sign. Your crew wonders whether the race has been shortened. What does the signal mean?
options: The next leg has been made shorter — the windward mark has been moved closer; the race continues
The time limit has been reduced; check the notice board after the race
The next leg is longer by one mark; the minus sign means a mark has been removed from the course
The course has been shortened and you finish at the windward mark
questions.why: Rule 33(b): flag C with repeated sounds and "−" — the length of the next leg is decreased ("+" — increased).

questions.q: On the run towards the leeward gate you see a committee RIB beside the gate showing flag C, repeated sounds and a board reading 215. What does the number tell you?
options: The time at which the race will be abandoned if no boat has finished
The new compass bearing of the next leg — the windward mark now lies on 215° from the gate
The sail number of a boat the race committee intends to protest
The distance to the next mark in metres, since the leg has been shortened
questions.why: Rule 33(a)(1): a change of direction of the next leg may be signalled by displaying the new compass bearing.

questions.q: You lead round the windward mark and are already ten lengths down the run when the race committee, behind you, hoists flag C with a green triangle at the mark to move the leeward gate. You never see it and sail to the old gate position, where there are no marks. Where do you stand?

figure.title: Leading down the run
lines: Flag C hoisted at the windward mark
after you were 10 lengths down the leg
You sailed to the old gate position:

options: You are scored NSC for missing the gate, and nothing can be done about it
The change is void for the whole fleet, which must sail the original course
The change was signalled improperly — it must be signalled before the boats begin the leg — so if your score suffers you may request redress
You must still find the new gate; the race committee may change a leg at any moment while boats are racing
questions.why: Rule 33: a change is signalled before boats begin the leg; a late signal is an improper RC action, a ground for redress under rule 61.4(b)(1).

questions.q: Flag C with a red rectangle is displayed at the windward mark as you round it. Looking down the run you cannot yet see the leeward gate in its new position; the mark-laying boat is still motoring with the buoys aboard. Is the change valid?

figure.title: Rounding the windward mark
lines: Flag C, repeated sounds, red rectangle

options: Yes, but you may wait at the windward mark until the new gate is laid
No — without a visible mark you may sail to the original gate position and round there
No — a change of leg is valid only once the new mark is already anchored in position
Yes — the next mark need not be in position when the change is signalled; head to port of the old leg and look for the gate being laid
questions.why: Rule 33: the next mark need not be in position when the change is signalled; the red rectangle means the leg is changed to port.

questions.q: After a 20° shift the race committee signalled a change at mark 2 with flag C and a green triangle. Rounding mark 3 later you find mark 4 has also been moved, but there was no flag C at mark 3. Was the race committee allowed to move mark 4 without signalling?

figure.title: After a 20° shift
lines: Flag C + green triangle at mark 2

options: Yes — to maintain the course configuration, legs after a changed leg may be changed without further signals
Yes, but only if mark 4 was moved by less than 100 m
No — every leg that is changed must be signalled with flag C at the mark where it begins
No — a second change in the same race requires the race to be abandoned
questions.why: Rule 33(c): to maintain the course configuration, subsequent legs may be changed without further signalling.

questions.q: Halfway up the first beat you see the mark-laying boat lift the windward mark and re-lay it 150 m to the right, with no flag C anywhere and the original mark in no way missing or adrift. Several boats on the left are now badly placed. Was that a proper race committee action?

figure.title: First beat
lines: No flag C; mark was not adrift

options: Yes — the race committee may move any mark at any time to keep the beat square to the wind
No — rule 33 allows changing only the next leg, signalled before boats begin it, and rule 34 covers only a mark missing or out of position
No — but only because the mark was moved more than 100 m; a smaller adjustment needs no signal
Yes — rule 34 allows a mark to be relaid wherever the race committee thinks best
questions.why: Rule 33 permits changing the next leg, signalled before boats begin it; rule 34 permits repositioning only a mark missing or out of position.

questions.q: The sailing instructions say course changes will be signalled under rule 33. At mark 1 a committee boat shows flag C with repeated sounds, a red rectangle and a board with 190. Mark 2 was on 230° from mark 1. Where do you look for mark 2 now?
options: On a bearing of 270° — the red rectangle means 40° further to starboard
At mark 1 itself — flag C with a bearing means the course is shortened to finish here
On a bearing of 190° from mark 1 — the leg has been changed to port, and the board gives the new compass bearing
On a bearing of 230° still — the red rectangle only warns that mark 2 is to be left to port
questions.why: Rule 33(a): the change of direction is signalled by the new compass bearing and/or a red rectangle (port) or green triangle (starboard).

questions.q: Running towards mark 2 you cannot find it; where it should be there is a committee RIB displaying flag M and making repetitive sound signals. What do you do?

figure.note: Mark 2 has disappeared; the RIB makes repeated sound signals

options: Pass the RIB on either side; a committee vessel is never a mark unless it anchors a line
Sail to where mark 2 was laid according to the sailing instructions and round that position
Stop and wait: flag M means the race will be abandoned once all boats have gathered
Treat the RIB as mark 2 — leave it on the required side and continue the course
questions.why: Rule 34(b): a missing mark may be replaced by an object displaying flag M with repetitive sound signals; it is then the mark.

questions.q: During the second lap the leeward mark drags 80 m downwind in a gust. The mark-laying boat tows it back to its original position without any flag or sound signal. Blue says the race committee had to signal the move with flag C. Is Blue right?
options: No — a mark out of position may be moved back to its correct position without a signal; flag C is for changing the next leg
No — but the mark should have been replaced by a vessel with flag M, not towed back
Yes — any movement of a mark while boats are racing must be signalled with flag C
Yes — the race committee should instead have abandoned the race
questions.why: Rule 34(a): if a mark is missing or out of position the RC shall, if possible, replace it in its correct position; no signal is required.

questions.q: The windward mark has sunk. There is no spare buoy and the only committee RIB is busy with a capsized Optimist. The leaders are approaching the spot where the mark was. What should the race committee do?

figure.title: Windward mark sunk
lines: Only RIB busy with a capsized Optimist

options: Score the boats by their order of arrival at the spot and continue to the next mark
If it cannot put a replacement or a vessel with flag M in position, it should abandon the race under rule 32.1(c), because a mark is missing
Shorten the course with flag S at the leeward mark after the boats have come back down
Let the boats round the GPS position of the mark; the sailing instructions give its coordinates
questions.why: Rule 34: replace a missing mark or substitute an object with flag M if possible; otherwise rule 32.1(c) — abandon because a mark is missing.

questions.q: Mark 3 has gone adrift. A committee RIB with flag M and repeated sound signals has anchored about 100 m from where the mark used to be. You round the empty spot where mark 3 was, ignoring the RIB, and sail on. How will you be scored?

figure.note: You rounded the empty spot where mark 3 used to be

options: DNF — a boat that does not round the replacement vessel is treated as not finishing
By your finishing place — the sailing instructions give the mark's position, and you rounded it
NSC — the RIB with flag M replaced the mark, so you did not sail the course
By your finishing place, since the RIB was not in the mark's exact position
questions.why: Rule 34(b): an object displaying flag M replaces the missing mark; rule 28 and A5.1 — a boat that does not sail the course is scored NSC.

questions.q: In race 2 you fouled Blue on port tack and took a Two-Turns Penalty. Twenty minutes later the race was abandoned and is now being resailed. Blue says you must take the two turns again at the start of the resail. Must you?

figure.title: Race 2 abandoned, now resailed
lines: You fouled Blue and took two turns

options: No — because you took the penalty at the time; had you not, you would be disqualified from the resail
Yes — penalties taken in an abandoned race do not count and must be repeated
Yes — but one turn is enough the second time
No — a breach in the original race is not a reason to penalise a boat in the resail, except for rules 2, 30.2, 30.4, 69 or rule 14 with serious damage or injury
questions.why: Rule 36(b): breaches in the original race are not a reason to penalise a boat in the resail, with the listed exceptions.

questions.q: In the original race Grey, on port, hit you at speed and holed your topsides — a clear breach of rule 14 with serious damage. The race was then abandoned for lack of wind and resailed. Grey sails the resail and says the abandonment wiped the slate clean. Is she right?

figure.title: Original race, then resail
lines: Grey on port hit you at speed

options: No — rule 36 excepts rule 14 breaches that caused serious damage or injury; Grey can still be penalised for the original incident
Yes — but you can request redress in the resail for the damage
Yes — a breach in an abandoned race can never be penalised in the resail
No — because any contact in an abandoned race carries over, with or without damage
questions.why: Rule 36(b): a boat may still be penalised for a breach of rules 2, 30.2, 30.4, 69 or rule 14 when she caused serious damage or injury.

questions.q: Under a black flag you were in the triangle in the last minute and the race committee displayed your sail number after the general recall. The class now restarts. May you sail the restart?

figure.title: Black flag start, general recall
lines: In the triangle in the last minute

options: Yes — but you must start at least one minute after the starting signal
No — a boat disqualified under rule 30.4 may not sail in the restart; rule 36 makes 30.4 the one breach that bars a boat from a restarted race
Yes — a general recall cancels all starting penalties, including the black flag
No — and you are also excluded from the rest of the regatta
questions.why: Rule 36(a): a breach in the original race does not prevent a boat from competing in a restart, except a breach of rule 30.4.

questions.q: In a race later abandoned for a wind shift, Red deliberately sailed through the finishing area to block a rival, breaking rule 2. The race is resailed. Red says the abandonment ends the matter. Does it?
options: Yes — once a race is abandoned nothing that happened in it can be penalised
No — but only a report under rule 69 can now be made, not a protest
No — rule 36 keeps rule 2 breaches alive: Red can still be penalised for the original race despite the abandonment
Yes — unless the rival requests redress in the resail
questions.why: Rule 36(b): a breach of rule 2, 30.2, 30.4, 69 or rule 14 with serious damage in the original race may still be penalised after a resail.

questions.q: Your hull has crossed the finishing line and you are turning away on port tack, still within a length of the pin. Blue, finishing on starboard, is converging. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: You have crossed but not yet cleared the line

options: Nobody — once a boat's hull has crossed the line the rules of Part 2 no longer apply to her
Blue — she must not interfere with a boat that has finished, under rule 23.1
Blue — a boat that has finished has right of way over boats still finishing
You do — until you clear the finishing line and marks you are still racing, so rule 10 applies as usual between you
questions.why: Definition Racing: a boat is racing until she finishes and clears the line and marks; Part 2 applies, rule 10 (opposite tacks).

questions.q: The sailing instructions for a coastal race say: "Mark 1 to port, mark 2 to starboard, mark 3 to port." Your crew assumes all marks are to port and plans to round mark 2 turning left. What is correct?

figure.title: SI 10.2: the course
lines: Crew plans to turn left at mark 2

options: Round mark 2 leaving it to starboard, turning right — each mark must be left on the side the sailing instructions specify for it
Round mark 2 either side — a single mark with a different side does not bound a leg
Round mark 2 to port and take a One-Turn Penalty for the error
Round all marks to port — marks of a course are always left on the same side
questions.why: Rule 28.1 and definition Sail the Course: each mark is passed on its required side as given in the sailing instructions.

questions.q: The sailing instructions name mark 2 as a rounding mark; the course doubles back from it towards mark 1. In a foul tide you turn back 50 m short of mark 2, well on its correct side, and head for mark 1. Have you sailed the leg?

figure.note: You turned back 50 m short of mark 2

options: Yes — the string stays on the correct side of mark 2, so the leg is sailed
No — the string must touch each rounding mark; by turning short of mark 2 you never passed it, and you must go back and round it before you finish
Yes — a rounding mark need only be approached within hailing distance
No — and because you turned short of a mark you are scored DNF
questions.why: Definition Sail the Course: the string touches each mark the SI designate a rounding mark; rule 28.2 allows the error to be corrected.
questions.ref: RRS 28, RRS definition Sail the Course

questions.q: At mark 2 the committee boat shows flag C with repeated sounds, a board with 040 and a minus sign. The leg to mark 3 was 1.2 miles on 020°. What do you now know about the leg to mark 3?

figure.title: At mark 2
lines: Old leg to mark 3: 1.2 M on 020°

options: It lies 40° to port of the old bearing and is shorter
It lies on 040° and is 1.2 miles minus 40 metres long
It now lies on 040° and is shorter than 1.2 miles — mark 3 has been moved to starboard and closer
It is unchanged — the signal concerns the leg after mark 3
questions.why: Rule 33(a) and (b): flag C with a new compass bearing changes the direction, and "−" means the leg has been shortened.

questions.q: You pass between the leeward gate marks and gybe round the right-hand mark, leaving it to starboard. Your crew protests that the sailing instructions say "marks to port". Did you round correctly?

figure.note: The left-hand gate mark is off the picture to the left

options: No — with marks to port the right-hand gate mark may only be passed on your port side
Yes, but only because your crew had not hailed which mark to take
No — you should have gone round the outside of the right-hand mark to keep it to port
Yes — at a gate a boat passes between the marks and may round either; rounding the right-hand mark means leaving it to starboard, which the gate definition allows
questions.why: Definition Sail the Course: at a gate the string passes between the marks from the previous mark and then round either gate mark.
questions.ref: RRS 28, RRS definition Sail the Course

questions.q: In a Hobie 16 race the only boat to cross the finishing line within the 90-minute time limit is later scored NSC because she left mark 3 on the wrong side. Three other boats crossed the line a few minutes after the time limit. Is the race valid?

figure.title: Time limit 90 min
lines: Only one boat crossed within 90 min
She is scored NSC (mark 3 wrong side)
Three boats crossed a few minutes later

options: No — a race is scored only if a boat started, sailed the course and finished within the time limit; an NSC boat did not sail the course, so the race must be abandoned
Yes — she crossed the finishing line within the time limit, and that is what the time limit measures
Yes — the first of the three later boats is treated as having finished within the limit
No — but the race committee may score the three boats by their order of crossing
questions.why: Rule 35 and 90.3(a): the race stands only if one boat starts, sails the course and finishes within the time limit; otherwise it is abandoned.

questions.q: A change of course was correctly signalled with flag C at the windward mark before you got there, but you did not notice it. You sailed to the original leeward mark, which had been removed, found nothing and eventually finished. How will you be scored?

figure.title: Flag C at the windward mark
lines: Sailed to the old leeward mark: removed

options: DNF — you did not finish the course as originally described
NSC — the changed course is the course; a boat that does not see a correctly made signal is still bound by it
By your finishing place — a boat that could not see the new mark is not responsible for the change
Average points — missing a signal is a ground for redress
questions.why: Rule 33 changes the course when signalled before boats begin the leg; rule 28 requires that course to be sailed; A5.1 — NSC.

questions.q: You capsize while tacking at the windward mark and, still capsized, drift past the mark on the wrong side; you right the boat three lengths beyond it. Your crew says a capsized boat is not sailing, so the drift does not count. Who is right?

figure.note: You capsized at the mark and drifted past it on the wrong side

options: Your crew — but you must take a One-Turn Penalty for passing the mark on the wrong side
Nobody can say — ask the race committee for a ruling before continuing
You must unwind — the string of your track passed the mark on the wrong side, however you got there; sail back and round it correctly
Your crew — a boat is not sailing the course while capsized, so her drift is ignored
questions.why: Definition Sail the Course: the string represents the boat's track from the start to the finish; rule 28.2 lets her correct the error before finishing.
questions.ref: RRS 28.2, RRS definition Sail the Course

questions.q: The race committee signals a general recall with the First Substitute and two sounds. Sailing back, you bump the committee boat while jostling at its stern. Must you take a One-Turn Penalty?
options: Yes — you remain racing until the First Substitute is lowered and the new warning signal is made
No — but you must return around an end of the line before the new start
Yes — the committee boat is a starting mark from the first preparatory signal until the class finally starts
No — the general recall ended your racing, so rule 31 no longer applied when you touched the committee boat
questions.why: Definition Racing: a boat stops racing when a general recall is signalled; rule 31 applies only while racing.

questions.q: Wednesday evening club race, ILCA 7 fleet, a run in 8 knots and flat water, no judges afloat. You trim the mainsheet in hard and ease it again in a steady rhythm, about six times a minute, and the boat accelerates with each pull. Is this allowed?

figure.title: Run, 8 knots, flat water
lines: ILCA 7, no judges on the water
Mainsheet trimmed in and eased again

options: No — repeated fanning of the sail by trimming and releasing it is pumping, prohibited by rule 42.2(a)
Yes — pumping is prohibited only on a beat to windward, not on a run
Yes — rule 42 is enforced only when judges are on the water
Yes — trimming the mainsheet is normal sail adjustment, allowed by rule 42.1
questions.why: Rule 42.2(a): pumping is repeated fanning of any sail by trimming and releasing it or by body movement, prohibited whatever the leg.

questions.q: You are helming a 420 on the first beat of a national championship in 12 knots. Your crew hikes flat out and keeps still; you trim the main in each puff and ease it in each lull. A rival later says you were breaking rule 42. Were you?

figure.title: First beat, 12 knots
lines: Crew hiking hard and keeping still
Main trimmed in puffs, eased in lulls

options: Yes — hiking is a body movement and rule 42.1 forbids all body movement that affects speed
No — rule 42.1 lets the crew adjust the trim of sails and hull and hike; nothing here propels the boat by body movement
Yes — trimming in every puff and easing in every lull is pumping under rule 42.2(a)
Only if the class rules of the 420 specifically permit hiking and trimming
questions.why: Rule 42.1: crew may adjust the trim of sails and hull and perform other acts of seamanship; only body movement that propels the boat is prohibited.

questions.q: Optimist regatta on a lake, the breeze has died to 3 knots. You are 100 m from the finishing line, dead downwind, and you start rolling the boat from side to side with your body, again and again; the boat picks up speed. Which rule, if any, do you break?

figure.note: Wind 3 knots; the boat is rolled from side to side

options: None — rule 42.3(a) allows a boat to be rolled to help her steer
None — in less than 5 knots of wind rule 42 does not apply
Rule 42.2(b) — repeated rolling of the boat induced by body movement is rocking, prohibited
None — only pumping the sail is prohibited, not moving your body
questions.why: Rule 42.2(b)(1): rocking is repeated rolling of the boat induced by body movement; no wind-speed exemption exists in rule 42 itself.

questions.q: You are racing at a windsurfing event. On the reach Red pumps her sail continuously, stroke after stroke, and pulls away. You intend to protest her under rule 42.2(a) for pumping. Will the protest succeed?

figure.title: Windsurfing event, reach
lines: She pulls away from the fleet
You want to protest under rule 42.2(a)

options: Yes — rule 42.2(a) prohibits pumping for every kind of boat, boards included
Yes — pumping is allowed on a board only when the race committee displays flag O
No — pumping is allowed for anyone on a reach, only on a beat is it prohibited
No — Appendix B changes rule 42 for windsurfing: a board may be propelled by the unassisted actions of the competitor, so pumping is allowed
questions.why: Appendix B (windsurfing) replaces rule 42: a board is propelled by wind, water and the unassisted actions of the competitor; pumping is not a breach.
questions.ref: RRS Appendix B, rule 42 as changed

questions.q: A Dragon on a 5-knot beat in the Saronic Gulf. You move your crew of three forward and to leeward to heel the boat, lift the transom and reduce wetted surface, and they stay there for the whole leg. Does rule 42 allow this?

figure.title: Beat, 5 knots
lines: Crew moved forward and to leeward

options: Yes — rule 42.1 allows the crew to adjust the trim of the hull; the weight is moved once and held still
Only if the weight is moved after the boat has reached full speed
No — the crew must stay on the windward side in all conditions under rule 49
No — moving crew weight to change the boat's trim is a body movement that propels her
questions.why: Rule 42.1: crew may adjust the trim of sails and hull; a single, held change of weight position is seamanship, not kinetics.

questions.q: A 29er on a tight reach in 9 knots, not enough to plane. The crew on the trapeze bounces up and down on the wire in a steady rhythm, and with each bounce the mainsail leech flicks and the boat surges. How do you judge this?

figure.title: Tight reach, 9 knots
lines: Crew bounces on the wire in rhythm
Leech flicks and the boat surges each time

options: It is allowed because the crew never touches the mainsheet
It is pumping — repeated fanning of the sail by vertical body movement is prohibited by rule 42.2(a)
It is allowed — body movement on the trapeze is part of normal crew work
It is rocking — rule 42.2(b) — because the body movement is repeated
questions.why: Rule 42.2(a): pumping includes fanning a sail by vertical or athwartships body movement, not only by working the sheet.

questions.q: Palma, 20 knots and a long swell, your Melges 24 on a broad reach. As each wave lifts the stern the trimmer gives the spinnaker sheet one hard pull and the boat starts to surf; one pull per wave, nothing more. Is the trimmer breaking rule 42?

figure.title: Broad reach, 20 knots, swell
lines: One hard pull on the sheet per wave
The boat starts to surf each time

options: No — in 20 knots and waves rule 42 is suspended automatically
Yes — pulling in a sail sharply to start surfing is pumping under rule 42.2(a)
No — when surfing is possible, each sail may be pulled in once for each wave to initiate surfing (rule 42.3(c))
Yes — the exception for surfing applies only to the mainsail, not the spinnaker
questions.why: Rule 42.3(c)(1): in surfing or planing conditions each sail may be pulled in once per wave or gust to initiate surfing or planing.

questions.q: Same breeze, 18 knots and steep waves, a 470 on a reach. On every wave the helmsman pumps the mainsheet three or four times in quick succession until the boat is surfing, then lets her go. Is that within the surfing exception?

figure.title: Reach, 18 knots, steep waves
lines: Then the sheet is left alone

options: Yes — any number of pulls is allowed as long as the boat does start to surf
No — pumping is never allowed on a 470, whatever the conditions
Yes — rule 42.3(c) only limits pumping on a beat to windward
No — the exception allows one pull per sail for each wave or gust; several pulls per wave is pumping under rule 42.2(a)
questions.why: Rule 42.3(c)(1) limits the surfing exception to one pull of each sail per wave or gust; more than that is pumping.

questions.q: A Finn running in 6 knots. The helmsman steers a continuous series of S-curves, up 10°, down 10°, up again, with hard rudder each time; the boat rolls from side to side with every turn and clearly goes faster than her neighbours. The sailor says he never moved his body. Who is right?
options: He breaks rule 42.2(b) — rocking includes repeated rolling induced by steering, not only by body movement
He breaks rule 42.2(e) — repeated changes of course are the same as repeated tacks
He is right — rocking is defined only as rolling caused by body movement
He is right — rule 42.3(a) allows a boat to be rolled to facilitate steering
questions.why: Rule 42.2(b)(3): rocking is repeated rolling of the boat induced by body movement, repeated sail or centreboard adjustment, or steering.

questions.q: ILCA 6 youth regatta, a run in 7 knots. You pull the daggerboard up and push it down again every few seconds; each movement makes the boat roll and she moves faster. Does rule 42 cover this?

figure.title: Run, 7 knots
lines: Daggerboard up and down every few seconds
The boat rolls with each movement

options: Yes — it is ooching, because the board is moved suddenly and stopped abruptly
Yes — repeated rolling induced by repeated adjustment of the centreboard is rocking, rule 42.2(b)(2)
No — rocking is only rolling induced by body movement
No — adjusting the daggerboard is a hull adjustment allowed by rule 42.1
questions.why: Rule 42.2(b)(2): rocking includes repeated rolling induced by repeated adjustment of the sails or centreboard.

questions.q: You roll-tack your 420 in 8 knots: both of you heel the boat hard to windward through head to wind, then flatten her with a snap. You come out of the tack visibly faster than you went in and faster than the boats that did not tack. Was this a legal roll tack?

figure.title: Roll tack in 8 knots
lines: 420, both crew roll the boat hard
Snap flatten after head to wind
Exit speed greater than entry speed
Faster than boats that did not tack

options: No — body movement during a tack is never allowed under rule 42.1
Yes — a roll tack is a single manoeuvre, and rule 42 prohibits only repeated actions
No — rolling through a tack is allowed only if the boat's speed just after it is not greater than it would have been without the tack (rule 42.3(b))
Yes — rule 42.3(b) allows the crew to exaggerate the roll in a tack without any limit
questions.why: Rule 42.3(b): crew may exaggerate rolling to steer through a tack or gybe, provided that just after it the speed is not greater than without the tack.

questions.q: At the gybe mark in 5 knots you roll your Optimist to windward, swing the boom across and flatten the boat as she settles on the new gybe. She turns neatly round the mark and comes out at the same speed as before. A parent on the shore shouts that you cheated. Did you?

figure.title: Gybe mark, 5 knots
lines: Optimist rolled to windward in the gybe
Same speed after the gybe as before

options: Yes — rolling the boat with body movement during a gybe is rocking under rule 42.2(b)
Yes — the exception for exaggerated rolling applies only to tacks, not to gybes
No — rule 42 does not apply to a boat while she is within the zone of a mark
No — rule 42.3(b) allows exaggerated rolling to steer through a gybe, provided the boat is not faster just after it
questions.why: Rule 42.3(b): exaggerated rolling to facilitate steering through a tack or a gybe is permitted if the boat is not faster just after it.

questions.q: Drifting conditions, 3 knots, on a Star. To bear away round the leeward mark without dragging the rudder, you both move to leeward, heel the boat and let her turn by herself, then sit her upright again. Is this allowed?

figure.title: Leeward mark, 3 knots
lines: Star, both crew move to leeward
Boat heels and bears away by herself

options: Yes — rule 42.3(a) allows a boat to be rolled (heeled) to facilitate steering
Only if the rudder is also used at the same time
No — in light wind any body movement that changes the course is prohibited
No — heeling the boat by body movement to make her turn is rocking
questions.why: Rule 42.3(a): a boat may be rolled to facilitate steering; a single heel to turn the boat is the classic case.

questions.q: An ILCA 4 on a reach in 6 knots. The sailor sits forward, then throws her upper body forward sharply and stops dead against the straps, again and again, every couple of seconds. The boat jerks forward each time. What is this called in rule 42 and is it allowed?
options: Rocking — repeated body movement; prohibited by rule 42.2(b)
Ooching — sudden forward body movement stopped abruptly; prohibited by rule 42.2(c)
Torquing — allowed, because the sail is not touched and the boat is not rolled
Pumping — repeated body movement that moves the boat; prohibited by rule 42.2(a)
questions.why: Rule 42.2(c): ooching is a sudden forward body movement stopped abruptly; it is a prohibited action.

questions.q: Hobie 16, 17 knots and a following sea. On the best waves the crew gives one hard lunge forward with the body, stopping abruptly, to get the boat to surf; one lunge per wave, as with a sheet pump. The skipper says the surfing exception covers it. Does it?

figure.title: 17 knots, following sea
lines: One hard body lunge forward per wave
Skipper: "same as one pump per wave"

options: No — because the surfing exception does not apply to catamarans
Yes — one movement per wave is allowed for any action that initiates surfing
No — rule 42.3(c) permits pulling in a sail once per wave, not a body lunge; a sudden forward body movement stopped abruptly is ooching under 42.2(c)
Yes — ooching is prohibited only when it is repeated and unrelated to waves
questions.why: Rule 42.3(c) relaxes only the pulling in of sails; ooching (42.2(c)) is a sudden forward body movement stopped abruptly, prohibited even once.

questions.q: Six minutes before your start, in a drifting 2 knots, you scull your ILCA 7 vigorously for a minute to get across to the favoured end of the line. The warning signal has been made; the preparatory signal has not. Have you broken rule 42?

figure.title: Before the start, 2 knots
lines: Warning signal made, prep not yet
You scull hard for a minute

options: Yes — rule 42 applies to every boat on the course area from the time she leaves the shore
Yes — rule 42 applies from the warning signal, when the starting sequence begins
No — sculling is always allowed before a boat has started
No — the rules of Part 4 apply only to a boat racing, and she is racing from her preparatory signal
questions.why: Preamble to Part 4: its rules apply only to boats racing; a boat is racing from her preparatory signal (definition Racing).
questions.ref: RRS Part 4 preamble, RRS definition Racing

questions.q: In a dying breeze your J/70 crosses the finishing line, but with no steerage way she lies with her stern still over the line, in the way of the boat behind. The trimmer pumps the main hard a dozen times to get clear of the line. Is that a breach of rule 42?

figure.note: You have crossed but your stern is still on the line

options: Yes — a boat is still racing until she has finished and cleared the finishing line and marks, so rule 42 still applies
Yes — but only because the pumping took place within the zone of a finishing mark
No — pumping to clear the line for the next boat is an act of seamanship under rule 42.1
No — rule 42 ceases to apply the moment any part of the hull crosses the finishing line
questions.why: Definition Racing: a boat is racing until she finishes and clears the finishing line and marks; Part 4 applies until then.

questions.q: Flat calm at the leeward mark of a club race. Your J/24 has stopped two lengths short of it, and the bowman takes a paddle from the cockpit locker and paddles the last few metres round the mark. Which rule is broken?

figure.title: Leeward mark, flat calm
lines: J/24 stopped two lengths from the mark

options: No rule — paddling is allowed when the wind speed is below 3 knots
Rule 42.1 — a boat shall compete using only the wind and water to increase, maintain or decrease her speed
Rule 45 — a boat may not use any equipment to move while racing
Rule 31 — propelling the boat round a mark is treated as touching it
questions.why: Rule 42.1: only wind and water may be used to increase, maintain or decrease speed; a paddle is neither.

questions.q: A shifty, puffy day on a river. On one beat you trim and ease the mainsheet of your Laser perhaps thirty times, each time because the wind heads, lifts, gusts or dies. A judge boat has followed you the whole leg. Have you given them anything to penalise?

figure.title: Shifty beat on a river
lines: Each time in response to a shift or puff
Judge boat watching the whole leg

options: Yes — on a beat to windward a sail may be trimmed only once per shift
No — but only because the judges did not display a yellow flag during the leg
No — trimming the sail in response to changes in the wind is adjusting trim under rule 42.1; pumping is fanning the sail unrelated to the wind
Yes — more than a few sheet adjustments per leg is pumping by definition
questions.why: Rule 42.1 permits adjusting sail trim; rule 42.2(a) prohibits repeated fanning of the sail, not repeated trimming in response to the wind.

questions.q: Snipe on a run in 10 knots with a short chop. On every wave both crew swing their torsos to windward and then to leeward, rolling the boat; the boat is noticeably faster than the fleet. The helmsman argues they are "rolling to steer down the waves" as allowed by rule 42.3(a). Does that defence hold?

figure.title: Run, 10 knots, chop
lines: Snipe, both crew swing torsos each wave

options: Yes — in waves, body movement in time with the waves is always permitted
Yes — any rolling that helps the boat steer down a wave is covered by the exception
No — rolling a boat is never allowed on a run, only on a reach
No — rule 42.3(a) permits rolling to facilitate steering, not repeated rolling by body movement that propels the boat; this is rocking under 42.2(b)
questions.why: Rule 42.3(a) allows rolling to facilitate steering; repeated roll by body movement that clearly propels the boat is rocking, rule 42.2(b)(1).

questions.q: Two minutes before the start of a J/70 race in 3 knots you tack six times in a small area to hold your spot near the committee boat while the fleet lines up. Each tack is a normal tack, no roll, and you come out no faster. A competitor hails that repeated tacks are prohibited. Is she right?

figure.title: 2 minutes to start, 3 knots
lines: J/70, six tacks in a small area
Holding a spot near the committee boat
No roll, no gain in speed

options: No — rule 42.2(e) prohibits repeated tacks or gybes only when unrelated to changes in the wind or tactical considerations; holding a position is tactical
No — rule 42 does not apply until the starting signal is made
Yes — repeated tacks are allowed only after the starting signal
Yes — more than two tacks within a minute is a prohibited action whatever the reason
questions.why: Rule 42.2(e): prohibited are repeated tacks or gybes unrelated to changes in the wind or to tactical considerations.

questions.q: A long run in 5 knots on flat water, no boat within ten lengths and the wind steady. Your Europe sailor gybes, gybes back, and gybes again every fifteen seconds down the whole leg, gaining a little speed from each gybe. What does rule 42 say?

figure.note: Steady 5 knots, flat water, no boat within ten lengths

options: It is allowed — rule 42.3(b) permits any number of roll gybes
It is prohibited — repeated gybes unrelated to changes in the wind or to tactical considerations (rule 42.2(e))
It is prohibited only if the sailor also pumps the sail during each gybe
It is allowed — a gybe is a change of tack, and rule 42 does not restrict tacking or gybing
questions.why: Rule 42.2(e): repeated tacks or gybes unrelated to changes in the wind or to tactical considerations are prohibited.

questions.q: Downwind in a 36-ft cruiser-racer in a lull, 4 knots. You send three crew across to the leeward side once, to heel the boat to windward so the spinnaker stays full, and they stay there until the breeze returns. The owner is nervous about rule 42. Should he be?

figure.title: Run in a lull, 4 knots
lines: Three crew moved to leeward once
Boat heeled to windward, held there

options: Yes — moving crew to leeward on a run is rocking under rule 42.2(b)
Yes — crew may move across the boat only when she tacks or gybes
No — one change of crew position, held still, is adjusting the trim of the hull under rule 42.1; rocking means repeated rolling
No — because rule 42 applies only to dinghies and small keelboats
questions.why: Rule 42.1: crew may adjust the trim of the hull; rule 42.2(b) prohibits repeated rolling, not a single held weight shift.

questions.q: After a knock-down in 25 knots your 470 is half full of water. Sailing on, the crew bails furiously with a bucket, throwing the water aft over the transom; each bucketful visibly nudges the boat forward. Is this bailing a breach of rule 42?

figure.title: After a knock-down, 25 knots
lines: 470 half full of water, sailing on
Water thrown aft over the transom

options: No — but only if the crew throws the water over the side, never over the transom
Yes — the crew may bail only while the boat is stopped or made fast under rule 45
Yes — throwing water aft is propelling the boat by means other than wind and water on the hull
No — bailing is an act of seamanship permitted by rule 42.1, even if the water thrown out happens to move the boat a little
questions.why: Rule 42.1: crew may perform acts of seamanship; bailing is one, and rule 45 even lets a boat make fast to bail.

questions.q: Thirty seconds before the start you are too close to the line in your Finn, so you push the boom out to windward by hand, back the mainsail and let the wind push you astern a few metres. Grey, just behind, protests you under rule 42 for "using your hands to move the boat". Who is right?

figure.note: Mainsail backed; you move astern towards Grey

options: You, under rule 42 — backing a sail uses the wind; but under rule 21 a boat moving astern by backing a sail must keep clear of boats that are not
Grey — pushing the boom out by hand to move the boat is a prohibited action, like sculling
You — and Grey, as the boat clear astern of you, must keep clear under rule 12
Grey — a boat may not move astern at all once her preparatory signal has been made
questions.why: Backing a sail is propulsion by the wind, not a 42.2 action; rule 21: a boat moving astern by backing a sail keeps clear of one that is not.

questions.q: Twenty seconds before the start, 3 knots of wind, your ILCA 7 has stopped head to wind just below the line. You move the tiller back and forth several times to swing the bow down onto a close-hauled course, and stop as soon as she is there. Allowed?

figure.note: Stopped head to wind, 20 s to the start, 3 knots

options: No — repeated movement of the helm is sculling, prohibited by rule 42.2(d) in every case
Yes — a boat above close-hauled and stationary or moving slowly may scull to turn to a close-hauled course (rule 42.3(d))
No — sculling is allowed only after the starting signal, to get off the line
Yes — sculling is always allowed when the wind is under 5 knots
questions.why: Rule 42.3(d): a boat above a close-hauled course, stationary or moving slowly, may scull to turn to a close-hauled course.

questions.q: Having sculled his stopped Laser down from head to wind, the sailor reaches close-hauled and keeps waggling the tiller, now driving the boat forward over the line in the last seconds before the gun. Where does the rule draw the line?

figure.title: Last seconds before the gun
lines: Boat driven forward over the line

options: At the starting signal — any sculling after the gun is prohibited, before it is allowed
Nowhere — once sculling has legally begun it may continue until the boat has speed
At close-hauled — the exception ends when the boat is on a close-hauled course; sculling that propels her forward breaks rule 42.2(d)
At the line — sculling is prohibited only on the course side of the starting line
questions.why: Rule 42.3(d) allows sculling only to turn to close-hauled; rule 42.2(d) prohibits helm movements that propel the boat forward.

questions.q: Start of a river race against a 1-knot current, no wind. Your Dragon, head to wind and stopped, begins to drift backwards towards the boat behind. You work the rudder hard from side to side; the boat does not go forward, but she stops moving astern. Is that permitted?

figure.title: River start, 1 knot of current
lines: Dragon stopped head to wind, no wind
Drifting astern towards the boat behind
Rudder worked hard side to side

options: No — but the breach is of rule 21, because a boat moving astern must keep clear
Yes — rule 42.3(d) allows a stopped boat head to wind to scull as she wishes
Yes — sculling is prohibited only when it propels the boat forward
No — repeated helm movement that prevents the boat moving astern is sculling, prohibited by rule 42.2(d)
questions.why: Rule 42.2(d): sculling is repeated helm movement that is forceful, propels the boat forward or prevents her moving astern.

questions.q: You are early for the start in your 29er and want to kill speed without luffing into the boat to windward. You push the tiller from side to side repeatedly, and the boat slows down sharply. A judge is watching from ten metres. Will you get a yellow flag?

figure.title: Early for the start
lines: Tiller pushed side to side repeatedly

options: No — a boat may reduce speed by repeatedly moving her helm (rule 42.3(f))
Yes — repeated movement of the helm is sculling, whatever its purpose
Yes — slowing down by helm movement is allowed only after the starting signal
No — but only because the boat is above close-hauled while doing it
questions.why: Rule 42.3(f): a boat may reduce speed by repeatedly moving her helm.

questions.q: Beating in 4 knots in a Melges 24, the helmsman gives the wheel a forceful quarter turn each way every two seconds, "to keep her alive". The course hardly changes, but the boat keeps moving. Which prohibited action is this?

figure.title: Beat, 4 knots
lines: Of the wheel, each way, every two seconds
Course barely changes, boat keeps moving

options: Pumping — repeated movement of a control to increase speed (rule 42.2(a))
Sculling — repeated movement of the helm that is forceful or propels the boat forward (rule 42.2(d))
Rocking — the wheel movements make the boat roll (rule 42.2(b))
None — the helm may be moved freely as long as the course does not change
questions.why: Rule 42.2(d): sculling is repeated movement of the helm that is either forceful or propels the boat forward or prevents her moving astern.

questions.q: Bodrum regatta, your 36-ft cruiser-racer cuts a corner and runs aground on a sandbank. Two crew jump in and push the bow round; a spectator RIB comes alongside and offers a tow. What may you accept under rule 42?

figure.note: Aground; two crew in the water pushing, a RIB offers a tow

options: Nothing — a boat aground must get off using only the wind in her sails
Everything — a boat aground may use any means at all, including an engine, to get free
The pushing by your own crew, and help from the RIB's crew by hand — but not a tow under engine unless the sailing instructions allow it (rule 42.3(h), (i))
Only the tow — crew in the water pushing the boat is a prohibited body movement
questions.why: Rule 42.3(h): a boat aground may use the force of her own or another vessel's crew and any equipment other than an engine; 42.3(i) lets the SI permit an engine.

questions.q: In a 20-knot squall your J/24 is blown into an anchored committee vessel and her rigging catches on its rail. The vessel's crew help you push off and untangle the shrouds, and you sail on. Did you receive prohibited outside help?

figure.title: Squall, 20 knots
lines: J/24 blown into the committee vessel
Their crew push you off and untangle

options: No — because the committee vessel is a mark and marks do not count as outside help
Yes — unless the vessel you hit was also a boat racing in the same race
Yes — any help from a person not on your boat is outside help under rule 41
No — help from the crew of another vessel to get clear after a collision is allowed (rule 41(b)), and 42.3(h) allows their effort to free you
questions.why: Rule 41(b): help from the crew of another vessel to get clear after a collision; rule 42.3(h): a boat that has collided may use their effort to get free.

questions.q: The sailing instructions of a Split regatta say: "A boat that runs aground may use her engine to get clear, provided she gains no significant advantage." Your 40-footer touches on a reef, motors astern for ten seconds to get off, stops the engine and continues racing. Have you broken rule 42?
options: No — rule 42.3(i) lets the sailing instructions permit an engine in stated circumstances, provided the boat gains no significant advantage
No — any boat may use her engine to get off a grounding, with or without such an instruction
Yes — rule 42.3(h) excludes the engine in every case, and the sailing instructions cannot change that
Yes — after using the engine a boat must retire from the race
questions.why: Rule 42.3(i): the sailing instructions may permit propulsion by engine or other means in stated circumstances if no significant advantage is gained.

questions.q: On the second beat of an offshore race you see a windsurfer separated from his board, waving an arm, 200 m to leeward. You start the engine and motor to him. Does rule 42 allow that?

figure.title: Second beat, offshore race
lines: You start the engine and go

options: No — the engine may never be run while a boat is racing
Yes — any means of propulsion may be used to help a person or vessel in danger (rule 42.3(g)); rule 1.1 even requires you to help
No — you must sail to him; only the wind may be used while racing
Yes — but only if you retire from the race before starting the engine
questions.why: Rule 42.3(g): any means of propulsion may be used to help a person or vessel in danger; rule 1.1 requires all possible help.

questions.q: After a gybe in a 470 the top batten of the mainsail is inverted, poking to windward. Your crew pumps the mainsheet three or four times until it pops through; the boat barely changes speed. Is the pumping a breach?

figure.title: After the gybe
lines: Mainsheet pumped 3–4 times until it pops

options: Yes — pumping is pumping; an inverted batten should be cleared by luffing the sail
Yes — unless the batten is cleared with a single pump only
No — when a batten is inverted the crew may pump the sail until it is back to normal, unless this clearly propels the boat (rule 42.3(e))
No — pumping is always allowed within ten seconds of completing a gybe
questions.why: Rule 42.3(e): if a batten is inverted the crew may pump the sail until it returns to normal, but not if this clearly propels the boat.

questions.q: At a foiling WASZP event the wind is 9 knots, marginal for take-off. Coming off the start line you pump the mainsail eight or nine times in a row and the boat lifts onto her foils. A rival who stayed in the water protests. What is the position under rule 42?

figure.title: WASZP, 9 knots, marginal foiling
lines: Eight or nine pumps in a row

options: Pumping is never allowed in a single-handed class without flag O displayed
Rule 42.3(c) allows one pull per gust only, so eight pumps break rule 42.2(a)
Pumping to take off is allowed only on a free leg, never just after the start
In foiling conditions each sail may be pulled in any number of times to initiate foiling (rule 42.3(c)(2)); no breach
questions.why: Rule 42.3(c)(2): when foiling conditions exist, each sail may be pulled in any number of times to initiate foiling.

questions.q: The notice of race says Appendix P applies. On the first run a judge boat sounds a whistle, points a yellow flag at your boat and hails your sail number. It is your first penalty of the event. What must you do?

figure.title: Appendix P applies
lines: Whistle, yellow flag pointed at you

options: Take a Two-Turns Penalty under rule 44.2 as soon as possible; if you do not, you are disqualified without a hearing
Take a One-Turn Penalty; the two-turns penalty is only for Part 2 breaches
Retire from the race immediately; a judge's penalty is never a turns penalty
Nothing on the water; the judge will file a protest and a hearing will decide
questions.why: Appendix P2.1: a first penalty under P1.2 is a Two-Turns Penalty under rule 44.2; failing to take it means disqualification without a hearing.

questions.q: Day three of a championship sailed under Appendix P. You were yellow-flagged once on day one and took two turns. Now a judge whistles and points the yellow flag at you again on the final beat. What is the penalty this time?

figure.title: Appendix P, day three
lines: One yellow flag already on day one
Judge signals you again on the last beat

options: Another Two-Turns Penalty, as for every yellow flag under Appendix P
Retire promptly from the race; if you fail to, you are disqualified without a hearing and the score cannot be excluded
Disqualification from the whole series without a hearing
A 20 % scoring penalty added to your finishing place
questions.why: Appendix P2.2: a second penalty in the event means promptly retiring; otherwise disqualification without a hearing, not excludable.

questions.q: At a youth worlds sailed under Appendix P, Blue has already been yellow-flagged twice. In race eight a judge penalises her a third time; she retires from the race at once. How is she scored for that race?

figure.title: Appendix P, race 8
lines: Blue already flagged twice this event
Third yellow flag from a judge

options: Two-Turns Penalty — Appendix P penalties start again from the first after two
RET — retiring is the penalty, and the score may be discarded like any other
Disqualified without a hearing with a non-excludable score (DNE), even though she retired; had she not retired, every race of the event would be DNE
DSQ for that race, excludable, as for any boat that breaks rule 42
questions.why: Appendix P2.3: a third penalty means retiring; the boat is then DNE for the race; not retiring brings DNE in all races and a possible rule 69 hearing.

questions.q: Under Appendix P a judge penalises you for rocking thirty seconds after the start, and you begin your two turns. Before you have finished them the race committee signals a general recall. What happens to the penalty?

figure.title: Appendix P, 30 s after the start
lines: General recall signalled before you finish

options: It is cancelled completely, as if it had never been given
It stands — you must complete the turns before the new start or be disqualified
It is carried over to the restarted race and must be taken after the new start
It is cancelled by the recall, but it still counts towards the number of times you have been penalised in the event
questions.why: Appendix P3: a P1.2 penalty is cancelled by a postponement, general recall or abandonment, but it counts towards the number of penalties in the event.

questions.q: A 470 championship; the class rules permit pumping, rocking and ooching when the wind exceeds 10 knots. With the warning signal the race committee displays flag O. It is blowing 14 knots. What does this mean for your race?

figure.title: Warning signal, 14 knots
lines: Flag O displayed on the committee boat

options: Pumping, rocking and ooching are permitted for this race, as specified in the class rules (Appendix P5)
Nothing until the starting signal; flag O takes effect only after the start
Rule 42 is switched off entirely, including sculling and repeated tacks
Flag O means Appendix P judges are on the water and rule 42 will be enforced
questions.why: Appendix P5.2: flag O displayed no later than the warning signal means pumping, rocking and ooching are permitted as specified in the class rules.

questions.q: A Finn race started under flag O in 13 knots. By the second beat the wind has dropped to 7 knots, and at the windward mark a committee vessel displays flag R with repeated sound signals. What applies after you round that mark?

figure.title: Second beat, wind down to 7 knots
lines: Race started under flag O in 13 knots
Flag R with repeated sounds at the mark

options: The race is abandoned because the wind fell below the class limit
Rule 42 applies again, as changed by the class rules — pumping, rocking and ooching are no longer permitted after the mark
Flag R is a warning only; pumping remains permitted until the finish
Rule 42 applies again in full, but only on the next downwind leg
questions.why: Appendix P5.3(b): flag R at a mark with repetitive sounds means that after the mark rule 42 applies as changed by the class rules.

questions.q: A club regatta whose notice of race and sailing instructions say nothing about Appendix P. During the run a RIB with a club official whistles, waves a yellow flag at you and shouts your number for "pumping". What is the legal effect?
options: You must take a One-Turn Penalty, since the breach is not of a Part 2 rule
You must take a Two-Turns Penalty at once or be disqualified without a hearing
None — Appendix P applies only when the notice of race or sailing instructions say so; a breach of rule 42 can only be dealt with by protest and a hearing
You must retire; any official may penalise rule 42 on the water at any event
questions.why: Appendix P preamble: it applies only if the notice of race or sailing instructions say so; otherwise rule 42 goes through protest and hearing.

questions.q: From close astern you watch Red, a Laser, pumping her main stroke after stroke down the whole run of a club race; there are no judges. Can you do anything about it yourself?

figure.title: Club race, the run
lines: Red pumps her main all the way down
You are close astern and see it all

options: No — only the race committee or judges may protest a boat for breaking rule 42
No — a boat may protest another only for breaches of Part 2 or rule 31
Yes — you may penalise her yourself by hailing her to take two turns
Yes — you may protest her: hail "Protest" at the first reasonable opportunity and lodge a written protest; the protest committee decides on the evidence
questions.why: Rule 60: a boat may protest another boat; a rule 42 protest is decided by the protest committee at a hearing on the evidence given.

questions.q: Under Appendix P a judge penalises Blue for sculling at the leeward mark and she takes her two turns. You were next to her, hailed "Protest" and lodge a written protest for the same sculling. What should the protest committee do about the penalty?

figure.title: Leeward mark, Appendix P
lines: You protest her for the same incident

options: Not penalise her further — a boat penalised under P1.2 shall not be penalised again under rule 42 for the same incident
Hear the protest and impose a 20 % scoring penalty in addition to the turns
Make her retire — two penalties for one incident add up to a second Appendix P penalty
Disqualify her — a protest by a boat takes precedence over a judge's on-the-water penalty
questions.why: Appendix P1.2: a boat penalised by a judge under P1.2 shall not be penalised further under rule 42 for the same incident.

questions.q: Club race, no Appendix P, nothing in the sailing instructions about rule 42 penalties. Halfway down the run you realise you have been pumping without thinking about it. You want to put it right. What does the rule book offer you?
options: Take a One-Turn Penalty, which rule 44.1 provides for breaches other than those of Part 2
Rule 44.1 covers only Part 2 rules and rule 31; for rule 42 the only penalty you can take yourself is to retire (Basic Principle, Sportsmanship and the Rules)
Nothing — a breach of rule 42 that no boat or judge protests needs no penalty at all
Take a Two-Turns Penalty under rule 44.1, as for any rule you break while racing
questions.why: Rule 44.1 applies to Part 2 and rule 31 only; the Basic Principle requires a boat that broke a rule to take a penalty, which may be to retire.

questions.q: A judge gives your Optimist a yellow flag under Appendix P for rocking in 14 knots. You take the turns, but after the race you learn that flag O had been displayed with the warning signal and the class rules allow rocking above 12 knots. Can you get redress?
options: Yes — any penalty a boat considers wrong is a ground for redress under rule 61
No — a judge's decision under Appendix P can never be reviewed or give grounds for redress
Yes — redress is normally excluded for a judge's Appendix P action, except when it was improper because an RC signal or class rule was not taken into account (P4)
No — redress is available only for errors of the race committee, never of judges
questions.why: Appendix P4: no redress for a judge's P1.2 action, except when it was improper because an RC signal or a class rule was not taken into account.

questions.q: Your skiff's class rules change rule 42 so that pumping is permitted at all times, with no wind limit and no flag O. At a mixed-class regatta a Laser sailor protests you for pumping on the run. Is the class rule valid?
options: No — pumping can be permitted only through flag O under Appendix P5
No — rule 42 can be changed only by the sailing instructions, not by class rules
Yes — but only in races where every class present has the same rule
Yes — class rules may change rule 42 (rule 86.1(c)); the protest should be dismissed
questions.why: Rule 86.1(c): class rules may change rule 42 (among others); the change applies to boats of that class.

questions.q: A beat up a narrow lake in a gusty, shifting northerly. You tack on every header and sail eight tacks in one leg, far more than anyone else. A competitor mutters about "repeated tacks". Is there a case against you?

figure.note: Gusty, shifting wind; a tack on every header

options: No — repeated tacks are prohibited only when unrelated to changes in the wind or tactical considerations; tacking on shifts is exactly what the rule allows
No — rule 42 does not apply on a beat to windward
Yes — rule 42.2(e) limits a boat to a reasonable number of tacks per leg
Yes — more than four tacks on a beat is a prohibited action unless flag O is displayed
questions.why: Rule 42.2(e) prohibits repeated tacks or gybes only when unrelated to changes in the wind or to tactical considerations.

questions.q: A Hobie 16 crew in a near calm rock the boat and swing the boom in and out repeatedly to creep towards the mark. Their coach told them that "under 5 knots anything goes". Is the coach right?

figure.title: Near calm
lines: Hobie 16 rocked, boom swung in and out

options: No — but only because catamarans are excluded from every rule 42 exception
No — rule 42 has no wind-speed exemption; kinetics may be permitted only by class rules, signalled with flag O where Appendix P5 applies
Yes — rule 42.3 suspends the rule when the wind is below 5 knots
Yes — in a calm the only way to finish is to rock and pump, so it is seamanship
questions.why: Rule 42 contains no wind-speed limit; only class rules (86.1(c)) may permit pumping, rocking or ooching, signalled by flag O under Appendix P5.

questions.q: Halfway up the first beat of a 29er regatta your coach's RIB comes within 20 m and he shouts: "Big right shift in five minutes, go right!" You tack and go right. Has anything gone wrong under the rules?

figure.title: First beat, coach RIB 20 m away
lines: Coach shouts: "Big right shift, go right!"

options: No — information about the wind is freely available to everyone who looks at the water, so rule 41(c) covers it
Yes — but the breach is the coach's alone; the boat that used the information cannot be penalised
Yes — tactical information shouted by your coach is outside help under rule 41: not freely available to all, and not from a disinterested source
No — a coach may give any information he likes as long as he does not touch the boat or pass equipment
questions.why: Rule 41: a boat shall not receive help from any outside source, except information freely available to all or unsolicited from a disinterested source.

questions.q: During a race the committee boat announces on the VHF channel listed in the sailing instructions that the course has been shortened at mark 3. You hear it and alter your plan. Is using this information outside help?

figure.title: During the race
lines: VHF announcement on the SI channel

options: Yes — a boat may act only on visual signals, never on information received by radio
Yes — unless every boat in the fleet confirms that she also heard the announcement
No — because the race committee is a disinterested source and you asked for nothing
No — information freely available to all boats is permitted by rule 41(c)
questions.why: Rule 41(c): help in the form of information freely available to all boats is not outside help.

questions.q: On a long coastal race leg you open a public weather app on your phone to check the forecast for the afternoon sea breeze; nothing in the NoR, SI or class rules restricts electronics. Is that a breach of rule 41?

figure.title: Coastal race leg
lines: Public weather app on your phone

options: No — a public forecast is information freely available to all boats (rule 41(c)); only a rule restricting such devices could change that
No — because weather information is never covered by rule 41 whatever its source
Yes — any information received by electronic means while racing is outside help
Yes — forecasts may be consulted only before the preparatory signal
questions.why: Rule 41(c): information freely available to all boats is permitted; the NoR, SI or class rules may restrict devices, but rule 41 itself does not.

questions.q: A crash gybe in 22 knots and your bowman takes the boom on the head. He is dazed and bleeding; a safety boat comes alongside, takes him off and gives first aid, and you sail on with the rest of the crew. Have you received prohibited outside help?

figure.title: Crash gybe, 22 knots
lines: Bowman hit by the boom, dazed, bleeding
Safety boat takes him off, first aid

options: Yes — unless the sailing instructions specifically permit medical help on the water
No — help for a crew member who is ill, injured or in danger is allowed by rule 41(a)
Yes — any contact with a safety boat while racing means outside help and you must retire
No — but only because the safety boat belongs to the race committee
questions.why: Rule 41(a): help for a crew member who is ill, injured or in danger is not prohibited outside help.

questions.q: In the dusk before the start of a night race your 36-footer sails over an unlit mooring and the chain wraps round the keel. You are already racing. A passing RIB offers to tow you clear with its outboard; its crew also offer to lean on your bow and push. Which help may you accept?

figure.title: Before the start of a night race
lines: Mooring chain wrapped round the keel
RIB offers a tow — or a push by hand

options: The tow only — people in another vessel pushing your hull by hand is prohibited body movement under rule 42
Neither — after the preparatory signal a boat may accept no physical help at all from another vessel
The pushing — another vessel's crew may use their effort and any equipment other than an engine to free you (rule 42.3(h)); a tow under engine needs the SI to allow it
Both — a boat that has fouled an obstruction may accept any help whatever to get clear, engine included
questions.why: Rule 42.3(h): a boat that has fouled an object may use her crew's or another vessel's crew's force and any equipment except an engine; 42.3(i) needs the SI.

questions.q: Just after the start Blue, a competitor in the same race, sails past and calls to you, unasked: "You were over, 4471, go back!" You had not heard the recall signal. You return and restart. Was using Blue's warning a breach of rule 41?

figure.title: Just after the start
lines: Blue, unasked: "You were over, go back!"
You did not hear the recall

options: No — because recall information is always freely available to every boat
Yes — unless the race committee later confirms the information was correct
Yes — any information from another competitor in the same race is outside help
No — unsolicited information from a disinterested source is permitted, and the rule says that source may be another boat in the same race (rule 41(d))
questions.why: Rule 41(d): unsolicited information from a disinterested source, which may be another boat in the same race, is not prohibited outside help.

questions.q: Approaching the windward mark in a dying breeze you hail a spectator boat anchored near it: "Which side has more wind up there?" They point to the left and you go left. What, if anything, is wrong?

figure.title: Windward mark, dying breeze
lines: You hail an anchored spectator boat
They point left; you go left

options: You solicited it, so rule 41(d) does not apply, and one spectator boat's view of the wind is not information freely available to all — a breach of rule 41
Nothing — spectators are a disinterested source and may be asked anything at any time during a race
The spectators broke rule 41 by answering; the boat that asked the question cannot be penalised
Nothing — information about where the wind is never counts as outside help under rule 41
questions.why: Rule 41(d) protects only unsolicited information from a disinterested source; asking for it and acting on it is receiving outside help.

questions.q: A six-hour distance race in the Gulf of Bodrum. At the halfway mark your team RIB hands over two bags of sandwiches and fresh water bottles while you sail past. The sailing instructions say nothing about supplies. How do the rules see this?

figure.title: Distance race, halfway mark
lines: Team RIB hands over food and water
You sail past and take it aboard

options: As allowed — food and water are not equipment, so rule 41 does not cover them
As outside help under rule 41 — receiving food and water from a support boat is prohibited unless the NoR or SI permit it
As a breach by the RIB driver only; the boat racing is not responsible
As allowed — rule 41 permits any help that does not make the boat go faster
questions.why: Rule 41: a boat shall not receive help from any outside source except as listed; supplies are not among the exceptions unless the NoR or SI permit them.
