questions.q: The tiller extension of your ILCA 7 snaps on the second beat. At the next mark your coach throws you a spare from his RIB; you fit it and continue. How many rules does this touch?

figure.title: Second beat, ILCA 7
lines: Coach throws a spare at the next mark

options: None — replacing a broken part is a repair, which rule 45 allows while racing
One — rule 41 only; equipment taken aboard during a race is a class-rule matter
Two — the spare is outside help under rule 41, and equipment not on board at your preparatory signal under rule 48.1
One — rule 48.1 only; a coach is a disinterested source under rule 41(d)
questions.why: Rule 41: help from a coach boat is outside help; rule 48.1: a boat shall use only the equipment on board at her preparatory signal.

questions.q: Before a club race you agree with a friend that he will stand on the breakwater and raise a red jacket when he sees more wind on the left of the first beat. He does, you go left and win. A protest follows. What is the outcome?

figure.title: Club race, first beat
lines: Friend on the breakwater, as agreed
Red jacket raised: more wind left

options: No breach — rule 41 applies only to help received from boats, not from the shore
No breach — a friend who gains nothing himself is a disinterested source
No breach — anything visible from the water is information freely available to all
You broke rule 41 — a pre-arranged signal from the shore is help from an outside source, not freely available and not unsolicited
questions.why: Rule 41: an arranged signal from a helper ashore is outside help; it is neither available to all boats nor unsolicited.

questions.q: Three minutes before your warning signal the race committee displays flag Y with one sound signal. Your crew in the Melges 24 are in shorts and T-shirts, lifejackets stowed below. What must they do?

figure.title: 3 minutes before the warning
lines: Flag Y with one sound on the RC boat
Crew in shorts, lifejackets stowed below

options: Put on personal flotation devices and wear them for this race; flag Y afloat before or with the warning signal makes rule 40.1 apply
Nothing — flag Y is advice only; wearing a PFD is each competitor's own choice
Nothing — flag Y displayed afloat applies only to dinghy classes
Wear PFDs only while on the trapeze or while on the foredeck
questions.why: Rule 40.2(a): when flag Y is displayed afloat with one sound before or with the warning signal, all competitors shall wear PFDs during that race.

questions.q: At a national championship flag Y is displayed ashore with one sound signal at 09:00, together with the 25-knot forecast. You launch at 10:30 and the first warning signal is at 11:55. From when until when must PFDs be worn?
options: From the preparatory signal of the first race until the last boat finishes
The whole time competitors are afloat that day — flag Y displayed ashore applies to the day, not to one race (rule 40.2(b))
From the warning signal of each race until each boat finishes, as for flag Y afloat
Only during the races; sailing out and back in is not covered
questions.why: Rule 40.2(b): flag Y displayed ashore with one sound means PFDs shall be worn at all times while afloat that day.

questions.q: Flag Y is flying for the race. On the run your 470 crew takes her lifejacket off for about half a minute to pull a dry top on underneath it, then puts it back on. A judge saw it. Has she broken rule 40?

figure.title: Flag Y, the run
lines: Crew removes her lifejacket for ~30 s
Pulls on a dry top, puts the PFD back

options: Yes — under flag Y a PFD must be worn without interruption while the boat is racing
Yes — clothing may be changed only while the boat is not racing
No — rule 40.1 allows a PFD to be removed briefly while changing or adjusting clothing or personal equipment
No — because the crew, not the helmsman, is the one who removed it
questions.why: Rule 40.1: PFDs shall be worn except briefly while changing or adjusting clothing or personal equipment.

questions.q: A Wednesday evening race in 25 knots. Flag Y is not displayed, the SI and the class rules say nothing about PFDs. Your foredeck crew on a J/24 decides not to wear his lifejacket. Which rule, if any, is engaged?

figure.title: Evening race, 25 knots
lines: No flag Y; SI and class rules silent

options: None — PFDs are required only when flag Y is displayed; nothing else in the rules touches it
Rule 46 — the person in charge decides, and his decision is binding on the crew
Rule 40.1 — in more than 20 knots PFDs are compulsory without any signal
Rule 40.1 does not apply, but rule 1.2 makes each competitor individually responsible for wearing a PFD adequate for the conditions
questions.why: Rule 40.1 applies only as rule 40.2 provides; rule 1.2 makes each competitor responsible for wearing a PFD adequate for the conditions.

questions.q: Flag Y is displayed with the warning signal of race 2 and lowered at the starting signal, as usual for class flags. On the last beat of race 2 your crew takes off his PFD because it is hot. He argues the flag is no longer flying. Is he right?

figure.title: Race 2, last beat
lines: Flag Y shown with the warning signal
Crew removes his PFD: "flag is down"

options: No — flag Y displayed afloat before or with the warning signal applies for the whole of that race, whether or not it is still flying
Yes — flag Y lowered with the starting signal means the requirement has ended
Yes — rule 40.1 applies only while flag Y is actually displayed on the committee boat
No — flag Y shown in any race applies to every race of the day
questions.why: Rule 40.2(a): flag Y displayed afloat with one sound before or with the warning signal makes rule 40.1 apply during that race.

questions.q: Flag Y is flying. The helmsman of a Hobie 16 wears a thick neoprene wetsuit and says it floats better than any lifejacket, so he needs no PFD. Does rule 40 agree?

figure.title: Flag Y flying
lines: Hobie 16 helmsman in a thick wetsuit

options: Yes — any buoyant clothing counts as a personal flotation device
No — wetsuits and drysuits are not personal flotation devices under rule 40.1
Yes — provided the wetsuit is at least 5 mm thick
No — but only because catamaran sailors must always wear a PFD
questions.why: Rule 40.1: wetsuits and drysuits are not personal flotation devices.

questions.q: Your crew is late and your Dragon is still tied to the club mooring when the preparatory signal is made. You cast off forty seconds later, start correctly and finish third. Have you broken a rule?

figure.title: Preparatory signal
lines: Dragon still on the club mooring

options: No — rule 45 applies from the warning signal, so being late at the preparatory signal does not matter
No — a boat only has to be off her mooring before her starting signal
Yes — rule 45 requires a boat to be afloat and off moorings at her preparatory signal
Yes — rule 42, because the mooring held the boat in position
questions.why: Rule 45: a boat shall be afloat and off moorings at her preparatory signal.

questions.q: The mainsail of your 470 tears along a seam on the first reach. You sail to the committee boat, tie alongside for ten minutes while the crew tapes the seam, cast off and finish the race. Was tying up allowed?

figure.title: First reach, torn mainsail
lines: Tied alongside the committee boat 10 min

options: Yes — a boat may tie up to anything at any time as long as she does not gain places
No — a boat may be made fast only to a mark, never to the committee boat
No — once racing a boat may not be made fast to anything for any reason
Yes — after the preparatory signal a boat may be made fast to make repairs, reef sails or bail out (rule 45)
questions.why: Rule 45: after her preparatory signal a boat shall not be hauled out or made fast except to make repairs, reef sails or bail out.

questions.q: A river race, the wind dies and a 1.5-knot ebb starts carrying the fleet back downstream from the windward mark. You drop your anchor and hold position while the others drift away. When the breeze returns you weigh anchor and sail on. Legal?

figure.note: No wind; 1.5-knot ebb sets the fleet away from the mark

options: Yes — a boat may anchor (rule 45); she shall recover the anchor before continuing if possible
No — a boat may anchor only to make repairs, reef or bail
Yes — and the anchor may be left behind if recovering it would lose places
No — anchoring while racing is prohibited; only the wind and water may hold a boat
questions.why: Rule 45: a boat may anchor or her crew may stand on the bottom; she shall recover the anchor before continuing in the race if possible.

questions.q: Flat calm in shallow water near the leeward mark of an Optimist race. You hop out and stand on the sandy bottom holding the boat so that the current does not carry her backwards, then climb back in when the wind fills. Is that permitted?

figure.title: Flat calm, shallow water
lines: You stand on the bottom holding the boat
Climb back in when the wind fills

options: Yes — and the sailor may also walk the boat forward towards the mark
Yes — rule 45 lets the crew stand on the bottom; holding the boat against the current is not propelling her
No — a competitor may never leave the boat while racing except to swim
No — standing on the bottom is prohibited outside help from the sea bed
questions.why: Rule 45: a boat may anchor or her crew may stand on the bottom; walking her forward would be propulsion other than by wind and water, rule 42.1.

questions.q: Having anchored against a foul tide, your Star cannot get the anchor back: it is fouled on something on the bottom and will not budge. The wind has returned and the fleet is sailing away. What does rule 45 allow?

figure.title: Anchored against a foul tide
lines: Star, anchor fouled on the bottom

options: She must wait for a support boat to recover the anchor before continuing
She may always leave the anchor behind; rule 45 does not require its recovery
She shall recover the anchor if possible; when it genuinely cannot be recovered she may slip it and continue racing
She must retire — a boat that leaves her anchor behind cannot continue in the race
questions.why: Rule 45: a boat shall recover her anchor before continuing in the race if possible — recovery is required only when it is possible.

questions.q: A thick clump of weed is on the centreboard of your Laser during a club race near the shore. You sail onto the beach, drag the boat half out of the water, pull the weed off and relaunch. Was hauling out allowed?

figure.title: Club race near the shore
lines: Boat dragged half out onto the beach

options: Yes — hauling out is allowed for any purpose as long as the boat does not gain places
No — a boat may never touch the shore while racing under any circumstances
Yes — removing weed is a repair to the boat's underwater profile
No — after the preparatory signal a boat may be hauled out only to make repairs, reef sails or bail out; clearing weed is none of these
questions.why: Rule 45: a boat shall not be hauled out or made fast except to make repairs, reef sails or bail out.

questions.q: A chartered 40-footer at a Mediterranean regatta: the owner is not aboard, the entry was made by a sailing club, and five friends share the helm. Who must be on board under rule 46?
options: A person in charge designated by the club that entered the boat — the entrant names the person in charge
The owner, or nobody; if the owner is not aboard there is no person in charge
The oldest person aboard, unless the sailing instructions say otherwise
Whoever is steering at the time; the helmsman is automatically the person in charge
questions.why: Rule 46: a boat shall have on board a person in charge designated by the member or organisation that entered the boat (see rule 75).

questions.q: On the long run of a Palma regatta a crew member finishes a banana and flicks the peel over the side, saying it is biodegradable. Does any rule object?

figure.title: Long run, Palma
lines: Banana peel flicked over the side

options: Yes — rule 42, since throwing anything overboard changes the boat's weight
Yes — rule 47: competitors shall not intentionally put trash in the water; the penalty may be less than disqualification
No — rule 47 applies only to plastic and other non-biodegradable items
No — organic matter such as fruit peel is not trash under the rules
questions.why: Rule 47: competitors and support persons shall not intentionally put trash in the water; the rule applies at all times while afloat.

questions.q: A coach following the fleet in a RIB during a 420 regatta is seen throwing an empty plastic bottle into the water. Does the trash disposal rule reach him, and can this affect the boats he coaches?

figure.title: 420 regatta, coach RIB
lines: Coach throws a plastic bottle overboard

options: No — the racing rules bind only boats and their crews, never coaches
No — rule 47 applies only while a boat is racing, and the RIB is not racing
Yes — rule 47 applies to support persons as well as competitors, at all times while afloat; a support person breach can be dealt with under rule 62
Yes — the coach's boats are automatically disqualified from the race
questions.why: Rule 47: competitors and support persons shall not intentionally put trash in the water, at all times while afloat.

questions.q: Your J/70's spinnaker blows out on the first run of a championship race. At the leeward gate the team RIB passes you a spare kite that had been left ashore; you hoist it for the next run. Apart from outside help, which rule is broken?

figure.title: First run, spinnaker blown out
lines: Spare kite handed over by the team RIB

options: Rule 45 — a sail may be replaced only while the boat is made fast for repairs
Rule 55.1 — a boat may carry only one spinnaker during a race
No other rule — once rule 41 is broken nothing else applies
Rule 48.1 — a boat shall use only the equipment that was on board at her preparatory signal
questions.why: Rule 48.1: a boat shall use only the equipment on board at her preparatory signal; a sail brought out during the race is not.

questions.q: Hot day, 6 knots, a long run on a lake. Your 29er crew slips over the side for a swim to cool off, holding the trapeze handle, while you keep sailing slowly towards the mark. Is this allowed, and what is the condition?

figure.title: Hot day, 6 knots, the run
lines: 29er crew over the side to cool off
You sail slowly on towards the mark

options: Leaving the boat to swim is allowed by rule 48.2, but the swimmer must be back in contact with the boat before the crew continues to sail towards the next mark
Allowed without condition — swimming is listed in rule 48.2 as a permitted reason to leave the boat
Not allowed — a person may leave the boat while racing only if ill, injured or in danger
Allowed only after the boat has finished and cleared the finishing line
questions.why: Rule 48.2: no one shall intentionally leave the boat except when ill, injured, to help someone in danger, or to swim; the swimmer must be back in contact first.

questions.q: In 20 knots your 470 crew falls off the trapeze and is left astern. A safety RIB picks her up within a minute. The RIB driver offers to bring her to the next mark and hand her back there so you lose less. What does rule 48.2 require?

figure.note: Crew in the water astern, picked up by a RIB; 20 knots

options: Nothing — a crew member recovered by a safety boat may rejoin at any point of the course
The crew must be back in contact with the boat before you continue sailing towards the next mark — you have to go back and recover her first
You may finish single-handed and the crew rejoins after the finish
You must retire at once; a boat that loses a crew member overboard cannot continue
questions.why: Rule 48.2: a person who leaves the boat by accident shall be back in contact with the boat before the crew continues to sail towards the next mark.

questions.q: During a Laser race you see a swimmer in trouble near the shore, nobody else around. You sail over, jump in, hold him up until a rescue boat arrives, then climb back aboard and continue. Have you broken rule 48.2 by leaving the boat?

figure.title: Laser race, near the shore
lines: You jump in and hold him up
Rescue boat arrives; you climb back

options: No — because the boat was not racing while you were in the water
Yes — a competitor may leave the boat only to swim or when ill or injured, not to rescue others
No — rule 48.2 allows a person to leave the boat to help a person or vessel in danger; rule 1.1 requires the help
Yes — but the protest committee will reduce the penalty because of the circumstances
questions.why: Rule 48.2 lists helping a person or vessel in danger as a reason to leave the boat; rule 1.1 obliges a boat to give all possible help.

questions.q: An ILCA 7 sailor has fitted a short bar under the gunwale so he can hook his feet and sit further outboard than the hiking strap allows. The class measurer objects. Does rule 49 support the measurer?

figure.title: ILCA 7, equipment check
lines: Bar fitted under the gunwale for the feet
Sailor sits further out than the strap

options: No — any hiking aid is allowed provided it is attached to the hull rather than worn
Yes — but only because the bar changes the boat's measured weight
No — rule 49 prohibits only trapezes on boats whose class rules do not allow them
Yes — competitors shall use no device designed to position their bodies outboard, other than hiking straps and stiffeners worn under the thighs
questions.why: Rule 49.1: competitors shall use no device designed to position their bodies outboard, other than hiking straps and stiffeners worn under the thighs.

questions.q: A 36-ft cruiser-racer with upper and lower lifelines on a 20-knot beat. The crew sit on the rail facing outboard, legs over the side, waists inside the lower lifeline and their upper bodies leaning out beyond the upper lifeline. A competitor says that is illegal hiking. Is it?

figure.title: Beat, 20 knots, double lifelines
lines: Crew on the rail facing outboard
Upper bodies beyond the upper lifeline

options: No — on boats with upper and lower lifelines a crew member sitting facing outboard with waist inside the lower lifeline may have the upper torso outside the upper lifeline
Yes — no part of the torso may be outside the lifelines except briefly to do a necessary task
Yes — legs over the side are allowed, but the torso must stay inside the upper lifeline
No — rule 49.2 does not apply to boats longer than 10 m
questions.why: Rule 49.2: with upper and lower lifelines, a crew member facing outboard, waist inside the lower lifeline, may have the upper torso outside the upper one.

questions.q: On a 40-footer with a single lifeline, the bowman leans his whole upper body outside the lifeline for a few seconds to skirt the genoa foot over the rail after a tack, then comes back inside. Is this a breach of rule 49.2?

figure.title: 40-footer, single lifeline
lines: Bowman leans out to skirt the genoa
A few seconds, then back inside

options: No — rule 49.2 applies only to the helmsman
No — the torso may be outside the lifelines briefly to perform a necessary task
Yes — with a single lifeline no part of the body may ever be outside it
Yes — skirting a sail is a tactical gain, not a necessary task
questions.why: Rule 49.2: competitors shall not position any part of their torsos outside the lifelines, except briefly to perform a necessary task.

questions.q: Before a windy regatta the crew of a J/24 slacken the lifelines by 15 cm so that they can lean further out when hiking. Class rules say nothing about lifeline deflection. Is that permitted?
options: No — lifelines may not be adjusted at all once the boat has been measured
Yes — provided the lifelines are tightened again before the boat finishes
No — unless class rules or another rule specify a maximum deflection, lifelines shall be taut (rule 49.2)
Yes — lifeline tension is the owner's choice when class rules are silent
questions.why: Rule 49.2: except where class rules or any other rule specify a maximum deflection, lifelines shall be taut.

questions.q: At equipment inspection of a 470 regatta the crew's clothing and equipment, wet, weigh 9.2 kg, trapeze harness excluded. The class rules and the notice of race say nothing about clothing weight. Does this pass?

figure.title: Equipment inspection, 470
lines: Clothing and equipment weigh 9.2 kg wet

options: Yes — the racing rules set no weight limit for clothing; only class rules may set one
No — the limit is 8 kg including the trapeze harness, so he is even further over the limit
Yes — the limit in rule 50.1(b) is 10 kg for every class, so 9.2 kg is comfortably within it
No — clothing and equipment shall not weigh more than 8 kg, trapeze harness and clothing below the knee excluded, unless class rules or the NoR prescribe more
questions.why: Rule 50.1(b): clothing and equipment shall not exceed 8 kg, excluding a trapeze harness and clothing below the knee; class rules or NoR may allow up to 10 kg.

questions.q: A Finn sailor soaks a sweater in the water and puts it on under his spray top before the start "for a bit more weight to hike with". Which rule does he break?

figure.title: Before the start, Finn
lines: Soaked sweater worn under the spray top
"For a bit more weight to hike with"

options: Rule 50.1(a) — competitors shall not wear or carry clothing or equipment for the purpose of increasing their weight
None — a sailor may wear what he likes if the total weight stays below 10 kg
Rule 51 — the sweater is movable ballast that was not properly stowed
Rule 42 — extra body weight increases hiking power and therefore speed
questions.why: Rule 50.1(a): competitors shall not wear or carry clothing or equipment for the purpose of increasing their weight.

questions.q: At a 2026 regatta a 29er crew turns up with an old trapeze harness whose hook has no quick-release mechanism. The 29er class rules do not change rule 50. The equipment inspector refuses it. Is he right?

figure.title: Equipment inspection, 29er
lines: Old harness, hook without quick release
Class rules do not change rule 50

options: Yes — but only because the harness is older than five years
Yes — a trapeze harness shall have a quick-release mechanism complying with ISO 10862 unless class rules change this, which they have not
No — quick-release harnesses are required only when flag Y is displayed
No — a quick-release hook is only a recommendation in the racing rules
questions.why: Rule 50.1(c): a trapeze harness shall have a quick-release device complying with ISO 10862; class rules may change this, but not the ISO requirement.

questions.q: A 36-ft cruiser-racer in a club series. On every tack the crew drag the sail bags, the toolbox and four water jerrycans across to the new windward side. The skipper says it is just tidy stowage. Is it?

figure.title: Club series, every tack
lines: Dragged to the new windward side

options: Yes — rule 51 restricts only water ballast and lead, not everyday gear
Yes — crew may move anything that is not bolted down as part of adjusting trim
No — movable ballast, including sails not set, shall be properly stowed, and weight shall not be moved to change trim or stability (rule 51)
No — but only the water jerrycans count; sails and tools may be moved freely
questions.why: Rule 51: movable ballast, including sails not set, shall be properly stowed; water, dead weight or ballast shall not be moved to change trim or stability.

questions.q: A 45-ft cruiser enters the club's Wednesday race. Her genoa is trimmed with electric winches and her mainsail furls with a powered in-mast system; the class (a local handicap fleet) has no rules about this. May she use them while racing?

figure.title: Wednesday race, 45-ft cruiser
lines: No class rule on the subject

options: No — and she must also remove the winches before she may enter
Yes — powered winches are allowed as long as the engine is not used for propulsion
Yes — rule 52 applies only to one-design classes, not handicap fleets
No — standing and running rigging, spars and movable hull appendages shall be adjusted and operated only by manual power (rule 52), unless a class rule changes it
questions.why: Rule 52: rigging, spars and movable hull appendages shall be adjusted and operated only by manual power; class rules may change rule 52 (86.1(c)).

questions.q: Before launching for a Dragon regatta a crew sprays the hull with a polymer coating advertised to make the water "slip off" and improve boundary-layer flow. Which rule is engaged?

figure.title: Before launching, Dragon
lines: Hull sprayed with a polymer coating

options: Rule 53 — a boat shall not eject or release a substance or have specially textured surfaces to improve the flow of water in the boundary layer
Rule 51 — the coating is a change of ballast distribution
No rule — hull coatings are a matter for class rules only
Rule 42 — the coating reduces friction and so increases speed by means other than wind
questions.why: Rule 53: a boat shall not eject or release a substance, such as a polymer, or have specially textured surfaces that could improve boundary-layer flow.

questions.q: On a long reach in a 470 the helmsman unclips the jib tack from the stem fitting and re-attaches it to the windward rail, 40 cm off the centreline, to open the slot. The jib fills well. Is this allowed?

figure.title: Long reach, 470
lines: Jib tack moved to the windward rail

options: No — but only because the 470 class rules specifically forbid moving the jib tack
No — forestays and headsail tacks shall be attached approximately on the centreline, except for spinnaker staysails when not close-hauled (rule 54)
Yes — rule 54 applies only to the forestay itself, not to the tack of the sail
Yes — a headsail tack may be moved anywhere on the boat when she is on a free leg
questions.why: Rule 54: forestays and headsail tacks, except those of spinnaker staysails when the boat is not close-hauled, shall be attached approximately on the centreline.

questions.q: On a 40-footer the wind drops on the beat and you change from the No. 3 to the No. 1 genoa. The No. 1 is hoisted and trimmed on the second groove while the No. 3 is still drawing, and only then is the No. 3 dropped. Is sailing with two genoas set for that minute a breach?

figure.title: Headsail change on the beat
lines: No. 1 hoisted and trimmed, second groove
No. 3 still drawing for about a minute

options: No — but only if the change takes less than thirty seconds
Yes — the old sail must be lowered before the new one is hoisted
No — when changing headsails the replacing sail may be fully set and trimmed before the replaced sail is lowered (rule 55.1)
Yes — a boat may have only one headsail set at any time
questions.why: Rule 55.1: when changing headsails or spinnakers, the replacing sail may be fully set and trimmed before the replaced sail is lowered.

questions.q: Running in 12 knots, a Dragon crew set the spinnaker on its pole and also pole out the jib on a whisker pole on the other side, to carry both. Does rule 55 allow two poles at once?

figure.title: Run, 12 knots, Dragon
lines: Jib poled out on a whisker pole

options: Yes — one spinnaker pole and one whisker pole are different equipment and may both be used
No — a whisker pole may never be used on a boat that carries a spinnaker
Yes — provided both poles are attached to the mast
No — only one spinnaker pole or whisker pole shall be used at a time, except when gybing (rule 55.2)
questions.why: Rule 55.2: only one spinnaker pole or whisker pole shall be used at a time except when gybing; when in use it shall be attached to the foremost mast.

questions.q: A J/24 on a run with the spinnaker set. The crew also hold the jib clew out to windward with a boathook so that the jib draws too. The skipper quotes the rule that a headsail clew may be attached to a whisker pole. Is he right here?

figure.title: Run, spinnaker set, J/24
lines: Jib clew held out with a boathook
Spinnaker flying at the same time

options: No — a headsail clew may be connected to a whisker pole only when no spinnaker is set (rule 55.3(a)); with the spinnaker up this is outboard sheeting, prohibited
No — a jib may never be set at the same time as a spinnaker under rule 55.1
Yes — the clew of a headsail may be held out by a pole or a boathook at any time on any leg
Yes — provided the boathook is held by hand and is not attached to the mast or the deck
questions.why: Rule 55.3: no sail shall be sheeted over a device that exerts outward pressure outboard, except (a) a headsail clew on a whisker pole when no spinnaker is set.

questions.q: A Star crew running in light air lead the jib sheet to the end of the main boom and ease the boom right out, so that the jib clew is held well outboard by the boom. Is that legal sheeting?

figure.title: Run in light air, Star
lines: Jib sheet led to the end of the main boom

options: No — the boom may carry only the sail it was designed for
Yes — sheets of any sail may be led to or along a boom regularly used for a sail and permanently attached to the mast (rule 55.3(b))
No — a jib may be sheeted only inside the hull or to a whisker pole
Yes — but only when the boat is on a beat to windward
questions.why: Rule 55.3(b): a sail's sheets may be led to or along a boom regularly used for a sail and permanently attached to the mast from which that sail is set.

questions.q: Night leg of an offshore race. To hide your position from a rival two miles astern, the watch leader switches off the navigation lights until dawn. Which rule does this break?

figure.title: Offshore race, night leg
lines: Navigation lights switched off until dawn
To hide from a rival two miles astern

options: No rule — navigation lights are a matter for the skipper's judgement
Rule 56.3 — navigation lights are a tracking system that may not be switched off
Rule 56.1 — when equipped, a boat shall exhibit lights as required by the IRPCAS (COLREGs)
Rule 41 — hiding from a competitor is interfering with her access to information
questions.why: Rule 56.1: when safety requires, a boat shall sound fog signals and show lights as required by the IRPCAS or applicable government rules.

questions.q: The notice of race of a 200-mile race requires every boat to carry an AIS transponder switched on. On the second night your navigator sets it to receive-only so competitors cannot see you. Is this a breach?

figure.title: 200-mile race, second night
lines: NoR: AIS transponder on at all times

options: Yes — but only rule 41 is broken, since the AIS gives information to other boats
No — the AIS is required for safety only and how it is used is the boat's business
No — receive-only is allowed as long as the unit is powered up
Yes — rule 56.3: when a rule requires an AIS transponder or other tracking device, it shall not be switched off or its effectiveness deliberately reduced
questions.why: Rule 56.3: an AIS transponder or other tracking device required by a rule shall not be switched off or have its effectiveness deliberately impaired.

questions.q: An offshore race course crosses a traffic separation scheme. To save a mile your navigator plans to cross it at a shallow angle, running along the lane for half an hour; the NoR does not mention Appendix TS. What do the racing rules require?

figure.title: Offshore race, TSS ahead
lines: Plan: cross at a shallow angle
Half an hour running along the lane

options: Compliance with rule 10 of the IRPCAS (COLREGs) on traffic separation schemes — rule 56.2 — so cross as nearly as practicable at right angles
That the boat avoid the TSS altogether, whatever the course
Only that the boat does not impede ships; the angle of crossing is free
Nothing — the racing rules replace the COLREGs between boats racing, including in a TSS
questions.why: Rule 56.2: a boat shall comply with rule 10 of the IRPCAS, Traffic Separation Schemes; the NoR may instead apply Appendix TS.

questions.q: A glassy calm at the windward mark of a Hobie 16 race. Your crew slides into the water, swims to the bow and, kicking hard, pushes the bow round and the boat forward until she is past the mark. He says rule 48.2 allows swimming. Does that settle it?

figure.title: Glassy calm, windward mark
lines: Hobie 16 crew swims to the bow
Kicks hard, pushes the boat past the mark

options: No — because swimming is allowed only after the boat has finished
No — swimming is a permitted reason to leave the boat, but propelling her by swimming breaks rule 42.1: only wind and water may be used
Yes — rule 42 applies to the boat, not to a crew member who is not aboard
Yes — a crew member who has legally left the boat may do anything in the water
questions.why: Rule 48.2 permits leaving the boat to swim; rule 42.1 still requires the boat to be propelled only by wind and water, and 42.3(h) applies only when aground.

questions.q: In 25 knots on the run the tape holding your Melges 24's batten pocket rips off and blows away, and a torn piece of the spinnaker goes into the water. The boat astern protests under rule 47. Should it succeed?

figure.title: Run, 25 knots, Melges 24
lines: Batten-pocket tape rips off and blows away
Torn piece of spinnaker in the water

options: No — because rule 47 does not apply while the boat is racing
Yes — any material that ends up in the water from a boat counts as trash disposal
No — rule 47 prohibits intentionally putting trash in the water; pieces lost accidentally are not a breach
Yes — unless the boat turns back and recovers the pieces
questions.why: Rule 47: competitors and support persons shall not intentionally put trash in the water; accidental loss of material is not intentional.

questions.q: You have finished, cleared the finishing line and are sailing your 36-footer back to the harbour when a crew member flicks a cigarette butt into the sea. He says the race is over, so the racing rules no longer apply. Is he right?

figure.title: After finishing, sailing home
lines: Cigarette butt flicked into the sea

options: Yes — after a boat has cleared the finishing line only the COLREGs apply to her
Yes — the rules of Part 4 apply only to a boat that is racing
No — but only because the boat was still within the race area
No — rule 47 applies at all times while competitors are afloat, not only while racing
questions.why: Part 4 rules apply to boats racing unless a rule says otherwise; rule 47 says it applies at all times while afloat.

questions.q: Wednesday evening club race, ILCA 7s. On the first beat you are on port tack and misjudge a cross: Grey, close-hauled on starboard, has to bear away hard to miss your transom. No contact. You know you broke rule 10. What penalty do you take?

figure.note: Grey bears away to miss your transom

options: A Two-Turns Penalty, as soon as possible after getting well clear of the other boats
No penalty — without contact there is no breach to pay for
Retire — a breach of rule 10 cannot be repaired by turns on the water
A One-Turn Penalty — that is the penalty for forcing a boat to change course without contact
questions.why: Rule 44.1: a boat that may have broken a rule of Part 2 may take a Two-Turns Penalty; rule 44.2 says when and how.

questions.q: National championship, 470 class, second lap. Rounding the leeward mark cleanly, with no other boat within five lengths, your boom brushes the buoy. What is the penalty?

figure.note: The boom brushes the mark; nobody else near

options: A 20 % Scoring Penalty, shown by displaying a yellow flag until you finish
A One-Turn Penalty — one tack and one gybe, taken as soon as possible after getting well clear of other boats
No penalty — touching a mark with the rig rather than the hull is allowed
A Two-Turns Penalty — two tacks and two gybes, the standard penalty on the water
questions.why: Rule 31 forbids touching the mark; rule 44.1 gives a One-Turn Penalty for a breach of rule 31 alone.

questions.q: Leeward mark of a Melges 24 regatta in Split. You are the windward boat, overlapped with Red inside you. As you squeeze in, your boom hits Red's shroud and in the same moment your bow touches the mark. What penalty covers this?

figure.note: Your boom hits Red, your bow hits the mark

options: Three turns — two for the contact with Red and one more for the mark
One turn only — touching a mark is the more specific breach and replaces the two turns
One Two-Turns Penalty — when a boat breaks a Part 2 rule and rule 31 in the same incident she need not take the penalty for rule 31
Retire — a boat that breaks two rules in one incident cannot take turns
questions.why: Rule 44.1(a): a breach of Part 2 and rule 31 in the same incident is settled by the Two-Turns Penalty alone.

questions.q: J/70, Lake Garda. After fouling a boat on the run you take your penalty: you luff, tack, bear away, gybe and come back to course — then you do the second turn the other way round, starting with a gybe to the opposite side. Your tactician says the penalty is complete. Is it?

figure.title: Your penalty on the run
lines: Turn 1: luff, tack, bear away, gybe
Turn 2: gybe the other way, then tack

options: Yes — as long as both turns are finished within two minutes of the incident
Yes — each turn had a tack and a gybe, and the rule does not care about the direction
No — a penalty turn must always begin with a tack, never with a gybe
No — both turns must be made in the same direction; the second turn does not count
questions.why: Rule 44.2: the required number of turns in the same direction, each including one tack and one gybe.

questions.q: 29er, windward mark, 18 knots. You hit Blue while tacking in front of her — clearly your fault. You round the mark and the offset, hoist the kite, and only 150 m down the run, where it is quieter, do you take two turns. Blue protests. What will the protest committee most likely decide?

figure.title: Windward mark, Lake Garda
lines: Rounded mark and offset, hoisted kite
Two turns taken 150 m down the run

options: You are disqualified — the turns were not taken as soon as possible after getting well clear, so they do not count
No further penalty — the rule says to get well clear first, and you did
A 20 % Scoring Penalty is added for the delay, but the turns otherwise stand
No further penalty — you completed two full turns before finishing, which is all rule 44 asks
questions.why: Rule 44.2: get well clear of other boats as soon after the incident as possible, then take the turns promptly; a delayed penalty is no penalty.

questions.q: Melges 24 worlds, thirty seconds after the start, the fleet is tight. You are on port and foul a starboard-tack boat. You start spinning on the spot, in the middle of the pack, and three boats have to alter course to avoid you. What is wrong with that?

figure.note: You begin your turns inside the pack

options: You should have waited until after the first mark; penalties are not allowed on the first leg
You should first have sailed clear of the other boats, and while turning you must keep clear of them — rule 21.2
Nothing — a penalty must start immediately after the incident, and the others must keep clear of you
Nothing — a boat taking a penalty has right of way over boats that are not
questions.why: Rule 44.2: get well clear first; rule 21.2: a boat taking a penalty keeps clear of one that is not.

questions.q: Dragon, Saronic Gulf. Ten metres short of the finishing line you fail to keep clear of Red to leeward (rule 11). You cross the line, take two turns on the far side of it and sail off to the harbour. Have you finished?

figure.note: Your turns are on the far side of the line

options: No — turns are not permitted near the finishing line at all; your only option was to retire
Yes — provided the turns were completed within the finishing area
No — after the turns your hull must come completely back to the course side of the line, and then you must cross it again
Yes — you finished when your bow crossed, and the turns after it complete the penalty
questions.why: Rule 44.2: taking a penalty at or near the finishing line, her hull must be completely on the course side before she finishes; definition Finish.

questions.q: Palma, 20 knots, a 36-ft cruiser-racer. On port you hit a starboard-tack boat; one of her crew is taken ashore with a broken wrist. You immediately take two turns and carry on. Is that the right penalty?

figure.title: Bay of Palma, 20 knots
lines: You on port, hit a starboard boat
You took two turns at once

options: No — with injury you must take three turns instead of two
Yes — two turns is the penalty for any breach of a Part 2 rule, whatever the consequences
Yes, provided you also display a yellow flag and tell the race committee at the finish
No — because the incident caused injury, your penalty is to retire from the race
questions.why: Rule 44.1(b): if the boat caused injury or serious damage, her penalty shall be to retire.

questions.q: Club regatta on the river, 30-footers. Misjudging a duck, you T-bone Grey amidships: a 30 cm hole in her topsides, she retires and motors home. You take a Two-Turns Penalty and finish third. What should you have done?
options: Retired — you caused serious damage, so turns are not the applicable penalty and the protest committee will disqualify you
Taken one extra turn for the damage, three in all
Displayed a yellow flag and accepted a 20 % Scoring Penalty
Nothing more — two turns were taken promptly and that settles a Part 2 breach
questions.why: Rule 44.1(b): serious damage means the penalty is to retire; a boat that takes turns instead is still liable to be disqualified.

questions.q: Star class, crowded windward mark, 40 boats. You come in on port, foul two starboard-tack boats in the queue, but by forcing your way through you avoid the pile-up and gain about fifteen places. You take two turns and lose four of them. Is the penalty enough?

figure.title: Windward mark, Star fleet
lines: You on port, foul two starboard boats
You slip past the pile-up: +15 places

options: Yes — but you must also show a yellow flag so the committee can add 20 %
No — despite the turns you gained a significant advantage from your breach, so your penalty is to retire
Yes — two turns taken promptly settle any number of Part 2 breaches in one incident
No — you fouled two boats, so you owe four turns
questions.why: Rule 44.1(b): a boat that gained a significant advantage in the race or series despite taking a penalty shall retire.

questions.q: Optimist regatta, light air. Your bow nudges the transom of Blue, who is clear ahead of you on the same tack — a touch at walking pace, no mark, no damage. Blue says nothing and sails on. What does the basic principle of sportsmanship expect of you?

figure.note: Your bow nudges Blue's transom; no damage

options: Nothing — contact that leaves no damage is not a breach of any rule
To take a One-Turn Penalty — contact without damage counts like touching a mark
To take a Two-Turns Penalty anyway — a boat that breaks a rule and is not exonerated promptly takes the appropriate penalty
Nothing — a penalty is only required when the other boat hails "Protest"
questions.why: Basic principle Sportsmanship and the Rules, rule 12 and rule 44.1: you broke rule 12, so you take the penalty whether or not anyone protests.

questions.q: Beat in a J/24 fleet. Red, on port, cannot cross you on starboard. You could have borne away behind her in good time but hold on and hail; the boats collide and Red's gunwale cracks. Red takes two turns. What about you?

figure.title: Port–starboard, J/24s
lines: Red on port cannot cross you
You could have borne away in time
You hold on and hail; collision
Red's gunwale cracks; Red takes two turns

options: Nothing — the right-of-way boat is never penalised in a port–starboard incident
You must retire — any right-of-way boat involved in a collision with damage must retire
Nothing — Red has already taken the penalty for the incident, and one penalty per incident is enough
You too may have broken a rule — rule 14, and with damage you are not exonerated — so you should take a Two-Turns Penalty as well
questions.why: Rule 14: a right-of-way boat must avoid contact once it is clear the other is not keeping clear; rule 43.1(c) exonerates her only if there is no damage.

questions.q: The sailing instructions of a J/24 championship say that rule 44.3, the Scoring Penalty, applies. Rounding the leeward mark you fail to keep clear of a leeward boat. How do you take your penalty?

figure.title: SI: rule 44.3 applies
lines: Leeward mark, you are windward boat
You fail to keep clear — your breach
No damage, no other boat affected

options: Display a yellow flag at the first reasonable opportunity, keep it up until you finish, and draw the race committee's attention to it at the finishing line
Hail "Twenty per cent" to the other boat and continue racing
Display a red flag until you finish and report to the race office
Take two turns anyway — the sailing instructions cannot replace the Two-Turns Penalty
questions.why: Rule 44.3(a) and (b): the Scoring Penalty is taken by displaying a yellow flag promptly, keeping it until finishing and informing the race committee.

questions.q: Forty-nine boats are entered in a Laser regatta where the Scoring Penalty applies. You take it for an incident on the run and finish 7th. What is your score for the race?

figure.title: Scoring Penalty taken
lines: SI do not specify another figure

options: 17 points — and every boat that finished behind you moves up one place
17 points — 7 plus 20 % of the DNF score (50 points), i.e. 10 points; the other boats' scores do not change
57 points — 7 plus 20 % of 49 entries is 9.8, rounded up to 50 added points
8.4 points — 7 plus 20 % of your own finishing score
questions.why: Rule 44.3(c): 20 % of the score for DNF (entries + 1), added to the boat's own score; the scores of other boats are not changed.

questions.q: A twelve-boat Dragon fleet. You take a 20 % Scoring Penalty and then finish last, 12th. The committee enters 15 points against your name. Is that right?
options: Yes — 12 points plus the penalty, rounded, is 15
No — the penalty is 20 % of 12, so you get 14.4 points
No — a Scoring Penalty may not make your score worse than the score for DNF, which here is 13 points
No — a boat that finishes last is not penalised further; 12 points stand
questions.why: Rule 44.3(c): the penalty shall not be worse than the score for Did Not Finish.

questions.q: Scoring Penalty allowed by the sailing instructions. At the gybe mark you lose control in a gust and hit the boat ahead; her bowman is cut on the forearm and needs stitches. Your crew hoists the yellow flag. Does that settle it?

figure.title: Gybe mark, 22 knots
lines: You hit the boat ahead in a broach
Her bowman: a cut that needs stitches
Your crew hoists the yellow flag

options: No — for injury the penalty is 40 %, so you need two yellow flags
Yes — where the sailing instructions allow it, the yellow flag replaces every other penalty
Yes — but you must also do two turns because there was contact
No — when the boat caused injury or serious damage the penalty is to retire; the Scoring Penalty is not available
questions.why: Rule 44.1(b) overrides rule 44.3: injury or serious damage means retirement, not turns and not a Scoring Penalty.

questions.q: You show the yellow flag at once after an incident on the first beat, but on the last run it blows out of the shroud and you do not replace it; at the finish you say nothing to the committee boat. The other boat protests. What is your position?

figure.title: Scoring Penalty, your race
lines: Yellow flag up at once after the foul
Flag lost on the last run
Not replaced; nothing said at the finish

options: Weak — the Scoring Penalty requires the yellow flag to be displayed until you finish and the committee to be told at the finishing line; you have taken no valid penalty
Strong — you displayed the flag at the first reasonable opportunity, which is what matters
Neutral — the protest committee will simply apply the 20 % for you
Strong — the committee boat should have seen the flag earlier in the race
questions.why: Rule 44.3(b): display the yellow flag until finishing and call the race committee's attention to it at the finishing line.

questions.q: The notice of race of a big-fleet Optimist regatta says: "Rule 44.1 is changed: the Scoring Penalty, rule 44.3, replaces the Two-Turns Penalty." You foul a boat at the windward mark and, out of habit, take two turns instead of showing the yellow flag. The boat protests. Outcome?

figure.title: NoR: Scoring Penalty replaces turns
lines: You foul a boat at the windward mark
You take two turns, no yellow flag

options: No further penalty — the protest committee just converts your turns into 20 %
You are disqualified — the specified Scoring Penalty replaces the turns, so your turns were not an applicable penalty
A warning only, because you did take a penalty of some kind
No further penalty — two turns is always at least as severe as a yellow flag
questions.why: Rule 44.1: the NoR or SI may specify the Scoring Penalty, in which case it replaces the One-Turn and Two-Turns Penalties.

questions.q: National championship, flag Z displayed with the preparatory signal. In the last minute before the start part of your hull is inside the triangle formed by the ends of the line and the first mark. The start is otherwise clean and the committee identifies you. What happens?

figure.title: Flag Z with the preparatory
lines: 0:40 to the start: your bow in the triangle

options: You are disqualified without a hearing
You must take a Two-Turns Penalty as soon as you are clear
You get a 20 % Scoring Penalty without a hearing — and it stays even if the race is restarted or resailed
You must sail back round an end of the line before starting
questions.why: Rule 30.2: the Z flag rule — a boat identified in the triangle in the last minute gets a 20 % Scoring Penalty without a hearing.

questions.q: Flag U is the preparatory signal. At 0:30 you are inside the triangle and the committee notes your number; then too many boats are over and First Substitute goes up with two sounds. What happens to your penalty?
options: You may start, but only after sailing round an end of the line
It becomes a 20 % Scoring Penalty because the race is restarted
It stands — you are UFD and must not start the restarted race
It is lifted — under flag U the disqualification does not apply if the race is restarted or resailed; you may start again
questions.why: Rule 30.3: disqualified without a hearing — except when the race is restarted or resailed.

questions.q: Black flag preparatory signal. You are over in the last minute; the committee signals a general recall and then displays your sail number on the committee boat. What are your options?

figure.title: Black flag start
lines: You in the triangle in the last minute
Your sail number displayed on the RC boat

options: None — you are disqualified (BFD) and may not sail the restarted race; if you do, the disqualification becomes non-excludable
Start again, but do a Two-Turns Penalty right after the starting signal
Start again, accepting a 20 % Scoring Penalty
Start again — a general recall wipes out all starting penalties
questions.why: Rule 30.4: the black-flag disqualification stands after a general recall; a boat whose number is displayed shall not sail again in that race.

questions.q: Black flag race. At 0:45 your bow is well inside the triangle. At 0:20 the race committee hoists AP with two sounds and postpones the start. Does the black-flag penalty apply to you?
options: Yes, but it is reduced to a 20 % Scoring Penalty
No — the penalty does not apply when the race is postponed or abandoned before the starting signal
No, but you must sail round an end of the line before the new start
Yes — you were identified in the last minute, so you are BFD for this race
questions.why: Rule 30.4: the penalty does not apply if the race is postponed or abandoned before the starting signal.

questions.q: Flag I is displayed with the preparatory signal. With 40 seconds to go, you drift over the line near the pin. Your crew says: "Do a quick turn and go." What actually fixes the error?

figure.note: Flag I; 0:40 to go, you are over near the pin

options: A Two-Turns Penalty taken after the starting signal
Dipping back across the line anywhere, as under flag P
Sailing to the pre-start side round an end of the line before you start — a penalty turn does nothing for a starting error
A One-Turn Penalty taken immediately on the course side of the line
questions.why: Rule 30.1: a boat on the course side in the last minute shall sail round an end of the line to the pre-start side before starting.

questions.q: P flag start in a 36-ft cruiser-racer fleet. You did not notice flag X and sailed on; after finishing you learn you were on the course side at the gun. The owner suggests doing two turns before the committee boat "to be safe". Will that help?

figure.title: After the finish
lines: P flag start, you did not see flag X
Part of your hull over at the gun
Owner: "Two turns now, to be safe"

options: Yes, if the turns are completed on the course side of the finishing line
Yes — a Two-Turns Penalty taken before the finishing line is removed closes any breach of the race
No — but you can take a 20 % Scoring Penalty instead of OCS
No — a starting error is corrected only by returning and starting correctly; now you are scored OCS without a hearing, and no turns change that
questions.why: Rule 29.1 and definition Start: a boat that does not return and start correctly has not started; she is scored OCS under Appendix A.

questions.q: The sailing instructions say Appendix T, Arbitration, applies. After a port–starboard incident with no damage you did not take turns, and the starboard boat has lodged a protest. On reflection you think you were in the wrong. What can you do before the hearing?

figure.title: SI: Appendix T applies
lines: No turns taken on the water
Protest lodged by the starboard boat
You now think you were wrong

options: A 30 % Post-Race Penalty — a written statement to the arbitrator or a protest committee member before the hearing begins
Do two turns in the harbour in front of the committee boat
Nothing — once a protest is lodged only the hearing can penalise you
Take a 20 % Scoring Penalty by hoisting a yellow flag at the dock
questions.why: Appendix T1: a boat that may have broken a Part 2 rule or rule 31 may take a 30 % Post-Race Penalty any time after the race and before the hearing starts.

questions.q: Beat in a Hobie 16 fleet off Bodrum. You are close-hauled on starboard; a port-tack boat ducks you late, her bow a metre from your stern, and her skipper hails "Protest!" You held a straight course throughout. What do you do?

figure.note: Red ducks a metre behind you and hails "Protest"

options: Hail "Protest" back at once, which cancels her protest
Keep racing — if you broke no rule there is nothing to pay for; a hail of "Protest" only announces a hearing, which will decide
Take a Two-Turns Penalty — a boat that is protested must take a penalty or be disqualified
Retire — the starboard boat is responsible for any near miss on a beat
questions.why: Rule 44.1 lets a boat that may have broken a rule take a penalty; a boat that broke none need not — the protest committee decides the facts.

questions.q: Reaching leg, 470s. Red to leeward hails "Protest" and says you, the windward boat, touched her. You felt nothing but cannot be sure — the boats were very close. What is the sensible course of action under the rules?

figure.note: Red hails "Protest"; you are not sure there was contact

options: Do not take turns — doing them is an admission and you would be disqualified anyway
Wait for the hearing — once "Protest" has been hailed, turns can no longer be taken
You may take a Two-Turns Penalty now: a boat that may have broken a rule can take it, and if the committee later finds you did, you will not be penalised further
Take one turn as a compromise, since the contact is uncertain
questions.why: Rule 44.1 applies to a boat that 'may have broken' a rule; rule 60.5(c): a boat that has taken the applicable penalty is not penalised further.

questions.q: You took two turns promptly after a windward–leeward incident with Blue, yet Blue lodged a protest anyway. The protest committee finds that you broke rule 11, that there was no damage and that you gained no advantage. What is its decision on your penalty?
options: A 20 % Scoring Penalty on top of the turns
A non-excludable disqualification, because you were protested after taking turns
Disqualification — a protest that is upheld always ends in DSQ
No further penalty — you had already taken the applicable penalty for the breach
questions.why: Rule 60.5(c): a boat that has taken the applicable penalty shall not be penalised further, unless the penalty for the rule broken is a non-excludable DSQ.

questions.q: After a collision at the leeward mark you took two turns at once. In the hearing the protest committee finds you broke rule 18.2 and that the other boat's pulpit was bent and her forestay fitting cracked — serious damage. What does the committee decide about your penalty?

figure.title: Hearing: leeward mark collision
lines: Other boat: bent pulpit, cracked fitting
You took two turns on the water

options: Disqualification — with serious damage the applicable penalty was to retire, so your turns do not protect you
Retirement entered retroactively — RET instead of DSQ
No further penalty — you took a Two-Turns Penalty promptly after the incident
A 20 % Scoring Penalty to reflect the damage
questions.why: Rule 44.1(b): serious damage means retirement; rule 60.5(c) protects only a boat that took the applicable penalty.

questions.q: A protest committee at a club championship finds that you broke rule 10 on the second beat and took no penalty at all. No damage, no injury, no advantage worth mentioning. What is the penalty it imposes?
options: A non-excludable disqualification, because you did not take turns
Disqualification from the race — the default when a boat broke a rule and no other penalty applies; excludable in the series
A 20 % Scoring Penalty — the committee applies rule 44.3 for you
A Two-Turns Penalty to be sailed before the next race
questions.why: Rule 60.5(c): the protest committee shall disqualify a boat that broke a rule unless she is exonerated or another penalty applies.

questions.q: Last race of a club series. At the final mark you deliberately sail into your rival so that your clubmate gets past her, then take a Two-Turns Penalty "to pay for it". Your rival protests under rule 2. Do the turns settle the matter?

figure.title: Final mark, last race
lines: You deliberately sail into your rival

options: No — the penalty for a deliberate foul is four turns instead of two
Yes — a Two-Turns Penalty settles any breach of a Part 2 rule, whatever the intention
No — deliberately breaking a rule is a breach of rule 2, and the penalty for that is a disqualification that cannot be excluded (DNE)
Yes, provided there was no damage and no injury
questions.why: Rule 2: a boat may be penalised for a clearly established breach of sportsmanship; the penalty is a non-excludable DSQ.

questions.q: The sailing instructions list rule 40 as [DP] and flag Y is displayed afloat. A jury boat reports you for sailing the second beat without a lifejacket. What penalty can you expect?

figure.title: SI: rule 40 [DP]; flag Y afloat
lines: Second beat sailed without a lifejacket

options: Automatic disqualification — rule 40 breaches always score DSQ
A 20 % Scoring Penalty without a hearing
A Two-Turns Penalty, which you may still take after the race
A discretionary penalty decided by the protest committee — which may be less than disqualification
questions.why: [DP] in the NoR or SI means the penalty is at the discretion of the protest committee and may be less than disqualification.

questions.q: Leeward mark, 470s. Blue is overlapped to windward of you and does not keep clear: she leans on you and pushes you onto the mark, which you touch with your hull. Who takes what?

figure.note: Blue pushes you onto the mark

options: Blue takes a Two-Turns Penalty for breaking rule 11; you are exonerated for touching the mark and take nothing
You take one turn — touching a mark is always the touching boat's responsibility
Both of you take a One-Turn Penalty, since both were involved in the mark contact
You take a One-Turn Penalty for the mark and Blue takes two turns
questions.why: Rule 43.1(a): a boat compelled to break a rule by another boat's breach is exonerated; rule 44.1 for Blue's Part 2 breach.

questions.q: Beat in a Dragon fleet. You are on port, overlapped to windward of Grey, also on port. Grey luffs hard without giving you room to respond and you are pushed up into the path of Red on starboard, who has to bear away. Red protests you under rule 10. Who should take a penalty?

figure.note: Grey luffs without room; you are pushed into Red

options: Nobody — Red had to bear away only slightly, so there was no breach
Grey — her breach of rule 16.1 compelled you to break rule 10, so you are exonerated; Grey takes a Two-Turns Penalty
You — rule 10 is absolute and the port-tack boat always pays for a starboard boat's alteration
Both you and Grey, two turns each
questions.why: Rule 43.1(a): exoneration for a boat compelled to break a rule by another boat's breach; rule 16.1 for Grey's luff.

questions.q: Gate mark, J/70s, 15 knots. You are the inside boat, entitled to mark-room; Yellow outside gives you so little that, rounding as tightly as a seamanlike turn allows, your quarter touches the mark. Must you take a turn?

figure.note: Yellow gives too little room; your quarter touches the mark

options: Yes — one turn for you and two for Yellow
Yes — a One-Turn Penalty, as any boat that touches a mark must take one
No — you were sailing within the mark-room you were entitled to, so you are exonerated for touching the mark; Yellow should take two turns
Yes — but you may delay it until the next leg to avoid the crowd at the gate
questions.why: Rule 43.1(b): a boat sailing within the mark-room she is entitled to is exonerated for breaking rule 31 in an incident with the boat required to give it.

questions.q: You are close-hauled on starboard in a 29er when a port-tack boat tries to cross and fails. You bear away at the last second but her transom clips your bow — a light touch, no marks on either boat. Did you break rule 14, and do you need to take a penalty?

figure.note: Blue fails to cross; a light touch, no damage

options: Yes — you take one turn as the boat that caused less of the contact
No — a right-of-way boat can never break rule 14
Yes — both boats were in contact, so both take a Two-Turns Penalty
You may have broken rule 14, but as right-of-way boat you are exonerated — no damage, no injury — so no penalty
questions.why: Rule 43.1(c): a right-of-way boat that breaks rule 14 is exonerated when the contact causes no damage or injury.

questions.q: At the windward mark Grey, overlapped outside you, fails to give you mark-room and you are forced onto the buoy. Grey then hails "Protest — you hit the mark!" Your crew suggests doing a turn "just to be safe". Is a turn required?

figure.note: Grey gives no mark-room; you are forced onto the buoy

options: No — a boat that is exonerated need not take a penalty and shall not be penalised; the hearing, if any, will find that Grey compelled the contact
Yes — a boat that touches a mark and is protested cannot be exonerated
Yes — a Two-Turns Penalty, since there was contact with a boat and with the mark
Yes — exoneration can only be granted by the protest committee after a hearing, so take the turn now
questions.why: Rule 43.2: a boat exonerated for breaking a rule need not take a penalty and shall not be penalised for it.

questions.q: In an ILCA 6 you take what you think is a penalty turn: you tack, sail a few lengths, tack back and call it one turn. Your coach shakes his head afterwards. Why?

figure.note: Tack — few lengths — tack back

options: A turn must start with a gybe when taken on a beat
A turn must include one tack and one gybe — two tacks is not a turn
A turn must be made in under ten seconds, and yours was slower
A turn must include two tacks and one gybe
questions.why: Rule 44.2: each turn includes one tack and one gybe.

questions.q: Taking a Two-Turns Penalty just past the windward mark, you misjudge the second turn and your transom hits the mark. What do you owe now?

figure.note: Your transom hits the mark during the second turn

options: Two turns in all — rule 44.1(a) says a mark touch in the same incident needs no extra penalty
Nothing more — the Two-Turns Penalty covers everything that happens while you take it
The two turns plus an additional One-Turn Penalty — touching the mark during the turns is a new incident, not part of the first
You must retire — a boat that fouls a mark while being penalised cannot continue
questions.why: Rule 44.1(a) merges a mark touch with a Part 2 breach only in the same incident; a mark touched during the turns is a separate breach of rule 31.

questions.q: You are doing penalty turns on the run after an incident with another boat. Yellow, sailing her normal course with the fleet, has to alter course sharply to miss your stern as you gybe. Who has to keep clear?

figure.note: You are mid-gybe in your turns; Yellow has to alter course

options: Neither — the normal Part 2 rules are suspended around a boat taking a penalty
Yellow — she was clear astern of you when the turns began
Yellow — a boat taking a penalty has right of way until the turns are complete
You — a boat taking a penalty shall keep clear of a boat that is not; Yellow must only avoid interfering with you if reasonably possible
questions.why: Rule 21.2: a boat taking a penalty keeps clear of one that is not; rule 23.2 asks others only not to interfere if reasonably possible.

questions.q: Blue has sailed off to the side of the run and is doing her penalty turns. You leave your proper course and sail over to sit on her wind so that she loses more distance. Blue protests. Did you break a rule?

figure.note: You leave your course to blanket Blue in her turns

options: Yes — a boat shall not interfere with a boat taking a penalty if reasonably possible, and you were not sailing your proper course
Yes — you broke rule 21.2 by not keeping clear of Blue
No — a boat taking a penalty has no rights, so anyone may do what they like near her
No — after the starting signal rule 23.2 never applies
questions.why: Rule 23.2: if reasonably possible, a boat shall not interfere with a boat taking a penalty; the proper-course exception did not apply to you.

questions.q: You foul a boat at the windward mark of a 40-boat ILCA fleet. You round the mark, sail three lengths off to the side of the reach away from the pack, and about twenty seconds after the incident take two turns. Does that satisfy rule 44.2?

figure.note: You pull three lengths clear before turning

options: No — the turns must begin at the exact spot of the incident
Yes — you got well clear of other boats as soon as possible and then took the turns without delay
No — rule 44.2 allows at most ten seconds between the incident and the first turn
No — the turns must be taken before you round the mark
questions.why: Rule 44.2: after getting well clear of other boats as soon after the incident as possible, the boat promptly makes the turns.

questions.q: Twenty seconds before the start in a Melges 24 fleet you misjudge the committee boat and your bow touches its hull. What penalty, if any, do you owe?

figure.note: 0:20 to go; your bow touches the committee boat

options: A Two-Turns Penalty — contact with a committee boat counts as contact with a boat
None — a committee boat is a vessel, not a mark, so rule 31 does not apply
A One-Turn Penalty — the committee boat is a starting mark, and touching it before starting breaks rule 31
None — rule 31 applies only after the starting signal
questions.why: Rule 31: while racing a boat shall not touch a starting mark before starting; rule 44.1 gives a One-Turn Penalty for rule 31.

questions.q: A minute before the start in an Optimist fleet you touch the pin-end buoy. A friend shouts that you have to wait for the starting signal and then do your turn on the course side. Is he right?

figure.note: 1:00 to go; you touch the pin

options: Yes — a penalty taken before the start does not count because you are not yet racing
Yes — penalties can only be taken while on a leg of the course, after the start
No — before the start a mark touch needs two turns, not one
No — you take the One-Turn Penalty as soon as possible after getting well clear, which may well be before the starting signal
questions.why: Rule 44.2 says to take the turns promptly after getting well clear; you are racing from the preparatory signal, so the penalty is available before the start.

questions.q: On one lap of a windward–leeward course you break rule 10 at the windward mark and, later, rule 18.2 at the leeward mark — two separate incidents, no damage. Your crew proposes four turns at the bottom of the course to cover both. Correct?
options: No — each incident requires its own Two-Turns Penalty, taken promptly after that incident; the first penalty is already late
No — one Two-Turns Penalty covers every breach in a race
Yes, provided the four turns are all in the same direction
Yes — four turns in one place are the same as two separate penalties
questions.why: Rule 44.1 and 44.2: the penalty is for an incident and must be taken promptly after it; separate incidents mean separate penalties.

questions.q: Flag Z displayed. At the first attempt you were identified in the triangle in the last minute; the race was generally recalled. At the restart you are again inside the triangle at 0:30 and are identified again. What is your penalty for the race?
options: Disqualification without a hearing — a second offence under flag Z means UFD
Two 20 % Scoring Penalties — the first stays after the restart and a second one is added
One 20 % Scoring Penalty — a boat cannot be penalised twice for the same race
No penalty — the general recall cancelled the first and the restart is a new race
questions.why: Rule 30.2: the penalty stands after a restart, and a boat identified again at a later attempt receives an additional 20 % penalty.

questions.q: The sailing instructions of a 90-boat Optimist event say: "Rule 44.1 is changed so that the Two-Turns Penalty is replaced by the One-Turn Penalty." You break rule 11 on the first reach. How many turns do you take?

figure.title: SI: one turn replaces two
lines: You break rule 11 on the reach

options: None — a changed penalty rule means penalties are taken only ashore
Two for the breach, plus the one-turn penalty from the instructions
One — the sailing instructions may change rule 44.1, and here they replace the two turns by one
Two — the sailing instructions cannot change a penalty in Part 4
questions.why: Rule 44.1 allows the NoR or SI to specify another penalty, which replaces the One-Turn and Two-Turns Penalties.

questions.q: Appendix P is in force at a Finn regatta. On the second beat a jury boat sounds a whistle, points a yellow flag at you and hails your sail number. It is your first rule 42 penalty of the event. What must you do?

figure.title: Jury boat: whistle, yellow flag
lines: Second beat, pumping in the chop
First rule 42 penalty for you this event

options: Take a One-Turn Penalty — rule 42 is not a Part 2 rule
Display a yellow flag of your own and accept a 20 % Scoring Penalty
Retire from the race immediately
Take a Two-Turns Penalty promptly under rule 44.2; if you do not, you will be disqualified without a hearing
questions.why: Appendix P2.1: a boat penalised under P1.2 for the first time takes a Two-Turns Penalty; failing that she is disqualified without a hearing.

questions.q: Same Finn regatta, two days later: a jury boat penalises you under rule 42 for the second time in the event. You take two turns as before and finish 5th. What is your result?

figure.title: Second yellow flag of the event
lines: You take two turns and sail on

options: A non-excludable disqualification — the second penalty required you to retire promptly, and you did not
An ordinary DSQ that can be excluded as your discard
5th — a Two-Turns Penalty is the penalty for any rule 42 breach under Appendix P
5th plus 20 % — the second penalty is a Scoring Penalty
questions.why: Appendix P2.2: a boat penalised a second time shall promptly retire; if she fails to, she is disqualified without a hearing and the score is not excludable.

questions.q: A long week at an ILCA 6 event sailed under Appendix P: a jury boat penalises you under rule 42 for the third time. You retire at once, as the rule requires. How is this race scored for you?

figure.title: Third rule 42 penalty of the event

options: As RET — you retired as required, and the score can be discarded
As a non-excludable disqualification — a third penalty means DSQ that cannot be discarded even though you retired promptly
As an ordinary DSQ that can be used as your discard
As DNF plus a 20 % Scoring Penalty
questions.why: Appendix P2.3: for a third or subsequent penalty the boat retires promptly and is disqualified without a hearing, with the score not excludable.

questions.q: Appendix P event, Europe class. Two minutes after the start a jury boat penalises you for rocking; you begin your turns — and the committee signals a general recall. What happens to that penalty?

figure.title: Appendix P, general recall
lines: 2 min after the start: penalised for rocking

options: It is converted into a 20 % Scoring Penalty for the restarted race
It stands — you must complete the turns after the restart
It is cancelled for the race, but it still counts when the jury adds up how many times you have been penalised in the event
It is cancelled completely, as if it had never happened
questions.why: Appendix P3: after a postponement, general recall or abandonment the penalty is cancelled but still counts toward the number of penalties in the event.

questions.q: Club race in a dying breeze, no jury on the water. Halfway up the last beat you realise you have been fanning the mainsail repeatedly for a minute — plain pumping. Nobody saw it. What does the rulebook expect of you?

figure.title: Dying breeze, last beat
lines: No jury boats on the water
You pumped the main for a minute

options: To take a One-Turn Penalty, since rule 42 is in Part 4
To take a Two-Turns Penalty, as for any breach of a rule while racing — rule 44 covers them all
Nothing — rule 42 can only be enforced by judges on the water
To retire — turns are only for Part 2 and rule 31; unless the sailing instructions provide another penalty for rule 42, you retire
questions.why: Basic principle: a boat that breaks a rule promptly takes the appropriate penalty, which may be to retire; rule 44.1 covers only Part 2 and rule 31.

questions.q: You retire after causing serious damage at the gybe mark, in a 24-boat Dragon fleet. How is the race scored for you?
options: RET — points for the finishing place one more than the boats entered, i.e. 25; excludable as a discard
DNF — the same as not finishing, with a 20 % penalty added
The points of the last boat that finished, plus one
DNE — a disqualification that cannot be excluded from the series
questions.why: Appendix A: a boat that retired is scored RET, points for the finishing place one more than the number of boats entered; it is excludable.

questions.q: On the final beat you cross a starboard boat by a whisker — you know you should have ducked — but she does not hail and nobody protests. You keep your 2nd place and tell the story in the bar. How do the rules see this?
options: As perfectly fine — a breach that is not protested has no consequences
As a breach of the basic principle Sportsmanship and the Rules — you were expected to take the penalty unasked — and possibly of rule 2
As a breach of rule 44.3 — you should have displayed a yellow flag
As fine — rule 10 only requires a penalty when there is contact
questions.why: Basic principle: a boat that breaks a rule and is not exonerated promptly takes the appropriate penalty; knowingly not doing so can breach rule 2.

questions.q: Running in a 470 fleet, both on port. You are to leeward and luff sharply without giving Red, overlapped to windward, room to keep clear; Red reacts late and her boom hits your shroud. No damage. Who takes a penalty?

figure.note: You luff sharply; Red's boom hits your shroud

options: Neither — when both boats break a rule the breaches cancel out
Only you — the boat that altered course is always the one at fault
Both of you — you may have broken rule 16.1 and Red rule 11; each boat that may have broken a rule takes her own Two-Turns Penalty
Only Red — the windward boat must keep clear whatever the leeward boat does
questions.why: Rule 44.1 applies to each boat that may have broken a rule; one boat's breach does not excuse the other's unless it compelled it (rule 43.1(a)).

questions.q: Dead downwind in a J/70, you need to take a penalty. You gybe first, then round up, tack, and bear away back onto the run — once, and then repeat the same way. Your bowman says a turn has to start with a tack. Who is right?

figure.note: Gybe, round up, tack, bear away — one turn

options: The bowman — every penalty turn starts head to wind, with a tack
Neither — on a run only a Scoring Penalty can be taken
The bowman — on a run the penalty is two gybes rather than a tack and a gybe
You — a turn needs one tack and one gybe in either order, so on a run it naturally starts with a gybe
questions.why: Rule 44.2: each turn includes one tack and one gybe; the rule does not say which comes first.

questions.q: You took a Scoring Penalty with the yellow flag. At the finish you call the committee boat's attention to the flag, but when asked which boat was involved you say you did not see her number. What does rule 44.3 require of you now?

figure.title: At the finishing line
lines: Yellow flag shown since the incident
Asked: "Which boat?" — you do not know

options: To tell the race committee which boat was involved — at the finish if you can, otherwise at the first reasonable opportunity within the protest time limit
Nothing more — identifying the other boat is optional
To lodge a written protest against the other boat
To take two turns before clearing the finishing line, since the report is incomplete
questions.why: Rule 44.3(b): at the finish the boat also names the other boat involved; if impossible, at the first reasonable opportunity within the protest time limit.

questions.q: You break rule 11 at mark 1 of a trapezoid course. The Scoring Penalty applies. You decide to hoist the yellow flag only on the final leg, "so the committee boat actually sees it". Is your penalty valid?
options: Yes — what matters is that the flag is up when you cross the finishing line
No — the yellow flag must be displayed at the first reasonable opportunity after the incident and kept displayed until you finish
Yes — the rule only requires the flag to be displayed for at least one leg
No — the yellow flag must be hoisted before the incident is over
questions.why: Rule 44.3(a): the Scoring Penalty is taken by displaying a yellow flag at the first reasonable opportunity after the incident.

questions.q: You finish 5th in a Scoring-Penalty race with your yellow flag up; your score becomes 5 plus the penalty. The boat that finished 6th asks the race office to be moved up to 5th place. What happens?
