options: She gets 5.5 points, splitting the place with you
She gets 5th only if your penalised score is worse than 6 points
Nothing — your penalty does not change the other boats' scores; she keeps 6 points even if your total is now higher
She is moved to 5th and every boat behind her moves up one place
questions.why: Rule 44.3(c): the scores of other boats shall not be changed; two boats may therefore receive the same score.

questions.q: Flag Z. At 0:40 you are identified inside the triangle. At 0:10 the race committee hoists AP with two sounds — the start is postponed and later begun afresh. Do you carry a 20 % penalty into the new start?
options: No — but you must sail round an end of the line before the new start
Yes — once identified, the penalty stands for every later attempt at that race
Yes — but it is halved to 10 % because the start was postponed
No — the Z-flag penalty does not apply when the race is postponed or abandoned before the starting signal
questions.why: Rule 30.2: the penalty stands after a restart or resail, but not if the race was postponed or abandoned before the starting signal.

questions.q: Flag U start, your number is noted at 0:20 inside the triangle; the race starts, but after the first lap the wind dies and the committee abandons it (flag N) and resails it the next day. Are you still UFD for that race?

figure.title: Flag U, race abandoned later
lines: 0:20: your number noted in the triangle
Race starts; wind dies after lap 1

options: No — the U-flag disqualification does not apply when the race is restarted or resailed; you sail the resail without penalty
No — but it becomes a 20 % Scoring Penalty in the resail
Yes — a U-flag disqualification stays with the race number, whatever happens later
Yes — only a general recall before the start removes it
questions.why: Rule 30.3: disqualification without a hearing, except when the race is restarted or resailed.

questions.q: In a race that was later abandoned and resailed, your 36-footer hit Grey on port–starboard and holed her bow above the waterline; you took two turns at the time. Grey protests after the resail. Can you still be penalised for the original incident?

figure.title: Original race, later abandoned
lines: You on port hit Grey on starboard

options: No — an abandoned race is as if it never happened, with all its breaches
Yes — rule 36 does not protect a breach of rule 14 that caused serious damage, and the applicable penalty was to retire, not turns
Only for the resail — you must do the two turns again there
No — you took a Two-Turns Penalty at the time
questions.why: Rule 36: breaches in the original race are not penalised except rules 2, 30.2, 30.4, 69 and rule 14 when it caused injury or serious damage.

questions.q: In the first attempt at race 3 you forced a starboard boat to tack away (rule 10) and took no penalty; the race was then abandoned after a windward-mark drag and resailed. In the resail you sail cleanly. Can the other boat have you penalised for the first-attempt incident?
options: No — but you are scored with a 20 % penalty in the resail
Yes — a rule 10 breach is carried over into the resail and can be heard there
No — a breach in a race that is abandoned and resailed is not a reason to penalise, apart from the rule 36 exceptions
Yes — you must take two turns at the start of the resail
questions.why: Rule 36: a breach in the original race is not a reason for penalising a boat, except rules 2, 30.2, 30.4, 69 and rule 14 with injury or serious damage.

questions.q: You cross the finishing line in a 470 and, while clearing it, your rudder clips the finishing mark. You have finished, so your crew says it does not count. What does rule 31 say, and what do you do?

figure.note: Your rudder clips the pin as you clear the line

options: It does not count — rule 31 stops applying the moment you finish
It counts — you must retire, since a penalty cannot be taken after finishing
It counts — take a One-Turn Penalty and sail home; you have already finished
It counts — touching a finishing mark after finishing breaks rule 31; take a One-Turn Penalty, return completely to the course side and cross again
questions.why: Rule 31 covers a finishing mark after finishing; rule 44.2: a penalty near the finishing line means returning completely to the course side before finishing.

questions.q: Two lengths from the finishing line you foul a boat to leeward. You start your two turns at once, and during the second turn your bow pokes across the finishing line before you complete the gybe. What must you do to finish correctly?

figure.note: Your bow crosses the line in mid-turn

options: Complete the turns, get your hull completely back on the course side of the line, and then cross it to finish
Sail round the committee boat and cross the line from the other side
Cross the line again from either side — the turns reset the finish
Nothing special — you finished when your bow crossed the line during the turn
questions.why: Rule 44.2: when a penalty is taken at or near the finishing line the hull shall be completely on the course side before the boat finishes.

questions.q: P flag start, Wednesday evening. You are over at the gun, see flag X, sail back across the line and start properly about 40 seconds late. The boat next to you says you also owe a penalty turn. Do you?

figure.note: Flag X; you sail back and start again

options: Yes — a Two-Turns Penalty, as for any rule broken at the start
No — returning to the pre-start side and starting correctly is the whole remedy; while returning you simply had to keep clear of boats that were not
Yes — a One-Turn Penalty for being on the course side at the starting signal
Yes — a 20 % Scoring Penalty applies to every boat recalled individually
questions.why: Rule 29.1 and definition Start: a recalled boat returns and starts; rule 21.1 only makes her keep clear while returning.

questions.q: You were over the line at the start and are sailing back on starboard tack to return. A port-tack boat that started correctly is beating across your path. Who keeps clear?

figure.note: You return on starboard; Blue has started on port

options: The port-tack boat — but only until you reach the line
Neither — boats returning to start are not racing
You — a boat returning to the pre-start side after the starting signal keeps clear of one that is not, until her hull is fully on the pre-start side
The port-tack boat — you are on starboard and rule 10 applies to her as to any other port-tack boat
questions.why: Rule 21.1: a boat returning to start after her starting signal keeps clear of boats that are not, whatever her tack.

questions.q: On the run, Grey is doing penalty turns a little to one side of the rhumb line. You are sailing your proper course straight down the run and will pass close to her. Must you alter course to leave her more room?

figure.note: Grey in her turns; you hold your proper course down the run

options: No — because Grey is not racing while she takes a penalty
Yes — rule 23.2 requires you to keep well clear of any boat taking a penalty
Yes — a boat taking a penalty has the right to the water she needs for her turns
No — Grey must keep clear of you while taking her penalty, and after the starting signal a boat sailing her proper course need not avoid interfering with her
questions.why: Rule 21.2: the penalised boat keeps clear; rule 23.2 does not apply after the starting signal to a boat sailing her proper course.

questions.q: You break rule 11 against Red at the leeward mark and take two turns at once, losing three places. Red, undisturbed, sailed on but later parked in a hole and finished behind you anyway. Red protests, arguing that you still beat her so the turns were not enough. Is she right?

figure.title: Leeward mark, later a hole
lines: Red sails on, later parks in a lull

options: No — the test is a significant advantage from the breach despite the turns; you lost places and Red lost nothing from the incident, so the turns stand
Yes — any boat that is protested after taking turns must take them again
Yes — a boat that fouled another must finish behind her or retire, whatever the turns
No — but the protest committee will add a 20 % Scoring Penalty to be fair
questions.why: Rule 44.1(b) requires retirement only when the boat gained a significant advantage despite taking the penalty; finishing ahead for other reasons is not that.

questions.q: After an incident at the gybe mark you notice that Blue is sailing on with a yellow flag tied in her shroud. The sailing instructions say rule 44.3 applies. What is Blue doing?

figure.title: After the gybe mark
lines: Blue sails on, yellow flag in her shroud

options: Protesting the boat she met at the gybe mark, as the rules require
Taking a Scoring Penalty — she keeps the flag up until she finishes and tells the race committee at the line
Acknowledging a rule 42 penalty signalled by the jury
Signalling that she is retiring from the race
questions.why: Rule 44.3: a boat takes the Scoring Penalty by displaying a yellow flag at the first reasonable opportunity and until she finishes.

questions.q: On a reach in a Star fleet you got your leeward overlap from clear astern and then luffed Blue well above your proper course. Blue hails "Protest" and you agree you were wrong. What penalty do you take?

figure.note: You luff Blue above your proper course

options: A 20 % Scoring Penalty — the default for rules outside Section A
No penalty — rule 17 breaches can only be dealt with in a hearing
A Two-Turns Penalty — rule 17 is a rule of Part 2
A One-Turn Penalty — rule 17 is only a limitation, not a right-of-way rule
questions.why: Rule 17 is in Part 2 Section B; rule 44.1 gives the Two-Turns Penalty for any Part 2 rule.

questions.q: You took two turns after barging in at the windward mark. In the hearing the committee finds that, even after the turns, the barge gained you twelve places you could not otherwise have gained. What is the decision?

figure.title: Hearing: windward mark barge
lines: Net gain from the barge: 12 places

options: A 20 % Scoring Penalty, which reflects the advantage
No further penalty — you took the Two-Turns Penalty promptly
The committee orders you to be scored twelve places lower
Disqualification — you gained a significant advantage despite the penalty, so the applicable penalty was to retire
questions.why: Rule 44.1(b): significant advantage despite the penalty means retirement; a boat that did not retire is disqualified under rule 60.5(c).

questions.q: You finish, clear the finishing line and its marks, and head home. Half a mile later you brush a turning mark of the course that is still being used by a later fleet. Do you owe a penalty?
options: No — you are no longer racing once you have finished and cleared the line and marks, and rule 31 applies only while racing
Yes — a One-Turn Penalty, and you must then cross the finishing line again
Yes — a One-Turn Penalty, to be taken at once
Yes — you must report to the race office and accept a Scoring Penalty
questions.why: Definition Racing: a boat stops racing when she finishes and clears the finishing line and marks; rule 31 applies 'while racing'.

questions.q: At a crowded leeward gate, you and Yellow each foul a different boat and both sail off to the same patch of clear water to take your turns. As you both spin, you converge. Which rules apply between the two of you?

figure.note: Both of you are taking penalty turns

options: Rule 21.2 — the boat that fouled first has priority in her turns
The ordinary rules of Part 2 — rule 21.2 only makes a penalised boat keep clear of a boat that is not taking a penalty
Rule 21.2 — the boat that started her turns later keeps clear
None — boats taking penalties are temporarily outside Part 2
questions.why: Rule 21.2 applies between a boat taking a penalty and one that is not; between two penalised boats the normal rules of Part 2 govern.

questions.q: A new crew member in your J/24 asks, as you spin after a foul, how many manoeuvres a Two-Turns Penalty involves in total. What do you tell her?
options: One tack and one gybe — two half-turns make the penalty
Two tacks only — a tack and then a tack back
Two tacks and two gybes — two full turns in the same direction, each with one tack and one gybe
Two gybes only — the boat must pass through dead downwind twice
questions.why: Rule 44.2: the required number of turns in the same direction, each including one tack and one gybe.

questions.q: After contact between you and Grey on the second beat, Grey hoists a red flag and keeps racing without doing any turns. Your crew says: "Fine, she has taken her penalty." Has she?
options: Yes — a flag of any colour shows that the boat accepts the penalty
No — a penalty is only taken by retiring
Yes — a red flag is the signal for the Scoring Penalty
No — a red flag means she is protesting; a penalty is turns, or a yellow flag where the SI allow the Scoring Penalty
questions.why: Rule 60.2 (red flag = protest) versus rule 44.2 (turns) and 44.3 (yellow flag = Scoring Penalty).

questions.q: Windward mark, Hobie 16s. Blue, overlapped outside you, fails to give you mark-room and you are squeezed onto the buoy. What penalty does Blue owe?

figure.note: Blue squeezes you onto the buoy

options: A Two-Turns Penalty — rule 18 is a Part 2 rule; you, forced onto the mark, are exonerated
A One-Turn Penalty — the incident involved a mark, so rule 31 governs
None — only the boat that touched the mark owes a penalty
A One-Turn Penalty each — one mark incident, one turn per boat
questions.why: Rule 18.2 is in Part 2, so rule 44.1 gives Blue a Two-Turns Penalty; rule 43.1(a) exonerates the boat compelled to touch the mark.

questions.q: Beat in a Laser fleet. Red, on port, hails "Hold your course!" as she tries to cross you on starboard. You hold on; her transom scrapes your bow, no damage. Red says the hail bound you and that you fouled her. Who takes a penalty?

figure.note: Red hails "Hold your course"; her transom scrapes your bow

options: Both — contact means both boats broke rule 14 and both take turns
Red — a hail of "Hold your course" gives a port-tack boat no rights; she broke rule 10 and owes a Two-Turns Penalty, while you are exonerated for the contact
Nobody — the boat that hails first has priority in a crossing
You — once Red hailed, you had to hold your course and avoid contact at the same time
questions.why: Rule 10 is not changed by any hail; rule 43.1(c) exonerates the right-of-way boat for rule 14 when there is no damage.

questions.q: Beating along a shore in a Dragon, you hail "Room to tack!" to Grey on your windward side — though you could easily have sailed on for another twenty lengths. Grey tacks, loses two places and protests. If the committee finds your hail broke rule 20.1, what is your penalty?

figure.note: Twenty lengths from the shore, you hail for room

options: A warning — breaches of rule 20 carry no penalty
None — a hail cannot break a rule, only a manoeuvre can
Disqualification unless you took a Two-Turns Penalty on the water — rule 20 is a rule of Part 2
A One-Turn Penalty, since no boat was touched
questions.why: Rule 20 is in Part 2 Section C; a boat that breaks it may take a Two-Turns Penalty under rule 44.1 or be disqualified.

questions.q: On the run you come up on an ILCA 7 lying capsized with her sailor in the water. You could have steered round her but hold your course and your bow bumps her hull — no damage, nobody hurt. What penalty do you owe?

figure.note: Grey is capsized; you could have steered round her

options: You must retire — any contact with a capsized boat is serious by definition
A One-Turn Penalty — a capsized boat counts as an obstruction, like a mark
None — a capsized boat is not racing, so no rule applies between you
A Two-Turns Penalty — rule 22 requires you to avoid a capsized boat if possible, and it is a rule of Part 2
questions.why: Rule 22 (Part 2 Section D): if possible, avoid a capsized boat; rule 44.1 gives a Two-Turns Penalty for the breach.

questions.q: On a 36-footer your crew sits with their legs over the lifelines through most of the first beat. Realising this breaks rule 49.2, the skipper orders two turns "to clear it". Does that work?

figure.title: First beat, 36-footer
lines: Most of the beat sailed that way

options: No — rule 44 turns are only for Part 2 and rule 31; a breach of rule 49 goes to the protest committee, or the boat retires
Yes — one turn would have done, since no other boat was involved
No — but a yellow flag and 20 % would settle it
Yes — a Two-Turns Penalty settles any breach noticed while racing
questions.why: Rule 44.1 covers only Part 2 and rule 31; other breaches are penalised by the protest committee (often [DP]) unless the boat retires.

questions.q: Two legs after a close mark rounding, Red sails up and hails "Protest" for that rounding. You now think she may be right. Will taking two turns now help you?

figure.title: Two legs later
lines: Close rounding at the windward mark
You now think she may be right

options: No — but a yellow flag now would convert it into a 20 % penalty
No — turns two legs after the incident are not prompt and do not count; wait for the hearing, where Red's late hail may make her protest invalid
Yes — turns can be taken at any time before finishing, so take them now and you are safe
Yes — a penalty taken after a hail of "Protest" is always timely
questions.why: Rule 44.2: turns are taken promptly after the incident; rule 60.2 requires the hail at the first reasonable opportunity.

questions.q: Club race; the sailing instructions say nothing about penalties. After fouling a boat at the gybe mark you hoist a yellow flag and sail on, planning to report 20 % at the finish. Is this a valid penalty?

figure.title: Club race, SI silent on penalties
lines: You foul a boat at the gybe mark

options: Yes — a boat may always choose between turns and the Scoring Penalty
Yes — provided the race committee acknowledges the flag at the finish
No — the Scoring Penalty is available only when the notice of race or sailing instructions say so; otherwise the penalty is two turns
No — the yellow flag must be hoisted before the incident
questions.why: Rule 44.3(a): the Scoring Penalty applies when the NoR or SI say so; rule 44.1 otherwise gives the Two-Turns Penalty.

questions.q: Final race of a championship: you and Blue are tied on points. At the last mark you foul her, take two turns at once, still finish one place ahead of her and win the title. In the hearing the committee finds the foul decided the series. What is the right penalty?

figure.title: Championship decider
lines: You and Blue tied on points
Two turns at once; you finish one ahead
You win the title by that place

options: Disqualification from the whole series
A 20 % Scoring Penalty, which costs you the title anyway
None — the turns were taken promptly and the advantage was only one place
Retirement — and since you did not retire, disqualification: you gained a significant advantage in the series despite taking the penalty
questions.why: Rule 44.1(b): a significant advantage in the race or series despite the penalty means retirement; otherwise DSQ under rule 60.5(c).

questions.q: Rounding the offset mark in a 29er, you felt nothing, but thirty seconds later your crew says: "We clipped the mark with the spinnaker sheet." What do you do?

figure.title: Offset mark, 29er
lines: Rounded with the kite going up
Crew, 30 s later: "We clipped the mark"

options: Take the One-Turn Penalty now — as soon as possible after the incident, which for you is the moment you learn of it
Nothing — contact with a sheet rather than the hull is not touching the mark
Take a Two-Turns Penalty — late mark penalties are doubled
Nothing — a penalty must be started within ten seconds of the incident or not at all
questions.why: Rule 31 covers any part of the boat; rule 44.2 requires the penalty as soon as possible after the incident.

questions.q: After a collision in which you holed Red's bow you retire at once and motor in. Red still lodges a protest and the committee finds you broke rule 10. Can it penalise you further?
options: Yes — a retired boat can still be disqualified, which is worse than RET
No — retirement was the applicable penalty for the breach, so no further penalty; only a rule 2 finding could add a non-excludable DSQ
Yes — a 20 % Scoring Penalty is added to your RET score
Yes — the committee can order you to miss the next race
questions.why: Rule 60.5(c): a boat that has taken the applicable penalty shall not be penalised further unless the penalty for the rule broken is a non-excludable DSQ.

questions.q: At the leeward mark you touched the buoy but took no turn, sure that Yellow had pushed you onto it. In the hearing the committee finds that Yellow kept clear and that you simply cut the corner. What is the outcome?

figure.title: Hearing: leeward mark
lines: You touched the buoy, no turn
Your claim: Yellow pushed you on
Facts: Yellow kept clear, you cut the corner

options: A 20 % Scoring Penalty for the mark contact
No penalty — you genuinely believed you were exonerated
Disqualification — you were not compelled to break rule 31, so no exoneration, and you took no penalty
A One-Turn Penalty, which the committee converts into one place
questions.why: Rule 43.1(a) exonerates only a boat compelled by another's breach; rule 60.5(c): DSQ when a boat broke a rule and took no applicable penalty.

questions.q: Passing the end of a long pier on the same tack, you are the inside boat and Blue, outside and to windward, is giving you room. You luff to clear the pier head and Blue has to respond sharply; she protests you under rule 16.1. Are you liable?

figure.note: You luff to clear the pier head; Blue must respond

options: No — rule 16 never applies at an obstruction
Yes — the inside boat at an obstruction has no right to alter course
Yes — rule 16.1 applies to every course change, and you must take two turns
No — you were sailing within the room you were entitled to, so you are exonerated for breaking rule 16 against the boat obliged to give it
questions.why: Rule 43.1(b): a boat sailing within the room she is entitled to is exonerated for breaking a rule of Section A, rule 15, 16 or 31 in that incident.

questions.q: Leeward mark, you are the inside windward boat with mark-room. Grey, outside and to leeward with right of way, gives you so little room that your hulls touch as you round — no damage. Grey protests you under rules 11 and 14. Result?

figure.note: Grey gives too little room; hulls touch, no damage

options: You are exonerated for both — you were sailing within your mark-room, and the contact caused no damage or injury; Grey should take a Two-Turns Penalty
You are penalised under rule 14 only, Grey under rule 18
Both boats are penalised — any contact breaks rule 14 for both
You are penalised under rule 11 — the windward boat must keep clear whatever her mark-room
questions.why: Rule 43.1(b) exonerates a boat sailing within her mark-room for a Section A rule; rule 43.1(c) for rule 14 when there is no damage or injury.

questions.q: Thirty seconds before the start, parked below the committee boat, you back your jib to drop astern and your transom bumps the boat behind, which is holding station normally. No damage. What do you owe?

figure.note: 0:30; you back the jib and drop onto Red

options: A One-Turn Penalty — pre-start contact is treated like touching a mark
A Two-Turns Penalty — a boat moving astern by backing a sail keeps clear of one that is not, and that is a Part 2 rule
Nothing — before the starting signal the rules of Part 2 do not apply
Nothing — the boat behind was clear astern and had to keep clear of you
questions.why: Rule 21.3 (Part 2 Section D): a boat moving astern by backing a sail keeps clear; rule 44.1 gives the Two-Turns Penalty.

questions.q: The sailing instructions say: "The Scoring Penalty, rule 44.3, applies; the penalty is two places." You take it and finish 4th in a 30-boat fleet. What is your score, and what happens to the boats behind you?
options: 6 points, and the 5th and 6th boats move up to 4th and 5th
4 points — a places penalty is applied only to the series total
6 points — and the boats behind you keep their scores, so the 5th and 6th boats stay on 5 and 6
4 plus 20 % of 31, about 10 points — the places clause does not change the arithmetic
questions.why: Rule 44.3(c): the score is worsened by the number of places stated in the NoR or SI, and the scores of other boats are not changed.

questions.q: Milling about before the preparatory signal of a J/24 race, you are on port and force a starboard boat to tack away to avoid you. No contact. She hails "Protest". Can you be penalised?

figure.title: Before the preparatory signal
lines: You on port, in the starting area
A starboard boat tacks away to avoid you

options: Yes — but only with a 20 % Scoring Penalty, not disqualification
No — rule 10 does not apply at all before the starting signal
Yes — Part 2 applies from the moment you are in the racing area, so take two turns
No — you are not yet racing, and a boat not racing is not penalised for a Part 2 breach except rule 14 with injury or serious damage, or rule 23.1
questions.why: Preamble to Part 2: a boat not racing shall not be penalised for breaking a Part 2 rule, except rule 14 with injury or serious damage, or rule 23.1.
questions.ref: RRS Part 2 preamble, RRS definition Racing

questions.q: After causing serious damage at the windward mark you decide to retire, as rule 44.1(b) requires. What do you do next?
options: Leave the course without interfering with boats still racing, and inform the race committee as the sailing instructions require
Take two turns first and then retire, to cover both possibilities
Sail the rest of the course anyway so that you are scored DNF rather than RET
Display a yellow flag and finish, so that the committee can score the penalty
questions.why: Rule 23.1: a boat not racing shall not interfere with boats racing; the SI normally require a retiring boat to notify the race committee.

questions.q: You are close-hauled on starboard, holding a steady course, when Blue on port hits your bow and hails "Protest — you bore away into me!" You did not change course. What do you do?

figure.note: Blue hits your bow and hails "Protest"

options: Take a Two-Turns Penalty — in a collision both boats always take turns
Keep racing without taking a penalty — you broke no rule; Blue should be taking two turns, and the hearing will decide the facts
Retire — a boat hit on a beat must assume she is at fault
Take a One-Turn Penalty as a goodwill gesture
questions.why: Rule 10: Blue keeps clear; rule 44.1 only concerns a boat that may have broken a rule; the protest committee establishes the facts.

questions.q: River course with a strong ebb. Rounding the windward mark in almost no wind, the current sets you sideways onto the buoy despite everything you try. Nobody else is near. Do you owe a penalty?

figure.note: Ebb sets you sideways onto the buoy; no wind

options: No — a boat that touches a mark because of current or lack of wind is exonerated
No — exoneration applies whenever the contact was unavoidable
Yes — rule 31 does not ask whose fault it was; you touched the mark while racing, so take a One-Turn Penalty
Yes — a Two-Turns Penalty, since there was no other boat to blame
questions.why: Rule 31 is broken by the touch itself; exoneration under rule 43.1 needs another boat's breach or room entitlement.

questions.q: Black flag preparatory signal, the race starts normally. You know you were in the triangle in the last minute, so you sail back round the pin end, restart behind the fleet and finish 2nd. How are you scored?

figure.title: Black flag, clean start
lines: You go back round the pin and restart

options: 2nd with a 20 % Scoring Penalty added
2nd — you corrected your error before starting, as under flag I
OCS — a boat that restarts late is scored as not having started
BFD — disqualified without a hearing; returning and restarting does not remove a black-flag penalty
questions.why: Rule 30.4: a boat identified in the triangle in the last minute is disqualified without a hearing; only a postponement or abandonment before the start lifts it.

questions.q: Flag U is displayed. In the last minute you realise part of your hull is inside the triangle, so you dip back round the pin end as you would under flag I and start cleanly after the signal. Does that save you?

figure.note: Flag U; you go back round the pin end

options: No — flag U disqualifies her without a hearing; rounding an end is for flag I
Yes — sailing round an end of the line cures any starting error
Yes — flags I and U have the same round-an-end remedy
No — but the penalty is only 20 %, as under flag Z
questions.why: Rule 30.3: UFD without a hearing unless the race is restarted or resailed; the round-an-end remedy belongs to rule 30.1.

questions.q: The results show ZFP against your name after a Z-flag start. You go to the race office to demand a hearing because you were "only just" inside the triangle. What will you be told?
options: That the penalty will be reduced to 10 % because you were only just inside
That a Z-flag penalty is applied without a hearing — your only route is a request for redress if you think the committee made an error
That a hearing will be scheduled, as for any penalty
That you can replace it with two turns before the next race
questions.why: Rule 30.2: the 20 % penalty is applied without a hearing; a boat disputing the facts may request redress.

questions.q: Arbitration under Appendix T. After hearing both of you, the arbitrator says the protest committee would probably find that you broke rule 11. What can you do now?
options: Nothing — the arbitrator's opinion is the final decision
Accept a 20 % Scoring Penalty, as on the water
Accept a 30 % Post-Race Penalty, or let the protest go to a full hearing where you risk disqualification
Take two turns ashore in front of the arbitrator
questions.why: Appendix T4: after the arbitrator's opinion a boat may take the Post-Race Penalty (30 %) or the protest may proceed to a hearing.

questions.q: Appendix T applies. In the incident you are protested for, the other boat's rudder was broken off and she withdrew from the regatta. You ask for an arbitration meeting to take the 30 % penalty. Will you get it?
options: Yes — but the penalty is raised to 50 % because of the damage
Yes — any Part 2 incident can be settled by a 30 % Post-Race Penalty
No — arbitration is only for incidents without a protest
No — when the arbitrator decides rule 44.1(b) may apply there is no arbitration and no Post-Race Penalty; it goes to a full hearing
questions.why: Appendix T1(a) and T2: the Post-Race Penalty and the arbitration meeting are not available when rule 44.1(b) — injury or serious damage — may apply.

questions.q: Wednesday evening club race on the lake. Ashore, Grey's crew tells you that Red crossed her on port far too close on the first beat; you were two legs away and saw nothing. You want to protest Red yourself. Can you?

figure.title: Ashore after the race
lines: Red crossed Grey on port, first beat
You were two legs away, saw nothing
Grey's crew tells you at the bar

options: No — for a Part 2 incident only a boat that was involved in it or saw it may protest; Grey herself can
Yes, but only as a joint protest signed by you and Grey together
Yes — any boat in the race may protest any other boat for any rule she hears about
Only if the race committee countersigns your protest form
questions.why: Rule 60.4(a)(2): a boat's protest about a Part 2 or rule 31 breach is invalid unless she was involved in or saw the incident.

questions.q: ILCA 7 nationals, 6 knots. After the race Blue's helm tells you that Grey pumped her mainsail all the way down the last run; you did not see it yourself. Can you protest Grey under rule 42, and what must you do?

figure.title: After the race
lines: Blue says Grey pumped down the run

options: Yes, and nothing more is needed: a written protest within the time limit is enough
Yes — the "involved or saw" limit applies only to Part 2 and rule 31; but since you did not see it, you must inform Grey at the first reasonable opportunity
No — a boat may protest a rule 42 breach only if she was involved in or saw the pumping
No — only the jury on the water may protest a boat under rule 42
questions.why: Rule 60.4(a)(2) limits only Part 2 and 31 protests; rule 60.2(b)(3): incident not seen in the racing area — inform her at the first reasonable opportunity.

questions.q: Dragon regatta in Split. After the finish the helm of 4471 screams abuse at the mark-boat crew and throws a winch handle at them. You write a protest against 4471 under rule 69 and lodge it. What happens to it?

figure.title: After the finish
lines: Throws a winch handle at them
You lodge a protest citing rule 69

options: It is valid only if you hailed "Protest" at the moment of the incident
It is heard as an ordinary protest and 4471 is disqualified from the race if the facts are proven
It is invalid — an alleged rule 69 breach cannot be protested; your report goes to the protest committee, which decides whether to open a rule 69 hearing
It is valid only if the race committee co-signs it, since race officials were the victims
questions.why: Rules 60.4(a)(3) and 69.1(c): a report of misconduct is not a protest; the protest committee decides whether to act under rule 69.

questions.q: You request redress, writing that the committee boat dragged after the preparatory signal; in the form you also mention that Blue, next to you, was over the line and never returned. The race committee then protests Blue using only your form. Is its protest valid?

figure.title: Race office
lines: RC protests Blue on that alone

options: Yes, provided Blue is informed before the protest time limit expires
No — a race committee may never protest a boat for a starting error; it only scores her OCS
Yes — the race committee may protest any boat on any information it receives
No — a committee protest based on information from a request for redress is invalid
questions.why: Rule 60.4(b)(1): a protest by a committee based on information from a request for redress is invalid.

questions.q: 29er Europeans. The race officer on the windward mark boat sees Grey hit the mark and sail on without taking a turn. The race committee wants to protest her. What must it do?
options: Inform Grey of its intention to protest after the race, within the protest time limit — a notice on the official notice board is enough — and lodge a written protest in time
Nothing — a committee may protest only breaches of the sailing instructions, not rule 31
Score Grey DSQ for the race without a hearing, as it would for OCS
Hail "Protest" at Grey from the mark boat and hoist a red flag
questions.why: Rules 60.1, 60.2(a)(2) and 60.2(d): a committee informs the boat after the race within the protest time limit, e.g. by a notice on the official board.

questions.q: Before the medal race at a Palma regatta the technical committee measures your 470 jib and finds its luff 4 cm over the class maximum. What may the technical committee do?
options: Ask the race committee to protest, since a technical committee cannot
Protest your boat — it has inspected the equipment and decided it does not comply with the class rules
Nothing — only another competitor may protest a class-rule breach
Disqualify you on the spot, without any hearing
questions.why: Rules 60.1 and 60.4(c)(3): the technical committee may protest after it has inspected and found non-compliance with class rules or rule 50.

questions.q: In a hearing between you and Red about a leeward-mark incident, the evidence shows that Green — outside, not protested, present as a witness — forced Red down onto you. Can the protest committee penalise Green in this hearing?

figure.note: Three boats overlapped entering the zone

options: Yes, but only if you or Red amend your protest form to name Green
Yes — any boat shown by the evidence to have broken a rule can be penalised at once
Not in this hearing — it must close it, protest Green itself, then hear both protests together with Green as a party
No — a boat not named in the original protest can never be penalised for that incident
questions.why: Rules 60.4(c)(2), 60.5(b) and 63.2(d): a boat is penalised only as a party; the PC protests her, closes the hearing and hears both protests together.

questions.q: At the dock after a club race you tell the race officer loudly that Blue tacked right in front of you at the windward mark and that you protest her. Then you go home. Has a protest been made?

figure.title: At the dock
lines: You tell the race officer about Blue

options: Yes — your hail on the water was already the protest; the dock conversation only confirmed it
No — only the race officer may write a protest form, and he did not
Yes — telling the race officer within the protest time limit is enough at club level
No — a protest must be in writing, identifying the protestor, the protestee and the incident, and be delivered to the race office within the time limit
questions.why: Rule 60.3(a)–(b): a protest is written, identifies protestor, protestee and incident, and is delivered to the race office within the protest time limit.

questions.q: Saronic Gulf, J/24 fleet (hull 7.2 m). Blue, on port, crosses too close and you bear away to avoid her. You hail "Protest" at once but never show a red flag, and lodge the form in time. Is the protest valid?

figure.note: J/24, hull 7.2 m — you hailed, no flag

options: No — a boat with a hull longer than 6 m must also display a red flag at the first reasonable opportunity
Yes — the flag is needed only when the other boat does not acknowledge the hail
No — the protest also needed a second hail at the finishing line
Yes — the hail at the first reasonable opportunity is enough for any boat
questions.why: Rule 60.2(a)(1): hail "Protest" and, if the hull is longer than 6 m, display a red flag at the first reasonable opportunity, until no longer racing.

questions.q: ILCA 7 club race on the river. Red, on port, forces you to bear away sharply. You hail "Protest" immediately but have no flag aboard; your written protest is lodged in time. Valid?

figure.note: ILCA 7, hull 4.2 m — hail only

options: No — every boat must display a red flag; carry one on the boom
Yes — a boat with a hull under 6 m needs only the hail; no red flag is required
No — a single-hander must instead report the incident to the race committee at the finish
Yes, but only because Red answered your hail
questions.why: Rule 60.2(a)(1): the red flag is required only when the protesting boat's hull length is more than 6 m.

questions.q: 36-ft cruiser-racer, Bodrum. After a mark-room incident you hail and hoist a red flag within seconds. Two legs later the crew takes the flag down because it fouls the runner. You finish and lodge a protest. Valid?

figure.title: Mark-room incident
lines: Hail and red flag within seconds
Flag taken down two legs later

options: Yes — the flag only needs to be shown at the first reasonable opportunity, however briefly
Yes — a flag shown for a full leg satisfies the rule
No — the red flag must stay displayed until you are no longer racing, i.e. until you have finished and cleared the line
No — but only because a 36-footer must display two flags, one on each shroud
questions.why: Rule 60.2(a)(1): the flag is displayed until the boat is no longer racing (definition Racing: finished and cleared the line and marks).

questions.q: Windward mark, 25 knots. Grey, tacking inside you, hits your 470 and you capsize. After righting and bailing, about three minutes later, you hail "Protest" towards Grey, who is now far away, and lodge a protest in time; no damage. Grey says the hail came too late. Validity?

figure.title: Windward mark, 25 knots
lines: Righted and bailed in about 3 min
Then you hail; Grey is far off

options: Invalid — the hail must come within a few seconds of the incident in every case, whatever happened to the boat
Invalid — a hail that the other boat could not hear counts for nothing, so you should have sailed after Grey
Valid only because there was contact; after contact no hail is needed at all, whenever it comes
Valid if the PC finds that three minutes after a capsize was the first reasonable opportunity; Grey, beyond hailing distance, only had to be informed then
questions.why: Rule 60.2(a)(1) and (b)(1): "first reasonable opportunity" is a question of fact; a boat beyond hailing distance is informed at that first opportunity.

questions.q: Trapezoid course, Melges 24 nationals. Black, the windward boat, touches your boom on the first reach; nothing is said. On the last beat, having thought it over, you hail "Protest" at Black and show a red flag. Valid?

figure.title: Melges 24 nationals
lines: Black touches your boom, first reach
Hail and flag on the last beat

options: No — the hail and the flag came nowhere near the first reasonable opportunity after the incident
No — Black had to be hailed by her sail number, not just "Protest"
Yes — contact with the boom replaces the need for a timely hail
Yes — any time before finishing counts as a reasonable opportunity
questions.why: Rule 60.2(a)(1): the hail and the flag must come at the first reasonable opportunity after the incident, not legs later.

questions.q: On the run you see Yellow, in your fleet about 300 m ahead, hit the offset mark and sail on without a turn. She cannot possibly hear you. What do you have to do to protest her?

figure.title: The run
lines: She is 300 m ahead, out of earshot

options: Nothing on the water — a boat that hits a mark is penalised by the race committee without a hearing
Inform Yellow at the first reasonable opportunity — hail her when you next come close, or tell her at the dock — then lodge a written protest in time
You cannot protest — only boats within two hull lengths of the mark may protest a touch
Hail "Protest" loudly at the moment you see it; nothing else is needed
questions.why: Rule 60.2(b)(1): when the protestee is beyond hailing distance, the protestor need only inform her at the first reasonable opportunity.

questions.q: You watch Blue, five lengths ahead of you, leave the offset mark to starboard when the sailing instructions require port, and carry on down the run. Do you need to hail "Protest" and show a flag?

figure.note: Blue left the offset mark to starboard

options: Yes — hail "Protest" and display the red flag at once, as for any incident in the racing area
No — nothing at all is needed before the written protest, since there was no contact
No — when the incident was a failure to sail the course, you need only inform Blue of your intention to protest at the first reasonable opportunity
No — rounding errors can be protested only by the race committee
questions.why: Rule 60.2(b)(2): when the incident was a failure to sail the course, the only requirement is to inform the protestee at the first reasonable opportunity.

questions.q: Star fleet. Red, on port, hits your bow: pulpit bent, a hole in the topsides. In the chaos nobody hailed or showed a flag. You lodge a protest within the time limit. Valid?

figure.title: Port–starboard collision
lines: Red on port hits your bow
Pulpit bent, hole in the topsides
No hail, no flag from anyone

options: No — the hail and the flag are required in every case for a boat over 6 m, however bad the damage
No — a boat with serious damage must retire and request redress instead of protesting
Yes, but only because the race committee saw the collision and can confirm it to the hearing
Yes — with injury or serious damage from the incident no hail or flag is required, but you must try to inform Red within the protest time limit
questions.why: Rule 60.2(c): with injury or serious damage from the incident, 60.2(a) and (b) do not apply; the protestor tries to inform the other boat within the time limit.

questions.q: At the gybe mark Grey's boom hits your crew, who goes overboard. You stop, recover him and sail in; no hail, no flag. Later you lodge a protest. Grey objects that there was no flag — both boats are 8 m long. Is the protest valid?

figure.title: Gybe mark
lines: Grey's boom hits your crew — overboard

options: Yes — when it was clear a crew member was in danger, the hail and flag are not required; you need only try to inform Grey within the protest time limit
Yes, but only if the race committee or a rescue boat witnessed the man overboard
No — once the crew was back aboard you had to hoist the flag and hail, and continue racing to keep the protest alive
No — a boat that stops racing to recover her crew loses the right to protest over that incident
questions.why: Rule 60.2(c): when a crew member is in danger, rules 60.2(a) and (b) do not apply; the protestor tries to inform the other boat within the protest time limit.

questions.q: Hobie 16 club race. Blue barges in at the committee boat and you shout "Hey, no room, you're out!" Later you lodge a protest; Blue says you never hailed "Protest". Was your shout enough?

figure.note: Blue barges in at the committee boat

options: Yes — at the start no hail at all is needed, since rule 18 does not apply
No — the rule requires the hail "Protest"; shouting about the incident is not a protest hail
No — only a hail of the other boat's sail number counts
Yes — any hail that makes clear you object to her action is enough
questions.why: Rule 60.2(a)(1): the protesting boat shall hail "Protest" at the first reasonable opportunity.

questions.q: Dragon (8.9 m), Lake Garda. Grey fails to give you room at the breakwater. Your crew hoists the red flag at once, but nobody hails; Grey clearly saw the flag. Is your protest valid?

figure.title: Breakwater
lines: Grey gives no room at the obstruction

options: Yes — a boat over 6 m may choose either the hail or the flag
Yes — seeing the flag is as good as hearing a hail
No — the hail "Protest" is required as well as the flag; the flag alone does not satisfy the rule
No — because the flag should have been shown only after finishing
questions.why: Rule 60.2(a)(1): both the hail at the first reasonable opportunity and, for hulls over 6 m, the red flag are required.

questions.q: You finish last. On the VHF channel given in the sailing instructions the race committee calls: "Sail 17, we intend to protest you under rule 42 for the last run." Is that a proper notification?

figure.title: After your finish
lines: RC on the SI radio channel

options: No — a race committee cannot protest under rule 42; only an Appendix P jury can
Yes, but only if it is repeated in writing on the notice board before you reach the shore
No — the committee had to hail "Protest" and show a red flag on the committee boat at the time
Yes — a committee informs the boat of its intention to protest after the race, within the protest time limit; it does not hail or fly a flag
questions.why: Rule 60.2(a)(2): a committee protestor informs the boat of its intention to protest after the race, within the protest time limit.

questions.q: After a port–starboard incident near the pin, both you and Red hail "Protest" at each other and both lodge protest forms. Will there be two separate hearings?

figure.title: Race office
lines: You protest Red; Red protests you

options: Normally one — the protest committee may combine hearings about the same incident into a single hearing with both boats as parties
One — the protest lodged second is automatically invalid
Two — each protest must be heard separately, in the order lodged
None — when both boats protest each other, the protests cancel out
questions.why: Rule 63.2(b): the PC may combine hearings about the same or closely connected incidents (never with a rule 69 hearing).

questions.q: A rescue boat reports to the jury that during race 3 a boat was holed in a collision that nobody protested. Can the jury protest the boat it believes was at fault, and what must it do first?
options: No — without a protest from one of the boats involved, the incident is closed once the time limit passes
Yes — a protest committee may protest a boat when it learns of an incident with possible injury or serious damage; it informs her at the first reasonable opportunity
No — a protest committee may only hear protests lodged by others; it can never lodge one itself
Yes, but only if it hails "Protest" and shows a red flag from the jury boat before the boat finishes
questions.why: Rules 60.4(c)(1) and 60.2(b)(4): the PC may protest on learning of possible injury or serious damage; it informs the boat at the first reasonable opportunity.

questions.q: The sailing instructions say nothing about a protest time limit. The last boat finishes at 15:40. You deliver your protest form to the race office at 17:50. In time?

figure.title: Protest time limit
lines: SI silent on the time limit

options: Yes — the default limit is two hours after your own finish, whatever the others do
Yes — without a limit in the SI, protests may be lodged until the end of the day
No — the default time limit is two hours after the last boat finishes, i.e. 17:40
No — the limit is 30 minutes after the committee boat docks
questions.why: Rule 60.3(b)(1): the default protest time limit is two hours after the last boat finishes the race, unless the SI say otherwise.

questions.q: Sailing instructions: "Protest time limit: 60 minutes after the committee boat docks." The last boat finished at 14:00, the committee boat docked at 14:30 and you lodge your protest at 15:45. Valid?

figure.title: Protest time limit
lines: SI: 60 min after the RC boat docks

options: No — but only because the limit is counted from your own finish
Yes — the two limits add up, so you had until 16:30
Yes — the rulebook's two hours after the last finish (16:00) always overrides the SI
No — the sailing instructions' limit applies: 60 minutes after docking, i.e. 15:30
questions.why: Rule 60.3(b): when the sailing instructions state a different protest time limit, that limit applies.

questions.q: Your protest form names Blue and describes the leeward-mark incident, where and when — but you left the "rules alleged to have been broken" box empty. Blue asks the protest committee to declare it invalid. Will it?
options: No — a written protest must identify the protestor, the protestee and the incident; naming a rule is not required for validity
Yes, unless you fill in the rule before the hearing starts
No, but the committee may then consider only the rules you name orally at the hearing
Yes — a protest that cites no rule number is invalid
questions.why: Rule 60.3(a): a protest is written and identifies the protestor, the protestee and the incident; no rule need be cited.

questions.q: Protest time limit 17:00. At 16:00 you hand your completed form to the bar manager and go for a shower; it reaches the race office at 17:30. Valid?

figure.title: Protest time limit 17:00
lines: Form handed to the bar manager 16:00
SI: deliver to the race office

options: No — it should have been handed to the protestee rather than to the race office
No — the protest must reach the race office (or follow the method in the SI) within the time limit; handing it to someone else is not delivery
Yes — the time you signed the form is what counts, not the time it arrived
Yes — handing it to any club employee within the time limit stops the clock
questions.why: Rule 60.3(b): a protest is delivered to the race office, or by another method stated in the SI, within the protest time limit.

questions.q: Your protest arrives 25 minutes after the time limit because you stood by a dismasted Yellow and towed her into harbour. Yellow's helm is not the protestee. What can the protest committee do?
options: It must hear it — the time limit never applies to a boat that gave help
It must declare it invalid but award you redress instead
It may extend the time limit if there is good reason — helping a boat in trouble is a classic good reason — and hear the protest
Nothing — the protest is automatically invalid; the time limit can never be extended
questions.why: Rule 60.3(b): the protest time limit applies unless the protest committee decides there is good reason to extend it.

questions.q: Next morning, in the photographer's gallery, you spot Grey's crew hiking with his torso outboard of the lifelines for a whole leg of yesterday's race 4. Race 4's protest time limit expired yesterday. Can you still protest?

figure.title: Next morning
lines: Grey's crew outboard of the lifelines

options: No — the time limit for race 4 ran out two hours after the last finisher yesterday, whatever you find later
No — only the technical committee may protest equipment or crew matters found from photographs
Yes — a protest based on photographs has no time limit at all and needs no notice to Grey
Yes — the limit is then two hours after the information became available to you, and you must inform Grey at the first reasonable opportunity
questions.why: Rule 60.3(b)(2): for other protests the limit is two hours after the information became available; rule 60.2(b)(3): inform the protestee.

questions.q: The sailing instructions forbid using the engine inside the race area. At 13:00, in the lunch break between race 2 (finished 12:00) and race 3 (started 14:30), Grey is seen motoring through the course. The protest committee finds a breach. To which race is her penalty applied?

figure.title: Lunch break
lines: SI: no engine in the race area

options: Race 2 — a penalty for a breach when not racing is applied to the race sailed nearest in time to the incident
No race — a boat cannot be penalised for anything done when she is not racing
Race 3 — penalties always apply to the next race sailed
Both races 2 and 3
questions.why: Rule 60.5(c): if a boat broke a rule when not racing, her penalty applies to the race sailed nearest in time to the incident.

questions.q: The jury protests you after the safety boat reported that you "holed" Red in a collision. At the hearing it turns out there was only a scratch in Red's gelcoat and no injury. What happens?
options: The hearing continues as an ordinary Part 2 protest between you and Red
The hearing is closed — a protest committee's own protest about a reported collision proceeds only if there was injury or serious damage
The hearing is converted into a request for redress for Red
You are disqualified anyway — a protest committee's protest is always valid
questions.why: Rule 63.4(a)(2): a hearing on a PC protest under 60.4(c)(1) is closed when there was no injury or serious damage.

questions.q: Blue protests you citing rule 10. The protest committee finds that both boats were on starboard and that you, clear astern, hit her transom — a breach of rule 12, which the form never mentions. Can it disqualify you?

figure.title: Hearing
lines: You, clear astern, hit her transom

options: Yes, but only with a lesser penalty than disqualification, since the rule was not cited
No — the protest must be dismissed and Blue may lodge a new one citing rule 12
Yes — when the committee decides a boat broke a rule, it disqualifies her whether or not that rule was mentioned in the protest
No — a boat can be penalised only under the rule written on the protest form
questions.why: Rule 60.5(c): the PC disqualifies a boat it finds broke a rule, whether or not the applicable rule was mentioned in the protest.

questions.q: You touched Red at the gybe mark as the windward boat, no damage, and did two turns straight away. Red still protests. The committee finds you broke rule 11. What is the outcome for you?

figure.title: Gybe mark
lines: You, windward, touch Red — no damage

options: A 20 % scoring penalty on top of the turns
Disqualification — the turns do not count once a protest has been lodged
Disqualification, unless Red agrees to withdraw her protest
No further penalty — you already took the applicable penalty for that breach
questions.why: Rule 60.5(c)(2): a boat that has already taken the applicable penalty is not penalised further (unless the penalty is a non-excludable DSQ).

questions.q: On port you hit Grey hard: her pulpit is torn off and the forestay fitting cracked. You take a Two-Turns Penalty and finish third. Grey protests. What should the committee decide about your penalty?

figure.title: Port–starboard
lines: Pulpit torn off, forestay fitting cracked
You did two turns, finished third

options: Disqualify you — with serious damage the applicable penalty was to retire, so the turns were not an applicable penalty
Order you to pay for the repair instead of a scoring penalty
Add a 20 % scoring penalty to your third place
Nothing further — a Two-Turns Penalty always closes a Part 2 incident
questions.why: Rule 44.1(b): with serious damage the penalty is to retire; rule 60.5(c)(2) protects only a boat that took the applicable penalty.

questions.q: You protest Blue under rule 11. The committee finds that you, the leeward boat, luffed suddenly without giving her room to keep clear (rule 16.1) and that Blue kept clear. What can happen to you?

figure.note: You, leeward, luffed sharply; Blue kept clear

options: Only a warning — a protestor is at most warned
You can be disqualified — the committee may penalise any party to the hearing, including the protestor, for a rule it finds was broken
Nothing — the protestor cannot be penalised in her own protest
Nothing — the committee may only rule on the rule the protest cites
questions.why: Rule 60.5(b)(1) and (c): a boat may be penalised as a party to a hearing, whether or not the rule was mentioned in the protest.

questions.q: At a week-long championship the committee finds your keel 3 mm outside class tolerance and disqualifies you from race 1; you are sure the measurement was wrong. Can you sail race 2 tomorrow with the boat unchanged?
options: Yes, but only with the written consent of every other competitor
Yes — a DSQ applies to one race only and has no effect on later races
Yes, if you state in writing that you intend to appeal — but if you do not appeal or lose it, you are disqualified without a hearing from all later races you sailed
No — after a class-rule DSQ the boat may not race until the fault is corrected, appeal or not
questions.why: Rule 60.5(d)(4): a boat may race on unchanged after declaring in writing an appeal; if she loses or does not appeal, DSQ without a hearing for those races.

questions.q: A rival protests your J/70 for a mast step 6 mm out of the class position. The committee finds the deviation was caused by a grounding last month and gives no advantage in speed. What does it decide?

figure.title: Class-rule hearing
lines: Mast step 6 mm out of position

options: Disqualification from the whole series, as for any measurement breach found during an event
No penalty and no further action — damage is always a complete excuse for a class-rule breach
Disqualification from the race — a class rule is a class rule, whatever caused the deviation
No penalty — the deviation came from damage and gave no advantage — but you may not race again until it is fixed, unless that is not reasonably possible
questions.why: Rule 60.5(d)(1)–(2): no penalty when the deviation is from damage or wear and gives no performance gain; the boat must be fixed before racing again.

questions.q: The sailing instructions mark rule 55 (trash disposal) as [DP]. A bottle slipped overboard from your cockpit during the race; within the protest time limit you report it yourself to the jury. What happens next?

figure.title: Self-report
lines: You report it to the jury in time

options: The protest committee decides on an appropriate discretionary penalty, taking into account the evidence it finds relevant — no hearing is required
You are disqualified from the race without a hearing, as for a black-flag start
Nothing — a boat cannot be penalised for a breach she reports herself
A full hearing must be held, with you as protestor and protestee
questions.why: Rule 64: when a boat reports within the protest time limit that she broke a DP rule, the PC decides the penalty; no hearing is required.

questions.q: You are disqualified in race 3 after losing a port–starboard protest. The series of seven races has one discard. May you discard the DSQ?

figure.title: Series of seven, one discard
lines: Race 3: DSQ after a rule 10 protest

options: No — only DNF, DNC and OCS scores may be discarded under the Low Point System
Yes — a disqualification from a protest hearing is excludable unless the rule broken prescribes a non-excludable one (rule 2, rule 69)
Yes, but only if the protest committee expressly says so in its written decision
No — any disqualification counts in the series total and cannot be discarded
questions.why: Rule 90.3(b) and A2.1: the worst score is excluded unless it is a non-excludable DSQ (DNE); an ordinary DSQ is excludable.

questions.q: At the start the committee boat dragged its anchor downwind, swinging the line. At the signal you were behind the line as laid, but the race committee, sighting from its new position, scored you OCS. Do you have grounds for redress?

figure.note: Committee boat dragged; the line swung

options: Yes, but only if at least two other boats were affected by the same error
No — a boat is always responsible for judging the starting line herself, whatever the committee boat does
Yes — an improper action or omission of the race committee that made your score significantly worse through no fault of your own
No — redress is available only for injury or physical damage, not for starting errors
questions.why: Rule 61.4(b)(1): redress for a score made significantly worse, through no fault of the boat, by an improper action or omission of a committee.

questions.q: Leading the second beat, you see a sailor from another fleet in the water, separated from her capsized Optimist and not moving. You stop, pull her aboard and hand her to a rescue boat, then finish 14th. Redress?

figure.title: Second beat
lines: Sailor in the water, not moving
You stop and pull her aboard
Hand her to a rescue boat

options: No — redress for help given applies only when a rescue boat was not available
Yes, but only as a first place, since you were leading
No — helping other fleets is voluntary and carries no compensation
Yes — giving help to a person in danger under rule 1.1 is a ground for redress when it made your score significantly worse
questions.why: Rule 61.4(b)(4): redress for a score made significantly worse by giving help under rule 1.1 (not to the boat herself or her crew).

questions.q: Red, on port, holes your bow at the windward mark. She takes a Two-Turns Penalty and sails on; you retire to stop the leak. Is redress available to you?

figure.note: Red holes your bow, takes two turns

options: Yes — physical damage caused by a boat breaking a Part 2 rule that took a penalty or was penalised is a ground for redress
Yes, but only if you also win a protest against Red
No — redress is never given for incidents between boats; that is what protests are for
No — because Red took her penalty, the matter is closed
questions.why: Rule 61.4(b)(2): injury or physical damage because of the action of a boat that broke a Part 2 rule and took a penalty or was penalised.

questions.q: Grey, on port, forces you to crash-tack to avoid her and you lose five places; no contact, no damage. Grey takes two turns. You want your five places back through redress. Will you get them?

figure.title: First beat
lines: Grey on port forces you to crash-tack

options: No — because Grey took her penalty; otherwise redress would be due
No — losing places because of another boat's breach, without injury or physical damage, is not a ground for redress
Yes, provided Grey's turns were taken too late
Yes — any loss of places caused by a boat breaking a Part 2 rule is a ground for redress
questions.why: Rule 61.4(b)(2) requires injury or physical damage from the other boat's breach; places lost without damage are not a ground.

questions.q: Lake race, 5 knots dying to nothing. You were leading by 200 m when the breeze shut off on your side; the fleet sailed round you in a new breeze and you finished 12th. Redress?

figure.title: Dying breeze
lines: Wind shuts off on your side

options: Yes — the race committee should have abandoned, so its omission is a ground
Yes — losing the lead through no fault of your own is exactly what redress is for
No — the weather is not a ground for redress; your score was not worsened by anything listed in the rule
No — but only because you did not request it before finishing
questions.why: Rule 61.4(b) lists the grounds for redress; a wind shift or dying breeze is none of them, and abandoning is the RC's discretion.

questions.q: At the leeward mark your spinnaker halyard jams, the kite goes in the water and you drop from 3rd to 15th. Nobody else was involved. You request redress for the places lost. Outcome?

figure.title: Leeward mark
lines: Halyard jams, kite in the water

options: The request is refused only because you did not retire
Redress granted — equipment failure is an "improper omission" by the boat
Redress granted — average points, since the gear failure was not deliberate
The request is refused — your score got worse through your own boat's fault, and no listed ground applies
questions.why: Rule 61.4(b): redress needs a score made worse through no fault of the boat and one of the listed grounds; a gear failure is neither.

questions.q: On the first reach a harbour ferry, not racing and required to keep clear of you, alters towards you and hits your quarter, bending the rudder stock. You limp in last. Is this a ground for redress?

figure.title: First reach
lines: Hits your quarter, rudder stock bent
Ferry was required to keep clear

options: Yes — physical damage caused by a vessel not racing that was required to keep clear is a ground for redress
No — only damage caused by another racing boat counts
No — incidents with commercial traffic are outside the racing rules
Yes, but only if the race committee abandons the race
questions.why: Rule 61.4(b)(3): injury or physical damage because of a vessel not racing that was required to keep clear or found at fault under IRPCAS or government rules.

questions.q: You lose a protest hearing in which you were a party and are disqualified. You think the committee got the rules wrong. You lodge a request for redress against its decision. What will the committee do with it?

figure.title: After the hearing
lines: You were a party, got DSQ
You think the rules were misapplied
You request redress against the PC

options: Hear it — an improper action of any committee is a ground for redress
Refuse it — a protest committee decision in a hearing where the boat was a party is expressly not a ground for redress; the remedy is an appeal
Hear it, but only with a differently composed protest committee
Refuse it — redress is never available against a protest committee for any reason
questions.why: Rule 61.4(b)(1): improper action or omission of a committee, but not a PC decision when the boat was a party; appeal under rule 70 instead.

questions.q: Your rudder is damaged by a port-tack boat at 11:30; you retire and reach the shore at 12:00. The last boat finishes at 12:30; the protest time limit is 14:30. By when must your request for redress be delivered?
options: By 12:30 — before the last boat finishes
Any time during the regatta — requests for redress have no time limit
By 14:30 — within the protest time limit, or two hours after the incident, whichever is later
By 13:30 — two hours after the incident, which is all the rule allows
questions.why: Rule 61.2(b)(1): a request based on a racing-area incident is delivered within the protest time limit or two hours after the incident, whichever is later.

questions.q: Last day of the series. At 16:10 the protest committee posts a decision in a hearing you were not party to, which moves you from 3rd to 5th overall. You want redress. By when must you request it?
options: You cannot — a decision in a hearing you were not party to cannot be challenged
Within two hours of the posting — by 18:10
Within 24 hours, as for a request to reopen a hearing
Within 30 minutes after the decision was posted — by 16:40
questions.why: Rule 61.2(b)(2): a request based on a protest committee decision on the last scheduled day of racing is delivered no later than 30 minutes after it was posted.

questions.q: You catch the principal race officer on the dock and say: "You finished me in the wrong place — I want redress." He nods. Have you requested redress?

figure.title: On the dock
lines: You tell the PRO you want redress

options: No — a request for redress must be in writing, stating the reason for it, and be delivered to the race office within the time limit
Yes — since the race officer agreed, no written request is needed
Yes — a verbal request to the race officer within the time limit is sufficient
No — redress can be requested only by the race committee on your behalf
questions.why: Rule 61.2(a)–(b): a request for redress is written, states the reason, and is delivered to the race office (or as the SI say) in time.

questions.q: You get redress for race 4 of a six-race series (you were scored OCS by the race committee's error). Your other scores are 3, 5, 2, 4 and 6. What is the usual way the committee will score race 4?
options: The same points as the boat that finished just ahead of you at the time of the incident
Usually the average of your other races to a tenth — here 4.0 — or another fair arrangement such as your place at the time of the incident
First place — the boat wronged by the committee always gets the best available score
Redress always means abandoning race 4 for the whole fleet and resailing it
questions.why: Rule 61.4(c) and A9: the fairest arrangement, e.g. average points of the other races (to a tenth) or the place at the time of the incident.

questions.q: Blue, out of contention, deliberately sails you into the committee boat at the finish to help her team-mate win the series; you finish 9th. The protest committee penalises Blue under rule 2 with a DNE. Can you have your own score corrected?

figure.title: Finishing line
lines: Blue deliberately pushes you into the RC boat

options: Only if Blue's team-mate is also disqualified
No — there was no physical damage, so no redress
Yes — a score made significantly worse by the action of a boat that was penalised under rule 2 (or rule 69) is a ground for redress
No — Blue's DNE is the end of the matter; redress is only for committee errors
questions.why: Rule 61.4(b)(5): redress when the score was worsened by an action of another boat (or her crew or support person) that led to a rule 2 or rule 69 penalty.

questions.q: Reviewing its finishing video in the evening, the race committee realises it recorded Yellow as DNF although she finished 6th; the protest time limit has passed and Yellow has gone home. What can the race committee do?

figure.title: Evening, race office
lines: Time limit passed, Yellow gone home

options: Nothing — once posted, results may be changed only by the protest committee after a hearing
Nothing — only Yellow may request redress, and the time limit has passed
Score Yellow 6th only if all other boats agree in writing
Correct its own error from its records, or request redress for Yellow itself — a race committee may request redress for a boat
questions.why: Rule 90.3(c): the RC corrects a scoring error from its records; rule 61.1(b): the race committee may request redress for a boat.

questions.q: Red is awarded redress and given 2.5 points for race 3 after being scored DNF by a committee error. You finished 3rd in that race and ask whether your score now drops to 4th. Does it?
options: No — when redress is given by adjusting a boat's points, the other boats' scores stay as they are unless the committee decides otherwise
No — but only because 2.5 points is not a whole place in the results
Yes — Red's 2.5 points push every boat with 3 or more points down a place
Yes — every boat that finished behind the redressed boat moves down one place
questions.why: Rule A6.2: when the PC adjusts a boat's points as redress, the scores of the other boats are not changed unless the PC decides otherwise.

questions.q: Your own crew falls overboard on the run; you stop, recover him and finish 20th instead of about 5th. You request redress citing rule 1.1 (helping a person in danger). Will it be granted?
options: Yes — but only average points of the other races
No — help given to your own boat or your own crew is expressly excluded as a ground for redress
No — because you should have left him to the rescue boat
Yes — recovering a person in danger is always a ground for redress
questions.why: Rule 61.4(b)(4): redress for giving help under rule 1.1 — but not to the boat herself or her own crew.

questions.q: You are the protestee in a hearing. The chairman opens by asking the protestor when she hailed, whether she showed a flag and when the form was delivered, before anyone describes the incident. Why?
options: Because the committee wants to check whether you agree with the protestor's account
Because the protestor always speaks first about everything, including the facts
Because the protest committee must first decide whether the protest is valid; if it is not, the hearing is closed
Because validity is checked only at the end, so the chairman is getting it out of the way early
questions.why: Rule 63.4(a): the protest committee first takes evidence and decides validity; an invalid protest or request means the hearing is closed.

questions.q: Grey was notified of the time and place of the hearing but does not turn up; her skipper is seen at the bar. You, the protestor, are present. What may the protest committee do?

figure.title: Hearing time
lines: Grey notified of time and place

options: Disqualify Grey immediately for failing to attend, without taking evidence
Postpone the hearing until Grey chooses to attend
Nothing — a hearing cannot be held unless all parties are present
Proceed with the hearing in Grey's absence, taking your evidence and deciding the protest
questions.why: Rule 63.1(b): when a party fails to attend after being notified, the protest committee may nevertheless decide the protest or request.

questions.q: After a rule 18 protest, the owner of Red, who watched from the club terrace, wants to represent Red at the hearing instead of the helmsman who was steering. May he?

figure.title: Rule 18 protest
lines: Red's owner watched from the terrace

options: Normally not — in a Part 2, 3 or 4 protest the representative must have been on board at the time, unless the committee decides otherwise for good reason
No — a boat may be represented only by the person who was steering at the time, never anyone else
Yes — provided the helmsman signs a written authorisation naming the owner as representative
Yes — the owner may always represent his boat in any hearing, whether or not he was aboard
questions.why: Rule 63.1(a)(4): for Part 2, 3 or 4 protests the representative shall have been on board at the time of the incident, unless the PC decides otherwise.

questions.q: One of the three protest committee members is the coach of Blue, the boat you protested. He says nothing about it. What should happen?
options: He may sit and take part as long as he does not vote on the final decision
He must declare it; he may sit only if all parties agree or the committee finds the conflict not significant — object as soon as you know
The hearing must be cancelled and the protest dismissed because of the conflict
Nothing — a coach is not a party to the hearing, so there is no conflict of interest
questions.why: Rule 63.3: a member declares any possible conflict of interest; a party objects as soon as possible; he sits only if all consent or it is not significant.

questions.q: You bring the helm of Green as a witness to your protest against Red. He wants to sit in the room for the whole hearing so as to understand the case. May he?

figure.title: Your witness
lines: Wants to stay for the whole hearing

options: Yes — witnesses may attend the whole hearing if the protestor agrees
Yes — at club level witnesses are treated like parties
No — a witness who is not a party or a committee member is excluded except while giving his evidence
No — a witness from another boat may give evidence only in writing
questions.why: Rule 63.4(e): a witness is excluded from the hearing except when giving evidence, unless he is also a party or a member of the protest committee.

questions.q: Your bowman was the only person on your 36-footer with a clear view of the port-tack boat at the moment of the incident. Can he give evidence in your protest hearing?

figure.title: Your witness
lines: Bowman had the only clear view

options: No — crew members of a party boat count as parties and may not testify as witnesses
Yes, but only in writing, since he was aboard a boat that is a party to the hearing
No — only people from boats not involved in the incident may be witnesses
Yes — a party may call witnesses, and a crew member is an ordinary witness whose evidence the committee weighs like any other
questions.why: Rule 63.4(b): the committee takes the evidence of the parties present and of their witnesses; a crew member may be a witness.

questions.q: At the hearing Red's helm says: "The mark-boat driver told me afterwards that you were clearly inside the zone." You object that this is hearsay. What does the committee do with it?
options: It may admit it — hearsay is admissible — and decides how much weight to give it; it may also exclude evidence it finds irrelevant
It must adjourn and summon the mark-boat driver before continuing
It must accept it as proven fact, since it comes from a race official
It must exclude it — hearsay is never admissible in a protest hearing
questions.why: Rule 63.4(b): hearsay evidence is admissible, but the PC may exclude evidence it considers irrelevant or unduly repetitive, and weighs it under 63.5(a).

questions.q: Blue's witness states that you were two lengths from the mark when the overlap was broken. You want to ask him how far away he was and what he was doing at the time. May you?

figure.title: Hearing
lines: Blue's witness: "two lengths from the mark"

options: No — a party may question only the other party, not her witnesses
Yes — a party present at the hearing may question anyone who gives evidence
No — only committee members may question witnesses
Yes, but only through written questions handed to the chairman
questions.why: Rule 63.4(c): a party present at the hearing may question any person who gives evidence.

questions.q: A member of the protest committee was on the windward mark boat and saw the incident between you and Grey. What must he do at the hearing?

figure.title: Protest committee
lines: One member was on the mark boat

options: Withdraw from the committee at once — a member who saw the incident may not take part
Give his evidence privately to the other members after the parties have left
State that he saw the incident, as soon as reasonably possible, in the presence of the parties; he may then give his evidence like a witness
Say nothing and simply vote according to what he saw
questions.why: Rule 63.4(d): a committee member who saw the incident shall, as soon as reasonably possible, state that fact in the presence of the parties.

questions.q: You and Red give flatly contradictory accounts of who tacked first at the port lay line; there are no witnesses. Red says the committee must dismiss the protest because nothing is proven beyond doubt. Is she right?

figure.title: Hearing
