lines: Who tacked first at the lay line?

options: No — the committee must accept the protestor's account whenever there is a conflict
Yes — with no witnesses a protest between two boats must always fail
Yes — a boat may be penalised only when the facts are proven beyond reasonable doubt
No — the committee finds facts on the balance of probabilities, deciding which account it finds more likely
questions.why: Rule 63.5(a): the PC weighs the evidence and finds the facts on the balance of probabilities (unless the rule applied requires otherwise).

questions.q: A four-member protest committee splits two to two on whether you broke rule 17. How is the decision made?
options: By a simple majority — and when the vote is tied, the chairman of the hearing may cast an additional vote
A tie means the protest fails and no boat is penalised
The decision must be unanimous, so the committee keeps deliberating
A tie means the protest must be reheard by a new committee
questions.why: Rule 63.5(b): decisions are by simple majority; when votes are equal, the person in charge of the hearing may cast an additional vote.

questions.q: The notice of race says a breach of the restricted-area rule carries a 10 % scoring penalty; the sailing instructions say disqualification. You broke it. Which does the committee apply?
options: Neither — when two event documents conflict no penalty can be imposed at all
The rule it believes will provide the fairest result for all boats affected — the conflict between the NoR and SI is resolved that way
The sailing instructions — the later document always prevails over the notice of race
The notice of race — the earlier document always prevails over the sailing instructions
questions.why: Rule 63.5(c): when rules in the NoR, SI or other event documents conflict, the PC applies the rule it believes gives the fairest result for all boats affected.

questions.q: The committee tells you orally that you are disqualified and why. You want the facts found, the rules applied and the reasoning on paper to decide about an appeal. What are you entitled to?
options: A written decision only if you announce the appeal first
Nothing further — decisions are given orally only, unless an international jury sits
The information in writing, provided promptly, if you request it in writing within seven days of being informed of the decision
A written decision only if you pay a fee set by the organising authority
questions.why: Rule 63.6(a)–(b): the parties are informed promptly; on a written request within seven days the PC gives the information in writing.

questions.q: Half an hour before the hearing you and Grey talk it through, agree you were both partly wrong and shake hands. You ask the committee to drop your protest. Can it?
options: No — once lodged, a protest must always be heard to the end
No — only the race committee can withdraw a protest
Yes — but only if Grey takes a Two-Turns Penalty ashore
Yes — the committee may allow a protest to be withdrawn; otherwise it must hear every protest lodged
questions.why: Rule 63.2(a): the protest committee shall hear all protests and requests delivered, unless it allows one to be withdrawn.

questions.q: You are told at the door that your hearing starts in two minutes; nobody has shown you the protest form against you. What are you entitled to before the hearing proceeds?

figure.title: At the jury room door
lines: You have not seen the protest

options: To be told the time and place, to see the protest, and to have reasonable time to prepare — ask for it before the hearing proceeds
To have the hearing postponed to the next day in all cases
Nothing — the committee sets its own timetable and parties attend when called
To refuse to attend, in which case the protest is dismissed
questions.why: Rule 63.1(a): parties are notified of the time and place, given access to the protest, and allowed reasonable time to prepare.

questions.q: Red brings a 40-minute GoPro video from her stern and insists the committee watch all of it, plus a friend's drone footage of other races. The committee watches two minutes around the incident and declines the rest. Did it act correctly?

figure.title: Hearing
lines: PC watches two minutes around the incident

options: No — video evidence must either be viewed completely or excluded completely
Yes — the committee takes the evidence it considers necessary and may exclude evidence it finds irrelevant or unduly repetitive
No — a party has the right to have all her evidence viewed in full
Yes — but only because video is never admissible in a protest hearing
questions.why: Rule 63.4(b): the PC takes the evidence it considers necessary and may exclude evidence it considers irrelevant or unduly repetitive.

questions.q: You lost a hearing at 18:00 on Tuesday. On Wednesday morning the fleet's tracking data is published and shows you were clearly outside the zone, contradicting the facts found. What can you do, and by when?

figure.title: Wednesday morning
lines: Tracking shows you outside the zone

options: Nothing — once the facts are found they cannot be challenged in any way
Lodge a fresh protest against the same boat for the same incident
Request that the hearing be reopened on new significant evidence — in writing, within 24 hours of being informed of the decision
Appeal to the national authority on the facts within 24 hours
questions.why: Rule 63.7(a)(3) and (b): a party requests a reopening in writing within 24 hours of being informed of the decision; new significant evidence is a ground.

questions.q: On the last scheduled day of racing the committee informs you of its decision at 15:05. You believe it made a significant error. By when must you request a reopening?

figure.title: Last day of racing
lines: You believe there was a significant error

options: Within 24 hours — by 15:05 tomorrow
Any time before the prize-giving
Within the protest time limit of the previous day
Within 30 minutes of being informed — by 15:35
questions.why: Rule 63.7(b)(2): on the last scheduled day a request to reopen is delivered within 30 minutes after the party was informed of the decision that day.

questions.q: The committee agrees to reopen your hearing because it may have made a significant error in applying rule 18.3. Who should sit on the reopened hearing?
options: If practicable, a committee that includes at least one member who was not on the original committee
Exactly the same members as the original hearing, nobody else
An entirely new committee with none of the original members
Only the chairman of the original hearing, sitting alone
questions.why: Rule 63.7(c): for a significant error, if practicable at least one new member; for new evidence only, if practicable a majority of the original members.

questions.q: The committee found as a fact that you were overlapped inside Grey at the zone, and penalised Grey. Grey wants to appeal on the ground that the overlap did not exist. Can she?
options: Yes — any party may appeal on any point, including the facts
No — a party may appeal the committee's decision or its procedures, but not the facts it found
No — appeals exist only for the protestor, never for the protestee
Yes — facts can be appealed if a witness signs a statement
questions.why: Rule 70.1: a party may appeal a protest committee's decision or its procedures, but not the facts found.

questions.q: You disagree with how a club protest committee applied rule 20 to your case and want to appeal. To whom is the appeal made?
options: To the commodore of the organising club, as the senior officer
To World Sailing directly, bypassing the national authority
To the national authority of the organising club, following the procedure in Appendix R
To the race committee of the event, which reviews protest committee decisions
questions.why: Rules 70.1 and 70.5: a party appeals to the national authority; appeals must conform to Appendix R.

questions.q: At an international regatta with an international jury properly constituted under Appendix N, the jury disqualifies you. You want to appeal to your national authority. Can you?
options: Yes — every protest committee decision may be appealed to the national authority
Yes, but only to World Sailing rather than to the national authority
No — but only because foreign competitors may never appeal
No — decisions of a properly constituted international jury cannot be appealed
questions.why: Rule 70.3(a): there is no appeal from the decisions of an international jury constituted in compliance with Appendix N.

questions.q: The sailing instructions of a club series state: "Decisions of the protest committee are final; there is no appeal." The club has not obtained approval from the national authority for this. Does the clause bind you?
options: No — the right of appeal may be denied under rule 70.3 only in the listed cases, with the national authority's approval where it requires it, and stated in the NoR or SI
Yes — at club level there is never a right of appeal anyway
No — because the right of appeal can only be removed by the race committee, not the SI
Yes — the sailing instructions may change any rule, including rule 70
questions.why: Rule 70.3: appeals may be denied only for the cases listed, several needing national authority approval, and only when stated in the NoR or SI.

questions.q: In the boat park after racing, the helm of 1192 punches a competitor who beat him on the last run. You saw it. What is the correct route under the rules?
options: Hail "Protest" at him and lodge a Part 2 protest form
Report it to the protest committee — this is possible misconduct under rule 69, handled in a rule 69 hearing, not a protest
Lodge a protest under rule 2 within the protest time limit
Nothing — events ashore after racing are outside the racing rules
questions.why: Rule 69.1: a competitor shall not commit misconduct; reports are dealt with under rule 69 and are not grounds for a protest (69.1(c)).

questions.q: The sailing instructions forbid support boats inside the course area while racing. Your coach drives his RIB through the fleet on the run to film you. The jury opens a hearing. Who can be penalised?

figure.title: Support person hearing
lines: Coach RIB inside the course while racing

options: Nobody — support boats are outside the jurisdiction of the protest committee entirely
Only your boat — a coach cannot be the subject of a protest committee hearing
The coach, as a support person, may be warned or excluded — and your boat too may be penalised if it may have gained an advantage from his breach
Only the coach — a boat can never be penalised for something her support person did
questions.why: Rule 62: the PC may hear a support person and warn or exclude him (62.3); under 62.4 the boat may also be penalised if she may have gained an advantage.

questions.q: Needing Blue to finish behind you for the series, you deliberately luff her into the committee boat at the finish, then do two turns. Blue protests. What penalty does the committee impose if it finds the collision was deliberate?

figure.note: You luff Blue into the committee boat on purpose

options: No further penalty — you already took a Two-Turns Penalty for the Part 2 breach
An ordinary disqualification, which you may discard
A 20 % scoring penalty, since Blue was not damaged
A disqualification that is not excludable — a clear breach of rule 2 (sportsmanship and fair sailing) carries a DNE, and the turns do not cure it
questions.why: Rule 2: a boat penalised under rule 2 receives a disqualification that is not excludable; a deliberate breach is not cured by turns.

questions.q: At the leeward mark you know you failed to give Grey mark-room; she says nothing, hails nothing, and nobody protests. What does the basic principle of sportsmanship expect of you?
options: To take the appropriate penalty promptly — or retire — even though no one protested
To wait for the committee to decide whether you broke a rule
Nothing — without a protest there is no breach
To offer Grey a place in the results after the race
questions.why: Basic Principle, Sportsmanship and the Rules: a boat that breaks a rule and is not exonerated promptly takes the appropriate penalty, which may be to retire.

questions.q: Twelve boats are entered in a club series scored under the Low Point System. In race 2 you finish fourth. How many points do you score for that race?
options: 9 points — entries minus place plus one
4 points — first place scores 1, second 2, and so on
3 points — fourth place minus one
0.75 points — the old Bonus Point System
questions.why: Rule A4: under the Low Point System first place scores 1 point, second 2, third 3 and each place thereafter one more.

questions.q: Twenty-three boats are entered in the regatta; eighteen started race 3. You retired with a broken boom and are scored DNF. How many points is that?
options: 19 points — the number of starters plus one
18 points — last of the boats that started
24 points — the number of boats entered in the series plus one
23 points — the number of boats entered
questions.why: Rule A5.2: a boat that did not start, sail the course or finish, retired or was disqualified scores the finishing place one more than the boats entered.

questions.q: The notice of race says rule A5.3 applies. 40 boats are entered; 31 came to the starting area for race 5. Red did not come out at all; Grey came out but did not start. What do they score?

figure.title: Race 5, NoR: A5.3 applies
lines: Grey: came out, did not start (DNS)

options: Red 41 points; Grey 31 points — last of those present
Both 32 points — boats in the starting area plus one
Both 41 points — entries plus one, as in the default rule
Red 41 points (entries plus one); Grey 32 points (boats in the starting area plus one)
questions.why: Rule A5.3 (when the NoR or SI say so): a boat in the starting area scores boats in the starting area + 1; a boat that did not come scores entries + 1.

questions.q: Six races, one discard. Your scores are 2, 7, 3, 7, 1, 4. Which race is discarded?
options: Race 2 — with two equal worst scores, the one from the race sailed earlier is excluded
Both sevens — equal worst scores are discarded together
You choose which of the two sevens to drop
Race 4 — the later of the two equal worst scores
questions.why: Rule A2.1: if a boat has two or more equal worst scores, the score(s) for the race(s) sailed earliest in the series are excluded.

questions.q: After discards you and Blue are tied on 15 points. Your race scores are 1, 2, 6, 6 (discard 8); Blue's are 1, 1, 5, 8 (discard 9). Who places ahead and why?
options: You — your worst counting score, 6, is better than Blue's 8
Blue — listing each boat's counting scores best to worst, 1-1-5-8 beats 1-2-6-6 at the second score
You — the boat with the best single race wins the tie
Blue — because her discarded score is worse than yours
questions.why: Rule A8.1: a series tie is broken by listing each boat's scores best to worst and comparing; the first difference decides. Excluded scores are not used.

questions.q: You and Grey are tied in the series and your counting scores, listed best to worst, are identical: 1, 2, 3, 4. In the last race you were 4th and Grey 2nd; in the second-last race you were 1st, Grey 4th. Who finishes ahead?
options: You — the boat with more first places in the series wins the tie
You — the better score in the second-last race is what decides first
Grey — with identical lists best to worst, the tie goes to the boat with the better score in the last race
The tie stands and the prize for the place is shared between you
questions.why: Rule A8.2: if a tie remains, the boats are ranked by their scores in the last race, then the next-to-last, and so on (excluded scores are used here).

questions.q: You and Red cross the finishing line at exactly the same moment, contesting third place, and the race committee cannot separate you. How are you scored?
options: Both get 4 points — a dead heat gives both boats the worse place
The committee tosses a coin to decide who is third
Both get 3 points — a dead heat gives both boats the better place
Both get 3.5 points — the points for third and fourth places are added together and divided equally
questions.why: Rule A7: boats tied at the finishing line share the points for the place they tie for and the following place(s), divided equally.

questions.q: Black finished second in race 6 but is disqualified after a protest hearing. You finished fifth. What happens to your score?
options: You move up to fourth place — every boat with a worse finishing place than the disqualified boat moves up one place
Nothing — a disqualification never changes other boats' scores
You move up only if the protest committee says so in its decision
You move up two places, since Black's points are shared out
questions.why: Rule A6.1: when a boat is disqualified, retires after finishing or is scored NSC, each boat with a worse finishing place moves up one place.

questions.q: Flag Z was displayed. You were in the triangle in the last minute and received a 20 % penalty; the sailing instructions say nothing more about it. 34 boats are entered and you finished 3rd. What is your race score?

figure.title: Flag Z start
lines: In the triangle in the last minute

options: 9.8 points — third place plus 6.8, with no rounding applied
10 points — 20 % of 35 (the DNF score) is 7.0, added to your 3 points
3.6 points — your third place plus 20 % of your own score of 3
35 points — a Z-flag penalty is scored the same as DNF
questions.why: Rule 44.3(c) via A5.2: 20 % of the DNF score, rounded to the nearest tenth of a point (0.05 upward), added to the boat's points — but never worse than DNF.

questions.q: The results sheet shows your sail number with "NSC" against race 2 — you had missed the offset mark and did not go back. What does NSC mean and how is it scored?
options: Not scored, the race was abandoned for you — no points
Did not start, corrected — scored as OCS
Did not sail the course — scored like DNF: boats entered plus one
No sail-number certificate — a measurement penalty
questions.why: Rule A10 and A5.2: NSC means the boat did not sail the course; she scores points for the finishing place one more than the number of boats entered.

questions.q: In a dying breeze only one boat, Yellow, finishes within the time limit; the other 20 are still a mile out. The race committee says it will abandon the race "since only one boat finished". Is that correct?

figure.title: Dying breeze
lines: Yellow finishes within the time limit

options: No — but only because Yellow could request redress if the race were abandoned
Yes — a race needs at least three finishers within the time limit to be scored
Yes — a race needs at least half the fleet to finish within the time limit to be scored
No — a race is scored if it is not abandoned and at least one boat started, sailed the course and finished within the time limit; the rest are DNF
questions.why: Rule 90.3(a): a race is scored if not abandoned and at least one boat started, sailed the course and finished within the time limit, even if later RET or DSQ.

questions.q: The posted results show you 11th in race 4, but the finishing sheet and the finish-boat video both put you 7th. The protest time limit has passed. What is the straightforward way to get this fixed?
options: Point it out to the race committee — it corrects an error it finds from its own records or observations without any hearing; if it refuses, request redress
Lodge a protest against the boat scored 7th
Nothing can be done — results are final once posted
Lodge a protest against the race committee within the protest time limit of the next race
questions.why: Rule 90.3(c): the RC corrects a scoring error it finds from its own records or observations, with no hearing; a committee error is also a ground for redress.

questions.q: The notice of race states that rule 90.3(e) applies. The regatta's last protest time limit ended Sunday at 15:00 and results were posted at 15:30. On Tuesday you notice a race committee adding error that cost you second overall. Can the results be changed?
options: Yes — a race committee must correct its own scoring errors whenever they are found, at any time
No — under 90.3(e) results cannot be changed by actions started more than 24 hours after the last time limit, decision or posting, except under rules 6, 69 or 71
No — results can never be changed after the prize-giving, whatever the notice of race says
Yes — the 24-hour rule applies only to protests and redress, not to scoring errors
questions.why: Rule 90.3(e): when the NoR says so, no score changes from actions started over 24 h after the last time limit, decision or posting, except rules 6, 69, 71.

questions.q: After a port–starboard incident Red suggests you both go to "arbitration" to avoid a full hearing. Neither the notice of race nor the sailing instructions mention Appendix T. Is arbitration available?

figure.title: After the incident
lines: NoR and SI silent on Appendix T

options: Yes — arbitration is always available for Part 2 protests under the racing rules
No — arbitration exists only for rule 69 cases
No — Appendix T (arbitration and the post-race penalty) applies only when the notice of race or sailing instructions say so
Yes — provided the jury has at least one international judge
questions.why: Appendix T preamble: all or part of the appendix applies only if the notice of race or sailing instructions so state.

questions.q: Appendix T applies at a J/24 nationals. You realise you broke rule 10 against Grey, who protested; no damage. Before the hearing starts you want to limit your loss. What can you do, and how much does it cost?
options: Take a 20 % scoring penalty by writing to the race committee before the hearing begins
Do two turns in the harbour before the hearing, which cancels the protest
Nothing — once a protest is lodged only the hearing can decide on any penalty
Take a Post-Race Penalty before the hearing begins — a 30 % scoring penalty, by a written statement to the arbitrator or a protest committee member
questions.why: Rule T1: a boat that may have broken a Part 2 rule or rule 31 may take a 30 % Post-Race Penalty at any time after the race but before the hearing starts.

questions.q: At an arbitration meeting under Appendix T you want to bring your mastman, who saw the incident, to describe it to the arbitrator. May you?

figure.title: Arbitration meeting
lines: You want to bring your mastman

options: No — at an arbitration meeting each party is represented by one person who was on board; witnesses are not permitted
Yes — but he may speak only after the arbitrator gives an opinion
No — but only because crew members can never testify in any proceeding
Yes — each party may bring up to two witnesses to arbitration
questions.why: Rule T2: an arbitration meeting is held only if each party is represented by a person who was on board; witnesses are not permitted.

questions.q: At arbitration the arbitrator gives her opinion that the protest committee would probably find you broke rule 11 and disqualify you. Grey is the protestor. What are the possible next steps?
options: Grey must withdraw her protest once the arbitrator has spoken
You may take the 30 % Post-Race Penalty; Grey may ask to withdraw her protest; if the protest is not withdrawn, a full hearing is held
The arbitrator's opinion is the decision — you are disqualified and the matter ends
You must accept the 30 % penalty; the protest is closed automatically
questions.why: Rules T3–T4: after the arbitrator's opinion a boat may take a Post-Race Penalty, a protestor may ask to withdraw; if not withdrawn, a hearing follows.

questions.q: In a request for redress hearing about a race committee error, Red's helm says the protest committee itself should be treated as a party because it is "the other side". Who are the parties here?
options: Every boat in the race, since redress may change all their scores
Red alone — committees are never parties to any hearing under the rules
Red, as the boat requesting redress, and the race committee as the body alleged to have acted improperly; a protest committee is never a party
Red and the protest committee, since the committee decides against one of them
questions.why: Definition Party: in a redress hearing, the boat requesting it and the body alleged to have made an improper action or omission; a PC is never a party.

questions.q: Arguing in the bar, Grey's helm says: "Case 50 in the Case Book is a rule, so the protest committee is bound by it." Is he right about its status?
options: No — only the Call Book for match racing has the status of a rule
Yes — the cases are published by World Sailing and are rules like any other document in the rulebook
No — the Case Book is informal guidance that a protest committee may ignore as it pleases
Not quite — the Case Book is World Sailing's authoritative interpretation of the rules, which a committee follows, but a case is not itself a rule
questions.why: Introduction and definition Rule: the Cases are World Sailing's authoritative interpretations; they are not listed among the documents that are rules.
